note: Kural 131 puts ஒழுக்கம் above life because it gives excellence; Acharakkovai 1 says what conduct grows from, naming eight inner virtues as its seed.
teaches: Read together, the Kural's command to guard conduct gets a source: the conduct to be guarded is not a set of rules but the outgrowth of gratitude, patience and the rest.
list_adds: It makes rule-bound conduct the fruit of eight ethical virtues, so a ritual code is founded on ethics before any ritual rule is given.

note: Kural 133 says conduct is noble birth and its lapse is low birth; Acharakkovai 2 makes good birth one of eight rewards that unfailing conduct earns.
teaches: Both tie birth to conduct, but the Kural collapses birth into present conduct while the Acharakkovai keeps birth as a real rank that conduct earns, so the same link can dissolve or confirm hierarchy.
list_adds: It sets birth among worldly rewards such as wealth, land and health, so birth becomes a prize of conduct rather than its definition.
audit_text_issue: l.4 ஒழக்கம் for ஒழுக்கம் | line 4 ஒழக்கம் for ஒழுக்கம்

note: Acharakkovai 3 lists sacrifice among four acts to be guarded and kept fruitful; Kural 259 rates abstaining from killing one creature above a thousand sacrifices.
teaches: The ritual code keeps sacrifice as a thing of value needing protection by conduct, while the Kural prices it below a single act of non-killing, so the two books weigh the same rite very differently.
list_adds: It groups sacrifice with fees, penance and learning as goods that conduct preserves, where the Kural sets sacrifice against non-killing and ranks it lower.
audit_text_issue: முப்பால் ஒழுக்கு is not explained in the verse.

note: Verse 4 has one rise worshipping father and mother; verse 16 names five elders, parents among them, to be worshipped as gods.
teaches: Verse 16 supplies the rank that verse 4's daily act presupposes, and shows the dawn rite honours only two of the five elders owed god-like worship.

note: Acharakkovai 5 bars one in எச்சில் from touching brahmins and other sacred things; Sivavakkiyar asks why water in the mouth is called எச்சில் while the Veda churned in the same mouth is not.
teaches: The Siddhar turns the category the Acharakkovai uses to protect the brahmin against the brahmin's own recitation, showing that the purity rule depends on exempting the sacred mouth from it.

note: On the reading that புலை names the outcaste person, Acharakkovai 6 makes the sight of a birth-group polluting; Kural 972 says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes from deeds.
teaches: The conflict holds only if புலை is a person and செய்தொழில் means conduct, so the pairing shows how the caste force of each verse rests on one disputed word.
list_adds: It sets a birth-group beside a dog and the heavenly bodies as one class of barred sights, a ranking by birth the Kural's verse denies.
audit_text_issue: sense of புலை and தக்கவீழ் மீன் uncertain | புலை may name an impure thing (flesh) rather than a person.

note: Acharakkovai 7 classes sexual union and eating as kinds of எச்சில்; Sivavakkiyar says the pure body itself came from எச்சில், and honey and milk are எச்சில் too.
teaches: The Siddhar takes the Acharakkovai's own classing of union as எச்சில் to its end: if union pollutes, every body and every food is born of pollution and the category cannot separate clean from unclean.

note: Acharakkovai 8 bars recitation while in எச்சில்; Sivavakkiyar says the mantra one recites is itself the mouth's எச்சில்.
teaches: One text guards recitation from impurity and the other calls recitation impure in itself, so the rule that protects the mantra is the Siddhar's evidence that purity of the mouth is a fiction.

note: Verse 7 defines the four kinds of எச்சில்; verse 8 says what they bar and what keeping them yields.
teaches: The pair shows the book's method: a definition followed by its prohibitions and a reward in learning, so purity rules are presented as a discipline of the scholar.

note: Kural 298 says water gives only outer purity and inner purity is seen through truth; Acharakkovai 10 lists ten occasions when water must remove impurity.
teaches: The Kural concedes the outer purity that the Acharakkovai regulates but makes it the lesser half, so the ten baths answer a question the Kural treats as minor; they are different things, not a contradiction.
list_adds: It turns the Kural's single clause on outer purity into an exact list of the occasions that call for a bath, among them dream, hair-cutting and contact with low people.
audit_text_issue: ஏனை மயலுறல் (line 4) is obscure.

note: Acharakkovai 10 makes bathing the removal of impurity on ten occasions; Sivavakkiyar addresses those who bathe daily and whose dirt never goes, asking where the dirt really lies.
teaches: The Siddhar denies the premise the bathing list rests on, that the impurity is where water can reach, whereas the Kural only ranks it below inner purity.
audit_text_issue: ஏனை மயலுறல் (line 4) is obscure and the count of ten depends on splitting ஊண்பொழுது and வைகு துயில். | Item list depends on counting ஊண்பொழுது and வைகு துயில் separately; ஏனை மயலுறல் is obscure.

note: Kural 1066 says asking even water for a cow degrades the tongue; Acharakkovai 12 says the worthy do not beg sandals even when they lack them.
teaches: The Acharakkovai brings the Kural's limit case of begging down to one's own bodily need and sets it inside a list of purity rules, so not begging becomes part of bodily propriety.
list_adds: It places the refusal to beg beside rules against touching oil and others' cloth, treating begging as a kind of defilement.

note: Both verses bar the sight of புலை, verse 6 to one in எச்சில், verse 13 to one who has oiled the body.
teaches: The bar on seeing புலை recurs under two different ritual states, which shows it is a standing rule of the code rather than a feature of one kind of impurity.
audit_text_issue: The oil/water order in 13 lines 3-4 is hard to fix; புலை may name a person or an impure thing. | acharakkovai:13 lines 3-4: order of oil and water uncertain; புலை may be person or impure thing

note: Acharakkovai 15 says one who scorns brahmins perishes; Kural 134 says a brahmin's birth itself is ruined when his conduct fails.
teaches: The Kural adds the condition the Acharakkovai leaves out: reverence owed to the brahmin by birth lapses with his conduct, so the two books disagree on whether birth alone commands it.
list_adds: It sets brahmins with the elements, the cow, the sun and the moon as cosmic things owed reverence, a rank the Kural makes conditional on conduct.

note: Acharakkovai 16 makes the teacher one of five elders to be worshipped as gods; Purananuru 183 says learning is worth serving and paying the teacher, and that learning outweighs both seniority and the order of birth.
teaches: Puram 183 gives the reason for the teacher's place and also cuts against the list: the elder brother the Acharakkovai reveres yields to the wiser younger, and a learned man of the lowest order draws the highest to him.

note: Kural 942 regulates the meal by digestion, eating only after the last meal is spent; Acharakkovai 20 regulates it by direction, posture, silence and worship.
teaches: The two books divide the same act between body and rite: the Kural cares when and how much one eats, the Acharakkovai how one sits and where one looks, and neither addresses the other's concern.
list_adds: It makes the meal a sequence of bodily disciplines, facing east, stillness, silence and worship, none of which concerns the food itself.

note: Kural 43 names five the householder must tend (ancestors, gods, guests, kin, self); Acharakkovai 21 names five who must be fed before the householder eats: guests, elders, the cow, caged creatures and children.
teaches: Read together, the Kural's general duty to five becomes a sequence at the meal, and the circle of dependants widens from kin and gods to animals and captives, while the self drops off the list.
list_adds: It turns a list of duties into an order of serving, and it puts the cow and the caged creature beside guests and elders as claimants on the same meal.

note: Naladiyar 94 asks for daily giving before eating, even a grain's worth, to anyone; Acharakkovai 21 names who must be served before the meal.
teaches: The Naladiyar makes giving before eating a matter of amount, however small, while the Acharakkovai makes it a matter of persons, so the two together fix both how little suffices and to whom it is owed.
list_adds: It replaces the Naladiyar's unnamed recipient with five named dependants of the house, human and animal.

note: Verse 21 names five to be fed before one eats; verse 39 bars cooking for oneself alone and requires the house offering to be fed first.
teaches: Together they show that the code puts others before the eater at both ends of the meal: in cooking (39) and in serving (21), with the house offering added to the living claimants.

note: Verse 22 bars laying the bed along the roof-ridge; verse 30 bars the head to the north and the corners when lying down.
teaches: Read together, the bed is governed by two separate direction rules, one tied to the house's ridge and one to the compass, so the code fixes sleep by both the building and the quarters.
audit_text_issue: acharakkovai:22 is obscure; முகட்டு வழி may be the roof-ridge or a direction.

note: Kural 946 grounds not eating to excess in health and joy; Acharakkovai 23 bars excess even when the food is choice, among rules of posture and place.
teaches: The same restraint has two grounds: in the Kural it pays in pleasure and freedom from disease, in the Acharakkovai it is decorum, binding even when the food tempts, so moderation is both prudence and conduct.
list_adds: It sets overeating beside eating lying down, standing, in the open and on the bed, so excess becomes a breach of form like a wrong posture rather than a danger to health.

note: Verse 20 sets the eater's direction, posture and silence; verse 25 sets the order of the food by taste, sweet first and bitter last.
teaches: Verse 20 governs only the eater's body, and verse 25 completes the meal code by governing the food's sequence, so the rule reaches what is eaten as well as how.

note: Acharakkovai 31 forbids passing between brahmins (பார்ப்பார்) as between gods; Tirumanthiram 231 denies the name of brahmin to those who lack truth, knowledge, restraint and devotion.
teaches: The Acharakkovai's deference attaches to the birth-name with no condition, while the Tirumanthiram makes the name itself depend on inner qualities, so the second would void the rule's deference for a brahmin who lacks them.

note: Verse 32 lists ten places barred for spitting and excretion; verse 34 says where these are allowed, a screened or secluded place, and sets the stake at refusing even Indra's throne.
teaches: Together they give the rule's two sides, the barred places and the permitted one, and verse 34 adds that the screening is also an act of mind, so the code of bodily acts reaches into intention.
audit_text_issue: Verse 32 வெண்பலி is doubtful; verse 34 அந்தரத்து may mean the open air. | 34 அந்தரத்து is uncertain (secluded spot or open air).

note: Kural 920 names double-minded women, toddy and dice as the company of those Fortune has abandoned; Acharakkovai 37 bars even looking at another's wife, toddy, theft, gambling and killing.
teaches: The Kural's sanction is loss of fortune in this life, while the Acharakkovai adds public scorn and hell, and it shifts the sexual fault from the courtesan to another's wife, so the same cluster of vices is judged on different grounds.
list_adds: It adds theft and killing to the Kural's three, so pleasures and crimes stand in one list, and it bars them at the level of sight.

note: Elathi 12 says it is good neither to desire nor to look at five places, among them the killing ground and the gambling ground; Acharakkovai 37 bars looking at five things, among them killing and gambling.
teaches: Both works bar the eye, but the Elathi bars the places where killing and gambling happen while the Acharakkovai bars the acts themselves and gives hell as the reason, so the ban on looking is applied once to sites and once to deeds.

note: Verse 37 bars looking at five wrongs; verse 38 bars even thinking of four more.
teaches: Read in sequence, the two verses move the ban inward from the eye to the mind, and both name hell as the end, so the code treats sight and thought as stages of the same fault.
audit_text_issue: 38 line 1 was repaired and is absent from one source.

note: Kural 282 says that even thinking of stealing another's goods is wrong; Acharakkovai 38 bars thinking of seizing, along with lying, slander and envy.
teaches: The Kural's thought-crime is confined to theft, and the Acharakkovai extends the same inward standard to speech faults and envy and names its sanctions, suspicion, hell and the deity's wrath.
list_adds: It groups seizing with lying, slander and envy, so faults of hand, tongue and heart are all forbidden at the stage of thought.

note: Kural 229 calls eating alone from one's hoard worse than begging; Acharakkovai 39 bars cooking for oneself alone and requires the house offering to be fed first.
teaches: The Kural condemns eating alone by its bitterness, while the Acharakkovai moves the bar back to the hearth, so the fault begins when the pot is set on the fire for oneself.
list_adds: It sets the bar on solitary cooking beside a purity rule for the kitchen and an offering rule, so sharing becomes part of the ritual order of the house.

note: Kural 987 asks one to do good even to those who have done harm; Acharakkovai 40 asks only that one not wound elders and young kin at their meal, even if they have done great harm.
teaches: Set beside the Kural's universal demand, the Acharakkovai's rule is narrower in scope (kin, at the meal) and lower in demand (not harming rather than doing good), so the code fixes a minimum where the Kural sets an ideal.
list_adds: It joins forbearance to a seating rule (not sitting above them), so restraint toward kin is part of the precedence of the table.

note: Acharakkovai 42 treats the menstrual days as days of no touch and sets the twelve days after the bath apart for the wife; Sivavakkiyar 134 says the monthly pollution is what grows into the body once the months stop, so no birth is free of it.
teaches: The ritual rule and the Siddhar's attack both join menstruation to conception, but one draws a line of pollution across the cycle while the other uses the same cycle to deny that any body stands outside pollution.

note: Verse 42 names the days a husband keeps to his wife after her bath; verse 43 lists hours and calendar days on which the couple do not come together.
teaches: Taken together the two verses make marital union a matter of the ritual calendar, with days prescribed by the wife's cycle and others barred by the moon, the gods and the hours.

note: Kural 560 says that when the guardian fails to guard, those of the six duties forget their books; Acharakkovai 47 lists affliction to the land's guardian among the days brahmins do not recite.
teaches: Both tie the reciting of the Veda to the king's state: the Kural through long neglect that makes the texts forgotten, the Acharakkovai through a single day of the king's distress that halts recitation at once.
list_adds: It sets the king's affliction among moon days, earthquake, thunder and impurity, so the ruler's distress counts as a cosmic disturbance rather than a failure of governance.
audit_text_issue: FLAG says the site lacks this verse; the text as printed reads cleanly.

note: Kural 43 makes tending ancestors, gods, guests, kin and oneself the householder's chief duty; Acharakkovai 48 names the days of gods, ancestors, wedding, festival and sacrifice as days for aram and for feeding guests.
teaches: The Kural's standing duties to gods, ancestors and guests are turned by the Acharakkovai into dated occasions, showing how a general householder's duty becomes a festival calendar.
list_adds: It replaces the Kural's five persons owed care with five kinds of day, so the duty is counted by occasion, and the guest is fed as an addition to the day's aram.

note: Kural 124 praises the restrained man who does not stray from his station (நிலை); Acharakkovai 49 says dress, gait, slack speech and rebuke must fit one's standing (நிலைமை), learning, manliness and family.
teaches: The Kural's 'not straying from one's station' is shown in concrete outward marks, and the Acharakkovai's addition of family as a measure shows how that station can be read as rank of birth.
list_adds: It names four outward behaviours, two of them faults, and four measures they must fit, so keeping one's station becomes a fitting of dress, walk and speech to learning and lineage.

note: Kural 988 says poverty is no disgrace to one with the firmness of worth; Acharakkovai 50 says the learned do not mock or deride the poor.
teaches: The disgrace of poverty is denied from two sides: the Kural says the poor man of worth carries none, and the Acharakkovai says the learned onlooker must not lay it on him.
list_adds: It sets not deriding the poor among the habits of the learned listener, beside not blaming and not sleeping among crowds, so respect for the poor becomes part of learned decorum.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 இசையாத நேர்ந்து கரவார் and தள்ளியும் uncertain.

note: Verse 6 bars a falling star from the sight of one in எச்சில்; verse 51 bars a falling star, lightning, harlots' finery and the low sun from anyone who wants to keep his radiance.
teaches: The same sight is barred on two grounds in the book, once as a matter of pollution and once to guard one's lustre, so the gaze rules do not rest on pollution alone.

note: Kural 196 calls the man who keeps up useless talk chaff among people; Acharakkovai 52 says those of unshaken mind never speak useless words, deceit, loose talk, abuse or backbiting.
teaches: The Kural judges the empty talker by what his talk shows him to be, while the Acharakkovai names the cause of not talking so, a steady mind, so useless speech appears as a symptom of an unsettled one.
list_adds: It makes useless speech one of five kinds with deceit, wanton talk, abuse and backbiting, all kept off by a single inner steadiness, where the Kural treats useless talk on its own.

note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken when slandered; Acharakkovai 52 says those of unshaken mind never backbite.
teaches: Held together the two verses make one steady mind both unmoved by slander and unwilling to slander, so steadiness works in both directions of backbiting.
list_adds: It sets backbiting last in a list of five faults of speech that the same unshaken mind avoids, where the Naladiyar shows only that mind receiving slander.

note: Kural 90 says a guest wilts when the host's face changes; Acharakkovai 54 puts a smile first among five honours given with food to a guest.
teaches: The Kural says what the wrong face does to a guest, and the Acharakkovai sets the right face at the head of a sequence of welcome, so the host's smile is the first act of hospitality, before word, water, mat and bed.
list_adds: It orders the welcome from face to word to body to rest, so the smile the Kural defends by a negative image becomes the first of five steps that accompany food.

note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from the work one does; Acharakkovai 56 says one does not leave the work of one's ancestral line even when famine makes one poor.
teaches: If செய்தொழில் in the Kural is occupation, the two clash: the Kural ranks people by their work and not their birth, while the Acharakkovai fixes the work by birth, so rank by work becomes rank by descent.
list_adds: It sets the bar on leaving hereditary work after plain rules of safety in fire, rain and forest, treating loyalty to one's descent as prudence of the same kind.
audit_text_issue: தொல்வரவின் தீர்ந்த தொழில் could also be read as work that breaks with good custom rather than hereditary work.

note: Verse 16 names the king, teacher, mother, father and elder brother as the குரவர் to be worshipped as gods; verse 58 ends by keeping the குரவர் on one's right.
teaches: Verse 16 says the elders are to be worshipped like gods, and verse 58 gives one bodily form of that worship, the circling to the right otherwise paid to the divine.

note: Kural 715 calls not speaking first among elders the best restraint; Acharakkovai 60 says that on the road with eminent elders one does not ride, wear sandals or shade oneself.
teaches: The Kural's deference to elders lies in speech, the Acharakkovai's in the body on the road, so respect is shown both by holding back the word and by sharing the elder's hardship.
list_adds: It turns deference into three bodily refusals, of mount, sandals and shade, which the Kural's single rule about speaking first does not cover.

note: Kural 134 says a brahmin's birth is ruined when his conduct fails, though a forgotten Veda can be relearned; Acharakkovai 61 says the four-Veda knowers, come by heaven's order, are honoured as one's own elders.
teaches: The Kural makes the brahmin's standing hang on conduct and treats the Veda as recoverable, while the Acharakkovai grounds his honour in the Veda and a heavenly origin and names no condition of conduct, so the two disagree on what earns the rank.
list_adds: It places the Veda-knowers inside the circle of one's own elders, so reverence for a birth-group is folded into filial reverence, which the couplet never does.

note: Verse 16 names the five peerless elders and says to worship them as gods; verse 62 names the three acts of ஆசாரம் owed to elders.
teaches: Verse 16 gives the rank and verse 62 the bodily acts by which god-like worship of elders is performed, so the book's worship of elders turns out to be bowing, timely attendance and rising.

note: Verse 16 says the elders are to be worshipped as gods; verse 72 says that in a great house or a temple one does not bow even to them.
teaches: The god-like worship verse 16 owes to elders gives way where a greater object of worship is present, so the book ranks reverence by place and the elder's claim is not absolute.

note: Verse 61 honours the four-Veda knowers as one's own elders; verse 64 puts பார்ப்பார் first among eight to whom one yields the road.
teaches: Verse 64 turns 61's honour into a gesture on the road and sets the brahmin at the head of a line of the burdened, the sick and cows, so rank by birth is enacted with the same act as care for the weak.

note: Kural 126 says that drawing in the five senses like a tortoise protects for seven births; Acharakkovai 65 says the five are hard to hold even for the worthy, so they must not stay alone with their nearest kinswomen.
teaches: Where the Kural trusts restraint of the senses as a power one can gain, the Acharakkovai doubts it even in the worthy and replaces it with a rule that removes the occasion, so self-mastery is backed by avoidance.
list_adds: It names mother, daughter and sister as the case, so the doubt about restraint is pressed to the women least suspected, a limit the couplet never tests.

note: Kural 700 says intimacy that does the improper because 'we are old friends' brings ruin; Acharakkovai 66 names கழிகிழமை, overstepping intimacy, among the things those who would last in service avoid.
teaches: The Kural states the danger of presuming on an old bond; the Acharakkovai puts that danger among gate, gift and dress, showing that presuming on intimacy is one of several small encroachments on a lord's dignity.
list_adds: It sets excessive intimacy beside anger at the gate, carelessness at gifts and dressing like the lord, so the couplet's single fault becomes one of a family of encroachments.

note: Kural 692 says not desiring what kings desire brings lasting gain through them; Acharakkovai 68 opens with not taking pleasure in what the great take pleasure in.
teaches: The couplet gives the rule and its reward; the Acharakkovai shows what it looks like in the house, joined to not bringing low men in and not slighting the house's child, so not rivalling the lord's pleasures is part of guarding his household.
list_adds: It joins the rule to two others about the great man's house, so restraint of desire is placed among household courtesies rather than left as a maxim.

note: Kural 698 says not to slight one as younger or as kin but to act by the light he stands in; Acharakkovai 68 says not to speak slightingly even of an undiscerning child.
teaches: Read together, the young one the Kural warns against slighting can be a mere child of the great house, so the rule against belittling youth reaches down to the child who cannot yet understand.
list_adds: It makes the child's undiscerning state the extreme case, not only youth, and ties the rule to the place where one is not intimate.

note: Pazhamozhi 281 says that even when an angry king does what one does not want, one should not act on one's resentment, for no one wakes a sleeping tiger; Acharakkovai 69 says one does not sulk or contradict even if the great one says the crow is white.
teaches: Pazhamozhi bars acting on resentment when the king wrongs one; the Acharakkovai extends the bar to speech and face when he speaks falsely, so the attendant's silence covers both injury and untruth.

note: Naladiyar 164 says those who anger the great do not escape even in a fortress, as the snake in its crevice dreads thunder; Acharakkovai 69 lists the small signs of displeasure one must not show before the great.
teaches: The Naladiyar gives the reason the Acharakkovai's courtesies are owed: the great one's anger reaches anywhere, so the rule not to sulk or contradict is a defence, not only a manner.
list_adds: It breaks the single danger into a list of guarded acts, sulking, facing, private talk and contradiction, so the quatrain's dread becomes a code of gestures.

note: Naladiyar 170 says the fitting quality of one who has some excellence is restraint; Acharakkovai 71 says those of good family do not spread out their wealth, learning, lustre and virtue before the lord.
teaches: The Naladiyar makes restraint the proper dress of excellence in general; the Acharakkovai names the place where it is tested, before the lord, and the risk of failing it, being taken for an enemy.
list_adds: It names four excellences, wealth, learning, lustre and virtue, as alike to be kept silent before the lord, and gives a reason, looking like an enemy, that the quatrain lacks.

note: Verse 63 bars speaking one's learning before elders; verse 71 bars displaying learning and three other excellences before the lord.
teaches: The same silence about one's learning is owed in the house to elders and at court to the lord, so the book treats display of learning as a breach of rank in both spheres.

note: Kural 694 says to suppress whispers and shared smiles before the great; Acharakkovai 73 bars laughter, yawning, hawking and sneezing before them.
teaches: The Kural bars the laugh as a sign that may be misread; the Acharakkovai puts it with yawning and sneezing, which carry no meaning, so the presence of the great governs the body itself and not only what it signals.
list_adds: It joins a meaningful act, laughter, to involuntary ones, so the couplet's guard against misread signs becomes a guard on the body as such.

note: Kural 694 says to suppress whispers before the great; Acharakkovai 75 says that in the house of the great one does not take in whispered words, nor look at the women, nor let the garment slip.
teaches: The Kural forbids whispering in the presence of the great; the Acharakkovai also forbids receiving a whisper, so the listener is as guilty as the speaker.
list_adds: It sets the whisper beside the gaze on the women and the slipping garment, so the couplet's rule on speech becomes one of several guards on eye, ear and body in the great house.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 செவிசொறுண்டார் is not a clear word. | Line 1 செவிசொறுண்டார் is unclear.

note: Kural 696 says to speak knowing the mood and the time, what is needed and not disliked; Acharakkovai 76 says to speak at the right moment with few syllables that hold the whole sense.
teaches: The Kural asks for the right time and the right matter; the Acharakkovai adds the right length, so speech before the great is judged by moment, content and brevity together.
list_adds: It lists four faults of manner, haste, going on, falsehood and sprawl, before giving the positive rule, so the couplet's advice is defined against its failures.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 காலந்தால் is unclear, perhaps காலத்தால்.

note: Kural 695 says not to listen in or press for anything, but to hear a secret when it is released; Acharakkovai 78 says not to take counsel with others or listen in, and if near, to stand turned away as if busy with something else.
teaches: The Kural states the inner restraint; the Acharakkovai gives the posture that makes it visible, standing turned away, so not listening must also be seen not to listen.
list_adds: It adds a staged posture of attention elsewhere to the bar on listening, which the couplet does not have.

note: Verse 6 lists புலை among five sights barred in எச்சில்; verse 80 bars addressing புலையர் by kinship terms, and both close on நன்கறிவார்.
teaches: Verse 80's plural personal form with a verb of address shows the book uses this root for persons, which weighs toward reading புலை in verse 6 as the outcaste person rather than an impure thing.

note: Kural 695 tells the king's servant not to listen in or press after secrets; Acharakkovai 81 names the palace places, the back gate, the assembly and the women's quarters, where looking in is barred, and exempts those whose office lies there.
teaches: Together they show that the courtier's discretion is spatial as well as verbal: what the Kural states as restraint of curiosity the Acharakkovai maps onto doors and rooms, and ties to office rather than to trust.
list_adds: It turns a general rule about secrets into three named places and adds the exception for those whose work lies there.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 தொழிற்குரிவர் is likely தொழிற்குரியவர்.

note: Kural 700 warns that intimacy which, presuming on old ties, does what is improper brings ruin; Acharakkovai 82 applies the same warning to sitting near the women, even with great intimacy (மிகக்கிழமை).
teaches: The pair show the period's fear of presumed closeness reaching its sharpest point in the women's place, where the Acharakkovai grounds the bar not in the king's anger but in a claim about women's changing liking.
list_adds: It names the one occasion where even the closest intimacy gives no right and adds a reason drawn from women rather than from the ruler.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 மகளிரி is likely மகளிர் miswritten; whose women are meant is unclear.

note: Acharakkovai 83 says those who would live long do not tell the size of the king's army; in Patitruppattu 77 the poet, asked by travellers how large Poraiyan's army is, says he could not count it and describes its elephants.
teaches: Read together, the courtier's rule of silence and the bard's praise give the same answer to the same question: no figure is told, and the bard turns the forbidden number into the uncountable.

note: Kural 698 says the king is not to be slighted as young or as kin; Acharakkovai 84 sets the king among the snake, fire and the lion and says slighting any of them as young, weak or familiar brings harm.
teaches: The Kural asks respect for the light the king stands in, while the Acharakkovai asks it because he can harm, so the pair show two grounds for the same deference, the office and the danger.
list_adds: It ranks the king with a snake, fire and a lion, so his claim to respect is made one with their power to harm.

note: Thirikadugam 42 says the vellala family behaves toward brahmins as toward fire even when familiar with them; Acharakkovai 84 says fire, like the king, harms one who slights it as familiar.
teaches: The two books use one image, fire that burns the familiar, for two superiors, the brahmin and the king, showing that the period's rule against contempt bred by familiarity covered ritual and political rank alike.

note: Kural 692 says not desiring what kings desire brings lasting prosperity through them; Acharakkovai 85 says that even great charity, weddings, enterprise and houses must not outdo the king's, or lasting wealth (மன்னிய செல்வம்) is lost.
teaches: The pairing turns the Kural's general restraint into a ceiling on display, and shows that in the period even a subject's virtue, charity included, could not be allowed to outshine the king.
list_adds: It names four kinds of display, charity first among them, so the limit is placed on virtue as well as on luxury.

note: Kural 103 praises help given by those who do not weigh the return; Acharakkovai 88 says those who would live rightly do not even speak of the return on help they gave.
teaches: The Kural's giver does not reckon the return before giving; the Acharakkovai adds that he does not mention it after, so the pair carry the refusal to weigh from the act into speech.
list_adds: It groups silence about one's help with not faulting food and not praising one's own vows, so the rule becomes part of a discipline of the tongue about one's own goods.

note: Kural 379 asks why those who welcome good fortune grieve at bad, on the ground of fate; Acharakkovai 89 says those of true vision do not grieve over what has passed or what is beyond their control.
teaches: The Kural grounds calm in fate, whereas the Acharakkovai limits it to the unattainable, the past and the uncontrollable and grounds it in vision, so the pair show calm resting either on what governs events or on seeing which events one can still change.
list_adds: It splits the Kural's single good and bad fortune into three cases, each scoped to what cannot be changed.

note: Acharakkovai 90 sets rules toward the பார்ப்பார், from whose hand a cow is not taken, and the புலை, to whom leavings are not held out; Sivavakkiyar asks what a Paraiyar woman and a Brahmin woman are, since no mark on flesh, skin or bone divides them.
teaches: Read against each other, the rule that ranks two birth-groups by what may pass between their hands meets a denial that the body carries any rank, so the purity rule is shown to depend on a mark the Siddhar says is not there.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 4 says a proud raised neck (ஏக்கழுத்தம்) in one who has nothing to be proud of draws the laughter of the good; Acharakkovai 91 says a raised neck (ஏக்கழுத்து) is blamed even in the forest, since there are always those older than oneself.
teaches: Sirupanchamoolam faults the raised neck when it lacks ground, but the Acharakkovai faults it anywhere, even unseen, so the pair separate pride as absurdity from pride as disrespect to elders.
audit_text_issue: acharakkovai:91 line 1 தாளிசைப்பு is uncertain.

note: Naladiyar 52 calls those who prattle endlessly (தொலைவில்லா) of grammar and astrology the greatest fools; Acharakkovai 92 tells one to fix the day of a rite from the unfailing (தொலைவில்லா) அந்தணர், whose word never errs.
teaches: The same word, தொலைவில்லா, marks the Naladiyar's endless and foolish astrology and the Acharakkovai's unfailing reckoners, so the two books take opposite views of consulting the day before acting.
list_adds: It sets the reckoning of days in a contrast between two birth-groups, so the question becomes whose reckoning to trust, not whether to reckon.

note: Kural 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous, kind to every living being; Acharakkovai 92 trusts the word of the அந்தணர் and distrusts that of the புலையர் on the day of a rite.
teaches: The Kural derives the name அந்தணர் from conduct, while the Acharakkovai uses it as a birth-group set against the புலையர், so the pair show the same word serving as a moral title in one book and a caste rank in the other.
list_adds: It pairs the அந்தணர் with the புலையர் as opposites, a contrast of birth that the Kural's definition by kindness does not make.

note: Kural 57 asks what use the guarding of women by confinement is, since the best guard is their own steadfastness; Acharakkovai 95 lists the wife among four things a man guards like gold.
teaches: The Kural moves the guard of a wife inside her, while the Acharakkovai keeps it in the husband's hands beside his body and his deposits, so the pair show two views of where a wife's keeping lies.
list_adds: It puts the wife in one list with the man's body, a deposit and his savings, so she is guarded as a possession.

note: Thirikadugam 62 names the man who wrongly keeps a deposit placed with him as one who loses his line; Acharakkovai 95 lists a deposit among four things to be guarded like gold.
teaches: One verse says what keeping a deposit asks and the other what breaking it costs, and together they show the deposit as another's property that the period held as close as one's own body and family.

note: Acharakkovai 1 names eight virtues as the seed from which ஆசாரம் grows; Acharakkovai 96 says ஆசாரம் comes in any case to those who hold to their own work like the ant, the weaver bird and the crow.
teaches: The book that opened by rooting conduct in inner virtues nears its close by rooting it in diligence, so ஆசாரம் is given two sources, character and steady work, and the second is learned from animals.

note: Kural 694 tells one to suppress whispers and shared smiles in the presence of the great; Acharakkovai 97 says one speaks before the great only with folded hands or a covered mouth and does not look into their eyes.
teaches: The Kural forbids the small private signs that the great may read as against them, and the Acharakkovai prescribes the posture of the mouth, hands and eyes, so together they show restraint before the great as a whole bodily discipline.
list_adds: It names the hands, the mouth and the eyes in turn, so the Kural's ban on two signs becomes a full posture of address.
audit_text_issue: acharakkovai 97 absent from one source

note: Elathi 12 says it is good neither to desire nor to look at five places, among them the killing ground and the ground where men gamble; Acharakkovai 98 says the wise do not enter the gamblers' hall or the ground of unceasing din, and that entering brings harm.
teaches: Both books treat the gambling place as a place to avoid, but the Jain Elathi bars even desiring or seeing it alongside the killing ground, while the Acharakkovai bars entering it for the harm it brings, so the pair show a moral and a prudential reason for the same avoidance.

note: Acharakkovai 1 makes eight virtues the seed of ஆசாரம்; Acharakkovai 100, the last verse, names nine persons freed from it: the stranger, the destitute, the old, the young, the bereaved, the frightened, one who has eaten, one on the king's work and the bridegroom.
teaches: Read as the book's frame, the pair show the code bounded at both ends: it grows from virtues that bind everyone, but its rules lapse for those whom ignorance, weakness, fear, grief or duty prevent from keeping them.

note: Elathi 35 promises kingship to one who feeds the renouncers, the powerless, the unknown, the dead or bereaved (இறந்தார்), the destitute and the young; Acharakkovai 100 frees from ஆசாரம் the stranger, the destitute, the old, the young and one who has lost a life.
teaches: The two books name nearly the same weak persons, but the Elathi makes them claims on the giver's food while the Acharakkovai lifts the rules of conduct from them, so the vulnerable are owed help in one code and excused in the other.
audit_text_issue: acharakkovai:100 உயிரிழந்தான் is uncertain (bereaved or near death); elathi:35 தோன்றார் and இறந்தார் are uncertain. | acharakkovai:100 and elathi:35 are both uncertain in sense.

note: Kural 260 says all creatures worship the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; Elathi 2 says the one who has the right to kill and does not, and is not deluded by flesh, rises above gods as well as men.
teaches: The pair shows the Jain ethics raising the stake: the Kural's worship by the spared creatures becomes rank above the gods, and the abstention counts most in the one who has the power to kill.
list_adds: It puts non-killing and refusing flesh first in a list with not tormenting, not deceiving and not swerving, so the two abstentions of 260 become the head of a five-part code rather than its whole.

note: Kural 263 chides householders who have forgotten penance in providing for renunciants; Elathi 3 says outright that penance is easy and giving is hard.
teaches: Read with 263, the verse reverses the ranking the Kural's chiding implies: if giving is the harder task, the householder who gives instead of doing penance has chosen the steeper road.
list_adds: It sets penance and giving as the first of several easy-hard pairs, so the ranking of the two is stated as a rule of difficulty rather than left to a rhetorical question.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 ends in the obscure அரிதுக் கார்க்கேல் and line 2 is damaged; only the first pair is clear.

note: Kural 391 says learn flawlessly and then stand by what is learned; Elathi 4 says that where six kinds of kindly conduct are seen, the books of learning may be let go.
teaches: The Kural makes conduct the completion of learning, while Elathi makes it a substitute: together they show two orders, learning that leads to conduct and conduct that makes the books unnecessary.
list_adds: It names the six acts that do the books' work (relieving distress, not scorning, shunning the base, relieving grief, avoiding blame, desired speech), so the conduct that replaces learning is specified, which 391 leaves general.

note: Kural 30 calls those who wear cool kindness toward every living being the அந்தணர்; Elathi 6 calls one who has six possessions a mother to all living beings.
teaches: Both give a title for care toward every creature, but Elathi grounds it in six restraints, keeping out lies and flesh among them, so universal care is built from abstentions, not only from a cool temper.
list_adds: It breaks the single quality of 30 into six possessions, two of them shutting out falsehood and flesh, and gives the outcome a mother's name instead of a status word.

note: Kural 86 says the host who tends the guest and watches for the next becomes a guest of the gods; Elathi 7 says the gods hasten to receive as guest one who gives sweet speech, mingling, a seat and good food without harsh words.
teaches: The couplet promises the reward and Elathi spells out the hospitality that earns it, so the pair shows the heavenly reciprocity resting on manner of speech as much as on food.
list_adds: It itemises hospitality into speech, mingling, a seat and food, with harsh words removed, a grading from word to meal that 86 does not make.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 69 counts the one who agreed to a killing among five who share its sin; Elathi 8 opens its list with not consenting and not killing as two separate acts.
teaches: Together the two Jain lists show consent treated as its own act of killing: one assigns it a share of the sin, the other makes refusing it a virtue in its own right.

note: Kural 226 says relieving the hunger of the destitute (அற்றார்) is where one should store wealth; Elathi 9 says giving food, shelter and clothing to the destitute (அற்றார்கட்கு) makes one live as a learned man.
teaches: The couplet makes the gift a bank for wealth and Elathi makes it a source of wisdom, so the same act toward the destitute is repaid in two different coins.
list_adds: It widens the gift from food to food, shelter and clothing and adds giving without regard to the receiver's learning or kinship, which 226 does not mention.
audit_text_issue: Lines 1-2 (கற்ற துணையார் எனமதியார், அன்னணம் ஓராமல்) are hard to construe.

note: Kural 367 says that if one cuts desire fully, the deeds that do not fail come; Elathi 11 echoes it (அவாஅறுப்பின் ஆற்ற) and adds the fate of one who does not cut it.
teaches: The near-verbatim echo shows Elathi reading the couplet and supplying its other half: what 367 leaves unsaid, the failure to cut desire, is rebirth under the five senses.
list_adds: It sets the one who cuts desire beside the one who does not, so the couplet's promise becomes one branch of a choice with a stated penalty.

note: Kural 24 guards the five with the goad of firmness, implying elephants without naming them; Elathi 11 names the five elephants (ஐங்களிறு) that toss the one who does not cut desire.
teaches: Elathi makes explicit the elephants the couplet only implies, and shows what happens when the goad is missing: the senses carry their rider into the hole of rebirth.
list_adds: It turns the goad image into a narrative of failure, the rider tossed by the five, which the couplet's image of control does not show.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 68 says long bathing at a ghat does not remove the blemish; Elathi 13 counts not bathing (ஆடாமை, on our reading) among the six marks of ascetics.
teaches: On this reading the two Jain lists move from denying bathing any cleansing power to making its refusal a mark of the renunciant, the reverse of the bathing rules of the Acharakkovai.
audit_text_issue: Elathi 13 line 2 division (உட்குடைத்தா வென்று களையாமை) and Sirupanchamoolam 68 வேகும்பம் are unclear.

note: Kural 834 calls the greatest fool one who studies, understands and teaches but does not restrain himself; Elathi 14 says that for one who keeps six restraints the books are beside the point.
teaches: Held together the two state the same principle from opposite ends: learning without restraint is folly, and restraint without learning already has what the books are for.
list_adds: It names the restraints (no lying, no flesh, no toddy, no evil, no base company, no reviling) that 834 leaves as a single self-restraint, and puts flesh and toddy among them.

note: Verse 4 lets the books go where six kindly acts are seen; verse 14 puts the books outside one who keeps six abstentions.
teaches: The repeated close shows the chapter treating conduct over books as a refrain, and the two lists divide that conduct into acts of kindness (4) and acts of refusal (14).

note: Thirikadugam 55 names a friendship that does not keep a precious secret (அருமறை) as one of three spies; Elathi 15 counts not letting a precious secret slip to sweet talkers as good.
teaches: Together they show the secret's danger from both sides: Thirikadugam names the friend who leaks it as a spy, and Elathi locates the leak in the listener's trust of pleasant speech.

note: Kural 42 makes the householder the support of those who renounced, those who have nothing and the dead; Elathi 16 names drawing near to renunciants, giving to those who have not renounced, speaking well of the dead and tending their kin.
teaches: The verse reads like a gloss on 42: it keeps the three figures and turns the dead into the living kin they leave, so the householder's duty to the dead becomes care of a household.
list_adds: It turns the three dependants of 42 into four acts and adds the kin of the dead, so the list says how the support is given, not only to whom.
audit_text_issue: துறவார்(கு) (line 1) may be a variant or corruption of the Kural's துவ்வார்; as printed it means those who have not renounced. | துறவார்(கு) may be a corruption of துவ்வார்க்கு; if so, the parallel with 42 is closer

note: Kural 632 names a minister excellent in resolve, guarding the people, learning and labour; Elathi 17 names guarding the people, resolve and strength in learning, then adds secret counsel, keeping off sloth and good company.
teaches: The two share three of their qualities in near-identical words (குடி, வன்கண், கற்றல்/நூல்வன்மை), and Elathi's additions show a minister judged also by the company he keeps and by his secrecy.
list_adds: It adds secret counsel and good company to the Kural's core, so ministerial fitness extends from capacity to discretion and associations.
audit_text_issue: Packet flags that the site's text lacks line 1, which carries the shared words; lines 2-3 divide uncertainly. | elathi:17 line 1 is missing from the site's text; the division of line 3 (முடியோம்பி நாற்றம் சுவைகேள்வி) is doubtful. | Site text lacks line 1 of Elathi 17, the line the link rests on; lines 3-4 doubtful

note: Kural 920 makes double-minded women, liquor and dice the company of those Fortune has abandoned; Elathi 18 lists indulgence, waste, hunting, toddy, gambling, harsh words, harsh punishment and unrestraint as what a king must guard against.
teaches: The couplet's three ruinous companions reappear inside Elathi's longer list of the king's vices, which shows the Kural's general warning taken up into a royal code where it secures the kingdom against rivals.
list_adds: It places the Kural's three vices among the seven of kingship (adding hunting, waste, harsh words and harsh punishment) and closes with unrestraint as their sum, carrying the warning into the king's domain.

note: Naladiyar 158 says one deaf to others' secrets, blind to a neighbour's wife and dumb in evil backbiting needs no teaching of virtue; Elathi 19 names the same deafness to secrets and dumbness to evil speech, with not killing and not lying, as the marks of one greater than a king.
teaches: The shared images of deafness and dumbness show the two Jain works using one figure for restraint, and Elathi's addition of non-killing turns the Naladiyar's man who needs no teaching into a rank above kings.
list_adds: It sets the Naladiyar's restraints of the senses after non-killing, not causing killing and not lying, so sense restraint is ranked behind non-violence and truth in a seven-part list.

note: Purananuru 43 recalls the Chola ancestor who entered the scales for a dove; Elathi 20 praises one who delights in giving even when it is like cutting off a limb.
teaches: Read with Puram 43, Elathi's simile carries the memory of the king who gave his own flesh: the heroic deed of an ancestor becomes the measure of ordinary giving for anyone.

note: Naladiyar 53 counts goods that fail (home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth, strength) as the reason to renounce; Elathi 21 counts the same failing goods together with what arrives, disease and old age.
teaches: Held together, the two show that the case for release can be argued from loss alone or from loss and arrival, and Elathi's version gives the body's afflictions equal weight with the goods that slip away.
list_adds: It pairs what leaves with what comes in one list of five, so the argument moves from fading goods to arriving afflictions, which the quatrain does not count.
audit_text_issue: line 4 வீதி is most likely விதி

note: Naladiyar 52 has the best reflect on impermanence, disease, old age and death and do their own work; Elathi 24 lists disease, birth, old age, death, sorrow and want and names the work as the way of release.
teaches: Read together, the quatrain's unnamed 'own work' is given a name and its four evils gain birth and want, so the round of births itself becomes the thing to escape.
list_adds: It adds birth and unending want to the Naladiyar's four, making the list the cycle of births rather than the ills of one life.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 புறப்பு is evidently பிறப்பு.

note: Both verses list what Death disregards and close with a book as the remedy; 22 names the defences Death does not fear, 23 the occasions and qualities he does not look at.
teaches: Together they show the chapter's argument that no strength, wealth, virtue or auspicious time stops Death, and that the Jain answer in both is scripture, not effort or rite.

note: Kural 686 names the envoy as learned, fearless of hostile eyes, persuasive and knowing the time; Elathi 26 has the same four and adds a tested beauty of mind and fame known to the world.
teaches: The pair shows the envoy's qualities carried from the Kural into a later list that makes reputation itself a qualification, so the envoy is chosen partly for being known.
list_adds: It sets world-known fame as a sixth excellence beside the Kural's four, ranking renown with skill as something an envoy must already have.

note: Kural 35 defines virtue as avoiding envy, craving, anger and harsh speech, mixing faults of mind and of speech in one four; Elathi 27 names three faults (coveting, anger, wrong view) and assigns them to the mind alone.
teaches: Set side by side, the Kural's single list is seen sorted in Elathi by the faculty that sins, and wrong view, a doctrinal error, enters a list the Kural keeps to passions.
list_adds: It sorts faults by faculty, mind here and speech and body in the next two verses, and adds wrong view to the passions, a sorting the couplet does not make.
audit_text_issue: Elathi 27 lines 1 and 3 (அஃகுநீ, கள்ளத்த அல்ல) are obscure.

note: Kural 360 names desire, anger and confusion as the three whose end ends pain; Elathi 27 names coveting, anger and wrong view as the three faults of the mind.
teaches: Both books build a triad of inner faults with anger at its centre, but where the Kural ends in confusion, a lack of seeing, Elathi ends in wrong view, a positive false belief, which shows the Jain stress on right doctrine.
list_adds: It replaces confusion with wrong view and puts the triad inside a scheme of ten faults across mind, speech and body.
audit_text_issue: Kural 360 as printed reads இநவ்முன்றன் for இவ்மூன்றன்; Elathi 27 line 3 கள்ளத்த அல்ல is obscure. | elathi:27 line 3 கள்ளத்த அல்ல is obscure.

note: 27 names three faults of the mind, 28 four faults of the mouth.
teaches: Read in sequence, the two verses (with 29) show the work laying out a full ten-part scheme of faults by faculty, mind three, speech four, body three, spread over consecutive verses.
audit_text_issue: மறலையின் (28, line 4) is obscure.

note: 29 names three faults of the body and closes the scheme begun in 27 and continued in 28.
teaches: With 29 the ten faults are complete, and the pairing shows that the counting form can carry one doctrine across several verses rather than finishing in each.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 18 lists not lying, not stealing, not desiring women and not eating flesh as what ends rebirth; Elathi 29 names killing, theft and lust as the body's faults.
teaches: Taken together, Elathi's body-faults are seen in Sirupanchamoolam as conditions of escaping rebirth, and the sister Jain work adds flesh-eating to the bodily code Elathi frames by faculty.
audit_text_issue: Sirupanchamoolam 18 வையாமை and நையாமை are uncertain.

note: 30 names six kinds of legal son and 31 names the remaining six.
teaches: Only read together do the two verses give the twelve kinds of son of the law-books, showing the work importing a Sanskrit legal classification whole into Tamil verse.
audit_text_issue: Elathi 30 ஓளரதனே and கிரிதன்பென கற்பவன் are garbled; Elathi 31 runs புத்ரனபவித்தன் together.

note: Kural 50 says one who lives on earth as life should be lived is placed among the gods; Elathi 32 says one who keeps six silences about himself and others and gives before eating is god of gods.
teaches: The pair fills the Kural's undefined 'as life should be lived' with particular restraints of speech and the act of giving, and raises the reward from a place among the gods to their head.
list_adds: It spells out the good life as six named silences, mostly about one's own birth, wealth and years, joined to giving before eating.
audit_text_issue: sense of some items uncertain

note: Kural 86 says the host who tends guests will be a welcome guest to the gods; Elathi 34 says the gods seek with love one who gives what fits and keeps from angry and boastful speech.
teaches: Both books put the giver's reward in the gods' welcome, and Elathi adds that restraint of speech and anger, not hospitality alone, is what the gods are drawn to.
list_adds: It sets the giving beside five restraints of speech and temper, so the gift alone does not earn the welcome.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 70 promises kingship to those who give to prisoners and to people keeping fasts; Elathi 35 promises rule of the earth to one who gives food to renouncers, the needy and the young.
teaches: The two Jain lists share the reward of kingship for feeding, but Sirupanchamoolam's recipients are mostly ascetics fasting by rule while Elathi's are mostly the needy, which shows the same promise attached to two different kinds of worthy receiver.
audit_text_issue: Both verses have uncertain words (தோன்றார், இறந்தார்; செந்தார்க்கு, உறைக்கிடந்தார்). | Elathi 35's recipients (தோன்றார், இறந்தார்) and Sirupanchamoolam 70's செந்தார்க்கு and உறைக்கிடந்தார் are uncertain.

note: Kural 226 calls removing the hunger of the destitute the place to store wealth; Elathi 36 names whom to feed (the lame, the blind, the mute, the kinless, the unlearned) and says the gods will desire such givers.
teaches: The pair turns the Kural's general 'destitute' into named kinds of person who cannot earn, and moves the giver's return from stored wealth to the gods' regard.
list_adds: It names five kinds of need, bodily, social and of learning, and puts the unlearned among the disabled as people owed food.

note: Kural 335 says to hurry to good deeds before the death rattle stops the tongue; Elathi 37 lists the pleas Death ignores, worship among them, and names penance as the remedy.
teaches: Together they show the urgency of the Kural's couplet sharpened into a Jain argument in which even worship fails before Death and only penance done in time avails.
list_adds: It counts six failed appeals to Death, including worship, so ritual is set aside before penance is named.
audit_text_issue: Lines 2-3 (ஈடற்றார் என்றும், ஈ(டு) ஓரான்) are compressed and uncertain.

note: Naladiyar 52 calls those who prattle endlessly of grammar and astrology the greatest fools; Elathi 38 says the great penance is not removed by letters, numbers or hymns but reached by conduct.
teaches: Read together, both Jain works set letters and number-lore against the real work, and Elathi names that work as conduct within penance where the quatrain leaves it as one's own task.
list_adds: It puts praise and hymns beside letters and numbers as three substitutes for conduct, adding the devotional to the learned ones the quatrain mocks.
audit_text_issue: Lines 1-3 are compressed and the subject of நீங்காது, ஒழியாது, மாறாது is unclear.

note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy and doing as spoken is hard; Elathi 39 lists four easy-hard pairs and ends that winning is easy and the word is hard.
teaches: The same easy-hard form ranks speech oppositely in the two books, because Kural 664 means announcing a plan while Elathi means the right and truthful word, so the pair shows how much 'speech' changes with what kind of speaking is meant.
list_adds: It sets four easy-hard pairs in a row, death against character and victory against the word, so speech is ranked among the hard things the Kural keeps for deeds.

note: 37 treats Death as the overpowering thing no plea escapes; 39 calls dying easy beside the hard work of character.
teaches: Within one chapter the work views death from two sides, as the terror that drives penance and as the easy thing beside lasting virtue, and the pair shows death's weight depends on what it is measured against.
audit_text_issue: In Elathi 39, (எளிது) in line 2 is an editorial restoration. | 39 (எளிது) restored by editor; 37 flagged uncertain

note: Naladiyar 92 sets death, age and disease before the reader and urges sharing food while wealth is in hand; Elathi 40 joins choosing the way out of impermanence with removing others' hunger.
teaches: Together they show the ethics group tying the feeding of the hungry to the escape from impermanence, and Elathi places it among inner disciplines like not doubting and not wavering.
list_adds: It sets removing hunger beside non-harm, steadiness and the choice of release, so feeding becomes one of the marks of one bound for heaven.
audit_text_issue: elathi:40 line 1 division (உற்றதற்கு ஓடி) and line 3 (பசியுண்டு) are uncertain.

note: Kural 232 says all that speakers say amounts to praise resting on those who give to askers; verse 41 says the books of the path will recite the worth of one who gives to the resourceless.
teaches: The couplet locates fame in what people say; the verse places it in the scriptures themselves, so giving earns a place in the texts that teach giving.
list_adds: It makes giving the last of six marks after five refusals (the mean, flesh, falsehood, theft, tight-fistedness), so the praise in the books is earned by a whole discipline and not by the gift alone.

note: Kural 260 says all beings worship the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; verse 42 widens the refusal to consenting to killing and to the company of killers, and rewards it with kingship on a killing elephant.
teaches: The couplet's reward is the reverence of the spared creatures; the verse pays the same abstention with conquest, showing a Jain work content to reward non-killing with a war elephant.
list_adds: It splits the couplet's one refusal into three degrees of complicity (killing, consenting, keeping killers' company) and then joins them to feeding, so non-killing is graded by distance from the act.

note: Kural 908 says those who act as a woman wishes fail their friends and do no good; verse 43 sets not trusting women's words beside feeding great ascetics, both as a giver's marks.
teaches: Read together, the period rule against heeding women is tied in both works to giving: the Kural says it stops good deeds, and Elathi sets it beside the meal for ascetics it protects.
list_adds: It puts distrust of women's words among gambling, deceit and disputes, as one more distraction a giver must refuse, where the Kural's chapter treats it alone as a fault of the husband.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 கலா(வு) and பேரான் are uncertain.

note: Kural 322 calls sharing one's food and sustaining many lives the chief of all virtues; verse 44's giver, who gives white rice before eating, is reborn a king whose lot is to share and eat.
teaches: The couplet ranks sharing first among virtues; the verse makes it also the shape of the reward, so the king of the next birth is the sharer of this one on a larger scale.
list_adds: It sets sharing after truthfulness, refusing flesh, not reviling and clearing the road, so the couplet's chief virtue closes a list that joins speech, diet and public work.

note: Kural 342 says to renounce while there is time; verse 45, on the reading that விடுப்பான் is letting the kingdom go, says the giver will rule, conquer and quickly give it up.
teaches: On that reading the verse makes kingship a stage on the way to renunciation, a reward meant to be left, where the couplet speaks of renouncing what one already has.
list_adds: It sets renunciation at the end of a reward sequence (rule, conquest, release) earned by six marks of conduct, so the couplet's counsel becomes the last step of a karmic career.

note: Kural 922 says not to drink and, if one does, to be one who does not care for the esteem of the worthy; verse 46 bars not only drinking but looking upon drinkers.
teaches: The couplet treats drink as the drinker's own loss of standing; the verse extends the bar to the sight of drinkers, so the rule reaches the company one keeps.
list_adds: It sets three degrees of avoiding toddy (revelry, drinking, seeing drinkers) beside three duties of the table, so abstention is joined to hospitality as one portrait of the householder.

note: Kural 527 says crows do not hide but call out and eat, and gain belongs to those of that nature; verse 48 counts announcing the meal in one's house before eating as a mark of the future king.
teaches: The verse gives the crow's call a human form, a spoken rice-call (சோற்றரவம்) in the house, and shows the couplet's image was a practice before it was a figure.
list_adds: It plays the rice-call against two other noises the householder avoids (strangers' clamour, hostile talk), so the sound he makes is defined by the sounds he refuses.

note: Naladiyar 271 says sharing what is cooked before eating is true cooking, and the door of the next world shuts on those who shut the door and eat; verse 48 has the householder call out the meal and rewards him with kingship.
teaches: The two give the same act opposite outcomes: the closed door and closed heaven in the Naladiyar, the public rice-call and a sword-held kingdom in Elathi, so the meal's openness decides the next life in both.
list_adds: It makes the open meal one of five household marks, with keeping guests and cherishing kin, where the quatrain argues the single act with a punishment.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu 23 calls giving gold with cows to brahmins foremost sweet; verse 49 names gold and herds among great gifts and sets with them food with ghee for great ascetics.
teaches: The same gifts of gold and cattle are aimed at brahmins in Iniyavai and joined to a meal for ascetics in Elathi, showing the two codes differ on who is the worthy recipient.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 65 says one who digs a tank, sets its bank, clears a road, breaks a field and digs a shared well goes sweetly to heaven; verse 51 rewards tanks, wells, shelters, water-booths and halls with a life of music, dance and love.
teaches: Two Jain works price the same public water works differently: heaven in one, sensual pleasure and the akam play of union and sulking in the other.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 72 says a mouthful given unasked to the weak, the old, those fasting to death, the sick and those who lost their land makes the giver a king; verse 52 makes kings of those who feed people who lost house, eyes, wealth, paddy or herds.
teaches: The two works state one rule, food to the ruined earns kingship, but Elathi defines need wholly by loss while Sirupanchamoolam includes the dying ascetic, so they draw the circle of the needy differently.

note: Kural 226 says removing the hunger of the destitute is where a man with wealth should store it; verse 53 names six kinds of destitute to be fed in the house and pays the store back as command of armies.
teaches: The couplet's metaphor of storage is made literal: the verse says what the stored wealth returns as, an army in a later life.
list_adds: It breaks the couplet's one class of the destitute into six (the indebted, unprotected, empty-handed, lame, old and young), so need is named by its causes.
audit_text_issue: தங்கான் in line 1 is best taken as தம் கால் before முடம்பட்டார்; மூப்பில்லார் is doubtful.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 7 says the பார்ப்பான் is one who shares his food; verse 54 lists பார்ப்பார் first among those to be fed, beside the hungry and ascetics.
teaches: One Jain work defines the brahmin by giving food, the other names brahmins by birth as receivers of it, so the same word marks a giver's virtue in one and a recipient's rank in the other.
audit_text_issue: Elathi 54 lines 2-3 (தூப்பால நிண்டாரால்) are corrupt.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 71 calls delivering a child, caring for the pregnant and taking up an infant great virtue; verse 55 counts feeding and curing new mothers, the pregnant and infants as acts that earn great wealth.
teaches: Both Jain works make the birth-room a field of merit; Elathi adds food and cure to the care and names a reward where Sirupanchamoolam cites the old books.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 75 says those who cured the diseases of five kinds of sufferer live now without disease; verse 57 says those who fed and cured six diseases become kings.
teaches: The two works pay the same act of healing differently: Sirupanchamoolam returns it in kind as health, Elathi converts it, like its other gifts, into rule.
audit_text_issue: elathi:57 கல்வளி may be one ailment or two, so the count is uncertain

note: Kural 441 counsels choosing the friendship of those mature in virtue and knowledge; verse 59 sets taking the words of the excellent among a learner's acts and makes them the making of a blameless king.
teaches: The couplet speaks to a king choosing counsellors; the verse shows the same habit begun as a learner's discipline of bowing and study, which yields the king.
list_adds: It sets taking counsel between bowing and close study, so heeding the great is one of six habits of learning rather than a separate policy of state.

note: Kural 460 says nothing brings more affliction than bad company; verse 60 names the afflictions, sin, blame, enmity, death, ruin and fear, and says they cling in both worlds like a curse.
teaches: The couplet's 'affliction' is left general; the verse itemises it and extends it beyond this life, so bad company is a karmic cost and not only a social one.
list_adds: It counts the evils that follow from bad company and joins worldly ones (blame, enmity) to otherworldly ones (sin), which the couplet's single word does not separate.
audit_text_issue: கேடச்சம் joins two evils in one word; line 1 may describe the unworthy or list what is lost.

note: Kural 360 names three, desire, anger and confusion, whose very names must perish; Elathi 61 names six defects of the soul.
teaches: Together they show the Jain list keeping desire and anger but trading the Kural's confusion for pride, avarice, hatred and partiality, so the root faults shift from error of mind to faults of self-regard.
list_adds: It doubles the Kural's three into six and adds pride and avarice, which 360 does not name, so the passions are counted as the Jain stains of the soul rather than as a triad of the mind.
audit_text_issue: ஒர்வமே in line 2 is an unknown form; the reading ஓர்வம் is a guess.

note: Elathi 12 says it is good neither to desire nor to look at the killing ground, the gaming place and the like; Elathi 62 says those of conduct do not go to dances, festivals, weddings, killing grounds or the battlefront.
teaches: Read together, the two verses show that the book's bar is on spectacle as such: 12 keeps the eye from scenes of violence, and 62 puts weddings and festivals under the same bar and names the cost of going.

note: Elathi 9 says those who give food, shelter and clothing to the destitute live as learned men; Elathi 63 says those who give food, clothing, stylus and book to students live amply in this life.
teaches: The pair shows the book twice making learning or its fruit the reward of a gift, and 63 narrowing the gift to the tools of study, so that the giver shares in the learning he supplies.
audit_text_issue: elathi:63 line 4 வேட்டெழுத is doubtful

note: Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Elathi 64 orders taking the Exalted one as lord, reciting his book, restraint and penance into a path to release.
teaches: The couplet makes worship the condition of learning, and the verse turns that condition into the first step of a sequence that ends in release, so worship, study and penance become stages rather than separate duties.
list_adds: It sets worship first in a ranked series of four steps ending in release, where the couplet only binds learning to worship.
audit_text_issue: Elathi 64 line 1 ஒப்புடைத்தான் is obscure.

note: Kural 269 says that even leaping past death is possible for those who have the power of austerity; Elathi 65 says that one who would see Death's strength cut down must study the all-knowing one's book and do a penance that harms nothing.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the verse names the conditions the Kural leaves out: the austerity that defeats death must be guided by scripture and must injure no creature, so non-harm becomes part of the power over death.
list_adds: It turns the Kural's bare power of austerity into a sequence of conditions (scripture, undistracted mind, harmless penance), each needed for the same victory over Death.
audit_text_issue: பாலனார், பாராது in line 2 are uncertain.

note: Kural 369 says that when craving, the sorrow of sorrows, perishes, joy is unbroken; Elathi 66 describes the high state only by six absences, sweet sleep among them.
teaches: The Kural names the goal as unbroken joy, while Elathi refuses even sleep's sweetness to it, so the pair shows two ways of naming release: as fullness of joy or as the cessation of every state, pleasant or painful.
list_adds: It defines the goal by a list of negations that strikes out goods (light, speech, sleep) along with ills, which the couplet's single positive term does not do.

note: Elathi 66 describes the high state by six things it lacks; Elathi 67 names the seven low states one by one.
teaches: Read in sequence, the two verses map both ends of the same cosmos: the summit is known only by negation, while the depths are given names and an order, so the book makes ruin more nameable than release.
audit_text_issue: Elathi 67 lines 1-2 (கூரம்பு, ஈர்மணி தூங்கலும், ஈரும்) are hard to construe; the list of seven is a reconstruction. | elathi:67 line 1-2 (ஈர்மணி தூங்கலும், புகையிரு ளோ(டு)) are hard to place and may be corrupt

note: Kural 72 says the loving belong to others even to their bones; Elathi 68 names dying for the beloved first among six marks of love.
teaches: The couplet states love's self-surrender as a claim about ownership, and the verse spells out what that surrender does in practice, from giving life and wealth down to grieving at a parting.
list_adds: It ranks love's marks from the gift of life down to feeling at union and parting, so the bones of 72 head a list that also counts speech and grief as love.
audit_text_issue: புணர்வுலத்தல் may stand for புணர்வு உவத்தல்.

note: Kural 263 asks whether the others have forgotten penance in wanting to provide for those who renounced; Elathi 70 says the one who gives alms, food and clothing to ascetics will rule earth and sky.
teaches: Where the couplet treats provisioning ascetics as the reason householders left penance aside, the verse makes that provisioning its own road to heaven, so the giver gains what the ascetic seeks.
list_adds: It lists the gifts in kind (alms, begged food, food, clothing) and adds a reward over two worlds, which the couplet's question leaves unstated.

note: Kural 43 names five to be tended (ancestors, gods, guests, kin and oneself); Elathi 71 names six to be fed: wayfarers, burden-bearers, the sick, kin, those of the sky and those of the other side.
teaches: Beside the Kural's five, the Elathi list drops the self and widens the circle to the stranger, the labourer, the sick and the adversary, so the household's duty is measured by need more than by bond or rite.
list_adds: It counts the sick, the porter and the adversary as equal claimants on the household's food, which the couplet's ancestral and kin-centred five do not include.
audit_text_issue: elathi:71 line 2 கேடின்று உடல்சார்ந்த is unclear

note: Kural 351 says a joyless birth comes from the confusion that takes the unreal for real; Elathi 72 traces not understanding to fault, karma, birth and suffering, and says it turns in a circle.
teaches: The couplet names ignorance as the cause of birth, and the verse adds the middle steps and closes the chain into a cycle, so birth becomes both the fruit and the renewer of ignorance.
list_adds: It sets ignorance at the head of six linked steps and closes them into a circle, where the couplet names only cause and result.
audit_text_issue: ஒத்தான் (line 1), தொண்டு (line 3) and மண்டிலமும் ... மதி (line 4) are doubtful.

note: Kural 46 asks what a man who lives household life in virtue would gain by going the outside way; Elathi 73 calls household life and great penance two noble ways of acting.
teaches: The couplet ranks the household above renunciation, while the verse sets the two side by side as one kind of noble life defined by their relation to attachment, so the pair shows Elathi declining the Kural's ranking.
list_adds: It pairs the two ways under one name (வினைவாழ்க்கை) and defines each by how it handles attachment, where the couplet sets them against each other.
audit_text_issue: Elathi 73 line 4 (பற்றுதல் பாத்தில் தவம்) is obscure.

note: Naladiyar 131 says the beauty of hair, garment border and saffron is not beauty and that learning's beauty is; Elathi 74 says the beauty of waist, shoulders, gait, modesty and neck is not beauty, and that of numbers and letters is.
teaches: The Naladiyar dismisses adornment, while Elathi dismisses the body itself and even modesty, so the pair shows the same verdict for learning reached against two different rivals, what one wears and what one is.
list_adds: It replaces the Naladiyar's adornments with six parts and graces of the body, modesty among them, so the rejection reaches a virtue as well as looks.

note: Kural 392 calls numbers and letters the two eyes of living beings; Elathi 74 calls the beauty of numbers and letters the only beauty.
teaches: The verse takes the Kural's very pair, எண் and எழுத்து, and moves it from the sense of sight to the standard of beauty, so learning is both how one sees and how one is seen.
list_adds: It sets the pair of 392 against six bodily beauties, so learning wins a contest the couplet never stages.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 33 says only he who leads one to the higher state is a teacher; Elathi 75 says a teacher's fitness lies in knowing the six schools and refuting a false teacher's word.
teaches: One verse defines the teacher by where he leads, the other by what he can defend, so together they give the Jain teacher's two tests: the goal he serves and his mastery of rival doctrine.
audit_text_issue: Elathi 75 lines 2-3 (மறுவரவு, மாசாரியன்) are obscure.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 35 says giving brings enjoyment, penance heaven and knowledge release; Elathi 76 says giving brings enjoyment, penance heaven and penance that does not cling brings release.
teaches: The two Jain works share the first two rungs word for word but differ on the third, knowledge in one and a deeper penance in the other, so the pair shows a live question within the group about what finally frees.
audit_text_issue: Sirupanchamoolam 35 line 3 போதும் does not construe; read as போகம்.

note: Elathi 64 says release comes to one who takes the Exalted one as lord, studies his book and fully performs his penance; Elathi 77 says such penance brings release in three, five or seven births.
teaches: Read together, the verses give the path and its timetable: 64 says what leads to release, and 77 says release is not immediate but measured in births.
audit_text_issue: வல்லைளீ(டு) (77, line 4) is corrupt; read as வல்லை வீடு. | elathi:77 line 4 வல்லைளீ(டு) needs emendation to வல்லை வீடு

note: Kural 221 says giving to those who have nothing is true giving; Elathi 78 names six kinds of the destitute: the motherless child, the widow, those without livelihood, the ruined trader, those who lost their wealth, and the blind.
teaches: The couplet defines giving by the recipient's want, and the verse names who the wanting are and how they came to want, so the general rule gets its cases.
list_adds: It names each recipient by what was lost (mother, husband, trade, wealth, sight), so the Kural's வறியார் become a list of the newly helpless rather than the poor as a class.

note: Kural 642 says gain and ruin both come from speech, so lapses must be guarded; Elathi 79 says death, ruin, enmity, sorrow, joy and exile all come by the tongue.
teaches: The couplet's two outcomes are spread into six, from joy to death and exile, so the pair shows speech held responsible for the whole range of a life's fortunes, not only for profit and loss.
list_adds: It splits the Kural's gain and ruin into six named fates, adding death and banishment, so the stakes of speech rise to life and country.
audit_text_issue: Lines 2-4 (நாக்காடு, நாட்டறை போக்கு, the close) are obscure and may be corrupt.
