note: Kural 226 says relieving the hunger of the destitute is where the wealthy should store their wealth; Elathi 80 says those who feed outcastes, the wounded, the blind, the immobile, the fallen and the eminent in need will live as kings.
teaches: The couplet calls feeding a store of wealth, and the verse names the stored return (living as kings) and widens the hungry to include the outcaste, so the gift crosses lines of birth the couplet does not mention.
list_adds: It names the hungry one by one and puts the outcaste first, so feeding is extended across rank as well as need.

note: Kural 395 has the learner yearn like the poor before the rich; Iniyavai goes further and calls learning sweet even if it must be had by begging.
teaches: The couplet makes the poverty a simile for the learner's humility, while the verse makes it literal, so together they show the tradition moving from 'learn as if a beggar' to 'learn even as a beggar'.
list_adds: It puts learning got by begging first among four sweet things, ahead of the assembly and the company of the great, so the list ranks learning above the dignity it costs.
audit_text_issue: நற்சலையில் (line 2) is not a known word; the marker reads நற்சவையில். | நற்சலையில் (line 2) is not a known word; probably நற்சவையில்.

note: Kural 46 asks what one gains by leaving a household run in dharma; Iniyavai 2 agrees while the household goes well but makes renunciation the highest sweetness when it does not prosper.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's rhetorical question turns out to carry a condition: household life wins only while it succeeds, and the verse names the failure that opens the outer path.
list_adds: It orders household and renunciation as first and highest under a stated condition, a ranking with a hinge the couplet's question does not supply.

note: Kural 251 asks how one who eats flesh to swell his own flesh can have grace; Iniyavai 4 uses the same phrase and calls abstaining foremost sweet.
teaches: The couplet condemns the act by what it costs the eater's compassion, the verse praises the abstention as a pleasure, so the pair shows non-eating of flesh argued both as a moral loss avoided and as a gain enjoyed.
list_adds: It ranks abstaining from flesh 'foremost' beside the sight of an elephant army and a riverside village, so a renunciant's rule is counted among a ruler's and a villager's delights.

note: Innaa Narpathu 22 is this verse's mirror: kings without elephants, eating flesh to swell flesh and a town cut off by a forest river are painful where elephant armies, abstaining and a town on the river's bank are sweet.
teaches: Side by side they show the two books built as paired catalogues, and the forest river item shows the method is not a simple negation: the same river is sweet as a bank and painful as a barrier.
audit_text_issue: Innaa 22 line 1 யானையின் is read as 'without elephants'; the form is unusual.

note: Kural 323 ranks not killing first and not lying after it; Iniyavai 5 also puts not killing foremost and closes with not speaking evil of anyone.
teaches: Both books place non-killing at the head of a short ranked list and a restraint of speech behind it, so the pair shows the Kural's ranking reused as the frame of a king's list, where justice of the sceptre is slotted between.
list_adds: It sets non-killing in a king's list beside unjust honours and the straight sceptre, so a universal vow is read as the first duty of rule.

note: Kural 33 bids one do dharma as far as one can and without ceasing; Iniyavai 6 calls dharma done to the measure of one's strength foremost sweet.
teaches: The couplet sets the measure as a demand, the verse as a pleasure, so the pair shows the capacity clause working two ways: it limits what is owed and it is what makes the act sweet rather than a burden.
list_adds: It joins measured dharma to hearing good counsel and choosing worthy guards, so doing good is ranked first among the supports of a life rather than stated alone.

note: Kural 134 says a forgotten Veda can be relearned but a brahmin's birth is ruined when conduct fails; Iniyavai 7 names brahmins' keeping of the Veda as very sweet.
teaches: The verse praises the recitation the couplet treats as recoverable, and the couplet ranks conduct above it, so a reader sees the Kural demoting the very possession the later list holds up as the brahmin's excellence.
list_adds: Its own third item puts restraint above even a father, so within the list conduct also outranks the ties of birth, which brings it closer to the couplet than its first item suggests.

note: Innaa Narpathu 28 calls painful the gallop of a spirited horse ridden by one who has not learned; Iniyavai 8 calls sweet the strength of the spirited horse one rides.
teaches: The same spirited horse is a pleasure or a pain according to the rider's training, so the pair locates the sweetness not in the horse but in the skill that can bear its strength.

note: Kural 57 says confinement is useless and a woman's own நிறை is her best guard; Iniyavai 10 calls putting away women who lack நிறை sweet.
teaches: The couplet moves the guard inside the woman, and the verse states the consequence when that inner guard is missing, so together they show நிறை made both the woman's defence and the ground on which she may be sent away.
list_adds: It sets dismissing such a wife beside living free of debt and avoiding the mean-minded, so the rule is filed among the household's protections, not among the virtues of marriage.

note: Kural 1065 says nothing is sweeter than thin gruel won by one's own effort; Iniyavai 11 says nothing is nobler than refusing to eat from unworthy hands even unto death.
teaches: Both close on the same 'nothing above it' form, but the couplet praises the food one earns and the verse the food one refuses, so the pair shows the two halves of a single code of eating with dignity.
list_adds: It caps a list about not living off the road and not taking crookedly with a refusal unto death, so the list climbs from avoiding gain to giving up life.

note: Kural 726 asks what use treatises are to those who fear the subtle assembly; Iniyavai 12 calls sweet the learning of one who does not fear the clamorous assembly.
teaches: The couplet denies the fearful scholar the worth of his books; the verse grants the fearless one sweetness, so the pair shows courage before the assembly as the condition on which learning pays.
list_adds: It sets fearless learning between a healthy child and lasting wealth, so learning appears as one of the household's goods kept safe from its typical failure.

note: Innaa Narpathu 35 names the sickness that infants suffer as painful; Iniyavai 12 names a child living without sickness as sweet.
teaches: The two books say the same thing from its two sides, and the pairing shows that the child's health is the first item in the sweet list but the third in the painful one, so each book ranks it by what surrounds it.
audit_text_issue: Innaa 35 line 2 குழலின் இனிய மரத்தோசை is obscure.

note: Kural 969 likens those who die when honour is touched to the yak that dies once its hair is lost; Iniyavai 13 calls not living after honour is lost foremost sweet.
teaches: The couplet treats the act as a matter of nature, the verse as a pleasure chosen first, so the pair shows dying for honour justified both as instinct and as preference.
list_adds: It ranks death before dishonour ahead of restrained living and flawless wealth, so honour is set above the two things that would make a long life comfortable.

note: Kural 66 implies children's babble is sweeter than flute and lute; Iniyavai 14 calls hearing it sweeter than amrita.
teaches: The couplet measures the child's voice against the best of art, the verse against the food of the gods, so the pair shows the babble outranking both human and divine sweetness.
list_adds: It sets the babble beside the child's first steps and then beside steadiness when one's deeds come home, so the household's joys and the courage to suffer are counted together.

note: Innaa Narpathu 38 calls painful the folly of following after another man's wife; Iniyavai 15 calls sweet the dignity of not looking after her.
teaches: The two lines use nearly the same words and say the same thing from two sides: what Innaa names as folly in the doer, Iniyavai names as dignity in the one who abstains, so the act is judged by its effect on the man's standing.
audit_text_issue: Innaa 38 line 1 prints பின்னோர்க்கும், most likely for பின்னோக்கும்.

note: Kural 148 calls not looking at another's wife great manhood and full conduct; Iniyavai 15 calls not looking after her a dignity that is very sweet.
teaches: The couplet names the restraint a heroism, the verse a pleasure, and the verse narrows the act to the backward glance, so the pair shows the restraint tested at the smallest motion of the eye.
list_adds: It sets the restraint beside rain on parched crops and elephants roaring at a king's gate, so a private abstention is ranked among the large public pleasures of the land.

note: Kural 722 says those who make their learning go home before the learned are the learned among the learned; Iniyavai 16 calls setting out one's learning before the learned very sweet.
teaches: The couplet makes the act the test of reputation, the verse makes it a pleasure, so the pair shows the same performance valued as proof to others and as delight to oneself.
list_adds: It joins speaking before the learned to joining one's betters and giving without asking, so the list ranks learned speech first among acts of standing among superiors.
audit_text_issue: iniyavai_narpathu:16 line 1 reads சுற்றார்முன்; கற்றார்முன் is an emendation

note: Iniyavai 17 nearly quotes Kural 679 (doing good to friends; winning over those not allied), but reads நாட்டார்க்கு, the land's people, and calls both sweet where the couplet ranks them by urgency.
teaches: The couplet's ranking is one of speed, the verse's one of sweetness, and the verse adds granaries and many allies, so the pair shows a counsel of timing turned into a picture of a secure ruler.
list_adds: It adds a third item, full granaries and true allies, so the couplet's two acts of alliance become part of a ruler's provisioning.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 நாட்டார்க்கு may be a misprint for the Kural's நட்டார்க்கு.

note: Kural 221 says giving to those who have nothing is the only true gift; Iniyavai 19 calls giving great wealth 'where it is fit' sweet.
teaches: The couplet makes need the test of a gift and the verse makes fitness of the recipient the test, so the pair shows two criteria in the tradition for where wealth should go.
list_adds: It places giving after making wealth without lack, and after truthfulness and humility, so giving is set as the last stage of a well-conducted life, not as an act prompted by another's need.
audit_text_issue: iniyavai_narpathu:19 line 1 வாழ்தால் for வாழ்தல்

note: Innaa Narpathu 32 calls painful the talk of those who speak behind one's back; Iniyavai 19 calls sweet living without backbiting one's friends.
teaches: They state one thing from two sides, the victim's pain and the speaker's restraint, and together show backbiting judged both by what it does to the hearer and what refraining does for the speaker.
audit_text_issue: Iniyavai 19 line 1 வாழ்தால் is a misprint for வாழ்தல்.

note: Verse 1 names the speech of women with pearl-like smiles as sweet; verse 37 names knowing such women as poison as sweet.
teaches: Within one book the same object is sweet to hear and sweet to know as poison, which shows the book addressing the householder in one verse and the would-be renouncer in another rather than holding one view of women.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 of verse 1, நற்சலையில், is not a known word; நற்சவையில் is likely.

note: Iniyavai calls giving with knowledge of one's income sweet; Innaa 39 counts the liberality of one with nothing to give as painful. They say the same thing from two sides.
teaches: Read as a pair, the twin books fix one measure for giving from opposite ends: the pleasure lies inside one's income and the pain begins outside it.

note: Naladiyar 65 calls the gift of one without wealth the true fruit of giving; Iniyavai calls giving within one's income sweet.
teaches: The pair shows the ethics group divided on where giving is best: the quatrain prizes the gift that strains one's means, while this verse prizes the gift that stays within them.
list_adds: It sets measured giving beside independence from others and refusal of indulgence, so giving is ranked as one form of self-limitation rather than a test of sacrifice.
audit_text_issue: Iniyavai 22 line 2 reads பங்கு where tamilvu has பாங்கு.

note: Iniyavai calls giving cows and gold to brahmins foremost sweet; Innaa 21 counts the speech of a brahmin without Vedic recitation as painful, and giving to the never-content as painful.
teaches: Together the twin books make the brahmin a privileged recipient but not an unconditional one: the Innaa line ties his standing to recitation, a condition this verse leaves out.

note: Naladiyar 65 calls true patience that of a strong man able to punish; Iniyavai calls sweet the austerity of one who wants to win and does not rage.
teaches: Both place the worth of restraint where the urge to strike is live, and the pair shows the group treating anger held back in a contest as a form of penance.
list_adds: It names the restraint நோன்பு, a word of austerity, and sets it beside endurance and freedom from craving, so mastering anger is filed with ascetic practice.

note: Kural 343, in the chapter on renunciation, says the field of the five senses must be crushed and all desires let go at once; Iniyavai calls curbing the craving of the five senses foremost sweet, with no renouncer named.
teaches: The pair shows sense-restraint moving from the renouncer's whole programme in the Kural to a first pleasure open to anyone, its demand softened from abandoning to curbing.
list_adds: It ranks sense-restraint first and pairs it with keeping away from the unlearned and the unsteady, so the inner gate and the outer company are guarded together.

note: Naladiyar 111 says refusing what one cannot give is no fault, but letting an asker's hope (நசை) die after keeping him waiting is worse than ingratitude; Iniyavai calls not killing the hope (நசை) of those who come sweet.
teaches: Both judge a giver by what happens to the asker's hope, the quatrain condemning its slow killing by false promise and the verse praising its keeping, so honesty to the hope matters as much as the gift.
list_adds: It ties keeping askers' hope to a spirit that will not live without regard and a bond that hides nothing, so generosity is grouped with self-respect rather than with promise-keeping.

note: Kural 966 asks why one should stand behind those who scorn one; Iniyavai calls very sweet the spirit that will not live where it is held in no regard.
teaches: The couplet argues from the loss of praise and heaven, while the verse calls the refusal a pleasure in itself, so the pair shows honour defended first by reckoning and then by taste.
list_adds: It places the refusal to live without regard between two items on giving, so the self-respect of the giver and of the one who will not cringe are made one temper.

note: Kural 969 says those like the yak give up life when honour is lost; Iniyavai calls not living on when dishonour comes foremost sweet.
teaches: The verse names as a pleasure what the couplet presents as the nature of a rare kind of person, so the pair shows an admired temperament turned into something anyone may prefer.
list_adds: It sets dying rather than living dishonoured between the giver's bearing and right receiving, so honour is framed by how one gives and how one takes.

note: Kural 1066 says even asking water for a cow is the most degrading thing for the tongue; Iniyavai calls not going about asking others to relieve one's distress foremost sweet.
teaches: The pair values not asking from both sides, as disgrace avoided and as the first of pleasures, and the verse's ஆற்றாமை widens it from asking for goods to asking for relief.
list_adds: It ranks not asking first and follows it with remembering death and holding to right speech under ruin, so refusing to beg sits among the disciplines of a man facing loss.

note: Kural 113 says to let go at once of gain that comes from leaving fairness; Iniyavai calls sweetest the discernment that speaks no wrong even when one's fortune is being destroyed.
teaches: The couplet refuses unfair gain and the verse refuses unfair speech even to escape ruin, so the pair carries fairness from getting to speaking under loss.
list_adds: It puts this item last as the sweetest of three, after not begging and remembering death, so integrity under ruin outranks the other two.

note: Kural 596 says whatever one thinks, think of rising; Iniyavai calls sweet the zeal born of thinking of rising, using the couplet's own word உயர்வுள்ளி.
teaches: The verse borrows the couplet's phrase and names what the thought produces, zeal, so the pair shows aspiration as the root and ஊக்கம் as its fruit.
list_adds: It brackets the thought of rising between leaving the base and not scorning the lowly, so aspiration is hedged on both sides by conduct toward others.

note: Thirikadugam 77 opens with கயவரைக் கையிகந்து வாழ்தல் and makes it a mark of those whose family has no stain; Iniyavai 29 opens with கயவரைக் கைகழிந்து வாழ்தல் and calls it sweet.
teaches: The near-identical line shows a saying circulating between the counted works, and the different predicates show each bending it: a sign of good birth in one, a pleasure open to anyone in the other.

note: Innaa 40 counts seizing a deposit (அடைக்கலம் வவ்வுதல்) as painful; Iniyavai calls the goodness that does not seize a deposit the finest. They say the same thing from two sides.
teaches: The Iniyavai line adds the temptation the Innaa line omits, the thought that no one knew of it, so the pair shows the deposit as a test of honesty without witnesses.
audit_text_issue: iniyavai_narpathu:30 line 3 was repaired (ௌ) and differs from the site; the sense is unaffected.

note: Kural 104 says those who know the fruit of a kindness count a millet's worth as a palm; Iniyavai calls living with the fruit of a kindness weighed very sweet.
teaches: The couplet says how to weigh a kindness and the verse says living by that weighing is a pleasure, so the pair shows gratitude as a habit of measuring that becomes a way of life.
list_adds: It joins gratitude to honest speech in the assembly and keeping a deposit, so the three become one virtue of rendering to each what is owed.
audit_text_issue: line 3 வௌவாத repaired from split ௌ

note: Kural 417 says those whose listening is gathered on close study do not speak folly even when they misunderstand; Iniyavai says even those of excellent learning by listening should speak only after examining.
teaches: The couplet trusts deep listening to protect speech even through error, while the verse still asks the learned to examine first, so the pair shows the counted work refusing learning as a guarantee.
list_adds: It ranks examined speech with protecting refugees and doing one's duties even on borrowed money, so careful speech is made a duty owed to others.

note: Kural 220 says loss through ஒப்புரவு is worth buying even by selling oneself; Iniyavai calls doing what is to be done even by borrowing sweet, if செய்வன covers duties of help.
teaches: The couplet's extreme, selling oneself, appears here in a household form, taking a loan, so the pair shows the ethics group pricing duty to others in debt.
list_adds: It sets duties done on credit beside protecting those who came for refuge, so borrowing to do one's part is grouped with protection rather than prudence.

note: Purananuru 330 praises one man who, sword raised, stopped a king's army from passing him as the shore stops the sea; Iniyavai calls checking the army of great kings in the crowded battle sweet.
teaches: The Purananuru makes the stand one hero's glory, and the counted verse files it with civic zeal and tireless effort, showing heroic memory folded into a general ethic of exertion.

note: Kural 800 says to leave the friendship of the unfit even at the cost of a gift; Iniyavai calls sweet leaving the friendship of the worthless even when they embrace one.
teaches: The couplet counts the cost of leaving in goods and the verse in affection refused, so the pair shows two prices a man may pay to be free of an unworthy friend.
list_adds: It closes a list that begins with keeping off the roads at night and speaking without slips, so ending a bad friendship is grouped with other kinds of self-guarding.
audit_text_issue: Line 4 கொள்ளர் does not construe cleanly; possibly a corruption.

note: Kural 588 says to confirm what one spy reports through another (ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றி); Iniyavai calls sweet for kings learning facts ஒற்றினான் ஒற்றி.
teaches: The verse's compressed phrase echoes the couplet's, and read through it the item can mean checking one spy by another, not merely using one.
list_adds: It sets spying beside full inquiry before judgment and sharing with all beings, so intelligence is ranked with justice and care as one royal pleasure.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 (பற்றினலாய், பாத்தூற்று) is obscure and line 4 வெற்வேறில் is corrupt (variant வெற்றிவேல்).

note: Kural 167 says the goddess shows the man of twisted envy (அவ்வித்து அழுக்காறு) to her elder sister; Iniyavai calls not speaking out of twisted envy foremost sweet, in the same words.
teaches: The couplet punishes envy held and the verse praises envy unspoken, so the pair shows the ethics group separating the feeling from its voicing and treating restraint of the tongue as a partial cure.
list_adds: It puts restraint of envious speech first, ahead of conquered anger and refusing to snatch, ranking a fault of the tongue above faults of temper and hand.

note: Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounced in childhood; Iniyavai calls knowing youth to be old age sweet.
teaches: The quatrain draws the conclusion, early renunciation, that the verse leaves implicit, and the verse calls that foresight sweet rather than grim.
list_adds: It joins the foresight of age to seeing desire as poison and to the comfort of safe kin, so two renunciant insights are framed by a household one.

note: Kural 524 says the fruit of wealth is to live surrounded by one's kin; Iniyavai says the feast for guests of one whose kin stand by him is sweet beyond measure.
teaches: The couplet makes kin the use of wealth and the verse names the guest-feast as the moment that use shows, so the pair links kinship to hospitality.
list_adds: It ranks the kin-supported feast above the fighter's weapons and allies with எத்துணையும் ஆற்ற, so the house's hospitality outranks martial strength.

note: Kural 1060 says the one who asks must not be angry; Iniyavai calls it foremost sweet that one who lives by alms does not clamour.
teaches: Both place restraint on the receiver rather than the giver, and the pair shows the ethics group laying a duty on the needy as well as on the rich.
list_adds: It moves the rule from askers in general to the one who lives by alms and joins it to calm in a borrowed lodging, so it becomes part of a renouncer's poverty.

note: Kural 340 calls the soul a lodger in a borrowed corner (துச்சில்) of the body; Iniyavai calls sweet not grieving while living in a துச்சில்.
teaches: Read through the couplet, the verse's lodger may be the soul in the body as well as a poor man in borrowed rooms, which would make its item an image of calm about mortality.
list_adds: It sets the lodger's calm between the alms-eater's restraint and freedom from greedy want, so the image is read inside a renouncer's poverty.

note: Kural 391 says to learn faultlessly what should be learned and stand by it; Iniyavai calls the firm core of learning what has worth, faultlessly and over many days, the sweetest thing.
teaches: The verse adds duration and names the result காழ், a hard core, so the pair shows flawless learning as something that hardens over time.
list_adds: It closes the book on learning after staying in one's town at a cost and not eating the seed-grain, so learning is grouped with the household's ways of keeping what feeds the future.
audit_text_issue: பத்துக் கொடுத்தும் is unclear.

note: Acharakkovai 6 lists the dog among things a person in எச்சில் does not look at; Innaa 2 counts a fowl and a dog entering a brahmin's house as painful.
teaches: Read together, the two show the dog as a standing source of pollution in the period's code, kept from the eye of the impure person in one book and from the threshold of the brahmin house in the other.
audit_text_issue: Innaa 2 line 3 புநடைவை is corrupt.

note: Pattinathar says not to talk of எச்சில் and of fit and unfit, since people do not know where the impurity lies; Innaa 2 counts animals entering a brahmin's house as a pain, on the reading that the pain is ritual defilement.
teaches: The Innaa locates defilement in what crosses a brahmin's threshold, while Pattinathar denies that impurity sits in outward things at all, so the pair shows the purity code and its later Siddha rejection.
audit_text_issue: line 3 பாத்தில் புநடைவை is corrupt (likely புடைவை); variant உடையின்னாது

note: Iniyavai 32 names not living under a king without care for his people as foremost sweet; Innaa 3 names living under fierce kings of bent sceptre as painful.
teaches: The two books say the same thing from both sides, and the Iniyavai adds that the sweet thing is a choice (not to live there), while the Innaa's float image shows the subject who has no such choice.

note: Kural 557 likens a king's want of kindness to the earth's want of rain; Innaa 3 sets living under a cruel king beside swimming long water without a float.
teaches: The couplet measures a cruel king by what the land loses; the Innaa measures him by the subject's helplessness, a swimmer with nothing to hold, which turns the public loss into a private danger.
list_adds: It puts life under a cruel king beside the floatless swimmer and the harsh speaker's company, so tyranny is counted among the dangers a person meets rather than among the faults of a ruler.

note: Kural 861 says to avoid opposing the strong and to favour enmity with the weak; Innaa 4 counts doing harm to the very strong as painful, and provoking the fortunate as well.
teaches: The Innaa keeps the couplet's first half and drops its second: the danger of opposing the strong stands without the counsel to turn on the weak, and it is widened to those who merely have fortune.
list_adds: It sets the harm done to the strong beside the ox-less farmer and the fleeing soldier, so the act is counted as self-inflicted loss rather than weighed as strategy.
audit_text_issue: கருவிகண் (line 2) may be a misprint for கருவிகள்.

note: Kural 663 says the strength of a deed is that it is revealed only at its end, and that it brings trouble if it comes out midway; Innaa 5 counts a deed done without secrecy (மறை) as painful.
teaches: The couplet explains when secrecy matters (until the end), and the Innaa supplies the images for an exposed undertaking: unfenced cane and a leaking roof.
list_adds: It pairs the open deed with rule without justice and gives both two images of unguarded keeping, so secrecy is grouped with protection rather than with cunning.
audit_text_issue: line 2 உறைசேர்/உறைசோர்/புரைசேர் variants

note: Kural 548 says a ruler who does not examine and do justice perishes of himself; Innaa 5 counts a kingship that rules without முறை as painful.
teaches: The couplet looks at the unjust ruler's own fall, while the Innaa, by placing him beside a cane field with no fence, looks at what his subjects suffer while he still rules.
list_adds: It makes injustice one of four unprotected things, so the verse judges rule by the protection it fails to give rather than by the king's fate.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 உறைசேர் has variants புரைசேர் and சோர்.

note: Kural 218 says those who know what is due do not falter in giving even when they have no means; Innaa 6 counts giving by those in distress as painful, on the reading that இன்னா marks a thing to be avoided.
teaches: On that reading the books disagree about the poor man's gift: the Kural praises it as a mark of discernment, and the Innaa ranks it with a warrior idle in battle and a crooked man's word.
list_adds: It sets the distressed giver's gift beside the virtuous man's harsh word, so the verse names gifts and words that go wrong because the giver is in the wrong state, not because he lacks virtue.

note: Kural 727 likens the learning of one who fears the assembly to a bright sword in a பேடி's hand among enemies; Innaa 7 counts a weapon held by one without strength as painful.
teaches: The couplet uses the powerless swordsman as a simile for useless learning, and the Innaa counts him plainly but puts beside him the speaker who cannot reply, so the verse holds both halves of the couplet's comparison as separate items.
list_adds: It lists the weak man's weapon and the speaker who cannot answer as two items of one kind, where the couplet joins them only as image and subject.

note: Kural 650 likens those who cannot expound what they have learned to flowers in bloom without scent; Innaa 7 counts the beauty of a scentless flower as painful.
teaches: The Innaa places the scentless flower directly beside the speech of one who cannot reply, which is the Kural's comparison spelled out as two counted pains.
list_adds: It turns the Kural's simile into two items, a scentless flower and a speaker who cannot answer, and adds weapon and daring as two more things without their ground.

note: Kural 784 says friendship is not for laughing together but for rebuking when one oversteps; Innaa 8 counts the lack of binding affection (நார்) in friends made in laughter as painful.
teaches: The couplet says what friendship is for, and the Innaa names the pain of the friendship that was only laughter: it has no fibre when it is tested.
list_adds: It sets the laughing friend beside the fair-seeming heart without character and the ungracious friend, so the verse ranks three counterfeits of friendship together.

note: Innaa 9 counts the absence of patrons as the foremost pain of gift-seekers; in Puram 375 a drummer finds no patron but Ay and wishes that, with Ay gone, there be no patrons at all, lest bards praise kings of worthless wealth.
teaches: The bard in the Puram poem prefers the very lack the Innaa ranks first among his pains to service under the ungenerous, which the Innaa counts as a separate pain in its third item.
audit_text_issue: purananuru:375 lines 17-18 (நிலவன்மாரோ புரவலர்) are uncertain

note: Kural 720 likens speaking before those not of one's circle to nectar spilled in a dirty yard; Innaa 10 counts reciting a song where no one grasps its meaning as painful.
teaches: The couplet locates the waste in the hearers' unfitness, and the Innaa, by setting the song beside the poor man's generosity, shows it as a gift wasted on both sides: the giver of words has no receiver, the would-be giver of goods has nothing.
list_adds: It sets the wasted recital beside a lonely dark path and the penniless man's liberality, so the song without listeners is counted among gifts that cannot arrive.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 prints பொருளணர்வா; read பொருளுணர்வார்.

note: Iniyavai 22 names giving with knowledge of one's income as sweet; Innaa 10 names liberality attempted by those without wealth as painful.
teaches: The two books say the same thing from two sides, and together they make the measure explicit: giving is judged against income, sweet when it fits and painful when it outruns it.

note: Kural 890 likens living with those not in accord (உடம்பாடு இலாதவர்) to living with a snake in a hut; Innaa 11 counts the embrace of a wife without உடம்பாடு as painful.
teaches: The couplet leaves 'those not in accord' open, and the Innaa narrows the same word to the wife, placing the discord at the closest point of the house, the embrace itself.
list_adds: It sets the discordant wife beside the petty friend, the intemperate companion and the creditor's eye, so marriage is counted among the bonds that can turn to pain.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 has a Project Madurai variant மனைவி தொழில் for மனைவிதோள், which would remove the 'embrace' point; line 2 has a vowel-sign misprint (சிறியரோடு யர்த்த).

note: Kural 890 likens living with those not in accord to living with a snake in a hut; Innaa 13 counts a house where people like a disease live as painful.
teaches: The couplet's image is sudden danger and the Innaa's is slow sickness, so the pair shows two ways a house of the wrong people harms: the bite and the wasting.
list_adds: It sets the diseased house among the king's and courtier's pains, so a household trouble is counted beside a bell-less elephant and submission to proud kings.

note: Iniyavai 32 names as sweet the purpose of an undertaking (கருமப் பொருள்) as those who know its surroundings explain it; Innaa 15 names the same thing explained by the unlearned as painful.
teaches: The same phrase is sweet or painful in the two books depending only on who speaks it, which shows that both make the counsellor's knowledge, not the undertaking, decide its worth.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 has a Project Madurai variant (விழைவின்னா) and line 4 a likely missing vowel sign (tamilvu பல்லாருள் நாணுப் படல்).

note: Kural 392 says numbers and letters are the two eyes of living beings; Innaa 16 sets the good looks of a man without eyes beside accounts kept by one who does not know numbers.
teaches: The Innaa places the literal blind man next to the innumerate one, which makes the Kural's metaphor into two counted pains of one kind: both are blind.
list_adds: By putting eyelessness and innumeracy side by side as items 3 and 4, the list enacts the couplet's equation of number with sight without stating it.

note: Kural 1001 says one who hoards great wealth and does not eat it is as good as dead; Innaa 16 counts storing great wealth without enjoying it as painful.
teaches: The couplet judges the hoarder as already dead, and the Innaa, by setting him beside the handsome blind man, makes him one who owns a good he cannot use.
list_adds: It pairs unused wealth with unseeing beauty, so the hoard is grouped with gifts that their owner cannot enjoy rather than with failures of giving.

note: Kural 840 likens a fool's entering the assembly of the worthy to putting an unwashed foot on a bed; Innaa 17 counts a fool's entering among the worthy (சான்றோருட் பேதை புகல்) as painful, in nearly the same words.
teaches: The couplet gives the image of defilement and the Innaa gives the worthy their mark, ஆன்றவித்த (full and self-subdued), which is what the fool's entry offends.
list_adds: It sets the fool's intrusion beside a penance without self-subduing, so both are counted as the unsubdued entering where self-mastery is required.

note: Kural 656 says not to do what the worthy condemn even to relieve one's mother's hunger; Innaa 17 counts abandoning the mother who bore one as painful.
teaches: The Kural uses the mother's need as the hardest case in which a wrong still may not be done, and the Innaa counts her neglect as a pain in its own right, so together they bound the duty: it is weighty, but it does not license blame.
list_adds: It sets the mother's neglect beside a fool among the worthy and a false penance, so care for her is counted among the duties of a person's standing rather than as a test case.

note: Iniyavai 34 names not going about at night as foremost sweet; Innaa 17 names going about when it has grown dark as very painful.
teaches: The same rule appears from both sides with matching intensifiers (முன் in the Iniyavai, பெரிது in the Innaa), so both books rank night travel above their other items.

note: Kural 600 says a man's உரம் is the abundance of his உள்ளம் (inner drive); Innaa 18 counts the உள்ளம் of a man who has உரன் lying idle as painful.
teaches: The Kural defines strength as drive, so the two cannot come apart; the Innaa names the case where they do, a strong man whose mind sleeps, and counts it as a pain.
list_adds: It sets the idle strong man beside the man who faces a warrior's chest, so lost strength and rash strength are counted together.

note: Kural 409 says the unlearned born high are worth less than the learned born low; Innaa 19 counts lack of learning in one born to a good family as painful.
teaches: Both make learning the test of birth, but the Kural overturns the ranking while the Innaa keeps it, counting the unlearned noble as a failed seed and union outside family rank as another pain.
list_adds: It sets the unlearned noble beside a seed that fails to sprout and a union without family standing, so birth is kept as the frame that learning fulfils, not one it overturns.

note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes from the work they do; Innaa 19 counts union where there is no family standing as painful, on the reading that குலம் is birth rank.
teaches: On that reading the two disagree on whether family rank is a ground of worth: the Kural denies it at birth, and the Innaa makes its absence a reason a union is a pain.
list_adds: It places union outside family rank beside the unlearned noble and the immodest woman, so birth, learning and women's conduct are counted as one order of standing.

note: Thirikadugam 84 joins people of a long line who lack the excellence of learning to poverty; Innaa 19 counts lack of learning in one born to a good family as painful.
teaches: Both books set the unlearned man of good family beside a failed source of growth (the badly made tank inlet, the unsprouting seed), so the two together show a shared image: lineage is a resource that learning must make flow.
audit_text_issue: thirikadugam:84 சேய்மரபில் is uncertain (a long line, or a distant or lesser descent).

note: Kural 13 says that if the sky fails, hunger torments the world though it is ringed by water; Innaa 20 counts the failure of the rain's plenty as painful to a town.
teaches: The couplet speaks of the world and its hunger, and the Innaa of the town and its plenty, flanked by the koel's ill-timed call and a sluggish ox, so the failure is set in the farmer's season rather than the cosmos.
list_adds: It sets failed rain between the out-of-season koel and the weak ox, so drought is counted as one of the farming year's mistimings and lacks.

note: Innaa 4 counts the soil's moisture passing unused for ploughmen without oxen; Innaa 20 counts ploughing with a sluggish ox as painful.
teaches: The book grades the ploughman's lack across two verses: with no ox the wet season is lost, and with a sluggish ox it is wasted, so the ox decides whether the rain is of use.

note: Thirikadugam 18 names old age and great disease as two separate things to fear more than thieves; the Innaa line joins them as one pain, sickness that comes once one is old.
teaches: Read together, the two dreads compound: the Innaa line shows disease and age not as two risks but as one in which each makes the other worse.

note: Both describe flesh-eating as feeding flesh with flesh (ஊனைப் பெருக்குதல், ஊன் பெருக்கற்கு); the Kural asks how such a person can hold அருள், the Innaa line ranks the act as the first of pains.
teaches: The pair shows one image doing two jobs: in the Kural it proves the loss of compassion, in the Innaa verse it is a pain ranked above even soured honey and kingless armies.
list_adds: It ranks flesh-eating first (முன்) among things that have lost their proper working, a king without elephants, honey gone sour, a cut-off town.
audit_text_issue: Innaa 22 line 4 has a source variant (கானாறு).

note: The Kural explains the image the Innaa line only names: the base are like a beaten drum because they carry every secret they hear to others.
teaches: With the Kural's gloss, the drum-like talker in the Innaa list is seen as a breach of keeping, matching the wall-less gate and the fouled ford beside him.
list_adds: It sets loose talk beside a gate with no wall and a ford fouled by washing, so the talker becomes one more failed guard.
audit_text_issue: innaa_narpathu:23 line 3 has a variant (அறைபறை யாயவர்)

note: Kural 262 says penance comes to those who have it and is futile for those without; the Innaa line names what such a man lacks, நிறை, self-restraint.
teaches: The Innaa line fills the Kural's circular condition with content: the 'தவம் one must already have' is the inner restraint without which penance is a pain.
list_adds: It names the missing quality (நிறை) and files the empty penance with other things whose holding power is gone.
audit_text_issue: Variant அறைபறை யாயவர் (line 3).

note: Verse 23 makes guarding the gate of a wall-less old town painful; 24 makes living in an old town without protection painful.
teaches: The second verse moves the pain from the guard's futile labour to the townsman's daily exposure, so one weakness is felt by both its defenders and its dwellers.
audit_text_issue: innaa_narpathu:24 line 4 has a vowel-sign variant (என்பவரொடு/என்பவரோடு).

note: After the town without wall (23) and without protection (24), verse 25 names the old town without கட்டு, bonds of order.
teaches: Across three verses the town's weakness moves from its stone to its order, teaching that a town is unsafe for lacking ties as much as for lacking walls.
audit_text_issue: Innaa 25 line 1 has printed variants (இடுக்க ணனிகண்டா னன்கின்னா / கண்டாற் பெரிதின்னா). | the packet flags a variant reading in line 1 of innaa_narpathu:25

note: Kural 788 defines friendship as clearing a friend's distress at once, like a hand catching a slipping garment; the Innaa line counts the mere sight of a friend's distress as a deep pain.
teaches: The pairing shows the feeling behind the Kural's reflex: the friend's hand moves so fast because seeing the trouble already hurts.
list_adds: It sets the friend's trouble against the enemy's pride in the next line, so friendship's pain is measured against its mirror in enmity.
audit_text_issue: Line 4 நட்ட கவறு is uncertain.

note: Kural 892 says neglecting the great brings ills through them; the Innaa verse counts doing evil to the great as painful and opens with letting go of a bond with them.
teaches: Together they show neglect and injury of the great as stages of one fault, the Innaa list naming the first step, loosening the bond, that the Kural leaves implicit.
list_adds: Its first and last items both concern the great, so harming them is shown as the end of a course that begins with letting go of them.

note: Iniyavai 28 calls not going about crying for relief from one's distress foremost sweet; the Innaa line calls telling one's suffering to those who do not care painful. They agree from two sides, but the Innaa line narrows the fault to an uncaring listener.
teaches: The pair separates self-restraint in grief from the choice of listener: the Iniyavai praises not complaining at all, the Innaa only counts complaint to the indifferent as a pain.

note: Iniyavai 37 calls knowing youth as old age sweet; Innaa 27 calls entering old age within youth painful. They do not disagree: one is foresight of age, the other its untimely arrival or imitation.
teaches: Read together they keep the counsel to remember age while young from turning into premature decline, the sweet awareness and the painful condition being kept apart.
audit_text_issue: innaa 27 line 2 variant

note: Kural 401 likens holding an assembly without full learning to a board game with no board; the Innaa line names the same act, கல்லாதான் கோட்டி கொளல், as painful.
teaches: The Innaa verse adds exposure to the Kural's emptiness: paired with the unlearned man on a prancing horse, holding court becomes a display that can throw him.
list_adds: It frames the verse with the unlearned man, mounting a spirited horse at the start and holding court at the end, two displays he cannot carry.

note: Kural 1046 says the words of the poor go slack even when well understood; the Innaa line counts the very grace of speech in a poor man's mouth as painful.
teaches: The pair moves the loss from the listeners to the speaker: the Kural notes that no one heeds, the Innaa line that fine speech which cannot land is itself a pain.
list_adds: It sets poverty beside want of learning and skill, so wealth and learning appear as the two things that give speech its weight.

note: Kural 61 prizes above all children who come to understanding (அறிவறிந்த மக்கட்பேறு); the Innaa line counts getting children without it (அறிவறியா மக்கட் பெறல்) as painful.
teaches: The Innaa line states the other branch of the Kural's condition, showing that its praise was never of children as such but of children with sense.
list_adds: It sets senseless children beside a snake charmed without knowledge and a secret in a careless ear, as power held without the knowledge to handle it.
audit_text_issue: innaa_narpathu:29 line 1 has variant readings flagged

note: 29 counts a secret heard by one who cannot hold it; 23 counts the talk of those who are like a beaten drum.
teaches: The two lines describe one leak from both ends, the careless hearer and the broadcasting talker, so the book shows a secret failing first in the ear and then on the tongue.

note: Kural 890 makes living with those not in accord like living with a snake in a hut; the Innaa line names the house with a hidden snake plainly, as a bodily danger.
teaches: Placed together, the Innaa line gives the literal fear on which the Kural's figure rests, so the reader sees why discord at home is felt as close, quiet and constant danger.
list_adds: It keeps the snake-house literal beside a high leap, a raging elephant and a tiger's path, four plain dangers with no moral item.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 has a source variant.

note: Kural 573 asks what use a melody is that does not fit the song, and an eye without kindly regard; the Innaa verse opens with a lute not set to its mode and ends with the enmity of those without coolness.
teaches: Both pass from music out of tune to a person out of tune, which suggests a shared idea of kindness as attunement, with the Innaa verse adding enmity as its opposite.
list_adds: It spreads the Kural's single analogy over four items, three instruments or reckonings out of true and then a hostile temper.
audit_text_issue: Variant தன்மையிலாளர் for தண்மை யிலாளர் (line 4) and எண்ணறிய (line 2).

note: Kural 184 grants that harsh words to the face are better than careless words behind the back; the Innaa line names the backbiter as one who will not speak to the face (முன்னை உரையார்).
teaches: Both rank the face above the back, and the Innaa wording makes the backbiter's fault a refusal of the open speech the Kural concedes, so cowardice is seen inside the malice.
list_adds: It sets backbiting beside failing to guard oneself and bad company, as ways a person is undone without seeing it.

note: Iniyavai 34 calls leaving the friendship of worthless people, even when they cling, sweet; the Innaa line calls association with those without goodness painful. The same thing from two sides.
teaches: Together they give both the cost and the remedy: the Innaa names the pain of the tie, the Iniyavai the sweetness of cutting it even when the other holds on.

note: Kural 929 says giving reasons to a drunk is like searching with a torch for a man under water; the Innaa line says the business a drunkard himself speaks of is painful.
teaches: Together they close talk with the drunk in both directions: reasons cannot reach him, and his own account of affairs cannot be relied on.
list_adds: It sets the drunk's counsel beside walking on thorns and the deceitful's company, as pains that come through trusting the wrong ground.
audit_text_issue: The packet flags a variant reading of line 2. | line 2 has a source variant (நடக்கி னனியின்னா)

note: Naladiyar 341 says the base man, though books of weighty meaning are opened for him, goes his own way like a hen scratching rubbish; the Innaa line says even an excellent book is a pain to one who does not want it.
teaches: The pair moves the loss from the learner to the teaching: the Naladiyar shows the base mind wasting the book, the Innaa line the book itself suffering a reader who does not want it.
list_adds: It sets the unwanted book beside counsel spoken to the unruly and friendship with the despised, all goods given where they do not fit.
audit_text_issue: line 4 கழிப்புவாய் மண்டிலங் கொட்பு obscure; line 1 variant குறைவுரைத்தல்

note: 27 counts beauty in those without means as painful; 35 counts a handsome man who is a fool as painful.
teaches: The poet twice makes beauty a pain when what should go with it is missing, wealth in one verse and sense in the other, so beauty is judged by its company.
audit_text_issue: 35 line 2 (குழலி னினிய மரத் தோசை) is obscure.

note: Kural 799 says friendship with those who desert one in ruin burns the heart even at death; the Innaa verse closes its run of poverty's pains with the friendship of those who abandon one at the time of ruin.
teaches: The Kural measures the desertion by the burn it leaves; the Innaa verse shows it as the last support lost, after the wish to give, the rich city and others' doors have already hurt.
list_adds: It places the desertion at the end of a falling householder's sequence, so betrayal is the last stage of poverty, not a separate fault.

note: Kural 218 says the discerning do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even without means; the Innaa line counts a man without wealth desiring to be liberal as painful. Not a tension on our reading: the Innaa line names a cost, not a fault.
teaches: The pair shows the pain hidden inside the Kural's praise: giving steadily in want is admirable, and the wish to give without means is also an ache.
list_adds: It sets the giving wish among the pains of want, a rich city around one and eating at others' doors, so it is seen from inside poverty.

note: Iniyavai 22 calls giving with knowledge of one's income sweet; Innaa 36 calls longing to be liberal without wealth painful. The same rule seen from two sides: giving should match means.
teaches: Together the two books set a measure on liberality, the sweet side naming the rule and the painful side the cost of breaking it.

note: Naladiyar 65 says the gift of one without wealth is the true fruit of giving; the Innaa line counts liberality in one who has nothing to give as painful. On the reading that the Naladiyar's giver has little and the Innaa's has nothing, they meet at a limit rather than conflict.
teaches: Together they mark where giving from want stops being the highest giving and becomes pain: the point where nothing is left to give.
list_adds: It files moneyless liberality with a stone in the chewed areca and broken patronage, as an act that breaks in the middle.

note: In Purananuru 101 Avvai tells her heart that whether Athiyaman's gift is delayed or not it is sure, since he greets her on the hundredth visit as on the first; the Innaa line counts a poet held back by the giver as painful.
teaches: The poem shows the pain the Innaa line names and how it is borne: a patron's constant welcome makes the delay of the poet's send-off endurable.

note: 36 counts a man without wealth longing to be liberal; 39 counts liberality practised by one who has nothing to give.
teaches: The poet counts the moneyless giver twice, once in the wish and once in the act, so the pain is not only frustrated desire but the giving itself carried on without means.
audit_text_issue: 39 line 3: tamilvu reads கொடுத்து விடாமை.

note: Kural 301 says only restraint of anger where it can take effect counts; the Innaa line counts rancour held against the small as painful.
teaches: Read together, anger toward the weak is both the Kural's true test of restraint and the Innaa verse's common failure of it, the same ground seen as trial and as fall.
list_adds: It sets rancour toward the weak beside a scentless flower and a fool under questioning, so cruelty is filed with exposures of one's own lack.

note: 29 counts jumping into water without knowing the stakes; 37 counts going down into water without knowing the ford.
teaches: The poet uses the water twice with two kinds of ignorance, of what lies beneath and of the way in, showing knowledge of place as the condition of entering.
audit_text_issue: Both lines carry Project Madurai variants (துறையறியா நீரிழிந்து; கீழ்நீர்ப்பாய்ந்தாடுதல்), which do not change the image.

note: Both call desire for another man's wife பேதைமை; the Kural says it is absent in those who have seen aram and porul.
teaches: The Innaa list explains the shared word by its company: the folly is that of a venture beyond one's strength, like a valourless king in battle, which those the Kural describes would never attempt.
list_adds: It sets the folly beside a valourless king in battle, a bareback ride on a fierce horse and unskilled work, so it is ranked as reckless overreach.

note: Iniyavai 30 calls the goodness that does not seize a deposit, thinking 'who knew of it then?', the sweetest; Innaa 40 calls seizing a deposit painful. The same thing from two sides.
teaches: The Iniyavai line names the thief's private reckoning that no one saw; set against it, the Innaa line shows the betrayal of trust as painful whether or not anyone knew.
audit_text_issue: the packet flags a repair and a site difference in iniyavai_narpathu:30 line 3

note: Thirikadugam 62 names the one who wrongfully keeps a deposit among three who live on with their line lost; the Innaa line counts seizing a deposit as painful.
teaches: The Thirikadugam names the consequence, loss of descendants, that the Innaa line's bare 'painful' leaves unspoken, so the ethics works together give the act and its price.

note: Kural 134 says a brahmin can relearn a forgotten Veda but his birth is ruined if conduct fails; saying 1 ranks conduct above recitation for all people.
teaches: The Kural's ranking of conduct over recitation, made for the brahmin whose role is recitation, is here lifted off birth entirely and given to everyone the frame line addresses.
list_adds: It sets the ranking first in a ten of rankings and removes the brahmin, so conduct over study becomes the opening rule for all people rather than a warning to one varna.

note: Both sayings place learning below something else: conduct in 1, serving the learned in 8.
teaches: Within one ten learning is twice ranked second, once to conduct and once to reverence for those who have learnt, so the book never lets learning be the highest good.

note: Kural 562 tells the ruler to raise the rod sharply but bring it down lightly; saying 2 ranks being held in awe above being loved, on the plainer reading of கண்ணஞ்சப் படுதல்.
teaches: The Kural allows awe only as a measured show that must not become harm, while the saying ranks awe over love outright and for anyone, so the pair shows how far the measure matters.
list_adds: It ranks awe directly against affection, a contrast the couplet lacks, and carries it beyond the king to every person the frame addresses.
audit_text_issue: Packet flags that the site's verse 2 is a different verse.

note: Kural 300 says nothing seen as true is better than truthfulness; saying 4 sets truthfulness specifically above liberality.
teaches: The Kural's absolute claim for truth is tested against the one virtue its rival tradition prizes most, open-handed giving, and truth still wins.
list_adds: It names the rival virtue that truth outranks, liberality, where the couplet compares truth with everything at once.
