note: Naladiyar 55 laments youth gone and disease and old age coming; saying 5 ranks freedom from disease above youth.
teaches: The quatrain counts youth's passing and illness's coming as one loss that urges renunciation, while the saying pulls them apart and says health, not youth, is the greater good.
list_adds: It ranks two goods the quatrain mourns together, making health a separate and higher thing than youth.
audit_text_issue: Packet flags that the site's verse 5 is a different verse.

note: Kural 1014 calls shame the ornament of the worthy; saying 6 ranks shame above beauty or good qualities.
teaches: The Kural's metaphor of shame as an ornament becomes a literal ranking: shame outranks the beauty that ornaments are meant to serve.
list_adds: It sets shame against beauty in a direct comparison, turning the couplet's figure into a ranking among goods.
audit_text_issue: Flagged site_diff: another source prints a different verse 6.

note: Kural 54 asks what is greater than a woman with the firmness of chastity; saying 7 names lineage as one of the things chastity outranks.
teaches: Where the Kural leaves chastity's superiority open-ended, the saying sets it against birth itself, so a woman's fidelity is made to count for more than the family she comes from.
list_adds: It pits chastity against lineage, one specific good of birth, a contrast the couplet does not draw.
audit_text_issue: The site's Muthumozhikkanchi 7 is a different verse (site_diff 0.34).

note: Kural 395 says the foremost are those who learnt while yearning before teachers like the poor before the rich; saying 8 ranks serving the learned above learning.
teaches: The Kural makes humility before the learned the posture of learning, while the saying ranks that reverence above the learning it leads to, so the means is put above the end.
list_adds: It ranks the service of the learned against learning itself, where the couplet only makes the one the manner of the other.
audit_text_issue: Packet flags that the site's verse 8 is a different verse.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 28 says the fit pupil serves his teacher with love; saying 8 ranks serving the learned above learning.
teaches: One counted work names service of the teacher as the mark of a fit pupil and the other ranks it above learning itself, so the group treats reverence for the learned as prior to knowledge.
audit_text_issue: The site's Muthumozhikkanchi 8 is a different verse (site_diff 0.28).

note: Kural 782 says the friendship of the good waxes like the moon and that of fools wanes after being full; saying 10 ranks not dwindling above a large beginning.
teaches: The Kural's moon image is about friendship; the saying states its principle bare, for any course of fortune or bond, and keeps only the half that matters: holding, not starting great.
list_adds: It strips the image and the domain of friendship and ranks endurance over a large start as a general rule.
audit_text_issue: Packet flags that the site's verse 10 is a different verse.

note: Line 11 reads great birth from kindness; line 12 reads kindness from giving.
teaches: Taken in order the two lines make a chain of evidence, so in this ten noble birth is finally proved by the act of giving.

note: Line 11 says a great house shows in kindness; line 16 says a small house shows in pride.
teaches: The pair shows the ten treating rank of birth as real yet legible only in conduct, with kindness and pride as its two marks.

note: Kural 959 reads lineage from a person's speech; the line reads great birth from kindness.
teaches: Both read birth from a sign, but the sign moves from what is said to what is felt, so the Muthumozhikkanchi's test is harder to counterfeit.
list_adds: Set in a ten of signs, the line makes kindness the test of birth and the next line makes giving the test of kindness, a chain the couplet does not build.
audit_text_issue: The site's text lacks line 2. | The packet flags that the site lacks line 2.

note: Kural 796 says ruin is the rod that measures one's people; the line names help as the mark of a friendship that does not fail.
teaches: The Kural gives the occasion of the test and the line gives its measure, so together they say what ruin reveals: who still helps.
list_adds: It places the friendship test among tests of birth, learning and ability, so friendship is judged by the same rule of outward proof as every other claimed virtue.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 prints சேரா; tamilvu's சோரா ('not slackening') is the sense the link needs.

note: Thirikadugam 37 says the extent of friendship shows in backbiting; the line says a good friendship shows in help.
teaches: The two give friendship a positive and a negative test, help given and slander withheld, so neither alone measures it.
audit_text_issue: line 1 சேரா; tamilvu சோரா

note: Kural 717 says learning shines among those who can examine words; the line says learning is known by the learner's own discernment.
teaches: The Kural needs a qualified audience for learning to appear, while the line finds the proof inside the learner, in how he sees.
list_adds: By setting learning between friendship and eminence in a run of signs, it treats learning as one more inner fact read from outward evidence rather than as display before an assembly.

note: Kural 978 says smallness adorns itself with self-admiration; the line says birth in a small house shows in pride.
teaches: The same mark of pride serves the Kural as a sign of small character and the Muthumozhikkanchi as a sign of small birth, which shows the ten tying character to family.
list_adds: Paired in the ten with line 11, it sets the small house against the great one, a contrast of birth the couplet, which speaks only of character, does not draw.
audit_text_issue: சிற்றில் may mean a poor or mean house rather than a birth-group.

note: Naladiyar 195 says good and bad lineage are only words and that lineage is made by austerity, learning and effort; the line treats a small house of birth as a fact that pride reveals.
teaches: Read together they show two answers in one group: the Naladiyar dissolves birth rank into achievement, while the Muthumozhikkanchi keeps rank and reads it from conduct.
list_adds: Its pairing with line 11 sets great and small houses as fixed ranks with opposite marks, which is exactly the distinction the quatrain calls empty words.

note: Kural 287 calls stealth a dark knowledge absent in those who love measure; the line names trickery as what shows a man to be a thief.
teaches: The Kural places theft in a kind of cunning, and the line turns that cunning into the evidence, so the thief is known by his method before any taking.
list_adds: Among signs of good birth, kindness and learning, it gives the one sign of a crime, so the ten's method of reading people from acts reaches the detection of a thief.

note: Kural 642 says gain and ruin come from speech and bids one guard against its lapse; the line says a lapse in speech reveals every other lapse.
teaches: The Kural treats a slip of the tongue as a cause of loss, while the line treats it as evidence, so the guarded tongue both protects and conceals.
list_adds: Set beside line 19, it makes speech and understanding the two windows through which all other failings are seen, a pairing the couplet lacks.

note: Lines 18 and 19 share one frame: a lapse in one place reveals lapses elsewhere, first in speech and then in understanding.
teaches: The repeated frame shows the ten holding that faults do not stay single: one visible slip is read as the index of hidden ones.

note: Kural 421 calls understanding the tool and inner fortress that guards against faults; the line says a lapse of understanding exposes the other lapses.
teaches: Read together, the fortress image explains the line: once understanding gives way, the faults it guarded behind it come into view.
list_adds: It moves understanding from a guard to a sign, placing its failure among the ten's ways of reading a person.

note: Kural 505 makes one's own deeds the single touchstone of greatness and smallness; the line makes deeds the test of manly ability only.
teaches: The Kural uses one test for all worth, while this ten assigns a different sign to each quality, kindness for birth and giving for kindness, and keeps deeds for ability.
list_adds: As the last of ten paired signs, it shows deeds as one test among several, each matched to its quality, rather than the one touchstone the couplet names.

note: 24 reverses the terms of 23: the rarity of the great is not blamed, then the greatness of the rare.
teaches: The chiasm makes greatness and rarity two faces of one value, so a reader learns that complaining of a thing's cost and grudging its esteem are the same error.

note: The Kural says the great accomplish deeds that are hard; the line says the hardness of great things is not to be complained of.
teaches: Together they show the link between பெருமை and அருமை from both ends: the great man takes on difficulty, and the onlooker should not resent that great things are difficult.
list_adds: Paired with its mirror line 24 in a ten on what is not blamed, it turns the couplet's praise of the great into a rule for those who judge them and their works.

note: The Kural grants effort its wage even when the end fails; the line adds that the unfinished work itself is not censured.
teaches: The couplet secures the striver's inner reward and the line secures his standing among others, so an honest shortfall costs neither the wage nor the name.
list_adds: Set among excuses for nature, poverty and foreign custom, the shortfall becomes one of the things beyond a person's power that the ten exempts from blame, which the couplet on effort does not frame.

note: On the reading that the world abandons those who leave a task short, the Kural blames the shortfall that this line excuses.
teaches: The pair divides the unfinished task in two: abandoning it in the middle draws the world's blame, while a work that simply could not be done in full does not.
list_adds: The ten's predicate puts the onlooker's verdict first, where the couplet speaks to the worker, so the line adds the case the couplet leaves open, a deficiency not chosen.

note: Innaa Narpathu counts living under fierce kings of bent sceptre as painful; the line says one living in such a land does not blame the king.
teaches: Read together, the pain of misrule and the silence of its subject belong to one situation: the subject suffers it and still holds his tongue, which is prudence, not approval.
audit_text_issue: muthumozhikkanchi:26 இருந்து as printed is awkward for the ten's noun slot

note: The Kural says having is worse than poverty under a ruler who does no justice; the line says the subject there does not voice blame.
teaches: The couplet names what the subject loses under misrule and the line names what he must also give up, the open word against the king, so the cost of a bent sceptre falls on speech as well as property.
list_adds: Among the ten's cases of withheld blame it makes silence under an unjust king a rule of the subject's conduct, a side of tyranny the couplet, which speaks of the king's guilt, does not state.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 is uncertain: இருந்து may go with the predicate or name the excused act. | The construal of இருந்து பழியார் is uncertain.

note: The Kural reads a friend's hurtful act as folly or great intimacy; the line extends forbearance to good kin who fail to do what they should.
teaches: The pair carries the Kural's charity of interpretation from friends' acts to kinsmen's omissions, and keeps its limit: in both, the tie must first be a good one.
list_adds: It moves the couplet's rule from friendship to kin and from a wrong done to a duty left undone, and sets it beside excuses for the poor and the small.

note: The Kural says understanding lives as the world lives; the line applies that to the customs of an unknown country.
teaches: The pairing shows the couplet's conformity turning outward: wisdom not only follows the ways of one's own world but withholds blame from a world whose ways it does not know.
list_adds: It names the thing the couplet leaves general, ஆசாரம் of a தேசம், and so makes custom local and the judge's ignorance a reason for restraint.

note: Acharakkovai fixes the posture and direction of the meal as ஆசாரம்; the line treats ஆசாரம் as varying by country and not to be faulted where it is unknown.
teaches: Holding them together shows that one ethics work treats ஆசாரம் as binding rule while another grants it is a country's custom, so the rule code is local even in the eyes of its own literature.

note: The Kural says those who know their duty do not slacken in helping even without means; the line says the poor man who is not generous is not blamed.
teaches: The pair separates the ideal from the verdict: the Kural praises the poor man who still helps, while the line forbids others to condemn the one who cannot, so excellence is not made a debt.
list_adds: In a ten on withheld blame the line speaks to the onlooker rather than the giver, a standpoint the couplet on ஒப்புரவு never takes.

note: The Naladiyar says if poverty makes giving impossible, not begging is worth twice giving; the line says the poor man's lack of generosity is not blamed.
teaches: Together they show the poor man's position from both sides: others owe him no reproach for not giving, and he keeps a virtue of his own in not asking.
list_adds: The quatrain gives the poor man a substitute duty; the line instead binds the onlooker, placing the poor man beside the untrained and the small as people whose shortfall is excused.

note: The Kural says greatness hides another's weakness while smallness tells faults; the line says even the excellent do not blame the conduct of the small.
teaches: The pair shows greatness proved on the very people who invite contempt: not publishing a fault is hardest and most telling when the faulty are the small.
list_adds: Closing a ten of withheld blame, it turns the couplet's portrait of greatness into the last case of a rule, with சிறந்தோரும் marking the eminent as those for whom restraint is due.

note: Kural 657 sets the utter poverty of the worthy above wealth won under blame; Muthumozhikkanchi 31 sets the wealth of the blameworthy level with poverty.
teaches: The couplet ranks clean poverty above tainted wealth, while the line only levels them, and holding both shows a scale with two steps: tainted wealth is already worth no more than want, and the worthy man's want is worth more still.
list_adds: It makes tainted wealth one of ten things measured against a plain lack (hunger, solitude, refusal), so blame is shown to empty wealth of what wealth is for, not merely to rank below virtue.

note: Kural 773 calls தறுகண் great manliness and gives it kindness to the fallen foe as its edge; the line says that தறுகண்மை in excess (கழி) is no better than the பேடி's lack of it.
teaches: The Kural refines valour by adding mercy as its edge, and the line limits it by measure, so the pair shows two separate checks on courage: mercy to the fallen and restraint in excess.
list_adds: Set in a ten where each thing is equated with its seeming opposite, it makes the over-bold and the coward one kind, a turn the couplet's praise of valour does not make.

note: Kural 1012 says food and clothing are common to all living beings and shame is the mark of humans; the line says a life without shame is no better than hunger.
teaches: The couplet sets shame above food as what makes a person human; the line turns the same order into a verdict on the shameless man, whose full table counts for no more than an empty one.
list_adds: It measures the lack of shame in the coin of food, the very thing the couplet put aside as common to all, so the ranking is applied as a judgement on a life rather than stated as a definition.

note: Naladiyar 268 sees the shameless feasting at home while those with shame walk far and eat scraps; the line counts a shameless life as no better than hunger.
teaches: The quatrain records the outward fact that shamelessness feeds well, and the line answers it by counting that full stomach as hunger, so together they give the complaint and its reply.
list_adds: The line states as a measure what the quatrain shows as a scene, setting the shameless life among ten counterfeit goods that equal their lacks.

note: Kural 1057 says the asker rejoices deep within on meeting givers who do not scorn; the line says giving without regard is no better than withholding.
teaches: The couplet locates the worth of a gift in the asker's inner joy at being spared scorn, and the line draws the conclusion from the giver's side: without that regard the gift is as good as refused.
list_adds: It puts the careless gift beside the shameless life and the false helper, ten things that keep the outward form of a good while lacking its substance, which the couplet, focused on the asker, does not do.

note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy for all and doing as one said is hard; the line counts an undertaking left undone as no better than folly.
teaches: The couplet names the gap between word and deed as a difficulty, and the line names its cost to the man who leaves it open: he is counted a fool, so failure to perform becomes a matter of judgement, not only of strength.
list_adds: By measuring the broken undertaking against சிதடி, it moves the couplet's point from firmness in action to the standing of the one who fails, among other things judged as their opposites.

note: Kural 110 says there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him; the line counts withdrawing regard after receiving as no better than cruelty.
teaches: The couplet ranks ingratitude as the sin without remedy, and the line names what it is in act: the ungrateful man, who strikes no one, is reckoned as cruel as one who does harm.
list_adds: It classes ingratitude with கொடுமை, an act of harm, where the couplet ranks it among sins by its consequence, so the list says what kind of wrong it is rather than how grave.

note: Kural 816 says being a stranger to the wise is ten million times better than close friendship with a fool; the line counts a fool's support as no better than solitude.
teaches: The couplet sinks the fool's friendship far below even estrangement from the wise, while the line only equates it with having no one, and the pair shows the range of the same judgement from mild to extreme.
list_adds: It measures the fool's company against solitude, the measure the same ten uses for unshared pleasure in 40, so a bad companion and a joy kept to oneself are shown to leave a person equally alone.

note: Both lines close on தனிமையின் துவ்வாது: a fool's support and pleasure enjoyed alone are each no better than solitude.
teaches: Read together, the two make solitude the measure from both sides: one may be alone though accompanied, by a fool, or alone though joyful, by not sharing, so company is defined by what is shared and not by who is present.

note: Kural 229 says eating alone to fill one's own store is more bitter than begging; the line says enjoying pleasure alone is no better than solitude.
teaches: The couplet ranks solitary eating below begging, a loss of goods and honour, while the line counts any unshared pleasure as loneliness, so the pair shows the same fault judged once as social shame and once as the self's own isolation.
list_adds: It widens the couplet's solitary eating to every pleasure kept to oneself and pairs it within the ten with the fool's company, both measured by solitude.

note: 41 denies the name of spouse to one who does not act knowing the other's nature; 42 denies the name of household life to a house whose wife is not excellent.
teaches: Read as written, the ten opens with a condition on the husband before it measures the house by the wife, so the household is made to fail from either side and not from the wife alone.
audit_text_issue: 41 line 2 masculine endings with தாரம்; site text lacks line 2

note: Thirikadugam 96 names the wife who knows her husband's hint as one at whose word rain falls; saying 41 denies the name of spouse to one who does not act knowing the other's nature.
teaches: The same virtue, knowing the partner's nature, is a power over the rains in one work and the bare minimum of being a spouse in the other, so it is both the ceiling and the floor of marriage.
audit_text_issue: Line 41 gender of ஒழுகாதான் / அல்லன் against தாரம் is unresolved.

note: Kural 52 says that if the wife lacks household excellence the life is nothing whatever else it has; saying 42 says the same in the அல்ல form.
teaches: The Kural's claim that a wife's excellence decides the household survives the move into a book of bare definitions, where it becomes one of the tests by which a thing earns its name.
list_adds: It sets household life beside kin-friendship, giving, learning and penance as things that lose their very name when one inner condition fails, so the wife's excellence becomes a defining condition of the same kind as aram in giving.

note: Naladiyar 56 says that even a wife without good qualities cannot be put away, and that this is why marriage is called கடி; saying 42 says a house whose wife is not excellent is no household life.
teaches: Put together, the two say that the life which the saying denies the name of household is one the man still cannot leave, so 'not a life' names a bond that persists as a hardship.
list_adds: Its list denies such a house the name of a life outright, where the quatrain keeps the marriage and counts its cost.

note: Saying 11 says birth into a great house is known by ஈரம; saying 43 says kin-friendship without ஈரம் is no kin-friendship.
teaches: The book uses the same moistness of heart twice, as the sign of good birth and as the condition of kin's bond, so blood and lineage are both made to depend on a tenderness that birth alone does not give.
audit_text_issue: ஈரலில் read as ஈரம் இல்

note: Kural 522 says kin whose love does not lapse bring ever-branching gains; saying 43 says a kin bond without tenderness is not a kin bond.
teaches: The Kural values kin by the gains their unfailing love brings, while the saying moves the test inward and denies the name of kin to those without tenderness, before any gain is counted.
list_adds: It puts the kin bond in a run of definitions by inner condition (spouse, house, friend, learning), so kinship is ranked with friendship as a bond made by feeling, where the couplet treats kin as a source of wealth.
audit_text_issue: ஈரலில் for ஈரமில் is an unusual spelling.

note: Kural 231 says giving and living with renown is the only gain of life; saying 44 says the man whose hand never loosens is no mountain of renown.
teaches: The Kural joins giving and fame as the one profit of living; the saying shows the same bond from its failure, that the closed hand loses the standing of one's name, on the reading of சொன்மலை as renown.
list_adds: It states the bond negatively and puts the miser among other false holders of a name (the unfeeling kinsman, the friend whose heart does not consent), a contrast of claim and substance the couplet lacks.

note: Kural 786 says friendship that smiles in the face is not friendship and friendship that smiles in the heart is; saying 45 says one whose heart does not agree is no friend.
teaches: Both deny the name of friendship by the same 'is not' form, and the saying narrows the Kural's heart-smile to consent, so the friend is one whose heart has come into agreement, not only one who feels warmth.
list_adds: It sets the false friend beside the false spouse, kinsman, learning, giving and penance, so the Kural's one test for friendship becomes a general method: each bond or practice is named by an inner condition.

note: Both sayings turn on நேர்தல்: the friend whose heart does not agree, the learning gained without consent or submission.
teaches: Placed side by side, the two make friendship and learning both depend on an act of assent, so the pupil's submission to learning is the same act as the friend's agreement of heart.

note: Kural 395 praises those who learned yearning before the learned like the poor before the rich; saying 46 says learning without நேர்தல் is not learning.
teaches: The Kural ranks the humble learner highest; the saying goes further and denies that learning without that assent or submission is learning at all, on the reading of நேராமல் as not submitting.
list_adds: It turns the couplet's ranking into a definition and puts learning beside friendship and penance as things that exist only when entered into by consent or undertaking.

note: Saying 8 ranks serving the learned above learning; saying 46 denies the name of learning to what is learnt without submission.
teaches: Across two tens, the book first puts reverence for teachers above learning and then makes it the condition of learning, so reverence moves from the greater good to the thing without which learning does not exist.

note: Kural 619 says that even where fate denies the end, effort pays the wage of bodily strain; saying 47 says strain that does not bring one to live is not strain, on the reading of வருத்தம் as effort.
teaches: The Kural promises effort a wage even in failure, while the saying refuses to count strain that brings no living, so the pair sets a floor (some wage) against a definition by result (a life gained).
list_adds: It names effort among things judged by an outcome or manner beside giving and penance, a measure by result the couplet explicitly sets aside.
audit_text_issue: Muthumozhikkanchi 47 is open to a second reading (deserved grief), which the marker flags.

note: Kural 221 says giving to those who have nothing is giving and all else is a measured return; saying 48 says what is not given in aram's way is not giving.
teaches: Both redefine giving by denying the name to gifts that look like it; the Kural fixes the test by recipient and expected return, while the saying fixes it by the road of aram and leaves its content open.
list_adds: It pairs the test of giving with a matching test of penance in the next line (அறத்தாற்றின் / திறத்தாற்றின்), so the householder's gift and the ascetic's vow are judged by one rule of right manner, which the couplet does not do.

note: Saying 34 reckons giving without care for the receiver no better than refusing; saying 48 says giving not along aram's way is not giving.
teaches: The book judges giving twice by its manner, once by care for the receiver and once by aram's road, so a gift's worth never rests on its size in either ten.

note: The two lines are built as twins: அறத்தாற்றின் ஈயாதது ஈனையன்று, திறத்தாற்றின் நேர்லாதது நோன்பன்று.
teaches: The twin form makes the giver's gift and the ascetic's vow two cases of one rule, that an act is named by the way it is done, so the householder's and renouncer's codes are tested alike.
audit_text_issue: நேர்லா (49) is read as a form of நேர்தல்; the sense is not certain.

note: Kural 261 defines தவம் as bearing pain and harming no living being; saying 49 says a vow not taken up in its proper way is no penance.
teaches: The Kural defines penance by its content, endurance and harmlessness, while the saying defines it by how it is undertaken, so the pair shows two separate tests a vow must pass.
list_adds: It sets penance as the twin of giving in a matched pair of lines, putting the ascetic's vow under the same test of right manner as the householder's gift, which the couplet does not.

note: Thirikadugam 96 names the ascetic who carries out what he has undertaken in the proper way as one at whose word rain falls; saying 49 says a vow not undertaken in its proper way is no penance.
teaches: One work denies the name of penance to a vow wrongly undertaken; the other promises rain to the ascetic who completes his vow rightly, so between them the proper manner is both the condition of penance and the source of its power.
audit_text_issue: நேர்லா ததுநோன் in muthumozhikkanchi:49 looks corrupt (perhaps நோலாதது); thirikadugam:96 line 3 repaired சொய்வான் to செய்வான்.

note: Purananuru 195 tells grey-haired elders in useless age that Death will bind them and urges them at least to refrain from harm; saying 50 says age without knowledge of the next birth is not old age.
teaches: The puram poet shames old men by the coming of Death, while the saying denies them the name of age unless they know what follows death, so the heroic warning about the end becomes a doctrine of rebirth.

note: Saying 39 reckons disgraced old age no better than anger; saying 50 says age that does not know rebirth is not old age.
teaches: The book judges old age twice and never by years: once by the disgrace it carries, once by what it knows of the birth to come, so elderhood is a moral and a spiritual standing.
audit_text_issue: 39 கதம் sense uncertain

note: Kural 61 knows no gain like children who come to know (அறிவறிந்த); the line names the getting of children the greatest gain with no condition.
teaches: The couplet's praise hangs on a single qualifier the line drops, so the pair shows the Kural deliberately narrowing a common saying that children are the greatest gain.
list_adds: Set first in a ten of superlatives that ranks fame as the greatest legacy (58) and giving as the greatest distinction (60), the line makes offspring one of several 'nothing greater' goods, so its supremacy is one claim among rival ones rather than the couplet's single ranking.
audit_text_issue: The packet flags that the site lacks line 2.

note: Innaa Narpathu 29 counts begetting children without understanding (அறிவறியா மக்கட் பெறல்) among painful things; the line calls the getting of children, unqualified, the greatest gain.
teaches: Read plainly, the two works give the same act opposite values, and only the qualifier about the child's understanding, which the Kural supplies, reconciles a supreme gain with a pain.
audit_text_issue: The site's text lacks line 2 of Muthumozhikkanchi 51. | The packet flags that the site's text lacks line 2 of Muthumozhikkanchi 51.

note: Kural 213 says nothing here or in the gods' world is as good as ஒப்புரவு; the line says nothing is a more fitting acquisition than knowing it.
teaches: The couplet ranks the duty itself above all goods; the line ranks the knowledge of the duty, so that merely learning what one owes the world already counts as the best thing one can gain.
list_adds: Placed in a ten of gains, losses and disgraces, the line turns ஒப்புரவு from a good done for others into an acquisition of the doer's own, set beside children and fame as things one gets.

note: 53 calls a desire that can come to pass the best desire; 54 calls a desire that cannot the worst.
teaches: Together the two lines judge desire by its outcome rather than its object, a scale on which the same wish is best or worst depending only on whether it can be fulfilled.
audit_text_issue: வாய்ப்புடை / வாயா: attainable or fitting is undecided

note: Thirikadugam 28 names the man who sits craving what he does not have (இல்லது காமுற்று இருப்பான்) as one who pounds husk; the line calls unattainable desire the worst desire.
teaches: Thirikadugam gives the image of the wasted labour and the line gives the verdict, so the pair says why futile wanting is worst: it spends effort with nothing to show.
audit_text_issue: வாயா uncertain: 'not coming about' or 'unfitting'

note: Thirikadugam 45 says the man who without love hides what he can (இயைவ கரப்பான்) from those who ask falls into hell; the line uses the same words and calls the act the greatest cruelty.
teaches: The two works share the phrase for withholding what one can give, and between them name its moral kind (cruelty) and its fate (hell), so refusal is treated as a harm done to the asker, not just a lack of virtue.

note: Kural 1069 says the heart melts at the thought of begging and is destroyed at the thought of concealment; the line makes concealment the greatest cruelty.
teaches: The couplet weighs concealment by what it does to the asker's heart, the line by what it makes the concealer, and both rank it below begging itself, which 59 calls the worst disgrace.
list_adds: In a ten that also names begging the worst disgrace (59) and giving to askers the highest distinction (60), the line completes a three-way scoring of one exchange (asking, refusing, giving) that the couplet treats only from the asker's side.

note: 37 sets turning one's regard away from those one has taken from as no better than cruelty; 55 sets hiding what one can give as the greatest cruelty.
teaches: The book uses cruelty as the measure twice, once as a floor for ingratitude and once as a summit for refusal, so withholding from an asker ranks as worse than the ingratitude it is compared with.

note: Kural 214 says one who knows what is fitting lives and anyone else is counted among the dead; the line calls being without understanding the worst death.
teaches: The couplet makes the living death a matter of not knowing ஒப்புரவு; the line widens it to any lack of understanding and ranks it below bodily death, while 52 in the same ten keeps the couplet's other half, knowing ஒப்புரவு as the best gain.
list_adds: The ten splits the couplet's antithesis across two separate lines (52 and 56), so knowing one's duty and lacking understanding become a highest gain and a worst death in a series of superlatives.

note: Kural 363 calls not wanting the finest wealth here and hereafter; the line calls wanting the greatest poverty.
teaches: The couplet makes desirelessness a wealth and the line makes desire a poverty, so together they move both wealth and poverty out of possessions and into the state of wanting.
list_adds: Placed two lines before begging is named the worst disgrace (59), the line sets desire as the poverty that leads to asking, a causal sequence the couplet does not draw.

note: Naladiyar 306 says a mind racked by desire (காதல் கவற்றும் மனம்) sends a man to beg of strangers when he could end his want by asking of himself; the line calls desire the greatest poverty.
teaches: The quatrain shows the mechanism the line only names: it is desire, not lack, that drives a man to beg, so the poverty that matters is the one inside.
list_adds: The line states the root in four words, as one of ten superlatives, where the quatrain needs a scene and a remedy; set beside 59, the ten's list makes desire and begging the worst poverty and the worst disgrace.

note: Kural 238 calls it a disgrace not to obtain the legacy called renown (இசையென்னும் எச்சம்); the line, using the same two words, calls renown the greatest legacy.
teaches: The couplet makes renown the minimum below which a life is disgraced; the line makes it the maximum above which there is no legacy, so the pair fixes fame as both the floor and the ceiling of what one leaves.
list_adds: In a ten that opens with children as the greatest gain (51), the line separates the legacy of fame from the gain of offspring, two senses that the couplet's எச்சம் leaves folded together.

note: 51 names the getting of children the greatest gain; 58 names renown the greatest எச்சம், a word that also means offspring.
teaches: Within one ten the two superlatives divide the field: children are the greatest gain in life, but what survives a person is ranked as fame, not progeny.
audit_text_issue: Packet flags that the site lacks line 2 of 51.

note: 59 makes begging the deepest disgrace; 60 makes giving to those who beg the highest distinction.
teaches: The ten scores one exchange twice, from both sides, so the asker's lowest point is the giver's highest, the same thing seen as shame and as honour.

note: Kural 1066 says nothing degrades the tongue more than asking, even for water for a cow; the line says no disgrace goes beyond begging.
teaches: The couplet tests the claim at its hardest case, a worthy cause and a tiny request, while the line states it bare, so the pair shows the superlative holds without exception for need or motive.
list_adds: Coupled with 60, the line's list sets the asker's disgrace beside the giver's distinction, so begging is judged inside an exchange rather than alone as the couplet judges it.

note: Purananuru 204 says giving at 'take' is high and refusing a gift is higher still (கொள்ளேன் என்றல் அதனினும் உயர்ந்தன்று); the line says no distinction exceeds giving to those who ask. The tension holds on the plain reading of the line's 'nothing greater'.
teaches: The bard's poem ranks the proud refusal of a gift above the gift, where the ethics line puts the giver at the summit, showing the puram ethic of honour placing the poet's self-respect above the patron's generosity.

note: Kural 231 says giving and living with renown are the only profit of life; the line ranks giving to askers as the highest distinction.
teaches: The couplet treats giving as a means to renown, the only profit; the line narrows the gift to one made to those who ask and makes its distinction an end, so the asker's presence is what makes the gift supreme.
list_adds: The ten sets giving to askers directly after begging as the worst disgrace (59), so the giver's distinction is ranked against the asker's shame, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: Naladiyar 68 grants that the worthy of standing (சீர்கொண்ட சான்றோர்) feel anger and says it cools of itself; the line says that a man of great standing (சீர்) being without anger is false.
teaches: Together they move the virtue of the eminent from having no anger to letting anger subside, since one says such a man will feel it and the other says how his anger differs from the low man's.
list_adds: Set beside the drunkard's lapses and the greedy judge, it counts anger as a thing that comes with high standing as surely as lapse comes with drink, a turn the quatrain's contrast of the worthy and the low does not make.
audit_text_issue: ஒன்றன் in line 1 looks corrupt; the reading assumes a person-noun such as பெருஞ்சீரோன்.

note: Kural 930 asks whether the drinker, seeing another drunk, does not think of the lapse (சோர்வு) of his own drinking; the line says a drinker without lapse is false.
teaches: The couplet hopes the drinker may see his own lapse in another man, and the line states that lapse as certain, so the pair shows the Kural's appeal resting on a fact the drinker refuses: that his lapse is not occasional but sure.
list_adds: It makes the drinker's lapse one of ten impossibilities with the greedy judge and the impure ascetic, a type-judgement on a kind of man rather than the couplet's question put to one drinker.

note: Innaa Narpathu 33 counts as painful the matter of business a drunkard speaks of; the line says a drinker free of lapses is false.
teaches: The Innaa line names the pain of dealing with a drinker's affairs and the Muthumozhikkanchi line gives its cause, the lapse that is certain in him, so one reports the effect and the other the reason no business with him is safe.

note: Kural 484 says even the world comes to hand (கைகூடும்) if one weighs the time and acts by the place; the line says gain coming to hand (கையுறல்) for one who does not know the time is false.
teaches: The couplet makes knowing the time enough for even the greatest gain, and the line makes it necessary for any gain, so together they give timing both halves of a condition: without it nothing comes to hand, with it even the world can.
list_adds: It states as an impossibility, beside nine others, the negative half that the couplet's promise leaves unsaid, and drops the couplet's second condition of place.

note: Kural 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming are not shaken by affliction; the line says one who does not know what is coming cannot guard himself.
teaches: The couplet joins knowing and guarding in one phrase and promises calm; the line pulls them apart and makes knowing the prior condition, so the pair shows that the Kural's guarding is itself a kind of knowledge, not a separate defence.
list_adds: In a ten that sets each act against the lack that makes it false, it isolates foresight as the single lack that undoes self-protection, where the couplet praises understanding in general.

note: Kural 978 says greatness always bows and smallness adorns itself in self-admiration; the line says one who cannot bear lowliness cannot rightly seek greatness.
teaches: The couplet describes greatness as bowing once it is had, and the line makes the bearing of low estate the road to it, so together they show humility as both the way to greatness and its mark once reached.
list_adds: Paired in its ten with its own mirror (68), it turns the couplet's contrast of two characters into a test of endurance applied to both high and low estate.

note: 67 denies greatness to one who cannot bear lowliness; 68 swaps the two words and denies lowliness to one who cannot bear greatness.
teaches: Read as a pair, the two lines make the capacity to bear one's station, high or low, the single condition of moving between them, so neither ambition nor humility is genuine in one who cannot endure the other state.
audit_text_issue: 68 is obscure; சிறுமைவேண்டல் may be the other's fall.

note: Kural 541 defines justice as inquiry, no favour to anyone, holding to the ruler's part and acting after thought; the line says justice done by one who craves wealth is false.
teaches: The couplet's definition is a procedure and says nothing of the judge's appetites; the line adds a condition on the judge himself, so the pair shows that the four steps can be kept in form and still be false if greed sits behind them.
list_adds: It sets greed for wealth among ten lacks that falsify an act, so justice is judged by the character of the one who does it, not by the steps the couplet lists.

note: Kural 262 says penance comes to those who have penance and is futile for those without it; the line says penance done by one who is not pure is false.
teaches: The couplet's condition for penance is circular, penance belongs to those who already have it, and the line names what that prior possession is, purity, so the pair turns the Kural's riddle into a stated precondition.
list_adds: In a ten that names the one lack that falsifies each act, it gives the precondition of penance a name, வாலியன், where the couplet leaves it as penance itself.

note: Thirikadugam 80 counts penance taken up by one without restraint of heart (நிறை) as seed sown on scrub; the line says penance by one who is not pure (வாலியன்) is false.
teaches: The two name different lacks, restraint of heart and purity, that make penance void, and one calls it barren where the other calls it false, so together they show the penance of the unfit failing both as fruit and as truth.

note: Purananuru 27 reports as hearsay (என்ப ... எனக் கேட்பல்) that those whom poets praise reach a sky-car no charioteer drives; the line states flatly that heaven is easy for those who desire fame.
teaches: The heroic poem hedges its heaven as something heard and grants it to the man others praise, while the maxim drops the hedge and grants it to the man who wants fame, so the pair shows a court belief hardening into a saying and its condition moving from the poet's praise to the seeker's own desire.

note: Kural 856 says the life of one who finds it sweet to excel in hostility is close to failure and ruin; the line says that a hard battle comes easily to one who loves contention.
teaches: Read together they give two links of one chain: the relish for rivalry brings battle near, and the man who relishes it has ruin near, so both texts measure the quarrelsome man by what lies close at hand rather than by what he chooses.
list_adds: In a ten where each desire draws its own easy consequence, battle is set beside disease for the glutton and blame for the lecher as the natural yield of an appetite, which the couplet, inside a chapter on hostility alone, does not do.

note: Kural 230 says nothing is more bitter than death, yet even death is sweet when giving cannot be done; the line says giving to the asker's wish comes easily to those who love kindness.
teaches: The line explains from the giver's side what the couplet asserts as a ranking: for one whose heart is moist, giving is so natural that being unable to give becomes, as the Kural says, worse than dying.
list_adds: It puts the ease of giving down to a disposition (ஈரம்) and sets it in a ten of desires and their yields, so generosity appears as the fruit of a love of kindness, where the couplet only ranks giving above life.

note: Kural 1076 likens the base to a beaten drum because they carry secrets they hear to others; the line says spreading secrets comes easily to those who love tale-bearing.
teaches: The couplet traces the spilling of secrets to a fixed baseness of nature, while the line traces it to an appetite for slander, so the pair shows that the drum-like betrayer is made by a taste he indulges, not only born base.
list_adds: Set among ten desires and their easy outcomes, it gives the betrayal of secrets a cause in a named desire (குறளை), where the couplet gives only an image and a class of person.

note: Kural 630 says that one who takes what hurts as pleasure gains a distinction his enemies admire; the line says pleasure comes easily to those who take on hardship.
teaches: The couplet pays the man who embraces hardship in esteem, the line pays him in pleasure itself, so together they show the old claim that welcomed toil returns both honour and the very joy that was given up.
list_adds: Paired in the ten with its mirror line 76, it turns the couplet's single reward into one half of a reversal law: what is chased flees and its opposite arrives, a symmetry the couplet does not draw.

note: 75 says pleasure comes easily to those who embrace hardship; 76, reversing the same two words, says pain comes easily to those who crave pleasure.
teaches: Placed side by side the two lines make one law from two sides: desire turns its object into its opposite, so the way to pleasure runs through accepted pain and the chase of pleasure ends in pain.

note: Naladiyar 60 says fools crave pleasure though suffering mounts, while the higher ones see the pain in each pleasure and do not cling; the line says pain comes easily to those who crave pleasure.
teaches: The Naladiyar finds pain lodged inside pleasure itself and so counsels detachment, while the line lays the pain on the craving and not on the pleasure, which leaves room, as its mirror 75 shows, for pleasure that comes to one who did not chase it.
list_adds: Its pairing with 75 makes pleasure attainable by the non-craving, a turn the renunciant quatrain does not allow, since it treats every pleasure as the seed of pain.

note: Kural 946 says joy stays with the one who eats knowing when to stop, as disease stays with the one who eats hugely; the line says grave disease comes easily to those who love food.
teaches: The couplet ties disease to the act of eating beyond measure, the line ties it to the love of food that precedes the act, so the pair moves the cause of illness back from the meal to the appetite.
list_adds: In the ten it stands beside blame for the lecher (78) and pain for the pleasure-seeker (76), so gluttony's disease is one instance of a general rule that a desire brings its own harm, where the couplet speaks in a chapter on medicine.
audit_text_issue: யோர்க்குப் before உறுபிணி is irregular sandhi.

note: Kural 146 says enmity, sin, fear and blame never leave one who crosses into another's home; the line says grievous blame comes easily to men who lust after women, naming no other's wife.
teaches: The Kural fixes blame on a single transgression against another man's house, while the line widens it to the roving desire itself, so the pair shows blame attaching first to the trespass and then, in the maxim, already to the appetite before any trespass.
list_adds: Among the ten's desires and their easy harms, the line gives blame as the natural yield of a craving, like disease for the glutton, where the couplet lists blame as one of four penalties for a specific act.

note: Kural 227 says the evil disease of hunger hardly touches one accustomed to பாத்தூண், sharing before eating; the line says பாத்தூண் comes easily to those who willingly bear a burden.
teaches: The couplet gives what the habit of shared eating protects against, the line gives what makes the habit easy, so together they show shared food as both the fruit of shouldering a charge and the guard against the hunger the miser fears.
list_adds: It traces the Kural's habit to a prior disposition to bear a load and sets it among good desires with good yields (fame, kindness, hardship), a cause the couplet does not give.

note: 38 reckons the support of a fool no better than being alone; 80 says that for those with no support, violent killing comes easily.
teaches: Joined, the two lines make an argument the book never states: a fool's support leaves one as good as alone, and to be without support is to be easily killed, so a foolish protector exposes a person to the same danger as none.

note: Kural 559 says that when the king bends justice the sky bends and withholds rain; the line says the land of a king without justice is poor.
teaches: The couplet gives a mechanism, the failed rain, and the line gives only the result, a poor land, so together they show the period's chain from royal injustice through the weather to the country's want.
list_adds: It sets the unjust king's land first in a ten of things that fail for lack of their ground, so misrule becomes the type of all such emptiness rather than a cosmic exception.

note: Line 26 says those living under a king who keeps no justice do not openly censure him; line 81 says his land is poor.
teaches: Read together, the subjects keep silent about an unjust king but the land itself shows the injustice through its poverty, so the blame the people withhold is spoken by the country.

note: Naladiyar 13 says aged men who cling to desire in the house have no path to safety; the line calls a very old woman's desire poor.
teaches: The quatrain condemns aged desire because it bars release, and the line condemns it with no thought of release and names a woman, so the pair shows one judgement on old age held on ascetic grounds and on plain worldly fitness.
list_adds: It places the old woman's desire among ten misfits of condition (a sick man's pleasure, an old man's ornament), judging it as unfitting rather than as a danger to the soul.

note: Both lines set an aged body against a good of youth: desire in an old woman (82), ornament on an old man (86).
teaches: The ten applies the same verdict to both sexes, desire for the woman and adornment for the man, so the pairing shows how the period divided what each was faulted for in age.

note: Kural 890 likens living with those not in accord to sharing a hut with a snake; the line calls joining with a hostile intimate poor.
teaches: The couplet stresses the danger of living beside the hostile, the line the futility of allying with them, so together they show the enemy within is both a threat and a bad bargain.
list_adds: It moves the couplet's fear into a reckoning of worth, counting such a union among things that are simply poor, which the snake image does not do.
audit_text_issue: The source has உறவோனை; tamilvu has உறைவோனை, which fits the link better.

note: Thirikadugam 4, item 3, counts taking into one's hand a man who once raged against one among the acts of one bound for death; the line calls joining with a hostile intimate poor.
teaches: Thirikadugam calls the embrace of a former foe deadly and Muthumozhikkanchi calls it worthless, so the same act is judged by its danger in one list and by its yield in the other.
audit_text_issue: muthumozhikkanchi:83 line 1 has உறவோன் where tamilvu reads உறைவோன்

note: Line 5 ranks freedom from bodily disease above youth; line 84 calls the pleasure of a sick man poor.
teaches: The first ten ranks health above youth and the ninth shows why, since disease empties even pleasure, so health appears as the ground other goods stand on.
audit_text_issue: Packet flags that the site's verse 5 is a different verse; the line as printed reads cleanly. | The packet flags that the site's verse 5 is a different verse (similarity 0.20), so the text of 5 is in doubt.

note: Kural 1308 asks what use suffering is where no lover knows of it; the line calls sulking poor where one is not cherished. Both turn on an absent beloved's care (இல்லா வழி, போற்றாவழி).
teaches: The couplet speaks of grief with no one to notice and the line of sulking with no one to appease it, so together they show that every display of hurt in love has worth only before someone who cares.
list_adds: It takes a lover's sulk out of the Kural's love book and sets it among public ills like misrule and empty anger, treating it as one more act that fails without its ground.

note: Innaa Narpathu 27, item 3, calls beauty in those without means painful; the line calls ornament on an aged body poor.
teaches: One list makes beauty depend on wealth and the other makes adornment depend on youth, so together they show that beauty in these works is never good alone and fails when either support is gone.

note: Kural 720 likens speaking before those not of one's set to nectar spilled in a drain; the line calls speech poor where words do not carry.
teaches: The couplet locates the waste in the hearers' unfitness, the line in the word's lack of force, so together they show that speech fails either from the audience or from the speaker's standing.
list_adds: It puts futile speech beside futile anger (89) and futile sulking (85) in one ten, making each a case of an act without the power to land.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 printed சொற்சொல்லாவழி; tamilvu reads சொல் செல்லாவழி. | Our text has சொற்சொல்லாவழி; the link depends on tamilvu's சொல் செல்லாவழி.

note: Kural 301 says restraint of anger counts only where anger can take effect; the line calls anger poor where it inspires no awe.
teaches: The couplet says restraining powerless anger is no virtue, and the line says indulging it is no gain, so together they show that anger without power is worth nothing whether held back or let loose.
list_adds: It judges anger by its effect, as one of ten things emptied by a missing condition, where the couplet judges the restraint of anger as a virtue.

note: Innaa Narpathu 21, item 2, calls going to eat with those who do not share their food painful; the line calls going where there is no friendship poor.
teaches: Innaa Narpathu names the particular case, the stingy table, and the line states the general rule behind it, so together they show the visit's worth lying in the host's bond, not in what is offered.

note: Line 10 ranks not dwindling later above swelling at first; 92 says the one who wants to swell does not leave off gathering renown.
teaches: Read together, the two lines say that greatness is kept from shrinking only by an unbroken run of creditable deeds, so the unslackening of the last ten is the answer to the dwindling feared in the first.
audit_text_issue: Packet flags that the site's verse 10 is a different verse; numbering of 10 is uncertain.

note: Line 8 ranks revering the learned above one's own learning; 93 makes unbroken reverent service the condition of learning at all.
teaches: The first ten treats reverence as a value above learning and the last treats it as the road to learning, so the book holds both that service is the means and that it outranks the end.
audit_text_issue: The packet flags verse 8 as differing from the site's text (similarity 0.28), so its numbering or reading may not be settled.

note: Kural 395 says the learned learnt by standing before those who know as the poor stand yearning before the rich; 93 says the would-be learner never drops வழிபாடு.
teaches: The couplet gives the learner's posture as a beggar's longing, and the line gives it as worship that never lapses, so the pair shows humility in learning as both a hunger and a sustained service.
list_adds: In a ten that pairs each goal with the practice its seeker never drops, reverence is set beside toil for plenty and penance for steadfastness, so it reads as the price of learning, where the couplet uses it to rank the learned above the unlearned.

note: Kural 265 says penance is pursued here because it gains whatever one wishes, as one wishes; 94 names one such wish, to stand firm, and says its seeker never leaves off penance.
teaches: The couplet makes penance a means to any wish at all, while the line ties it to one wish and requires it without a break, so the pair moves from penance's open promise to its continuing cost.
list_adds: It sets penance among nine other practices each tied to its own goal, so penance becomes one specialised means among learning, toil and justice rather than the universal means the couplet makes it.
audit_text_issue: நிற்றல் has no stated object

note: Kural 671 says deliberation ends in resolve and that delay after resolving is an evil; 95 says the one who wants a good life never leaves off deliberation.
teaches: For a single task the couplet closes deliberation once resolved, and for a whole life the line keeps it always open, so the pair shows deliberation ending task by task while never ending as a habit of living.
list_adds: It carries சூழ்ச்சி from the minister's work on one undertaking, where the couplet places it, to the making of a whole life, by setting it in a list of lifelong practices.

note: Kural 619 says effort yields its wage of bodily strain even where fate will not grant the end; 96 says one who wants plenty does not shun வருத்தம்.
teaches: The line makes toil necessary for plenty and the couplet makes it rewarding even against fate, so the pair gives both halves: there is no abundance without strain, and strain is never wholly unpaid.
list_adds: Among goals and their unbroken practices, the list makes toil the specific price of surplus, beside pain as the price of pleasure, a pairing of goal and cost the couplet's defence of effort against fate does not make.

note: Kural 628 says the one who does not desire pleasure and takes suffering as natural is never distressed; 97 says the one who wants pleasure does not shun pain.
teaches: Both bind pain to the pursuit of pleasure, but the couplet frees the man who stops desiring pleasure while the line binds the man who keeps desiring it, so the pair gives the two exits from the same bond.
list_adds: Placed beside its mirror in 98, the line makes pleasure and pain each the cost of the other, a symmetrical turn the couplet, which speaks of only one direction, lacks.

note: 97 says the seeker of pleasure does not shun pain; 98 reverses the terms, so the seeker of pain does not hold back from pleasure.
teaches: Taken as a pair the two lines say the same truth from both sides: pleasure and pain are tied so closely that whoever chases either is pursuing the other.

note: Naladiyar 60 says fools long for pleasure while suffering mounts, and the higher ones see the pain in each pleasure and do not cling; 98 names the unchecked pleasure-seeker as one who in effect wants pain.
teaches: The quatrain describes the wise seeing pain inside pleasure, and the line describes what follows when that is not seen, so the pair joins the renouncer's insight to the verdict it passes on the one who lacks it.
list_adds: The line compresses the quatrain's contrast of fool and sage into a single reversed formula, and its mirroring with 97 makes the point by form alone, without the quatrain's turn to renunciation.

note: Kural 547 says the king protects the world and just order (முறை) protects the king when he keeps it without fail; 99 says the one who wants safety does not leave off acting by just order.
teaches: The couplet explains why the king's safety lies in justice and the line states it as an unbroken practice, so the pair shows justice as the ruler's own shelter and not only a duty owed to the ruled.
list_adds: It puts the king's justice in a list where each seeker keeps a practice for his own end, so just rule is framed as what the ruler does for his own security, the same way the learner keeps reverence.

note: Purananuru 35 counsels Killivalavan that in a land of just rule, where the humble can reach the king when they seek முறை, rain comes when sought, and that if he protects his people the unsubmitting will bow; 99 states the bare rule that security needs just order.
teaches: The poem shows to a named Chola what just rule looks like and what it brings, the king reached by the humble and the enemy bowing, and the line reduces the same counsel to a maxim any ruler can carry.

note: Kural 1097 says small words without real anger and hostile looks are the signs of those who are close while seeming distant; 100 says the one who wants love does not give up hinted speech.
teaches: The line says the lover speaks by hint and the couplet shows how hints are read, even harsh ones turned inside out, so the pair gives both the speaker's practice and the hearer's skill.
list_adds: It closes a ten of public goals and their practices with love and its indirection, so hinting stands beside justice and toil as a discipline, where the couplet treats it as a sign within the lovers' scene.

note: Both invocations of the group open on Vishnu's stride across the earth: Thirikadugam counts it among three deeds of the feet, Nanmanikkadigai among four deeds of the 'son'.
teaches: Set side by side, the two invocations show the counted form fitted to the god before it is fitted to conduct: each book praises him in its own number, three deeds or four.

note: The Kural uses the strider of the earth as the measure of what a king free from sloth gains; the invocation worships the stride itself.
teaches: The same three steps serve the Kural as a measure of a diligent king's reach and the invocation as an act of the god, so the myth is shared ground between worship and statecraft.
list_adds: It puts the stride among three other cosmic deeds (swallowing the earth, lifting the hill, breaking Sho), so the step is one of the god's acts rather than a yardstick of gain.

note: The Naladiyar says true living is never to ask even of the dearest; Nanmanikkadigai forbids only taking so that the hand of those one should not receive from is above one's own.
teaches: Against the quatrain's ban on all asking, the verse draws the line at the giver: receiving is shameful when the hand above is one that should not be.
list_adds: It sets the rule on receiving beside rules against contempt for the lowly and rage at the humble-born, so the shame of the raised hand is one of four checks on rank-pride.
audit_text_issue: கொள்ளார் is ambiguous: those one should not receive from, or those who themselves would not take.

note: Kural 969 compares men who die when honour is lost to the yak that dies when its hair is gone; Nanmanikkadigai has the asunam die at the drum and nobility die at an unworthy word.
teaches: Read together, the couplet says honour's loss kills its owner, and the verse adds that a single unfit word is enough to kill nobility, so the threat is speech, not only deed.
list_adds: It sets nobility's death beside three natural deaths (the asunam, the strong, the seeding bamboo), so the word that kills it is ranked with the drum and the bamboo's own fruit as a fatal cause.

note: Kural 796 calls ruin a rod that measures one's people; Nanmanikkadigai says the use of kin is known by being ruined, after the washing of gems, riding of horses and burning of gold.
teaches: Together they show ruin as an assay: the couplet names its single benefit, and the verse sets it in the craftsman's sequence of tests, where the tester pays the cost.
list_adds: It makes testing kin by ruin the last of four assays with gem, horse and gold, so the kin test is the one that burns the tester, not the thing tested.

note: The Naladiyar prizes salt born in barren ground above rice from fertile fields and puts the learned of low origin in the highest place; Nanmanikkadigai says agil, orpiment and pearls come from mean sources and no one knows the family a good woman is born in.
teaches: Both books use a precious thing from a poor source to cut worth loose from birth, the Naladiyar for the learned man and Nanmanikkadigai for the good woman.
list_adds: Its three natural instances (spurge, deer's belly, sea) build to a question rather than a command, so the reader is left unable to trace goodness to a family.

note: Kural 959 says a person's words show the lineage he was born in, as a sprout shows the soil; Nanmanikkadigai asks who can know the family a good woman is born in.
teaches: On the plain reading the couplet treats the person as evidence of the family, while the verse denies that inference: goodness, like agil from the spurge, does not reveal its stock.
list_adds: Its three images of precious things from unlikely sources make the point by pattern: if agil comes from the kalli, the source cannot be read from the product.

note: Kural 247 says this world is not for those without wealth as the other is not for those without அருள்; Nanmanikkadigai says the way of virtue is born of அருள் and everything is born of wealth.
teaches: The same pair of அருள் and பொருள் appears in both, but the verse turns the couplet's two worlds into two sources: one of virtue, one of everything else.
list_adds: It sets the pair after the gem from stone and delight from the beloved's word, and closes on wealth as the source of all, which makes the couplet's balance end in wealth's favour.

note: Naladiyar 280 says earning, guarding, losing and ruin of wealth are all suffering; Nanmanikkadigai says those who plan to make wealth and those who guard it get no sleep.
teaches: The quatrain says wealth is suffering at every stage; the verse names the suffering as sleeplessness and gives it to the thief and the lover as well.
list_adds: It ranks the earner and guardian of wealth with the thief and the lovesick as sleepless men, so lawful wealth shares its unrest with theft and longing.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 பார்ககுந் is a misprint for பார்க்குந்.

note: Thirikadugam 73 names the man who says he will make bright wealth by begging as one who lives daring the hard; Nanmanikkadigai says the one who plans to make bright wealth gets no sleep.
teaches: The two books use the same phrase for the plan to make bright wealth and both make it a hardship: Thirikadugam a daring, Nanmanikkadigai a sleepless night.

note: Kural 304 says anger kills smile and joy and is the worst enemy; Nanmanikkadigai says before the angry everything fails to show and is ruined.
teaches: The couplet names what anger kills in the angry man; the verse widens it to everything before him, so anger blinds as well as destroys.
list_adds: It sets anger's ruin after three things that do not show before the learned, the resolved and the wrongdoer, so anger closes a list of what each kind of person cannot see.
audit_text_issue: உறாமுதல் uncertain

note: Kural 1014 calls shame the ornament of the worthy; Nanmanikkadigai calls modesty the ornament of a woman's beauty.
teaches: The Kural gives shame to the worthy of either sex as their ornament, while the verse assigns it to women's beauty, so the pair shows the virtue narrowed into a gendered adornment.
list_adds: It puts women's modesty in a row of ornaments with paddy for land and lotus for pond, which makes the virtue something that decorates a seen beauty, where the Kural makes it a guard of conduct.

note: Thirikadugam 52 calls modesty the ornament of a woman in love and learning the ornament for the next life; Nanmanikkadigai calls modesty the ornament of women's beauty and virtue the ornament for the world one goes to.
teaches: Both short works pair a woman's modesty with an ornament for the next life, so the gendered ornament and the otherworldly one are a shared pairing of the group, not one poet's choice.

note: Verse 9 calls virtue one's own ornament for the world one goes to; verse 15 says that if one wants what goes along with oneself, one should do virtue.
teaches: Within the book virtue is twice the one thing that crosses death, once as an ornament worn and once as a companion that goes along.

note: Kural 1078 says the worthy are of use at a word and the base only when crushed like cane; Nanmanikkadigai binds the base with iron and the worthy by courtesy.
teaches: The couplet speaks of what the two yield; the verse of how they are held, so the pair moves from extracting good to restraining harm with the same contrast.
list_adds: It puts the base and the worthy in a row with the raging elephant and the great serpent, so each kind of creature has its own binding and courtesy becomes a bond.

note: Kural 108 says it is not good to forget a good done and good to forget at once what is not good; Nanmanikkadigai asks one not to be embittered by harsh acts and to hold the good done as good.
teaches: Both pair forgetting injury with remembering help; the verse goes on to one's own anger and ruinous deeds, so the inward work follows the outward.
list_adds: It follows the couplet's pair with two rules about oneself (letting anger go, destroying the self-ruining deed), so forgiving others is set beside disciplining oneself.

note: Kural 29 says the anger of those who have climbed the hill of virtue is hard to withstand even for a moment; Nanmanikkadigai says sages give harm through their penance.
teaches: The couplet warns of the ascetic's anger; the verse names its weapon, penance itself, and sets it with the snake's tooth and the elephant's tusk.
list_adds: It ranks the sage's penance with the snake's tooth, the elephant's tusk and the sulking woman's face as four instruments of harm, so holy power is classed as a natural weapon.

note: Kural 968 asks whether feeding the body is a medicine once dignity is lost; Nanmanikkadigai says hunger is better than eating with dignity undone.
teaches: The couplet questions the worth of a life fed without honour; the verse states the choice as a meal: go hungry rather than eat so.
list_adds: It places the choice among three other preferences of the plain over the spoiled (drum over untuned lute, a firm woman over worthless men, fire over parting), so hunger is one of four lesser goods.

note: Kural 1159 says fire burns only when touched, but love burns when one moves away; Nanmanikkadigai says entering fire is better than parting from those one is bound to.
teaches: Both weigh separation against fire and find separation the worse, the couplet in a lover's voice and the verse as a general rule of attachment.
list_adds: It carries the lover's comparison into a list of plain preferences, so parting from one's own becomes a general loss, not only love's.

note: Kural 525 says one who gives and speaks sweetly is ringed by kin; Nanmanikkadigai says the throng of kin rises in the pit of sweet speech and liberality grows in the bed of plenty.
teaches: The couplet gives two causes of a crowd of kin; the verse splits them, puts each in its own soil, and pairs them with the bad crops of harsh speech and poverty.
list_adds: It makes each disposition a crop of its condition, two good and two bad, so kin-gathering is shown with its opposite, concealment from harsh speech.
audit_text_issue: line division of வன்சொல் (lines 2-3) uncertain; line 1 misprint repaired

note: Naladiyar 306 says poverty can be ended by asking oneself rather than begging from strangers; Nanmanikkadigai says begging springs up quickly in the pit of poverty.
teaches: The verse describes begging as poverty's quick crop; the quatrain answers that the crop need not grow if one begs of oneself, so the pair sets the natural course against the discipline that stops it.
list_adds: It sets begging as the last of four growths from their soils, so it appears as a natural consequence where the Naladiyar treats it as a choice.
audit_text_issue: The division of lines 2-3 (where வன்சொல் belongs) is uncertain.

note: Kural 36 says to do virtue now, since it is the companion that does not perish when one does; Nanmanikkadigai says that one who wants what goes along with oneself should do virtue.
teaches: Both make virtue the one companion past death, and the verse puts it as a means to a wish, beside fame for lasting here and giving up anger for winning.
list_adds: Its 'if you want X, do Y' frame sets virtue as the means for one wish among four, with begging as the ironic means to pain, so the virtues become instruments chosen by their ends.

note: Verse 11 says one must always let go of one's anger; verse 15 says one who wants to win should give up anger.
teaches: The two verses together give the rule and its reason: anger is let go not only as a duty but because giving it up is how one wins.

note: Verse 14 says begging rises quickly in the pit of poverty; verse 15 says one who wants pain should rise to beg.
teaches: Read together, the book gives begging both a cause and a fruit: it grows from poverty and it yields pain.
audit_text_issue: Nanmanikkadigai 14 line 1 is repaired (கிளைக்குழாம்).

note: Kural 725 says to learn by the proper path so as to answer without fear in the assembly; Nanmanikkadigai says the learned man crosses the deep of the assembly.
teaches: The couplet gives the purpose of learning as fearless reply; the verse calls the assembly a deep like the sea and a battle line, which shows why that fear is real.
list_adds: It ranks the learned man's crossing of the assembly with the sailor's sea, the horseman's army and the ascetic's penance, so speaking before an assembly is made as perilous as war or the sea.

note: Thirikadugam 7 names the hard learning of one who fears assemblies as a mute's dream; Nanmanikkadigai says the learned man crosses the deep of the assembly.
teaches: The same claim is put from two sides: learning that fails in the assembly is useless, and learning is what carries a man across it.

note: Naladiyar 53 lists home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength as not lasting, so the best renounce them; Nanmanikkadigai gives friendship, youth, wealth and life each its own end.
teaches: The quatrain says these things do not last; the verse says what each ends in, and three of the ends (falsehood, old age, excess) come from the thing itself.
list_adds: It assigns each thing its own end, so wealth ends in excess and friendship in falsehood rather than all ending alike, and it adds friendship, which the quatrain does not name.

note: Kural 523 says one who does not mingle with kin lives like a tank filling with no bank; Nanmanikkadigai says casting off kin is the gain of ruin.
teaches: The couplet shows the loss in an image of wealth spilling away; the verse names it ironically as ruin's prosperity, closing a list of what builds.
list_adds: It sets casting off kin after three true sources of prosperity (a good wife, uprightness, a king's good name), so the last item undoes the predicate by calling ruin a gain.

note: Kural 386 says the land of an accessible king who is not harsh of speech is spoken of above others; Nanmanikkadigai says the land's prosperity is people saying 'this king is good'.
teaches: The couplet gives the king's conduct that earns praise; the verse makes that praise itself the land's wealth.
list_adds: It sets the king's good name among the prosperity of house and work, so the realm's gain is one of a household series, measured by speech.

note: Verse 18 says excellent women are the prosperity of a house; verse 20 says the lack of a bright-browed wife lays a house waste.
teaches: The book states the same claim from both sides, prosperity with a good wife and waste without one, so the house is defined by the wife's presence.

note: Verse 16 says the learned man crosses the deep of the assembly; verse 19 says that if the learned man shakes, the meaning shakes.
teaches: The book qualifies its praise of the learned: he carries the meaning across the assembly only while he holds firm, and his faltering loses it.
audit_text_issue: அதிர் in Nanmanikkadigai 19 may mean tremble or roar; the sense is uncertain. | அதிர் may mean tremble or roar

note: Kural 406 likens the unlearned to barren saline ground; Nanmanikkadigai says a body without learned understanding is waste to oneself.
teaches: Both use waste land for the unlearned, but the couplet says they yield nothing to others while the verse says the body is waste to its owner.
list_adds: It sets the unlearned body after a house without a wife, a region without friends and an assembly without elders, so the ignorant self is one of four places laid waste by an absence.

note: Thirikadugam 10 names an assembly with no elders to settle quarrels among three things that yield no good; Nanmanikkadigai calls lack of elders waste to the assembly.
teaches: Both short works make elders the thing an assembly cannot do without, and Thirikadugam gives the reason the verse omits: elders settle disputes.

note: Naladiyar 177 says water mixed with milk becomes milk, so the small are hidden by joining the great; Nanmanikkadigai says the vessel spoils the milk, as bad company ruins a lineage.
teaches: The same mixing image runs both ways in the group, the good absorbing the small in one and the container corrupting the good in the other, so company is shown to work in both directions.
list_adds: It sets the spoiled milk among four kinds of ruin (disunity, falsehood, bad company), so mixing is counted as a cause of loss, not of concealment.

note: Verse 22 says learning gives eyes cleared of darkness; verse 28 traces learning step by step through lessened ignorance to the path of truth and the higher world.
teaches: Read together, the single sight learning gives in 22 becomes in 28 the first link of a chain that ends beyond this world.

note: Kural 805 tells one to read a friend's hurtful act as folly or intimacy; Nanmanikkadigai says friends, even angry, do nothing that makes one tremble.
teaches: The couplet expects friends to wound and supplies a charitable reading, while the verse sets a limit no anger crosses, so the pair marks how far a friend's hurt may go.
list_adds: It ranks the friend with the elephant and the beaten child as bonds that hold under strain, against the enemy who never stays, a contrast the couplet lacks.
audit_text_issue: line 1 மலைப்பினும் வாரணந் தாங்கும் uncertain

note: Both verses open with laughter among friends: in 24 its good grows there, in 37 it is sweet there.
teaches: The book twice makes friendship the condition of laughter, once as growth and once as pleasure, so laughter is never praised in itself but only in company.

note: Kural 428 calls not fearing what should be feared folly; Nanmanikkadigai says that if one fears anything, it should be fearlessness itself.
teaches: The couplet sorts objects of fear, while the verse turns fear on the fearless disposition, so the danger moves from the thing feared to the temper of the man.
list_adds: It makes the fear of fearlessness the first of four checks on oneself, with not falling short, not swerving for wealth and trusting friends, so fear opens a short code of integrity.
audit_text_issue: Line 1's division (அஞ்சாமை அஞ்சுதி ஒன்றின்) is not certain.

note: Kural 510 says doubting one already trusted brings endless trouble; Nanmanikkadigai says not to pry into a task left with friends.
teaches: The couplet states the general error of doubting the trusted, and the verse turns it into a working rule about checking up on a delegated task.
list_adds: It puts non-interference with friends' work beside refusing a crore against one's conscience, so trust in friends is counted as part of one's own integrity.
audit_text_issue: Line 1-2 (எஞ்சாமை எஞ்சல்) is hard to construe.
