note: Kural 256 argues that buyers cause the killing, since no one would sell flesh if none bought; Nanmanikkadigai counts buying and eating flesh as a fault in its own right.
teaches: The couplet needs an argument to make the buyer guilty, while the verse simply lists buying and killing as two faults, showing the group's code taking the Kural's conclusion as settled.
list_adds: It sets the buyer's fault beside the killer's and beside rearing beings to torment them and improper speech, so flesh-buying becomes one of four plain faults rather than the end of an argument.

note: Both lists put killing and eating flesh beside a fault of speech: Nanmanikkadigai saying what should not be said, Sirupanchamoolam speaking evil of a girl without inquiry.
teaches: Two counted works independently join a speech fault to the code of non-killing, so harmful words are filed with harm to bodies across the group.
audit_text_issue: Sirupanchamoolam 12 line 3 இளங்கிளியை is doubtful.

note: Kural 542 says the world looks to the sky and the people to the sceptre; Nanmanikkadigai keeps both and adds the infant at the breast and Death looking to the world's end.
teaches: The verse borrows the couplet's two dependencies and closes them with Death's grim watch, so the image of living by looking to a giver ends in the one watcher who takes.
list_adds: It adds the infant's dependence on milk and inverts the series with Death, so the king's sceptre is one giver among nurturers set against a taker.

note: Kural 398 says learning gained in one birth protects through seven; Nanmanikkadigai traces how learning reaches the other world step by step.
teaches: The couplet states that learning outlasts a life, and the verse supplies the stages by which it does so, ignorance lessening into insight, insight into the true path, the path into fame and the higher world.
list_adds: It turns the couplet's single benefit into a chain of four causes, so the reward beyond this life is earned through intermediate changes in the learner.

note: Kural 421 calls understanding the tool that guards against ruin; Nanmanikkadigai says understanding is found standing where trouble befalls oneself.
teaches: The couplet gives understanding its use as a guard, and the verse gives the place where it is proved, one's own adversity.
list_adds: It sets understanding among things known by where they settle (water in a hollow, sin under blame, desire in a crowding), so understanding is defined by its location in trouble.
audit_text_issue: Line 2-3 அழித்துச் செறிவுழி is obscure.

note: Kural 1041 says nothing is more painful than poverty except poverty itself; Nanmanikkadigai names poverty the most painful of all things.
teaches: The couplet leaves poverty incomparable, while the verse places the hand that never refuses right after it, so the extreme of want is paired with the extreme of giving.
list_adds: It makes the pain of poverty one of four superlatives and follows it with the generous hand, so the list supplies the remedy the couplet leaves out.
audit_text_issue: வன்பாட்டது (line 4) is uncertain.

note: Kural 871 says enmity should not be wanted even in jest; Nanmanikkadigai says enmity sprouts from a man's own prior intent and then becomes a seed of suffering.
teaches: The couplet warns against wanting enmity, and the verse explains why: it grows from one's own intention and multiplies into more pain.
list_adds: It sets enmity beside fire from smoke and joy from laughter, so laughter seeds joy while intent seeds enmity, a contrast to the couplet's 'not even in jest'.

note: Nanmanikkadigai likens the hard-hearted to stone; Naladiyar 334 ranks stones above base people because stones at least serve whoever uses them.
teaches: The two verses use stone in opposite ways, as hardness to be blamed and as plain usefulness to be praised, so the base man is lower than the very thing the hard-hearted resemble.
list_adds: It makes stone one of four likenesses (disease, ornament, weeds), so the image names a kind of person rather than ranking people against things.

note: Reading என்செயினும் with line 1, Nanmanikkadigai holds the brahmin's birth best whatever he does; Kural 134 says a brahmin's birth is ruined when his conduct fails.
teaches: On that reading the two make incompatible claims about whether conduct can forfeit a high birth, which shows the group divided on birth against conduct.
list_adds: It ranks brahmin birth alongside the mother, prosperity and youth as unequalled goods, so birth is treated as a fixed endowment like youth, not a standing to be kept.
audit_text_issue: என்செயினும் construal

note: Nanmanikkadigai ranks the brahmin's birth above all others; the Siddhar verse asks whether a number is marked on flesh or bone to tell a Paraiyar woman from a Brahmin woman.
teaches: Set together, a birth-rank stated as plain fact meets a later denial that birth leaves any mark on the body, showing the claim the ethics work takes for granted being contested.
audit_text_issue: Siddhar 1003 பணத்தி is read as the brahmin woman by tradition only.

note: Verse 33 ranks brahmin birth highest; verse 40 says fortune does not abide by rank or kind.
teaches: The book ranks births yet denies that birth secures fortune, so within one work high birth is honoured but given no hold on prosperity.

note: Kural 443 calls winning the great as one's own the rarest of rare things; Nanmanikkadigai says great things are reached through great men, as iron splits iron.
teaches: The couplet prizes the great as companions, and the verse explains the worth by a law of like working on like, so the great are needed because only they can reach great ends.
list_adds: It proves the claim with two physical cases (iron on iron, water rinsing after water), so the moral rule is given the force of a natural one.

note: Kural 1076 likens the base to a beaten drum that proclaims secrets; Nanmanikkadigai says the elation of the base blares through the town.
teaches: The couplet shows the base unable to keep others' secrets, and the verse shows them unable to keep their own joy quiet, so loudness marks them in both.
list_adds: It sets the base man's elation against the warrior's before kings and the giver's before the poor, ranking kinds of joy by where they show.

note: Kural 260 says all creatures fold their hands to the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; Nanmanikkadigai says others' not eating flesh is the refuge of living beings.
teaches: Both speak from the side of the creatures, the couplet as their worship and the verse as their shelter, so abstaining from flesh is a protection given, not only a purity kept.
list_adds: It puts abstention beside givers as the beggar's refuge and valour as an army's, so refusing flesh is counted among the supports others depend on.

note: Kural 1253 has a woman say her desire shows like a sneeze though she would hide it; Nanmanikkadigai says desire cannot be hidden however hard one tries.
teaches: The lover's confession in the couplet becomes in the verse a general law, so a moment of love poetry is used as ethical knowledge.
list_adds: It sets desire beside fortune and Death as things no one controls, so its showing is ranked with impersonal forces rather than one woman's weakness.

note: Kural 376 says what is one's lot will not stay though guarded nor go though thrown away; the verse says the same of life itself at birth and at death.
teaches: The couplet's law of lot, said of possessions, is extended to the life that holds them: being born and dying are the first goods one cannot keep or refuse.
list_adds: It sets life's coming and going beside Fortune's swelling and ruin's vanishing, so birth, death, gain and loss become one set of things outside command.
audit_text_issue: verse flagged uncertain by marker

note: Kural 761 ranks a complete, wound-fearing army first among a king's wealth; the verse says a king's glory withers without one.
teaches: Read together, the army is both the king's chief possession and the root his fame grows from, so losing it is not a loss of goods but a drying-up of renown.
list_adds: It puts the king's army in a row with war for warriors, roots for trees and the sluice for the neytal, so the army becomes the hidden supply of glory, not a holding.

note: Naladiyar 101 pictures an old deed seeking out its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the verse calls one's former deed one's mother.
teaches: The two images run the bond in opposite directions: in the Naladiyar the deed hunts the doer like a calf its mother, here the deed is the mother who bore the doer.
list_adds: It ends a list that redefines stranger, beloved and father, so karma takes the place of the mother in a whole remade family.

note: Kural 812 dismisses the friendship of misfits who come with gain and leave without it; the verse says friends' friendship perishes when the good changes.
teaches: The couplet blames a bad kind of friend, while the verse makes the fading of friendship with advantage a natural law, like a crop without water, so the fault may lie in friendship itself.
list_adds: It sets friendship's decay beside a crop dying without water, so the end of interested friendship reads as nature, not as a vice of some.
audit_text_issue: ஐவர் and பொறி uncertain

note: Kural 1019 says lasting shamelessness burns every good; the verse says fortune perishes the moment shame is lost.
teaches: The verse makes the couplet's slow burning instant (போழ்தே, the very moment), so the loss of shame is shown as a sudden rather than gradual ruin.
list_adds: It puts the loss of shame first in a list of four ruins of the same form, so shame stands with water for crops as the thing whose absence ends goods at once.

note: Kural 1308 asks what use suffering is where there is no lover to know it; the verse says a sulk dies in one who does not understand sulking.
teaches: Both put the life of oodal in the partner's understanding, and the verse adds that the same is true of gratitude, guests and song, so the lover's plight is one case of a general rule.
list_adds: It sets the sulk beside a kindness, a guest and a song, so love's quarrel becomes one of four gifts that die in an incompetent receiver.

note: Kural 90 says a guest wilts when the host's face changes; the verse says a guest dies before those without the wish to receive.
teaches: The couplet locates the guest's wilting in a visible face, the verse in the host's absent desire, so the face is shown as the sign of a want of welcome that kills even before it shows.
list_adds: It sets the guest beside gratitude, song and sulk, so hospitality is a gift that needs a fit receiver, like art.

note: Kural 707 asks whether anything is as knowing as the face, which reaches first in joy or anger; the verse says nothing tells the intention beforehand as the face does.
teaches: Both make the face faster than speech, and the verse sets this speed against slower signs, scent, weighed words and the mind, so priority in time is what makes the face the best witness.
list_adds: It ranks the face above three other signs (scent, words, mind), making the couplet's claim a contest won rather than a lone assertion.
audit_text_issue: முன்னம் may be 'before' or 'intention'

note: Kural 19 says giving and penance will not last if the sky does not give rain; the verse says rain does not fall where there are no ascetics.
teaches: The Kural makes penance depend on rain and the verse makes rain depend on penance, so together they describe a circle in which ascetic and sky sustain each other.
list_adds: It makes rain one link in a chain that ends with king and householder, so the couplet's dependence becomes a whole social order resting on the house.

note: Thirikadugam 96 names the knowing wife, the ascetic who keeps his vow and the good king as three at whose word rain falls; the verse makes rain rest on ascetics, ascetics on the king, the king on householders.
teaches: Both books make human virtue the cause of rain, but Thirikadugam sets three causes side by side while the verse lines them up, so one gives co-equal powers and the other a chain of dependence ending in the household.
audit_text_issue: Thirikadugam 96 line 3 is repaired (செய்வான்).

note: Naladiyar 111 says saying 'I have none' of what one cannot give is no disgrace and is the way of the world; the verse says saying 'nothing' to beggars is hard for anyone.
teaches: The quatrain frees refusal from blame and the verse says it is still hard to say, so together they separate guilt from difficulty: refusal is no fault but costs everyone.
list_adds: It ranks refusal as the hardest of four hard things, the only one hard for anyone, whereas the quatrain only judges it.

note: Kural 223 says not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing' and giving belong only to the well-born; the verse says saying 'nothing' to beggars is hard for anyone.
teaches: The couplet makes the refusal to refuse a mark of birth, the verse makes the reluctance to refuse universal, so lineage is no longer needed to explain it.
list_adds: It sets refusing beggars among difficulties tied to kinds of person (the eminent, the kin-born, the stingy) and frees this last one from any kind.

note: Kural 942 says the body needs no medicine if one eats after the last meal is digested; the verse says food burns a body that takes no pleasure in it.
teaches: The couplet gives the rule for eating, the verse the damage when the body cannot take food, so the pair shows food as medicine or fire depending on the body's state.
list_adds: It sets food beside words, past deeds and an army, all things meant to serve that turn and burn their holder.

note: Kural 423 says understanding is seeing the true substance of whatever is heard from whomever; the verse says the meanings of the many books are things to be examined.
teaches: The couplet gives the test for any utterance, and the verse applies it to the many books themselves, so even the written tradition must be sifted, not merely received.
list_adds: It puts sifting the books last in a sequence of right responses (deride contempt, ponder counsel, join dharma), so examination is the final act of a learner's conduct.

note: Kural 259 ranks not killing one creature above a thousand sacrifices; the verse says there is beneficence equal to sacrifice.
teaches: Both measure an ethical act against sacrifice, but the Kural puts non-killing above it and the verse puts beneficence level with it, so sacrifice stays the standard in one and is outranked in the other.
list_adds: It makes beneficence equal to sacrifice as a tank can hold a river and a song reach the Veda, so the claim is one of a set of lesser things rising to the greater.

note: Thirikadugam 12 defines the vellalan as one who does not eat while a guest waits; the verse defines him as one who owns oxen.
teaches: Both define the same birth-group name by a mark, but one by hospitality and the other by owning the plough-ox, so the period's ethics offered rival tests, conduct or possession, for who deserved the name.

note: Kural 56 says she is a woman who guards herself, cares for her husband and keeps their good name without flagging; the verse says the woman of household life has wisdom with her beauty.
teaches: Both make பெண் a title to be earned, but the Kural earns it by guarding and serving while the verse asks for wisdom joined to beauty, a different test of the same name.
list_adds: It puts the wife among definitions of the farmer, the brahmin, the cock and the commander, so a woman's title is one of a set of role-names each tied to a mark.

note: Kural 460 says nothing brings more affliction than bad company; the verse says the bad delighting in the bad is ruin.
teaches: The couplet warns the good against bad company, the verse looks at the bad among themselves, so ruin comes not only from joining them but from the pleasure they take in each other.
list_adds: It closes a list of fitting delights (kings in elephants and horses, good men in modest women) with a delight that is ruin, so the last item undoes the pattern.

note: Kural 61 says nothing that can be gained matches children who come to know; the verse says no wealth is brighter or fuller than children.
teaches: The couplet's praise is conditional on the children's understanding while the verse gives it unqualified, and the verse places it among other firsts, so children are the first of wealth as the mother is first above the gods.
list_adds: It ranks children as one of four superlatives (eye among organs, husband among kin, mother above gods), so their worth is placed in a hierarchy of bests.

note: Innaa Narpathu 30 counts a house where a snake lurks hidden as painful; the verse likens the small-minded who hide what has befallen them to an anthill where a snake dwells hidden.
teaches: The Innaa line names the hidden snake as a danger to live beside, and the verse turns it into a person, so the reader learns that the secretive man is that danger.
audit_text_issue: The grouping of lines 1-2 (கண்ணோடார்) is unclear.

note: Kural 348 says those who wholly renounce reach the head and the rest are caught in the net; the verse says those who delight in dharma are born again and those who renounce are of heaven.
teaches: The couplet's net becomes in the verse rebirth earned by dharma itself, so even the righteous householder is among those still caught, while renunciation alone leaves.
list_adds: It sets renunciation after the rule that deeds follow their doers, so release is the end of a sequence on karma rather than a standalone praise.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 is hard to divide.

note: Kural 336 says the world's greatness is that one who was here yesterday is gone today; the verse says the born and the dying always exist.
teaches: The Kural looks at the individual who vanishes and the verse at the pattern that stays, so impermanence of persons is shown to sit within a permanence of kinds.
list_adds: It places birth and death beside the sun and moon, disease and labour, and givers and takers, all fixtures of the world, so mortality becomes one more constant.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu 4 names not swelling one's flesh by eating flesh as foremost sweet; the verse says the one who eats sweetly is the one who eats without killing.
teaches: The two state one claim from two sides: Iniyavai calls the abstention sweet, and the verse calls the meal sweet only if it involves no killing, so sweetness belongs to the eating, not the food.

note: Kural 251 asks how one who eats flesh to swell his own can hold to grace; the verse redefines the sweet eater as one who eats without killing.
teaches: The couplet argues against flesh-eating from grace, the verse from the word 'sweet' itself, so the claim moves from the eater's heart to the meaning of a good meal.
list_adds: It sets the non-killing eater among redefinitions of the shunned, the lonely and the pleasant, so diet is judged by the same test of conduct as social standing.

note: Naladiyar 303 says the worthy go before no one except those who embrace them and say 'come in, eat'; the verse says begging from one who does not know one's plight becomes enmity.
teaches: The quatrain says whom the worthy may approach and the verse says what happens if they approach the wrong one: the request turns into enmity.
list_adds: It sets this cost beside the giver's fame, the taker's name and the laughter of going before strangers, so asking is weighed by its consequences on both sides.

note: Kural 85 asks whether the field of one who feeds guests and eats the leftovers even needs sowing; the verse says hospitality thrives when vessels are spread and guests fed.
teaches: The couplet claims the host's field prospers without seed; the verse supplies the mechanism by analogy, since fire grows by the ghee it consumes and the cow by the milk the calf takes, so the host's outflow is itself what increases.
list_adds: It sets guest-feeding beside fire fed with ghee, gods given praise and a cow let to its calf, so hospitality becomes one case of a general law that things thrive by being drawn on.

note: Kural 62 says blameless children of good character keep evils from a parent for seven births; the verse says a man's blamelessness is seen in his children.
teaches: The couplet makes good children a protection for the parent and the verse makes them the evidence of the parent's worth, so read together the child both shows and secures the father's blamelessness.
list_adds: It puts children among four kinds of evidence (ruin for friendship, wealth's movement for prosperity), so the child becomes a sign to be read rather than a blessing to be had.

note: Kural 409 says the unlearned of high birth lack the worth of the learned of low birth; the verse says that in one family the learned youth is praised over the unlearned elder.
teaches: The couplet reverses the rank of birth for learning; the verse reverses the rank of age within a single family, so together learning overturns both of the inherited orders a household runs on.
list_adds: It prefaces the reversal with one fire worshipped in a lamp and scorned in firewood, so the elder and the youth are shown to be one substance valued by what it does.

note: Kural 84 says the fair goddess dwells gladly in the house of one who tends guests with a glad face; the verse says a host of fortune comes when the bright lady looks on one.
teaches: The couplet tells what keeps the goddess in a house and the verse what her look does, so together hospitality is the cause and the goddess's glance the means by which fortune gathers.
list_adds: It ranks her glance with water for seed and wealth for desire, then adds that her grief undoes it, so fortune is shown as conditional where the couplet shows only her staying.

note: Kural 167 says the fair goddess, grudging the envious man, shows him to her elder sister; the verse says that if the bright lady is grieved the fortune perishes.
teaches: The verse states only that her displeasure ruins, and the couplet names one thing that displeases her, envy, so the pair turns a bare warning into a cause and its effect.
list_adds: It sets the loss of fortune as the reversal of its own previous item, so the list moves from gaining to losing with one goddess at both ends.

note: Naladiyar 200 says the base fill themselves on rice and fried dishes a great patron gives, while to the self-reliant water won by effort is nectar; the verse says all the low delight in rice from paddy.
teaches: Both books define the base by being satisfied with rice, but the quatrain sets against them those who live by their own effort and the verse those who delight in their due standing, so the opposite of the base is labour in one and honour in the other.
list_adds: It sets the low man's rice in a series with the tiger's flesh and the cattle's grass, so appetite for food is made a creature's nature, and the high are marked off by a delight that is not eaten.

note: Kural 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming meet no affliction that shakes them; the verse says deeds that recoil (அதிர்க்கும்) show themselves only later, except to those who knew beforehand.
teaches: Both use the verb அதிர் for the shock of what comes, and the verse adds that the shock is the delayed result of one's own deed, so the couplet's foresight becomes foresight of one's own acts rather than of outside events.
list_adds: It joins foresight to freedom from craving in one list, so knowing beforehand and wanting nothing are set as the two guards of a deed.
audit_text_issue: nanmanikkadigai:67 lines 1-2 are dense; one parse

note: Kural 367 says that if craving is cut off thoroughly, unfailing deeds (தவாவினை) come as one wishes; the verse says the deeds of those without craving do not fail (தவாவாம்).
teaches: The verse repeats the couplet's promise in its own words but sets beside it that the heart of those who have gained is ever craving, which shows why the couplet's condition is hardest for the one who already has.
list_adds: It sets the desireless deed against the craving of those who have obtained, a contrast between two kinds of person that the couplet, which speaks of one, lacks.
audit_text_issue: Nanmanikkadigai 67 lines 1 to 3 are dense, and the parse of அவாவாம் அடைந்தார்கட்கு உள்ளம் is uncertain.

note: Kural 228 asks whether hard-eyed hoarders who keep and lose do not know the joy of giving; the verse ranks those without wealth above those who have it and only guard it.
teaches: The couplet says the hoarder misses a joy; the verse goes further and ranks him below the man who has nothing, so wealth kept unused is shown to be worse than poverty, not merely less than giving.
list_adds: It frames the point as a ranking and repeats it with the poor over the hoarder, then sets forbearance over reviling in the same form, so hoarding is placed among vices of the same weight as abuse.
audit_text_issue: Line 4 (செய்தாரின் நல்லர் சிதையாதவர்) is obscure. | verse flagged uncertain in later lines

note: Kural 159 says those who bear the harsh words of transgressors are as pure as renouncers; the verse ranks those who bear above those who rise up and revile.
teaches: The couplet measures the forbearer upward against the renouncer and the verse measures him against the reviler beside him, so forbearance is placed both by its reward and by the act it refuses.
list_adds: It sets forbearance in a series of 'better than' rankings with poverty over hoarding, so restraint of anger and restraint of possession are judged by one standard.
audit_text_issue: Line 4 (செய்தாரின் நல்லர் சிதையாதவர்) is obscure.

note: Kural 706 says the face shows what is strongest in the heart, as crystal shows what is near it; the verse says a man's face tells the desire within him.
teaches: The couplet says the face shows whatever is strongest and the verse names that thing as desire (வேட்கை), so the pair makes the face chiefly a betrayer of wants.
list_adds: It ranks the face with a son revealing his father and rain revealing a land, so the face becomes one case of reading a hidden source from its outflow.

note: Kural 70 says the son's help to his father is that people ask what penance his father did; the verse says a son tells of his father's goodness.
teaches: The couplet makes the praise a debt the son repays; the verse states it as a fact of inference, so read together the son repays his father by being the evidence others read.
list_adds: It places the son among natural signs (the face, the field, the sky), so the father's repute is shown to be inferred as surely as rain is from cloud.

note: Thirikadugam 10 says a town without teachers yields no good; the verse says a town is good if many live in it.
teaches: The verse makes a town good by its numbers and Thirikadugam makes it worthless without teachers, so the pair shows the group measuring a town both by size and by learning, and a populous town can still fail the second test.

note: Kural 83 says the life of one who tends guests daily does not fall into ruin; the verse says a family gains glory by the food it gives.
teaches: The couplet answers the fear that giving food ruins a house; the verse claims more, that it is the source of the family's distinction, so feeding is shown as both safe and the very thing that ranks a house.
list_adds: It ranks the family's food-giving with a bull's herd and a town's people, so a house's glory is made to come from those it sustains.

note: Kural 33 tells one to do virtue without stopping as far as one is able; the verse says the doing of virtue is according to one's strength.
teaches: The couplet uses capacity as a floor (do all you can) and the verse uses it as a measure (each gives by his strength), so read together capacity both limits what is owed and forbids doing less.
list_adds: It sets virtue with a rider's horse, a tank's sluices and a household's spending, so the measure by capacity becomes a principle of proportion across unlike things.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 has a vowel-sign variant (tamilvu: அறம் செயல்; தோட்ட). | the packet flags a misprint candidate in line 2 (tamilvu: அறம் செயல்; தோட்ட)

note: Kural 478 says there is no ruin if the outflow is not wider than the inflow, using the image of channels; the verse says sluices are as wide as the dug tank and people live according to their means.
teaches: Both picture a household as water and channels, and the verse adds that the outlet should be cut to the size of the tank, so the couplet's rule of balance becomes a rule of construction made when the tank is dug.
list_adds: It sets the sluice beside the measure of virtue by strength, so spending and doing good are governed by the same proportion.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 வறஞ்செய்கை vs tamilvu அறம் செயல்; தொட்ட/தோட்ட.

note: Kural 99 asks why one who sees the good of sweet speech would use harsh words; the verse says the harsh delight in harsh words.
teaches: The couplet's question assumes harsh speech is a mistake; the verse answers that it is a pleasure to the harsh, so the pair shows that reasoning against harsh words will not reach those whose nature enjoys them.
list_adds: It places harsh speech after units of time and the clear-minded, so a speaker's words are shown as following from his nature as watches follow from naazhigai.
audit_text_issue: Lines 2-3 (தாழியாத் தெற்றென்றார்) are obscure.

note: Kural 415 says the words of the good are like a staff on slippery ground; the verse says the learned man rises if he stumbles while the fool breaks his leg.
teaches: The couplet gives the staff to the hearer as another's words; the verse puts the support inside the learned man himself, so learning is shown as the staff once it has been taken in.
list_adds: It sets the learned and the fool side by side in the same fall and then names the cause, a means made with single-minded care, which the couplet's image does not explain.

note: Kural 410 says others are to the learned as beasts are to people; the verse says those who love the learned are like the learned.
teaches: The couplet draws a line between the learned and all others; the verse lets those who love the learned cross it, so the pair shows the divide is passable through devotion rather than study alone.
list_adds: It closes a list in which each group is lifted to the rank of another (poets to gods, townsfolk to kin, servers to parents), so loving the learned becomes one of several ways nearness confers rank.

note: Kural 27 says the world lies with one who discerns the five sense-kinds; the verse names three senses with their objects and then thought.
teaches: The couplet ends its list at the five senses; the verse adds thought as a further faculty with its own object, done in company, so the pair shows the ethics group placing counsel beyond the discernment of sense.
list_adds: It pairs each faculty with its object and makes the last one collective (தொக்கிருந்து), a step from individual sensing to shared deliberation that the couplet lacks.

note: Naladiyar 2 says wealth turns like a cart wheel and urges sharing its food at once; the verse says no one has passed through prosperity without ruin.
teaches: The quatrain draws a counsel of giving from wealth's turning and the verse draws none, so set together they show the same observation used once as an argument and once as a bare fact.
list_adds: It compresses the impermanence of life, strength, youth and wealth into four negations in one verse, where the Naladiyar gives them separate chapters.

note: Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in childhood knowing grey hair would come; the verse says no one has gained unaging youth.
teaches: The quatrain turns the loss of youth into a reason to renounce early; the verse states only that the loss is universal, so the pair shows the Naladiyar's renunciation resting on a premise the other book states without that conclusion.
list_adds: It sets youth among strength, life and wealth, all lost alike, so the loss of youth is not singled out as the Naladiyar's chapter makes it.

note: Kural 986 says the touchstone of worth is accepting defeat even from those not one's equal; the verse says nobility is known by helpfulness toward anyone.
teaches: Both make the test of worth one's conduct toward those who are no match for one (துலையல்லார், யார்கண்ணும்), the couplet by yielding and the verse by helping, so the pair shows nobility tested where nothing is owed.
list_adds: It sets the sign of nobility with the signs of a man, a pool and toddy, so worth is known by its outflow as a pool by its water.

note: Kural 127 says whatever else one fails to guard one should guard the tongue; the verse says the tongue cuts friendship.
teaches: The couplet warns of the suffering an unguarded tongue brings to its owner; the verse names a particular loss, friendship, so the pair shows what is at stake in the couplet's general warning.
list_adds: It sets the tongue beside the fool who lets go and the resolve that fails, so speech is listed among the things that break bonds.

note: Kural 303 says to forget anger toward anyone, since evils are born from it; the verse says that if one destroys anything, it should be anger.
teaches: The couplet asks for anger to be let go of; the verse turns destruction itself toward anger, so the pair shows the same urge to destroy being redirected rather than given up.
list_adds: It frames each counsel as the best object of a verb (give food, lift fallen kin, destroy anger), so the destructive impulse is given a proper target like the giving and the lifting.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 உயிரிடை ஈட்டை is unclear.

note: Kural 226 says relieving the destroying hunger of the destitute is where one with wealth should store it; the verse says that if one gives, one should give food.
teaches: The couplet says where wealth is best stored and the verse which gift is best, so together food given to the hungry is both the best gift and the safest store.
list_adds: It ranks food first among gifts by setting giving beside letting go, lifting and destroying, each with its one right object.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 உயிரிடை ஈட்டை is unclear. | nanmanikkadigai:80 line 2 உயிரிடை ஈட்டை is unclear.

note: Thirikadugam joins people of a long line without learning to poverty; Nanmanikkadigai says lineage and family standing die beneath want of learning.
teaches: Thirikadugam names the outcome, poverty, and Nanmanikkadigai the death of the family's standing itself, so together they make unlearning ruin both the purse and the name of an old house.
audit_text_issue: சேய்மரபில் uncertain in sense

note: Innaa Narpathu calls beauty in those without means painful; Nanmanikkadigai says beauty and youth die beneath poverty.
teaches: The two books say the same thing from two sides: Innaa names the sight of beauty in want painful, Nanmanikkadigai says the beauty itself does not survive it.

note: Kural 409 ranks the learned low-born above the unlearned high-born; Nanmanikkadigai says lineage dies beneath want of learning.
teaches: Where the Kural keeps high birth as a rank that learning outweighs, the quatrain makes the rank itself die without learning, a stronger claim about birth.
list_adds: It puts lineage in a row with beauty, paddy and a draught ox, so birth becomes one more thing that needs a support beneath it to live.

note: Kural 397 says every land and town becomes one's own, and asks why one stays unlearned; Nanmanikkadigai gives the belonging to the good and the renouncer, and ends with the man of wealth.
teaches: The Kural ties belonging everywhere to learning alone; the quatrain shows virtue, renunciation and plain wealth also open every town, and names the base for whom none opens.
list_adds: It splits the Kural's single case into four holders, three by virtue or vice and the last by money, and the last item ironically undoes the first.

note: Purananuru 192 opens with every town as ours and everyone our kin, as the stance of one who sees through the wise; Nanmanikkadigai says every town belongs to those with something in hand.
teaches: The heroic poem makes belonging everywhere a philosophical stance; the ethics verse observes that wealth secures the same welcome, which sets the ideal against how towns in fact receive people.

note: Sirupanchamoolam counts the spider's eggs, the crab's young and abuse to the tongue as each one's own death; Nanmanikkadigai has the plantain's fruit and the unlearned man's own words.
teaches: Both books use a creature killed by its own offspring to say that speech kills the speaker, so the image of self-born death is a shared stock of the ethics group, applied each time to the tongue.

note: Kural 77 says dharma burns the loveless as the sun burns the boneless; Nanmanikkadigai calls dharma death to those who do wrong.
teaches: Read beside the plantain killed by its own fruit, the quatrain makes dharma a death the wrongdoer grows himself, which the Kural's sun, an outside force, does not show.
list_adds: It sets dharma's punishment among deaths that come from within the victim, so retribution becomes self-made rather than imposed.

note: Purananuru 187 says a land is good only where its men are good; Nanmanikkadigai says kings gain glory by the land they rule.
teaches: The pair runs the credit in opposite directions: the Purananuru makes the land's worth depend on its people, the ethics verse makes the king's glory depend on the land, so his glory rests on men he does not make good himself.

note: Kural 523 says life without mingling with kin is a tank with no bank; Nanmanikkadigai calls leaving one's kin striving after ruin.
teaches: The Kural shows the loss as waste, wealth spilling away; the quatrain names leaving kin as an effort, so ruin is something one works at rather than suffers.
list_adds: It sets abandoning kin as the one wrong striving after three right ones, so the last item reverses the verse's praise of effort.

note: Kural 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous, kind to every creature; Nanmanikkadigai names striving always after good as the mind of the அந்தணர்.
teaches: The Kural derives the name from the conduct; the quatrain lists the அந்தணர் with women and kings as a station with its proper striving, so read together they show the word moving between a status and a virtue.
list_adds: It puts the அந்தணர் in a row of stations, each with its own work, which turns the Kural's definition into a duty of a group.

note: Kural 284 says a love ripened in stealth yields undying sorrow; Nanmanikkadigai says not to steal because harsh things follow.
teaches: Both give the reason against theft as its consequence rather than its wrong, so the ethics books argue the point by outcome, not by rule.
list_adds: It sets theft beside rejecting the worthy, befriending the small and making enemies, so theft becomes one of four ways of making trouble for oneself.

note: Kural 871 says enmity should not be wanted even in jest; Nanmanikkadigai says one must not take up enmity with anyone.
teaches: The pairing shows the ban on enmity is absolute in both books: the Kural closes the gap of jest, the quatrain the gap of the opponent, with anyone at all.
list_adds: It sets avoiding enmity next to avoiding friendship with the small, so both who one befriends and who one opposes are guarded.

note: Kural 302 calls anger bad where it cannot avail and worse where it can; Nanmanikkadigai bids anger be curbed where it cannot avail.
teaches: The quatrain stops where the Kural's first half stops and, after bidding pride against enemies, leaves anger where one is strong unmentioned; the Kural's second half closes that gap.
list_adds: It sets curbing anger beside a call to be proud against enemies at the right time, so the anger left out is partly licensed by the list.

note: Kural 787 says friendship turns one from ruin and sets one on the path; Nanmanikkadigai says to increase friends by leading them to the good.
teaches: The Kural describes what a friend does; the quatrain turns that guidance into the way friendships multiply, so guiding friends is also how one gains more of them.
list_adds: It makes leading friends to the good a means of increase, set against diminishing food and anger, which turns a duty into a gain.

note: Kural 605 calls delay, forgetting, sloth and sleep the pleasure-boat of those bound for ruin; Nanmanikkadigai says sloth stays with those who are to perish.
teaches: The two books use the same phrase for the ruined (கெடுநீரார், கெடுவார்); the quatrain sets sloth's dwelling beside a tethered elephant, so sloth is pictured as a thing that stays, not a boat that carries one off.
list_adds: It puts sloth in a row with cruelty, women's shame and a tethered elephant under one verb, staying, so vice and restraint both become things that hold a person.

note: Kural 978 says greatness always bows and smallness adorns itself; Nanmanikkadigai says bowing is always the ornament of the worthy.
teaches: The Kural plays bowing against self-adornment; the quatrain makes bowing itself the ornament, and sets it beside the Veda and victory, so humility is the learning proper to the worthy.
list_adds: It ranks humility among the proper excellences of each station, the andhanar's Veda and the king's just victory, making it the worthy man's own accomplishment.
audit_text_issue: Line 4 அஃதன்றி அணங்கல் வணங்கின்று பெண் is obscure.

note: Kural 57 asks what use confinement is and says a woman's own steadfastness is the best guard; Nanmanikkadigai says a woman without a bond goes as she pleases though guarded.
teaches: The Kural moves the guard inside the woman; the quatrain adds desire that flows on though blocked and murder that clings though hidden, so the failure of guarding becomes a general law about inner nature.
list_adds: It sets the guarded woman beside desire and a hidden killing, so the claim widens from women to everything that outward control cannot hold.

note: Kural 1253 has a woman say her desire breaks out like a sneeze though she would hide it; Nanmanikkadigai says desire goes where it was going though obstructed.
teaches: The Kural gives the experience in a lover's voice; the quatrain states it as a law beside a hidden killing, which shows the ethics books treating akam's confession as a fact about desire in general.
list_adds: It turns a lover's admission into one of four laws of what cannot be stopped or hidden, placed next to murder.

note: Kural 575 calls kindly regard the eye's only jewel and an eye without it a wound; Nanmanikkadigai says where the gentle eye of the worthy grows dharma grows.
teaches: The Kural judges the eye by its kindness; the quatrain gives each kind of eye its harvest, and makes the hard eye a source of strength in one line and of sin in another.
list_adds: It sets the gentle eye among four eyes, two of them hard, so kindly regard is ranked against daring and cruelty rather than praised alone.

note: Kural 218 says those who know what is due do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even when without means; Nanmanikkadigai calls liberality at a time without means a fault.
teaches: On the plain reading the two disagree about giving when poor: the Kural praises it as knowledge of duty, the quatrain counts it a fault of timing, so the ethics books split over whether means limit generosity.
list_adds: It sets giving beyond one's means among faults of wrong timing, learning missed in youth and anger without kin, so liberality is judged by its season.

note: Innaa Narpathu calls the liberality of those without means painful; Nanmanikkadigai calls it a fault.
teaches: The two words differ: painful to see in Innaa, a fault in Nanmanikkadigai, so the same act is judged both by its cost to the giver and by its wrongness, and both books stand against the Kural 218 view.

note: Kural 306 says anger burns the raft of one's own kin; Nanmanikkadigai calls anger when one has no kin a fault.
teaches: Together they make kin and anger work both ways: anger destroys kin, and without kin anger has nothing to stand on, so the angry man loses the very support his anger needs.
list_adds: It counts anger without kin as a fault of wrong circumstance, beside youth without learning and giving without means.

note: Kural 67 says a father's good to his son is to place him in front in the assembly; Nanmanikkadigai calls letting children grow unlearned an evil.
teaches: The Kural states the father's duty as a gift; the quatrain states its neglect as an evil placed beside killing, which raises the weight of the duty.
list_adds: It ranks neglecting a child's learning with killing everywhere, so a parent's omission joins the gravest wrong in the list.

note: Kural 133 says conduct is noble birth and failing in it becomes low birth; Nanmanikkadigai says lineage is evil when its principle is destroyed.
teaches: The quatrain goes past the Kural's demotion to call the lost lineage itself an evil, and its கொள்கை, a held principle, names something narrower than conduct in general.
list_adds: It sets fallen lineage beside killing, unlearned children and shameless beauty, so birth is one more good turned evil by a loss.

note: Kural 541 says justice is investigating, showing favour to no one and acting after consideration; Nanmanikkadigai defines justice as having no favour toward anyone.
teaches: The same phrase (யார்மாட்டும் / யார்கண்ணும், no favour) defines justice in both, and the quatrain adds inner inquiry for the discerning ruler where the Kural asks for investigation, so the ruler's scrutiny is turned on himself as well.
list_adds: It sets the definition of justice beside definitions of conduct as learning and of wealth as enjoyment with dharma, making justice one of the ruler's set of defined virtues.
audit_text_issue: line 4 உண்ணாட்டம் இன்மையும் இல் is obscure and its division is uncertain

note: Acharakkovai 1 names learning as one of eight seeds of ஆசாரம்; Nanmanikkadigai says ஆசாரம் is learning.
teaches: The book of ஆசாரம் makes learning one root among eight and goes on to ritual rule, while the quatrain makes learning the whole of it, so the word is defined far more narrowly and less ritually here.
audit_text_issue: Lines 3-4 (தெரிந்தாள்வான் உண்ணாட்டம் இன்மையும் இல்) are hard to divide.

note: Kural 288 says deceit stands in the heart of those who know stealth; Nanmanikkadigai says the thief knows the misery of concealment.
teaches: The Kural shows deceit settled in the thief; the quatrain shows it as his torment, which only he knows, so the thief is both the home and the sufferer of his concealment.
list_adds: It sets the thief's misery among sufferings known only from inside, the drunkard's, the bird's and the many-wived man's.

note: Kural 139 says those with conduct cannot speak evil even by a slip; Nanmanikkadigai says deceitful words do not appear in the mouths of the learned even if they die.
teaches: The Kural rules out the accident, a slip; the quatrain rules out the extremity, death, so between them neither chance nor pressure draws evil speech from the good.
list_adds: It mirrors each good mouth with a bad one, the learned and worthy against the graceless and base, so the same kinds of word are shown present and absent.
audit_text_issue: சாயிறுந் (line 2) is probably a corruption of சாயினும். | Nanmanikkadigai 96 line 2 சாயிறுந் is probably corrupt. | Nanmanikkadigai 96 line 2 சாயிறுந் is probably corrupt; the 'even if they die' reading is an emendation.

note: Kural 720 likens holding forth before those not of one's kind to nectar spilled in a gutter; Nanmanikkadigai says even a learned man has no standing before the unlearned and foolish.
teaches: The Kural measures the waste of the speech; the quatrain measures the loss to the speaker, and pairs it with the unlearned man's loss before the fit assembly, so standing is shown to depend on the match of speaker and hearers.
list_adds: It makes the learned man's failure the mirror of the unlearned man's, so the list shows a mismatch failing in both directions.

note: Pazhamozhi 14 says fine points of learning spoken before the unlearned turn bad; Nanmanikkadigai says a learned man before the unlearned has no standing.
teaches: Pazhamozhi says the words go bad, Nanmanikkadigai that the man loses standing, so the group counts the damage to both the teaching and the teacher.
audit_text_issue: Pazhamozhi 14 has சுழிநுட்பம் where nearby verses have கழிநுட்பம்.

note: Naladiyar 347 says a sandal of gold and gems is still for the foot, so the base are known by their deeds though wealthy; Nanmanikkadigai says the base, though bound and polished, show their dirt.
teaches: The Naladiyar's base are dressed up by wealth, the quatrain's are scrubbed by force, and both fail, so neither fortune nor correction changes their nature.
list_adds: It sets the base against a gem that stays itself though soiled, so the base become the reverse of the gem, keeping their dirt as it keeps its worth.

note: Kural 784 says friendship is for going ahead to rebuke when one oversteps; Nanmanikkadigai likens friends' rebuking words to the lute.
teaches: The Kural states rebuke as the purpose of friendship; the quatrain says how it should be heard, as music, so the duty of the friend is matched by the response of the one rebuked.
list_adds: It sets the friend's rebuke among likenesses of company good and bad, so rebuke is counted as one of the pleasures of good company.
audit_text_issue: Line 1's எண்ணொக்கும் is doubtful.

note: Verse 99 likens a house without a good woman to a ruin; verse 103 calls the wife the light of the house.
teaches: The book says the same thing from both sides, ruin without her and light with her, and 103 continues the chain to sons, learning and understanding, so her worth is the first link, not the whole.

note: Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate, which arrives first whatever one devises; Nanmanikkadigai says deeds overrun one when earlier penance was small.
teaches: The quatrain makes fate's power depend on how much penance was stored before, which limits the Kural's unqualified claim for fate.
list_adds: It sets karma's overrunning beside water spilling from a small tank and enemies overrunning the weak, so fate becomes one more force that breaks a container too small for it.

note: Kural 754 says rightly gained wealth yields both dharma and pleasure; Nanmanikkadigai gives pleasure to wealth and dharma to softened grace.
teaches: Where the Kural lets good wealth bear dharma, the quatrain assigns dharma to grace alone, which separates the two that the couplet joins.
list_adds: It lays out a table of causes in which wealth and grace sit side by side with different fruits, so dharma is pointedly not among wealth's results.

note: Verse 101 says reviling yields reproach; verse 104 says harsh speech yields a reviling mind.
teaches: Read together, the book places the reproach first in others' mouths and then in the speaker's own mind, so harsh speech damages the speaker twice.

note: Kural 503 says even the learned and flawless are rarely without blankness when examined; Nanmanikkadigai says no one knows everything and no one knows nothing.
teaches: The Kural speaks of the best; the quatrain adds the worst, so knowledge is never total and ignorance never total, which leaves everyone open to examination.
list_adds: It pairs no one all-knowing with no one all-ignorant, and the same for virtue and fault, so the list denies both extremes.

note: Kural 504 bids one weigh virtues and faults and take what predominates; Nanmanikkadigai says no one has faults that hide all virtue.
teaches: The quatrain supplies the ground for the Kural's method: since no one is pure fault, there are always virtues to weigh against the faults.
list_adds: It makes the mixed nature of people a general law beside the limits of knowledge, which is what the Kural's weighing needs.

note: Kural 60 calls a home's excellence its blessing and good children its ornament; Nanmanikkadigai makes the wife the light of the house, sons hers, learning theirs and understanding learning's.
teaches: The Kural stops at children; the quatrain continues the chain to learning and understanding, so the household's worth is finally measured by knowledge.
list_adds: It turns the couplet's pair into a chain of four lights, each lit by the next.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 89 has nearly the same lines: sweet speech makes kin, harsh speech enmity, gentle speech grace, and grace release.
teaches: The one variant matters: Sirupanchamoolam has harsh speech make enmity (பகைமை), Nanmanikkadigai a reviling mind (வசைமனம்), which moves the damage from one's relations to one's own mind.
audit_text_issue: Sirupanchamoolam 89 line 2 பகைமைமன் and line 4 விடாய் (for வீடாய்) look corrupt.

note: Kural 96 says sweet speech of good things makes dharma grow; Nanmanikkadigai traces gentle speech through a mind of grace to release.
teaches: The Kural carries sweet speech to dharma in this life; the quatrain carries it through grace to வீடு, so speech becomes the first step of release.
list_adds: It makes speech the start of a chain ending in release, with harsh speech as the branch that turns the mind to blame.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 92 lists not learning in youth as one of four faults; Pazhamozhi 1 says why it is a fault: the chance does not return in old age.
teaches: The counted verse names the fault and moves on; the proverb supplies its logic, that learning is a toll only collectable while the road is still ahead.

note: Naladiyar 135 says learners have few days and so must choose what to learn; Pazhamozhi 1 locates those days in youth and says that once past they cannot be used at all.
teaches: Together they make two limits on learning, a short life that forces choice and a closing season of youth after which no choice remains.
list_adds: its proverb of toll and wages turns the quatrain's shortness of days into a deadline, a payment that lapses once the work is past.

note: Kural 1110 uses the learner's growing sense of ignorance as a simile for love; Pazhamozhi 2 states the same thing of learning itself and makes it the engine of study.
teaches: The Kural borrows from learning a fact Pazhamozhi takes as a method: the lament 'I have not learnt' drives the next round of pondering and labour.
list_adds: it gives the simile's base in its own right and adds the practice it drives, reflection on one thing at a time, which the love couplet has no room for.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 28 says that as one learns ignorance lessens, step by step toward truth; Pazhamozhi 2 says the earnest learner finds himself the more unlearned at each step.
teaches: Read together, ignorance shrinks in fact while the learner's sense of it grows, so the Nanmanikkadigai's ladder is climbed only by one who feels farther from the top.

note: Naladiyar 140 says worldly learning without the books of wisdom is clamour that removes no confusion; Pazhamozhi 3 compares learning that leaves confusion to a lamp bought that gives darkness.
teaches: The quatrain says which learning fails to clear confusion; the proverb adds the cost, that such learning is a price paid for darkness.
list_adds: its lamp-buying image frames learning as a purchase to be tested before paying, which the quatrain's judgement of book against book does not.

note: Kural 397 says every land and town is the learned man's own; Pazhamozhi 4 says the same and closes with the proverb that he needs no food for the road.
teaches: The Kural states belonging and asks why anyone stays unlearned; Pazhamozhi turns belonging into maintenance, the learned eat wherever they go.
list_adds: the proverb carries the couplet's claim of belonging into the traveller's practical case, provision for the journey.
audit_text_issue: line 1 ஆற்றவும் கற்றவும் is awkward as printed

note: Kural 414 offers listening to one who has not studied, the ஆயினும் keeping study first; Pazhamozhi 5 says outright that hearing is better than learning.
teaches: The two rank the same pair in opposite order: the Kural makes hearing the fallback for the unlearned, Pazhamozhi makes it the cure for the learned man's narrowness.
list_adds: its frog-in-the-well image gives a reason for ranking hearing above study, that one's own text is a single well, which the couplet lacks.

note: Kural 411 ranks the wealth of the ear first among all wealth; Pazhamozhi 5 ranks hearing above learning itself.
teaches: The Kural ranks hearing against wealth, Pazhamozhi against study, so together they set listening at the head of both outer and inner goods.
list_adds: it moves the ranking from wealth to learning and names what hearing cures, the well-frog's belief that its own water is the only water.

note: Kural 698 tells those who serve a king not to belittle him as young; Pazhamozhi 6 shows elders doing just that and the young Chola answering them.
teaches: The couplet gives the rule to the courtier; the story shows the king's side, meeting contempt for his youth with a disguise and a sound judgement.
list_adds: it supplies the episode and the cause of the king's competence, his family's craft, which the courtier's rule leaves unstated.

note: Naladiyar 195 says austerity, learning and effort make a lineage; Pazhamozhi 6 says a lineage gives half its craft without learning.
teaches: The pair disagree on which way the gift runs: for the Naladiyar learning makes the family, for Pazhamozhi the family half-supplies the learning.
list_adds: its named royal story stakes the claim for inherited capacity on a king's judgement, against the quatrain's denial that birth names anything.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 64 says the world passes over the elder who grew old unlearned and praises the young one who learned; Pazhamozhi 6 also has a young man outdo his elders, but by birth, not study.
teaches: Both set the able young against the doubting old, but the counted work credits learning and Pazhamozhi credits lineage, so youth's claim rests on two different grounds.

note: Kural 717 says the learning of the learned shines among those able to examine words faultlessly; Pazhamozhi 7 says it is visible only to the very learned and closed to common people.
teaches: The Kural names the audience where learning shines; Pazhamozhi adds that outside it learning is not dimmer but unseen, as a snake's feet are hidden from all but snakes.
list_adds: its proverb makes judgement of learning a matter of kind knowing kind, and shuts out the common people the couplet does not mention.

note: Pazhamozhi 7 says only the learned know the learned; 8 says the goodness of the good is known only by those better than they.
teaches: Read in sequence the claim tightens from peer to superior: learning can be judged by equals, but goodness only by one who exceeds it.

note: Naladiyar 256 says the learned keep silent for fear of a lapse while others chatter, like green and dry palm leaves; Pazhamozhi 9 says those ignorant of the learned man's restraint praise themselves, like a pot that is not full.
teaches: The quatrain gives the learned man's motive for silence; Pazhamozhi names what the noisy lack, knowledge of that restraint and attention to themselves, so the two halves of the contrast each get a cause.
list_adds: it narrows the others' chatter to self-praise and traces it to heedlessness, which the leaf image leaves unexplained.

note: Kural 978 says greatness bows while smallness adorns itself with self-admiration; Pazhamozhi 9 ties self-praise to not knowing the restraint of the learned.
teaches: The Kural sets self-admiration against greatness as a trait; Pazhamozhi makes it a symptom of shallow learning, so boasting becomes evidence of what one has not learnt.
list_adds: it moves the claim from greatness in general to learning and gives the full-pot proof that the deeply filled make no noise.

note: Kural 957 says a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon; Pazhamozhi 10 uses the same image for the misdeed of a learned man known in his town.
teaches: The image of the moon's spot passes from birth to learning, so the two together make visibility of fault the cost of any eminence, inherited or earned.
list_adds: it carries the couplet's image from lineage to the learned who live conspicuously, and makes their breach of their own texts the fault seen.

note: Kural 414 offers listening as the help left to one who has not studied; Pazhamozhi 11 names study and listening as the two routes and condemns the man who has taken neither.
teaches: Together they show listening as the fallback the Kural concedes and Pazhamozhi makes the minimum, so the man without even that has only luck left.
list_adds: it sets study and hearing side by side as two routes and adds a proverb that strips credit from any lucky hit.
audit_text_issue: l.1 சுற்றானும் சுற்றார்வாய் is corrupt for கற்றானும் கற்றார்வாய் | line 1 சுற்றானும் சுற்றார்வாய் read as கற்றானும் கற்றார்வாய் | Line 1 prints சுற்றானும் சுற்றார்வாய்; the heading கல்லாதார் and the sense require கற்றானும் கற்றார்வாய்.

note: Naladiyar 270 says those with understanding are as the learned though they have not studied; Pazhamozhi 11 says one who has neither studied nor listened does not understand clearly and is right only by chance. The conflict holds on the reading that 270's உணர்வுடையார் need no study or hearing at all.
teaches: The pair splits on whether native understanding can stand in for learning: the Naladiyar lets inner sense make a man learned, Pazhamozhi treats an untaught man's right judgement as a windfall.
list_adds: its proverb turns the untaught man's success into chance, the very case the quatrain credits to inner understanding.
audit_text_issue: l.1 சுற்றானும் சுற்றார்வாய் is corrupt; the sense depends on emending to கற்றானும் கற்றார்வாய் | line 1 சுற்றானும் சுற்றார்வாய் is read as கற்றானும் கற்றார்வாய்

note: Both say the unlearned man's standing falters (சோர்வு படும்) when he speaks; Pazhamozhi 12 places it before the learned and gives the cause through its proverb.
teaches: The Kural states the faltering bare and leaves the hearer unnamed; Pazhamozhi supplies the learned hearers and the mechanism, the questions every claim must meet.
list_adds: the proverb explains why the speech falters: among the learned every statement must survive a question it has never faced.

note: The two verses open with the same line on the unlearned man's fine point; 12 has it falter when spoken, 13 has it count for nothing when unspoken.
teaches: Read together they form a dilemma: speaking exposes the unlearned man's insight and silence erases it, so without learning there is no way for it to count.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 of 13, வெகுண்(டு)அரு கிற்பார்க்கும், carries an editorial bracket and is unclear. | pazhamozhi_nanooru:13 line 3 வெகுண்(டு)அரு கிற்பார்க்கும் is bracketed and obscure

note: Kural 403 calls the unlearned very good if they keep silent before the learned; Pazhamozhi 13 says silence leaves their insight unshown and so gives no ground for thinking themselves good.
teaches: The Kural's ironic praise of the silent unlearned is limited by Pazhamozhi: silence spares them shame but cannot make them one of the good.
list_adds: its proverb makes silence a nullity, so the goodness the couplet grants the silent unlearned is goodness with nothing in it.
audit_text_issue: Line 3, வெகுண்(டு)அரு கிற்பார்க்கும், is unclear. | line 3 obscure, not load-bearing

note: Naladiyar 254 says the unlearned man among the wise is a dog sitting if silent and a dog barking if he speaks; Pazhamozhi 13 says his unspoken insight is nothing.
teaches: Both refuse the unlearned any good way to be present among the learned, the Naladiyar by contempt for his person, Pazhamozhi by an argument that an unshown insight is no insight.
list_adds: it argues from the proverb on speech rather than from an insulting image, so the denial rests on how insight is shown, not on what the man is.
audit_text_issue: l.3 வெகுண்(டு)அரு கிற்பார்க்கும் is obscure | line 3 வெகுண்(டு)அரு கிற்பார்க்கும் is obscure

note: Kural 720 likens holding forth before those not of one's own group to nectar spilled in a dirty yard; Pazhamozhi 14 says learned speech before the unlearned turns good to bad, as a city is a forest to one without kin.
teaches: Both measure an audience by kinship (தங்கணத்தார், தமர்), but the Kural's nectar is only wasted while Pazhamozhi's good words become harmful, which makes the wrong audience an active danger.
list_adds: its proverb casts the speaker, not the speech, as the one stranded, a man among strangers in a city.
audit_text_issue: l.1 சுழிநுட்பம் where 12 and 13 have கழிநுட்பம் | line 1 சுழிநுட்பம் where verses 12-13 have கழிநுட்பம்

note: Naladiyar 255 has the worthy keep their learning unspoken, even when asked, where it will not be taken in; Pazhamozhi 14 gives the cost of speaking there.
teaches: The Naladiyar gives the practice, silence even when asked, and Pazhamozhi gives the reason, that good words among the unlearned turn bad.
list_adds: it names the outcome the worthy avoid, the reversal of good into bad, which the quatrain leaves implicit.
audit_text_issue: l.1 சுழிநுட்பம் for கழிநுட்பம் | line 1 சுழிநுட்பம் for கழிநுட்பம்

note: Kural 719 says those who speak well in a good assembly should not speak in a mean one, even by slip; Pazhamozhi 15 calls fine speech among the unlearned the worst thing for a man and a lapse of conduct.
teaches: Pazhamozhi moves the Kural's rule of assembly into the field of ozhukkam, so speaking to the wrong audience is a fault of character that lowers the speaker, not only a tactical error.
list_adds: it ranks the act as the worst of things for a man and proves it with the conduct maxim, which the couplet does not invoke.

note: Kural 137 says conduct brings high standing and lapses bring blame; Pazhamozhi 15 uses the same ozhukkam and izhukkam pair as a proverb to judge speech among the unlearned.
teaches: The pairing shows the Kural's conduct couplet circulating as a proverb and being applied to a case the couplet never names, the choice of whom to speak before.
list_adds: it applies the conduct maxim to a particular act, eloquence in the wrong company, and so widens what counts as a lapse.

note: Kural 402 likens the unlearned man's desire to speak to a desire for womanhood in one without breasts; Pazhamozhi 16 likens his challenge to the learned to a lame man wanting to play with an elephant.
teaches: Both frame the unlearned man's ambition as desire without the faculty, but Pazhamozhi moves it from wanting to speak to picking a fight, where the lame man's wish also courts danger.
list_adds: its image adds danger to incapacity, since an elephant can crush the lame man who wants to play.
audit_text_issue: பிடிப்பூணி, சொற்றாற்று and சுனைத்து are obscure

note: Naladiyar 312 has the bad scholar, worsted in assembly, slap his shoulders and rise to fight; Pazhamozhi 16 has the unlearned provoke the learned and rise itching for a contest.
teaches: The Naladiyar shows the fight as what follows defeat, Pazhamozhi as what the unlearned man starts; together they mark aggression as the unlearned man's response to learning before and after the contest.
list_adds: its proverb judges the challenge hopeless from the start, while the quatrain warns the disciplined to keep away.
audit_text_issue: சொற்றாற்று, சுனைத்து and பிடிப்பூணி are uncertain. | line 2 சொற்றாற்று, சுனைத்து and line 3 பிடிப்பூணி obscure

note: Kural 711 bids the speaker know the assembly and examine the matter before speaking; Pazhamozhi 17 names what is to be known, the hearers' desire about the matter, and calls speech that misses it a losing case.
teaches: Read together, knowing the assembly turns out to mean reading its appetite: the Kural asks for discernment, and Pazhamozhi says that discernment is of desire, so a true speech the hearers do not want is already lost.
list_adds: its bee image and proverb make the hearers' want the measure and recast unsuited speech as a defeat carried into the contest.

note: Kural 715 praises the restraint of not speaking first among elders; Pazhamozhi 19 applies the same rule of order to a dispute two have begun, where the later speaker pushes ahead of his turn.
teaches: The pair shows the Kural's rule of precedence is also a rule of relevance: speaking out of turn is not only immodest but misses the point at issue, as the bandage misses the torn knee.
list_adds: the proverb gives a reason the couplet lacks: speech before its turn lands on the wrong place.

note: Kural 729 holds the learned who fear an assembly of the good lower than the unlearned; Pazhamozhi 20 advises the learned to fear the unlearned who bandy words among them.
teaches: The Kural's demand for fearlessness in assembly has an exception: before the good, fear is a failing, but before the shameless unlearned, against whom even gods are powerless, wariness is wisdom.
list_adds: it names the one opponent in an assembly a learned man should fear, and its proverb grounds that fear in shamelessness rather than skill.

note: Naladiyar 314's fool, with one overheard sutra, walks unabashed (நாணாது) into the gathering of the good and shows his petty understanding; Pazhamozhi 22's man, knowing neither honour nor shame, sits among the wise and questions them.
teaches: Both trace the intrusion to a lack of shame rather than of learning alone, and Pazhamozhi adds that the shameless man need not even recite: questioning the wise is enough to make him laughable.
list_adds: it pairs மானம் with நாண் as what is missing and turns the exposure into ridicule through its proverb.

note: Naladiyar 255 praises the worthy who will not speak their learning even when asked, knowing it would not be taken in; Pazhamozhi 23 shows the chatterer scorning those whose learning keeps their tongues in check.
teaches: The pair exposes the cost of the worthy's silence that the Naladiyar praises: the low read restraint as emptiness and mock it, so the learned man's silence protects his learning but not his standing.
list_adds: it sets the restrained learned and the chattering intruder in one scene, so the silence the quatrain commends is seen from the scoffer's side.

note: Kural 719 tells the able speaker not to speak in a mean assembly even by slip; Pazhamozhi 24 condemns the man who does the reverse, silent before the good and boastful before the mean.
teaches: The pair fixes both halves of the rule: the Kural forbids good speech wasted on the mean, Pazhamozhi shows the inverted vice, where the mean assembly gets self-praise and the good assembly gets nothing.
list_adds: it joins silence among the good and self-praise among the mean as one fault and gives it a single image of cowardice.

note: Kural 727 likens the learning of one who fears the assembly to a bright sword in a பேடி's hand amid enemies; Pazhamozhi 24 likens the same fear to a man who strings his bow at home and shoots a pot.
teaches: The two martial images complete each other: the Kural shows the weapon useless in the field, Pazhamozhi shows it used where no enemy is, so fear of the assembly is both impotence before the learned and bravado before the mean.
list_adds: it adds the self-praise in a mean assembly to the fear the couplet names, so the coward's display is seen alongside his failure.

note: Kural 720 likens holding forth before those not of one's group to nectar spilled in a dirty yard; Pazhamozhi 25 likens counsel spoken among dull men to sifting flour in the sea.
teaches: The two waste images differ in what is lost: the Kural's nectar is fouled where it falls, Pazhamozhi's flour simply vanishes, and Pazhamozhi names the hearers as fools rather than outsiders, so the loss comes from incapacity, not from difference of group.
list_adds: it narrows the couplet's 'those not of one's group' to the dull and complacent and makes the counsel itself (உறுதி), not display, what is lost.

note: Innaa Narpathu 10 counts, as its first painful thing, reciting a song where none grasp its meaning as painful; Pazhamozhi 25 says counsel spoken among dull men is lost like flour sifted in the sea.
teaches: The counted work names the speaker's pain and the proverb names the speech's loss, so together they show that speaking to those who cannot take it in hurts the speaker and achieves nothing for the hearer.

note: Verse 18 forbids answering back so that an exchange becomes a two-sided quarrel; verse 19 forbids pushing ahead of one's turn in an exchange two have begun.
teaches: Read in sequence the two verses give a small order of debate in assembly: do not turn a speech into a contest by retort, and do not break into a contest out of turn.

note: Naladiyar 131 says the beauty of hair, garment border and saffron is not beauty and only learning's is; Pazhamozhi 26 keeps the ornaments but makes understanding the garment they must follow.
teaches: The quatrain discards outward adornment, while the Pazhamozhi verse keeps it and ranks it, so outer graces are not worthless but parasitic on the inner one.
list_adds: its string of jewels, sandal and garlands is not dismissed but placed in an order, ornaments after the cloth, which the quatrain's flat denial lacks.

note: Kural 846 calls it folly to cover one's nakedness while leaving faults uncovered; Pazhamozhi 26 makes understanding the cloth without which ornaments are absurd.
teaches: Both use clothing to name what must be covered first, and together they make the senseless man's lack a nakedness that neither dress nor jewellery can hide.
list_adds: it sets gems, gold, sandal and garlands on the naked body, turning the couplet's single garment into a whole toilette that is wasted without understanding.

note: Kural 410 sets the learned against others as men against beasts; Pazhamozhi 27 says a thousand of the senseless together do not equal one excellent man.
teaches: The couplet makes the gap one of kind; the Pazhamozhi verse draws the consequence that numbers cannot close it, so a crowd of fools adds up to nothing.
list_adds: its moon and many stars turn the couplet's two-term comparison into one against a multitude, adding the argument from number.

note: Kural 848 describes the man who neither does what he is told nor sees for himself; Pazhamozhi 28 says the senseless cannot be set firm and gives as the condition that learning has not gone in. The link rests on an uncertain reading of 28.
teaches: The couplet names the double failure of the unteachable, and the Pazhamozhi verse places its cause earlier, in learning that never entered, so telling fails because nothing is there to receive it.
list_adds: its image of the drum that answers a spoken cue supplies the responsive learner the couplet leaves out, so the fool is measured against an instrument.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 சொற்குறி கொண்டு துடிபண் உறுத்துவபோல் is obscure and may be corrupt.

note: Kural 678 and Pazhamozhi 29 close on the same proverb, binding an elephant with an elephant; the Kural applies it to using one task to achieve another, Pazhamozhi to winning a wise man through a wise man.
teaches: The pair shows one proverb serving two ethics: in the Kural a rule of method for tasks, in Pazhamozhi a rule of persons, that only an equal can draw in an equal.
list_adds: it moves the elephant image from the ordering of tasks to the gaining of people, and names the kings who practise the capture.

note: Kural 720 says speaking before those not of one's own kind is nectar spilt in a dirty yard; Pazhamozhi 30 says the discerning do not even enter among those who have no regard for them.
teaches: The couplet counts the waste after one has spoken in the wrong company; the Pazhamozhi verse moves the judgement earlier, to not going in at all, and makes that avoidance itself a mark of understanding.
list_adds: its jackal that keeps out of the reapers' sight turns the couplet's rule of speech into a rule of where to be seen, with the danger as well as the waste.

note: Both use the jackal as the creature that reads its ground: in Kural 500 it kills the elephant stuck in mud, in Pazhamozhi 30 it keeps out of the reapers' sight.
teaches: Held together, the jackal's cunning has two faces, striking where the ground favours it and vanishing where it does not, and the Pazhamozhi verse gives the second to the wise.
list_adds: it turns the Kural's lesson of place in war into a lesson of social company, applied to the discerning person rather than the commander.

note: Pazhamozhi 32 says those of wide strength cannot be hidden, as no hand hides the sun; Naladiyar 105 shows the palm-tall great shrinking to millet size and hiding their brightness through former deeds.
teaches: The pair limits the proverb's confidence: no man can cover real greatness, but the Naladiyar shows it dwindling from within through old deeds, so it is safe from suppression, not from fate.
list_adds: its moss and raised hand make concealment a deliberate act by others, which separates it from the self-hiding the quatrain attributes to deeds.

note: Kural 400 calls learning the imperishable wealth and says other things are not wealth; Pazhamozhi 33 grants that jewels and riches do return to the fortunate, and ranks understanding above them because it never leaves.
teaches: Where the Kural denies other goods the name of wealth, the Pazhamozhi verse concedes their worth and their power to come back, and rests understanding's superiority on its independence from fortune.
list_adds: it names the rival goods, priceless jewels and wealth, and gives them a real but conditional permanence, so the ranking is argued rather than asserted.
audit_text_issue: Sense uncertain; the subject of பிரிவின்று (line 3) is unstated.

note: Both set understanding against ornaments: in 26 ornaments come after the cloth of understanding, in 33 priceless jewels come and go with fortune while understanding stays.
teaches: Read together the chapter makes jewels doubly inferior to understanding, dependent on it for their sense and on fortune for their keeping.
list_adds: 33 adds time to 26's order of dressing, so the ornament is not only secondary but unstable.
audit_text_issue: Verse 33: the subject of பிரிவின்று is unstated and the proverb's sense uncertain.

note: Both prove excellence by a light in the sky: in 27 the moon that the many stars cannot equal, in 32 the sun that no hand can cover.
teaches: The two sky proverbs give the excellent man two properties at once, that a crowd cannot outshine him and a hand cannot put him out.
list_adds: 32 turns 27's contest of brightness into one of concealment, so the image moves from comparison to suppression.

note: Kural 133 makes conduct itself the substance of noble birth and its lapse low birth; Pazhamozhi 34 keeps old lineage as a good already held and makes conduct an addition upon it.
teaches: Read together they show two models of lineage: in the Kural birth is earned by conduct, in Pazhamozhi conduct enriches a birth already counted as excellent.
list_adds: its proverb of milk upon ghee makes conduct a second richness laid on lineage, a layering the couplet's identity of the two removes.
audit_text_issue: Proverb sense unclear: உக்கு விடல் (spilling) sits ill with the praise in lines 1-2; the construal with அஃதன்றோ is uncertain.

note: Naladiyar 195 says good and bad lineage are words with nothing behind them; Pazhamozhi 34 treats excellent descent from an old line as a real distinction. The conflict holds on reading 34's விழுத்தொடையர் and தொல் வந்தார் as birth.
teaches: The pair shows the ethics group divided on whether lineage is a fact before conduct: the Jain quatrain empties the word, the proverb collection banks on it.
list_adds: its abundance image treats birth and conduct as two goods to be summed, where the quatrain allows only austerity, learning and effort to make a line.
