note: Kural 423 says wisdom is seeing the true substance of what is heard from whatever mouth; Pazhamozhi 35 forbids scorning a good word from whatever mouth and proves it by low sources of prized things.
teaches: The Kural states the indifference to the speaker as a test of wisdom; Pazhamozhi shows its price, even the strictest abstainer taking what a dog has caught.
list_adds: it gives three low sources of good things, the spurge, the crow and the dog, and ends on a breach of a birth-group's diet as the extreme case.

note: Kural 505 makes one's own deeds the touchstone of greatness and smallness; Pazhamozhi 36 tells the hearer not to be like the small and to walk by his own conduct, which none knows apart from him.
teaches: The Kural gives the touchstone; Pazhamozhi places it inside the man, so the one who must test the deeds first is the doer.
list_adds: it sets the small man's three failures (not watching himself, not knowing his forebears, not joining the right path) before turning the touchstone on the hearer.

note: Kural 849 says one who shows things to the unseeing becomes unseeing himself while the other keeps what he saw; Pazhamozhi 37 says even the subtly learned cannot turn back one who has taken a wrong course.
teaches: The Kural mocks the would-be teacher; Pazhamozhi removes the blame from him, since even the wisest fail when the pupil's resolve is fixed like a drum's sound.
list_adds: it raises the adviser to the great and the keenly learned to show the failure is not his, and its drum gives the cause: a mind sounds only what it has resolved.

note: Kural 436 says a ruler who removes his own fault and then sees others' has no fault; Pazhamozhi 38 uses the same pair of own fault and others' fault to mock anyone who corrects others first.
teaches: Held together, the Kural's condition for a king's just correction becomes in Pazhamozhi a rule for anyone, and the reversed order is made ridiculous rather than unjust.
list_adds: it carries the king's condition into common life and adds the goat that cures others' wind and not its own, turning a rule into a jest.

note: Kural 656 forbids a deed the worthy condemn even to feed one's starving mother; Pazhamozhi 39 forbids a scarring deed even to save oneself from ruin.
teaches: The Kural tests the rule against duty to another, Pazhamozhi against self-preservation, and gives the reason both leave out: the word about the deed outlasts stone.
list_adds: its proverb supplies the reason behind the refusal, the lasting report, which the couplet leaves as a bare command.

note: Kural 129 says the scar (வடு) burned by the tongue never heals; Pazhamozhi 39 says one must do nothing that leaves a scar (வடு) on oneself, since a word does not wear away.
teaches: The pair turns the tongue's unhealing scar both ways: the Kural's falls on the one spoken to, Pazhamozhi's on the one spoken of, and both last for the same reason.
list_adds: it moves the scar from the wound of harsh speech to the reproach a deed earns, and sets it against stone for duration.

note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken by cruel slander like a flame in a lamp; Pazhamozhi 40 says undeserved reproach is a disease that, untreated by excellence of character, destroys a man.
teaches: The Naladiyar makes the pure immune to slander; Pazhamozhi denies immunity and asks for treatment, so worth must act against blame rather than merely survive it.
list_adds: its medical frame of disease, medicine and wasting gives reproach a course and a cure, where the quatrain gives only the steady flame.

note: Pazhamozhi 40 makes reproach a disease that wastes the man it strikes; 41 says great reproach does not exist for those who do not heed it.
teaches: Together they show that blame wounds only those who care for their name, so the disease of verse 40 is itself a mark of the man worth curing.

note: Naladiyar 189 sets the pure heart unshaken against cruel slander; Pazhamozhi 42 says the evil tongue never runs short and spares not even a god.
teaches: Pazhamozhi shows how far slander reaches, even to Mal's saving act, which is why the Naladiyar's steadiness must hold against slander that cannot be avoided.
list_adds: its example of a god called a cowherd shows slander turning a saving act into a slight on rank, a case beyond the quatrain's general slanderer.

note: Kural 320 says all pains rest on those who caused pain; Pazhamozhi 43 uses the same word, நோய், in its proverb and applies it to the man who hurts someone because they will forgive.
teaches: The pairing shows the rebound of pain is independent of the victim's response: forgiveness on one side does not stop the return of pain on the other.
list_adds: it names the excuse the couplet does not, that the victim will bear it, and makes gods and the steadfast fall under the same rule.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 (தேவர்க்கும் கைகூடத் திண்ணன்பினார்க்கேயும்) is hard to construe.

note: Kural 316 forbids doing to another what one has felt to be painful; Pazhamozhi 44 gives the same self-measure as its proverb and names what blocks it, the sense of the other as different (வேற்றுமை).
teaches: Read together, the self-measure of pain is the remedy and the sense of otherness is the disease: the Kural gives the rule, Pazhamozhi names what makes people break it.
list_adds: it adds the cause of the harm, a felt difference from the other, and narrows the case to harm with no gain at all.

note: Naladiyar 213 holds up the dog that wags its tail with its master's spear in its body as the loyal friend; Pazhamozhi 45 says even a dog shut in and beaten bites its owner.
teaches: The same animal marks the limit of loyalty: the Naladiyar praises the dog's endurance of injury, Pazhamozhi shows that cornering and steady abuse break even that endurance.
list_adds: its proverb adds the condition, the shut door and repeated beating, under which the quatrain's model of loyal endurance fails.

note: Both proverbs of this heading turn on a dog's bite: in 45 the abused dog bites its master, in 49 the worthy man does not bite back the dog that bites him.
teaches: The heading uses the dog from both sides, as the weak who will strike back when cornered and as the base whom the worthy will not answer, so the same bite warns the strong and restrains the worthy.

note: Kural 319 says hurts done to others in the forenoon come back in the afternoon; Pazhamozhi 46's proverb keeps the forenoon and afternoon but has the man only see (கண்டான்) another's ruin, and addresses the heart.
teaches: Together they move the rebound from the deed to the inner wish: the Kural times the return of harm done, Pazhamozhi applies the same timing to a cruel thought voiced in the heart.
list_adds: addressing the rebuke to the heart and using 'saw' for 'did' extends the couplet's rule from acts to wishes.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 நீயொளியை and line 2 அடியுளே are obscure; the sense of line 1 is not secure.

note: Kural 204 says that if one plots another's ruin, virtue plots the ruin of the plotter; Pazhamozhi 46 says one who looks on another's ruin sees his own soon after, and rebukes the heart for a cruel word.
teaches: Both make inner intent enough to set the return in motion, but the Kural names virtue as the agent while Pazhamozhi names no agent and only the speed of the return.
list_adds: it sets the counsel inside a dialogue with one's own heart and swaps the Kural's agent, அறம், for a bare law of time.

note: Kural 555 makes the tears of those who cannot bear their affliction the weapon that wears away a ruler's wealth; Pazhamozhi 47 uses the same phrase of tears wept unable to bear it, and makes them Death to any strong oppressor.
teaches: Read together, the victims' tears pass from wearing down a king's wealth to killing the oppressor, and from the king's subjects to four named kinds of the defenceless anyone strong might torment.
list_adds: it lists four kinds of victims, the ill-favoured, the friendless, the poor and those taken as foes for a word, where the couplet names none.

note: Kural 894 says the weak doing harm to the strong is beckoning Death; Pazhamozhi 47 says the strong tormenting the weak find the victims' tears fall on them as Death.
teaches: The pair makes Death the outcome on both sides of an unequal fight: the weak who strike the strong invite it by their act, the strong who strike the weak receive it from their victims' tears.
list_adds: it reverses the couplet's direction, making the strong the doer and the weak's tears, not the strong man's arm, the bearer of Death.

note: Kural 892 says disregard of the great brings ills through the great, with the conduct itself as agent; Pazhamozhi 48's image of the hand hurt by pinching rock makes the same point that the great need not act.
teaches: The proverb's mountain gives the couplet's grammar an image: the great do nothing and the attacker's hand is hurt by its own act against something harder, however easy the attack looks.
list_adds: it adds the apparent ease of the attack (நற்கெளி தாகி விடினும்) and a proverb that shows why the ease deceives.

note: Naladiyar 70 and Pazhamozhi 49 share the proverb that no one bites back a dog that bites; the Naladiyar applies it to low words, Pazhamozhi to harm done (நலிதல்).
teaches: The shared proverb carries non-retaliation from insult to injury: the Naladiyar asks the high not to answer low words, Pazhamozhi asks the worthy not to answer actual torment.
list_adds: it moves the proverb from speech to deed and names the offender's lack of worth (நீர்த்தகவு இல்லார்) as the reason the worthy hold back.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 கூர்த்தவரை is ambiguous.

note: Kural 312 says not hurting in return even those who hurt in hatred is the stand (கோள்) of the stainless; Pazhamozhi 49 uses the same word, கோள், for the worthy's refusal to retaliate but grounds it in the offender's likeness to a dog.
teaches: The two give the same rule different grounds: the Kural states non-retaliation as purity of the stainless, Pazhamozhi bases it on the offender's lowness, so the restraint becomes a mark of rank.
list_adds: its proverb ranks the offender with a dog, a contempt the couplet does not express, and limits the case to offenders lacking worth.
audit_text_issue: pazhamozhi_nanooru:49 line 2 கூர்த்தவரை is ambiguous. | pazhamozhi_nanooru:49 line 2 கூர்த்தவரை is uncertain.

note: Kural 158 says those who wrong one out of excess are to be defeated by one's own rightness; Pazhamozhi 50 says the superior should not rise against the low who wrong him at all, since it is a great weapon spent on a jackal.
teaches: The couplet still frames forbearance as a way of winning, while Pazhamozhi treats the contest with the low as not worth entering, so forbearance becomes economy of the superior's strength rather than victory.
list_adds: its proverb sets a measure of proportion, great means against a small target, that the couplet's language of victory does not.
audit_text_issue: Line 4 நல்லாநா ராயம் is obscure (நாராசம்?). | Line 4 நல்லாநா ராயம் is obscure.

note: Both verses forbid the worthy to answer the low in kind; 49 says it is not their way, 50 says it wastes their strength.
teaches: Side by side the two give two separate reasons for the same restraint: retaliation would lower the worthy to the dog's act (49), and it would spend great means on a little jackal (50).
audit_text_issue: 50 line 4 நல்லாநா ராயம் is obscure; only the sense of a great thing spent on a small target is secure

note: Naladiyar 68 says the worthy's anger cools of itself like heat taken on by boiled water; Pazhamozhi 51 uses the same heated water to say the well-born's heat, while it lasts, cannot burn the house.
teaches: Read together, the boiled-water image answers two questions: the Naladiyar says the worthy's anger does not last, Pazhamozhi says it does no harm even at its height.
list_adds: its proverb shifts the image from the cooling of the heat to the house that survives it, so harmlessness is added to brevity.

note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from deeds; Pazhamozhi 51 credits freedom from anger to those excellent by birth (பிறப்பினால் மாண்டார்). The tension holds on reading பிறப்பு in 51 as lineage rather than nature.
teaches: The pair shows two accounts of where restraint comes from: the Kural makes worth follow what one does, while Pazhamozhi makes a virtue of conduct the mark of a good birth.
list_adds: it sets the great by birth against the very small and makes forbearance the sign that separates them, the ranking the couplet refuses.

note: Naladiyar 71 says to speak nothing to a fool and slip away; Pazhamozhi 52 gives the same withdrawal as the answer to a man of unquenchable anger and grounds it in his untrustworthiness.
teaches: Together they show that withdrawal, not endurance, is the counsel for two cases, the fool and the man of lasting anger, and Pazhamozhi supplies the reason: neither can be trusted with one's words.
list_adds: it carries the quatrain's withdrawal from the fool to the man of lasting anger and adds a proverb that names distrust as the ground.

note: Kural 510 warns against trusting one not examined; Pazhamozhi 52 names unquenchable anger as a sign that a man fails the test and is to be avoided.
teaches: The pairing turns the Kural's general rule on examined trust into a usable test, since a man whose anger never cools shows by it that he is never clear and so not to be trusted.
list_adds: it names one observable trait, anger that never cools, as the mark of the untrustworthy that the couplet leaves unspecified.

note: Kural 158 says to defeat those who wrong one in excess by one's own fitness; Pazhamozhi 53 says the long feud dies of itself as grass does when paddy is grown.
teaches: The Kural states that rightness defeats excess and Pazhamozhi shows how: like a crop crowding out weeds, one's own good work starves the enmity without any act against the enemy.
list_adds: its farming proverb gives the mechanism, crowding out rather than fighting, that the couplet's language of victory leaves unstated.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 15 calls bearing a wrong greatness and counts living so that enmity ends as good; Pazhamozhi 53 says how the enmity ends: by tending one's own good rather than by force.
teaches: The counted verse names ending a feud as a good to aim at, and Pazhamozhi shows that the aim is reached by not aiming at the enemy at all, since the feud withers on its own.

note: Kural 995 says scorn hurts even in jest; Pazhamozhi 54 adds that the hearer takes the jest as abuse and the harm returns on the jester, like a rat burnt by the lamp it seized.
teaches: The Kural looks at the pain a jest gives the hearer, Pazhamozhi at the anger it rouses and the cost to the jester, so together they show a mocking word wounding both ends.
list_adds: its proverb turns the couplet's concern for the hearer into a warning about self-harm, the rat burnt by its own theft.

note: Naladiyar 72 bids silence before the unfit words of those not one's equals because the world counts a retort as disgrace; Pazhamozhi 55 bids the same silence because silencing strangers is as futile as bolting a public hall.
teaches: The pair gives two different grounds for one silence, reputation in the Naladiyar and futility in Pazhamozhi, which shows the counsel can rest on prudence alone without appeal to honour.
list_adds: its proverb replaces the quatrain's appeal to the world's judgement with the plain impossibility of shutting an open hall.

note: Kural 185 says backbiting exposes the meanness of the backbiter; Pazhamozhi 56 says the target of hired lies has no cause for grief, since the charge is false.
teaches: Held together, the two verses show slander's weight falling wholly on the speaker: the Kural says it exposes him, Pazhamozhi that it leaves the innocent target nothing to grieve.
list_adds: it adds the slanderer's motive, food from one's enemies, and the victim's side, which the couplet on the backbiter does not consider.
audit_text_issue: pazhamozhi_nanooru:56: the quoted words are only a clause of the question.

note: Naladiyar 70 says no one bites back a raging dog; Pazhamozhi 57 says no one gores back a cow. Both make a beast of the insulter to show that retaliation is beneath a person.
teaches: The two images differ in what they make of the insulter: the Naladiyar's biting dog is vicious, Pazhamozhi's goring cow is merely artless, so the unlearned are excused where the low are condemned.
list_adds: it puts a cow in the dog's place and the unlearned in the place of the low, softening the judgement on the offender.

note: Kural 153 calls bearing with fools the strength of strengths; Pazhamozhi 57 says the learned do not retort to the unlearned, for no one gores back a cow.
teaches: The Kural calls forbearance toward fools a strength, and Pazhamozhi gives the ground of that strength: a learned man who retorts makes himself the equal of an animal, so restraint keeps the rank between them.
list_adds: its proverb makes the fool a beast whose offence cannot be returned, a ranking the couplet's paradox of strength does not draw.

note: Pazhamozhi 51 says the well-born's heat, like hot water, cannot burn the house; 58 says that abuse returned is the very act of setting the house on fire.
teaches: Read side by side, the two verses draw the line between heat felt and heat spoken: anger held inside does no harm, while anger turned into a retort burns down one's own house.
audit_text_issue: Pazhamozhi 58 line 2 வயவுரை is unclear.

note: Naladiyar 63 says unguarded words burn the speaker without end; Pazhamozhi 58 says returned abuse sets fire to one's own house.
teaches: Both place the burn of an angry word on the speaker, and Pazhamozhi widens it from the speaker's self to his household, the house as the thing consumed.
list_adds: its proverb names the house, not the speaker's mind, as what the retort burns, widening the harm beyond the self.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 வயவுரை and the division of தீயில்லை in line 4 are uncertain.

note: Kural 987 says worth is useless unless it does good even to those who did harm; Pazhamozhi 59 says worth (சால்பு) comes from enduring such people rather than punishing them.
teaches: The pair sets two thresholds for nobility: Pazhamozhi grants சால்பு to one who merely endures the wrongdoer, while the Kural asks that the wrongdoer also be done good.
list_adds: it sets enduring against punishing and gives each its fruit, renown against nothing, where the couplet asks a third thing, doing good.

note: Naladiyar 65 says true patience is that of the strong who could punish all; Pazhamozhi 59 says punishing those who harmed one, though one could, brings no gain.
teaches: Both assume the power to punish, and together they show that forbearance counts as a virtue only when retaliation is open, and then gains what punishment cannot.
list_adds: it adds the outcome of the forgone punishment, no gain, and of the forbearance, renown and nobility, to the quatrain's test of strength.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 சுறுத்தாற்றி is a rare form.

note: Kural 891 ranks not slighting those able to act as the highest safeguard; Pazhamozhi 60 says calling the great small is neither wisdom, grace nor knowing, and brings harm.
teaches: The Kural values the restraint as self-protection; Pazhamozhi adds that the slight is also a failure of understanding, so the man who belittles the great is both unsafe and wrong about them.
list_adds: its threefold denial (not wisdom, not grace, not knowing) strips the slight of every merit before naming its harm, and the proverb says the slighted greatness itself survives.
audit_text_issue: Line 4 என்றூடு is obscure.

note: Both use a damaged great building that keeps its function: Naladiyar 147's decayed house still has a dry corner, Pazhamozhi 60's assembly hall stays a hall when cut into. The reading of 60's proverb is uncertain.
teaches: The same image works from two sides: the Naladiyar uses it for what the well-born still do in hardship, Pazhamozhi for how others must still regard the great when their standing is damaged.
list_adds: it turns the quatrain's image of the well-born man's own constancy into a warning to those who would belittle him.
audit_text_issue: Line 4 என்றூடு is obscure and may be corrupt; the proverb's construction is not secure. | Line 4 என்றூடு is obscure; the proverb's sense is not secure. | 60 flagged uncertain; என்றூடு obscure.

note: Kural 893 says, in grim irony, that one who wants ruin should offend the able; Pazhamozhi 61 has the small man offend the great because his senses are dazed and he cannot see his death.
teaches: The Kural frames offending the great as a choice of ruin, Pazhamozhi as blindness: held together they show the offence as willed in form and unseen in fact, the offender choosing what he cannot see.
list_adds: its proverb replaces the couplet's mock instruction with the dazed traveller, making the offender's fault a failure of sight rather than of will.
audit_text_issue: Only the closing quotation mark is printed; proverb start unfixed.

note: Naladiyar 64 says the excellent do not flare up when the low confront them with unfit words; Pazhamozhi 61 says the small who confront the great with insolence walk to their death.
teaches: The pair separates the great man's calm from the offender's fate: the great may not burn with anger, yet the insolent small man is lost all the same, so his safety never rested on their temper.
list_adds: it moves the scene from the great man's response to the offender's end, with the proverb's dazed traveller as the measure of his danger.
audit_text_issue: pazhamozhi_nanooru:61 prints only the closing quotation mark.

note: Kural 894 likens the weak doing harm to the strong to beckoning Death by hand; Pazhamozhi 62 likens the unlearned provoking the great to goading an elephant from behind an erukku shrub.
teaches: The Kural's weak man calls his death openly; Pazhamozhi's thinks he is hidden, so the pair adds a second folly to the first: misjudging one's cover as well as one's strength.
list_adds: the proverb adds the false shelter, the thin erukku, which the couplet's open gesture lacks, and names the provokers as the unlearned.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 சொல்வின் is likely சொல்லின்.

note: Naladiyar 164: a snake in a rock crevice still dreads thunder, and those who anger the great are not safe in a fortress; Pazhamozhi 62: the provoker hides behind an erukku shrub and goads an elephant.
teaches: Set side by side, the two hiding places run from the strongest to the weakest, a rock crevice and a fortress against a shrub, and both fail, so no shelter of any strength protects against the great.
list_adds: its proverb makes the shelter absurdly thin and the offender the one who starts the charge, where the quatrain's snake only fears.

note: Kural 152 says to bear with excess always (என்றும்) and better to forget it; Pazhamozhi 63 asks whether a man who errs again after a first fault will be borne, and answers with the plantain that bears once.
teaches: Against the Kural's 'always', Pazhamozhi sets a count: forbearance covers the first offence, and the repeated one is outside it, so the pair raises whether forbearance is unlimited or once given.
list_adds: the plantain proverb puts a number on forbearance, one bunch and no second, where the couplet sets no limit.

note: Naladiyar 161 warns not to offend even the faultless counting on their forgiveness, since once they turn away no one can undo it; Pazhamozhi 63 says a second offence after a first is not borne.
teaches: The quatrain warns against trading on forgiveness at all; Pazhamozhi shows when the trade fails, at the second offence, so together they mark forgiveness as real but single.
list_adds: it fixes the point at which the quatrain's turning away comes, the repetition, through the plantain that fruits once.

note: Kural 898 says those who seem to stand forever vanish with their line (குடியொடு) when the hill-like are slighted; Pazhamozhi 64 says the house (குடி) of the crooked perishes while the great only tremble and grieve.
teaches: Both make the offender's line the casualty, but Pazhamozhi has the great grieve rather than strike, so the ruin of the family comes from the offence itself and not from the great man's wrath.
list_adds: it makes the offenders the great man's own long-standing people and gives the great dread and grief, where the couplet gives them only height.

note: Kural 806 says those who keep bounds do not give up an old bond even when ruin comes; Pazhamozhi 64 has the great keep feeling for long-standing associates who go astray, yet their house perishes.
teaches: The pair shows the limit of old loyalty: the great do not cast the old associate off, they grieve for him, but their constancy cannot stop the ruin his crooked conduct brings.
list_adds: it sets the loyal great man's grief beside the old associate's ruin, so the couplet's constancy is shown to be powerless to save.

note: Both have the small or unlearned offend the great and end in an image of unseen danger: 61 a dazed man who does not see his death, 62 a man who thinks an erukku shrub hides him from an elephant.
teaches: Read together, the two proverbs name the two blindnesses of the offender: he does not see the danger at all, or he sees it and wrongly trusts a cover.

note: Naladiyar 340 says learning and birth win honour when others praise them but bring mockery when a man praises them himself; Pazhamozhi 65 condemns self-praise of a deed not yet accomplished.
teaches: Read together they give two grounds against self-praise: the quatrain's man owns real merits and is still mocked for voicing them, while Pazhamozhi's man claims a result that does not exist yet, so the second fault is falsehood on top of vanity.
list_adds: its proverb of selling uncaught birds adds the time element the quatrain lacks: praise claimed before the work is done is a sale of what one does not have.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 மெய்யா உணரவும் தாம்படார் is hard to construe.

note: Naladiyar 219 ranks abuse above praise of qualities one does not have; Pazhamozhi 66 says praise must be pushed away even when it comes from one's own kin.
teaches: The quatrain makes unfit praise worse than abuse in general; Pazhamozhi carries the refusal to the hardest case, the affectionate praise of one's own people, and gives the reason in the image of a jewel that is one's own and still does not fit.
list_adds: the proverb's own-but-unfitting jewel names the source the quatrain leaves open, one's own kin, and makes the test fit rather than giver.

note: 65 forbids praising oneself before the deed; 66 forbids settling into praise even from one's own people.
teaches: The two adjacent verses close off praise from both the self and the circle nearest the self, leaving only praise that fits the deed and comes from beyond one's own people as worth keeping.

note: Naladiyar 346 says the base man who gains a tiny fraction thinks himself Indra; Pazhamozhi 67 says those who extol such self-proclaimers call a hearth dog a tiger.
teaches: The quatrain describes the base man's inflated self-image; Pazhamozhi turns to the bystander who repeats it, so the pair shows the boast needs a flatterer to circulate and that the flatterer shares in the absurdity.
list_adds: it moves the fault from the boaster to the one who praises him and concedes that such praise is harmless, a qualification the quatrain does not make.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 மிகவின்றி is ambiguous.

note: Kural 1047 says a man in poverty is looked at as a stranger even by his own mother; Pazhamozhi 68 calls it a painful wrong for a man to set a poor kinsman apart among his many kin.
teaches: The Kural records estrangement from kin as one of poverty's miseries; Pazhamozhi names the kinsman who does the estranging as at fault, so the same fact appears once as the poor man's suffering and once as the kin's wrong.
list_adds: its proverb of a line drawn within a row makes the poor kinsman's exclusion a breach of the group's own unity, which the couplet states only as the poor man's loss.

note: 69 says the noble's light is his own and the covering will not cling; 72 says it is the discerning who see the gem through the mud.
teaches: Read together, worth that survives misfortune needs two things: its own shine and an eye that can find it under the dirt, so the verse after 69 hands the burden from the noble to the beholder.
audit_text_issue: தாறாப் படினும் (69) and இணரோங்கி (72) are obscure.

note: Naladiyar 300's tiger starves rather than eat a kill fallen on its left side; Pazhamozhi 70's tiger starves rather than graze grass. Both make the tiger's hunger the test of the excellent.
teaches: The two tigers refuse different things, one a proper meal improperly placed and one a meal beneath its kind, so honour is shown both in rejecting the base and in rejecting the ill-fitting.
list_adds: its proverb ties the refusal to poverty (ஒற்கம்) and to holding one's station, where the quatrain ties it to honour weighed against heaven.

note: Naladiyar 193 says a starving tiger will eat even a small frog and urges taking lowly work in need; Pazhamozhi 70 says the starving tiger will not graze grass and that the exalted keep their station in want. The conflict holds on reading 193 as counsel to stoop for a while.
teaches: The same starving tiger is made to argue both ways, so the pair shows where the line falls: the tiger may stoop to small meat but not to grass, stooping within one's kind but never out of it.
list_adds: it makes the tiger's refusal the proof that poverty must not move the high from their station, the opposite lesson from the same animal.

note: Kural 964 says those fallen from their position are like hair fallen from the head; Pazhamozhi 71 says the great keep their worth when their standing is gone, like the timber of a fallen mansion.
teaches: The pair splits on whether worth lies in place or in substance: the Kural's fallen hair is worthless off the head, the Pazhamozhi's timber is still building stuff off the ruin.
list_adds: its salvage image gives the fallen great a further use, where the couplet's hair has none once it leaves its place.
audit_text_issue: Pazhamozhi 71 line 2 கூடம் மரத்திற்குத் துப்பாகும் is compressed; the proverb's பாடு is ambiguous. | Line 2 கூடம் மரத்திற்குத் துப்பாகும் has an uncertain construction.

note: Naladiyar 347 says a gem-set golden sandal is still for the foot, so the base are known by their deeds though rich; Pazhamozhi 72 says a gem rolled in mud is still a gem to those who know.
teaches: Together they make one rule from both directions: wealth does not lift the base and mire does not lower the noble, so neither fortune changes what a person is.
list_adds: it gives the case the quatrain leaves out, the noble brought low, and adds that only the discerning see the worth through it.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 இணரோங்கி is uncertain. | Pazhamozhi 72 line 1 இணரோங்கி uncertain

note: Kural 409 says the unlearned, though born high, have not the worth of the learned born low; Pazhamozhi 73 says the well-born, though they learn nothing, are far better than those who know other things.
teaches: The two books rank the same pair, birth and learning, in opposite order, so the ethics group does not agree on whether lineage can stand in for study.
list_adds: its proverb makes the well-born the very source of what learning would bring them, so instruction is superfluous rather than merely outweighed.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 மற்றொனறறிவாரின் lacks a pulli; the comparison could be read otherwise.

note: Purananuru 200 presents Pari's daughters as the children of the man who gave his tall belled chariot to a jasmine creeper that never sang for him; Pazhamozhi 74 cites the same gift as hearsay of old givers.
teaches: The heroic poem uses the chariot to the creeper to claim a husband for the daughters, while the ethics verse turns the same act into a maxim that knowing folly adorns the worthy, so the patron's deed becomes a proof text.
list_adds: it sets Pari's chariot beside a second giver's mantle and names both as foolishness, a judgement the bardic poem never makes.

note: Purananuru 142 says Pekan is foolish (மடம்) only in giving, like rain on salt land, never foolish in battle; Pazhamozhi 74 says knowing foolishness (அறிமடம்) is an ornament to the worthy, citing the mantle given to a peacock.
teaches: The puram poem already calls Pekan's giving மடம் and limits it to the gift; the ethics verse adds அறி, knowing, and so makes the patron's folly a chosen virtue rather than a lapse.
list_adds: it pairs Pekan's mantle with Pari's chariot as one kind of act and gives the whole class a name, அறிமடம்.

note: Naladiyar 325 says it is a wonder if one who reviles another before an assembly survives when the reviled stays silent; Pazhamozhi 75 says the worthy say no wounding word in an assembly because any speaker is answered.
teaches: The quatrain gives the rare case, the reviled keeping silence, and the proverb the ordinary one, the retort, so between them reviling in company is shown to rebound whether it is answered or not.
list_adds: its proverb extends the rule to the highest speaker, Mal himself, so no rank exempts a reviler from reply.

note: Kural 293 says not to lie about what one's own heart knows, for the heart will burn its owner; Pazhamozhi 76 makes the king his own witness (தனக்குக் கரியாவான் தானாய்) who judges his hidden fault and cuts off his hand.
teaches: The Kural makes the heart the witness that punishes a lie; the Pazhamozhi shows a king acting on that witness and carrying out the sentence on his own body, so self-witness becomes self-justice.
list_adds: its proverb names the opposite motive, 'no one will see', and the story shows the inner witness overruling it in a king with no accuser.

note: Naladiyar 226 asks whether anyone cuts off his own hand because it poked his eye, to say one does not cast off a friend for a hurt; Pazhamozhi 76 praises a king who did cut off his own hand for its fault.
teaches: The same act is absurd as a response to a friend's offence and noble as a response to one's own moral fault, so the pair separates forgiving others from judging oneself.
list_adds: its story turns the quatrain's absurd hypothetical into a real and admired deed, by making the fault the king's own.

note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken by cruel slander, like a lamp's inner flame; Pazhamozhi 77 says the worthy do not join slanderers who pose as protectors but turn away at once like a crow from a bow.
teaches: The quatrain gives the inner response to slander, steadiness, and the Pazhamozhi the outer one, flight, so the worthy are shown both unmoved by the slanderer and unwilling to stay in his company.
list_adds: it names the slanderer's disguise, speaking as if guarding one, and answers it with withdrawal rather than endurance.
audit_text_issue: site's text lacks line 1; graded on the packet text

note: Kural 174 says those of faultless sight who have conquered the senses will not covet on the plea 'we have nothing'; Pazhamozhi 78 says the worthy do not covet others' goods even when hunger bends them.
teaches: The Kural rules out need as an excuse by the coveter's self-mastery; the Pazhamozhi makes the distance between the worthy and another's goods a fact of nature, like sea and forest, so non-coveting appears as character, not effort.
list_adds: its proverb turns the couplet's conquest of the senses into a fixed separation that needs no struggle.

note: 79 says the fault of the exalted never stops being spoken of, like a brand on a grey bull; 80 says a single fault of the exalted is seen by all, like a lamp on a hill, while the small man's many go unseen.
teaches: Taken together, the fault of the great is exposed in both dimensions, lasting for all time in 79 and seen across all space in 80, which is why the heading asks more of them than of the small.
audit_text_issue: 79 lines 1-2 (the மால் clause) are obscure

note: Kural 957 says a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon; Pazhamozhi 80 says one fault of the exalted is a lamp on a hill while the many faults of the small never show.
teaches: The Kural shows the fault against the bright moon; the Pazhamozhi adds the other side of the scale, that the small man's long-matured faults stay hidden, so visibility, not guilt, is what height changes.
list_adds: it sets the one fault of the great against the many of the small, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: Kural 955 says an old family does not part from its nature when what it can give has shrunk; Pazhamozhi 81 says a man of a giving house keeps up ஒப்புரவு without wealth, and adds that he does so though untended and unfed.
teaches: The Kural treats the shrunken means as the only test; Pazhamozhi adds neglect, so the inherited nature is shown to hold without either resources or nurture.
list_adds: its proverb of the unfed calf that still becomes a bull makes the claim one of nature against upbringing, which the couplet does not raise.

note: Both use grass and a beast to show that the well-born keep their nature in hardship: the lion will not chew creeping grass, the bull's calf grows into a bull though it grazes where there is no grass.
teaches: The same pasture image argues in two directions: the Naladiyar's lion refuses what is beneath it, while Pazhamozhi's calf needs nothing from the pasture at all, so lineage is shown both as refusal and as self-sufficient growth.
list_adds: it turns the image from what the well-born will not do to what they become regardless, and ties it to the act of ஒப்புரவு rather than to principle in general.

note: Kural 220 says ruin through ஒப்புரவு is worth buying even by selling oneself; Pazhamozhi 82 names the concrete form of that cost, borrowing to do what is due, and the excuse it refuses, waiting for a better time.
teaches: Read together they show the Kural's startling price, selling oneself, as the far end of an ordinary practice the worthy actually follow: going into debt rather than postponing a duty.
list_adds: its pun on கடன் as debt and duty makes the cost and the obligation one word, which the couplet keeps as ruin set against gain.

note: Naladiyar 80 forbids eating from the hands of those one should not eat from and speaking words mixed with falsehood; Pazhamozhi 83 grants that the worthy may have eaten from another's hand and says they speak the truth even so.
teaches: The Naladiyar guards truth by refusing the obligation that might bend it; Pazhamozhi allows the obligation and makes truth hold against it, a stronger and riskier claim.
list_adds: it sets the worthy man's truth beside the traitor's borrowed lie in battle, a contrast of two men under obligation that the quatrain's separate refusals lack.
audit_text_issue: Pazhamozhi 83 lines 1-2 (அறைபோய், மாற்றார்வாய்ப் பொய்கொண்டு) are compressed and their sense is uncertain.

note: Both proverbs rest on a public commitment: the man who strapped on the drum beats it, the man who made friends before the village feeds them; 84 applies this to those who came for shelter, 85 to friends who prove faulty.
teaches: Taken together the two verses ground loyalty not in the worth of the person protected but in the protector's own visible pledge, so the other's unworthiness is ruled out twice as an excuse.
audit_text_issue: 84 lines 1-2 are elliptical

note: Purananuru 203 tells a king that refusing a returning suppliant with 'you took before' is cruel and that protecting suppliants is his duty; Pazhamozhi 84 says those who took in seekers do not cast them off as worthless.
teaches: The puram poem closes the excuse of past giving and the ethics verse closes the excuse of the seeker's unworthiness, so together they show the protector's duty answering two different pretexts for withdrawal.
audit_text_issue: Pazhamozhi 84 lines 1-2 are elliptic; the subject is unstated.

note: Kural 806 says those who keep within bounds do not give up an old friendship even when it brings ruin; Pazhamozhi 85 says the worthy do not change toward cherished friends who lack good qualities, because the friendship was made before the village.
teaches: The Kural makes constancy a mark of the man who keeps bounds; Pazhamozhi adds a reason outside him, the village that witnessed the bond, so loyalty becomes a public obligation as well as a private virtue.
list_adds: its proverb names the friend's bad character outright and answers it with feeding as a duty, a concrete act the couplet does not specify.

note: Kural 579 ranks highest the disposition to show kindly regard and bear with those whose way is to hurt; Pazhamozhi 86 sets that regard at one moment, when an open and dangerous enemy is in distress.
teaches: The pairing fixes when the Kural's demand is hardest: not under the enemy's attack but at his fall, when sparing him is a choice and he may still bite.
list_adds: the snake proverb names the enemy as still dangerous and the assembly of the worthy as the place he is spared, a setting and a risk the couplet leaves out.

note: Both verses set the high-born beside those small by birth: in 87 the great go to the small and depend on them, in 88 the great take the small into their company.
teaches: Read together they show the edition's heading praising the great for crossing the birth-rank in both directions, as dependents and as patrons, while leaving the ranking itself in place.
audit_text_issue: 87 line 4 தால அடைக்கலம் is obscure.

note: Kural 451 says greatness fears small company and only smallness takes it as kin; Pazhamozhi 88 praises great families who conduct themselves as kin with those lesser than they. The conflict holds on the reading that 88's சிறியார் are the same small people the Kural warns against, not merely those of lower rank.
teaches: The two split on whether keeping company with the lesser degrades the great or raises the lesser: the Kural fears contamination, Pazhamozhi sees the flower lending itself to the string.
list_adds: its proverb reverses the direction of influence that the couplet assumes, making the great the ones who pass on their quality.
audit_text_issue: Pazhamozhi 88's sense is flagged uncertain.

note: Kural 960 says one who wants lineage must want humility toward all; Pazhamozhi 88 shows the great families in the act, keeping kin-like company with those below them.
teaches: The Kural states humility as the condition of lineage; Pazhamozhi gives its form and its effect, the lesser carried along like string with the flower.
list_adds: it turns the couplet's general humility into one practice, keeping the lesser as kin, and adds what the lesser gain from it.

note: Kural 657 sets the utter poverty of the worthy above wealth gained under blame; Pazhamozhi 89 sets the poverty of the great above the wealth the small have reached, calling that wealth shameful.
teaches: The Kural condemns wealth for how it was got; Pazhamozhi condemns it for who holds it, so the pair shows two grounds on which wealth can rank below poverty.
list_adds: the old-ghee proverb concedes the great man's decline and ranks him above the fresh lesser thing anyway, a turn the couplet's plain ranking lacks.

note: Both rank the poverty of the worthy above others' wealth through an image of what is drunk or eaten: the Naladiyar's small well beside the sea, Pazhamozhi's old ghee beside buttermilk.
teaches: The images argue differently for the same ranking: the Naladiyar's well is preferred because it can be used, Pazhamozhi's ghee because its kind does not change with age, so one rests the claim on use and the other on nature.
list_adds: it measures the worthy against the small rather than against those ignorant of the next world, making the ranking one of character rather than of foresight.

note: Kural 458 says that even the worthy, good of mind in full, are protected by good company; Pazhamozhi 90 reverses the same phrase to say the base, good of company in full, never become good of mind.
teaches: Held together they show the house view that company acts on the mind has a limit: it guards a good mind already there and cannot make one in the base.
list_adds: its salt-sea image and inverted wording set an exception beside the couplet: for the base, company runs one way only and leaves the mind as it was.

note: Kural 452 says water changes with the land it runs on, as understanding takes the nature of company; Pazhamozhi 90 uses water the other way, the fresh flood that cannot sweeten the sea.
teaches: The same water image proves opposite things depending on which is larger: the Kural's water yields to the soil, while the base man is the sea that absorbs every good influence unchanged.
list_adds: it turns the couplet's image around, making the base the vessel that alters what flows in rather than being altered.

note: Pazhamozhi 90 denies that good company changes the base; 106 denies that a patron's favour and prosperity change them.
teaches: Read in sequence the chapter closes both routes of reform it considers, the influence of good companions and the gift of fortune, so the base man's nature is fixed against both.

note: Naladiyar 262 says the wise do not seek the base however rich, as no one picks cactus buds; Pazhamozhi 91 says those who live as kin of the worthy do not go over to the small though they are called superior.
teaches: The Naladiyar grounds the refusal in judgement of the base, Pazhamozhi in belonging: settled among the worthy, one does not change sides, and the sweetness on offer is jaggery in sand.
list_adds: it gives the refusal a cause the quatrain lacks, the bond of living as kin of the worthy, and admits the small some sweetness while denying it is edible.

note: Naladiyar 351 says the petty-minded grow more practised in wrong as they age; Pazhamozhi 93 says some grow old without understanding, like trees that flower without fruit.
teaches: Together they deny that age brings wisdom from two sides: the Naladiyar says age deepens folly, Pazhamozhi that it can simply pass without yield, so telling the fool is one more seed that will not sprout.
list_adds: it sets old age among the failures of plant growth, flower without fruit and seed without sprout, so the old fool becomes a natural kind of barrenness.

note: Kural 849 says the one who shows things to the unseeing becomes unseeing himself while the other keeps what he saw; Pazhamozhi 94 says not to counsel the obstinate, who keep what they took up.
teaches: The Kural describes the failed lesson and Pazhamozhi draws the rule from it, adding the cause: the obstinate are already dyed, so the teacher has no blank cloth to work on.
list_adds: its indigo proverb explains why the lesson fails, a first colour that has set, and turns the couplet's observation into a counsel not to speak.

note: Kural 510 says that both trusting without examining and doubting one already trusted bring endless trouble; Pazhamozhi 95 says that once you have seen a man speak evil you should never trust him again.
teaches: Pazhamozhi names the case where withdrawing trust is not the fault the Kural warns of: one evil word plainly seen is taken as proof of a nature, as neem stays bitter whoever eats it.
list_adds: it adds a specific condition, evil speech plainly seen, that overrides the couplet's warning against doubting the trusted.

note: Naladiyar 350 says small bullocks fed cut grass never learn the yoke, and the base, though rich, are known by their deeds; Pazhamozhi 96 says forest men of cruel deeds granted a place in the country do not behave well.
teaches: The Naladiyar's care is feeding and wealth, Pazhamozhi's is a ruler's grant of settlement; together they show the period's ethics denying reform by provision whether the provider is a herdsman or a lord.
list_adds: it moves the claim from private wealth to a ruler's act of settlement and pins it on a people of a named way of life.

note: Kural 1075 says fear is the conduct of the base; Pazhamozhi 97 says the base do not care about the great blame that falls on them.
teaches: The pair separates two fears: the base may be held in line by fear of punishment, as the Kural says, but blame, which works on others through shame, has no hold on them at all.
list_adds: its proverb of eating fearlessly at a house of mourning shows what the base do not fear, the judgement of others, which the couplet leaves out.

note: Kural 1078 says the base, like sugar-cane, are of use only when crushed; Pazhamozhi 100 says those who have been punished go on doing evil, growing a span for every cubit cut.
teaches: Pressure may wring use out of the base, as the Kural says, but Pazhamozhi denies that it changes them: what is cut back grows again.
list_adds: its regrowth image separates getting use from the base by force and reforming them by punishment, which the couplet runs together.

note: Kural 1078 says the base yield use only when crushed; Pazhamozhi 101, on the reading that அலப்பின் means 'if pressed', says the base do wrong when pressed and also when left alone. The conflict depends on that reading of line 1.
teaches: The two disagree on whether pressure works on the base at all: the Kural makes it the one way to get good from them, Pazhamozhi makes it one more occasion for harm, like the jackal that feeds in any year.
list_adds: it sets the pressed and the unpressed case side by side and finds harm in both, removing the couplet's one remedy.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 is mis-split (ஆகிச்சி தைத்தெழுப for ஆகிச் சிதைத்து எழுப) and the division of lines 1-2 is uncertain.

note: Naladiyar 260 says the base man kicks away the subtle teaching of the learned and sets up a petty assembly with one like himself; Pazhamozhi 102 says those who refuse the good words of the keen-minded and act harshly are known to everyone.
teaches: The Naladiyar follows the refuser into a small circle of his own kind; Pazhamozhi follows him into the village's notice, so refusing counsel ends both in a narrowed company and in public notoriety.
list_adds: it adds the consequence the quatrain lacks, harsh action that makes the fool as known as a rogue bull.

note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from the work one does; Pazhamozhi 103 says those who come down in a base line have no one of good character among them. The conflict holds on the reading of 972's செய்தொழில் as conduct or work rather than hereditary occupation.
teaches: The pair puts the period's two accounts of character side by side: the Kural makes worth follow deeds and denies birth a role, Pazhamozhi makes it follow descent so firmly that a whole line is written off.
list_adds: its monkey proverb treats a line of descent as a species, the very ranking by birth that the couplet rejects.

note: Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every folly; Pazhamozhi 104 says clearing out the fit to raise up the useless base is like felling the jackfruit to plant the kanjirai.
teaches: The Kural warns against the wrong appointment, Pazhamozhi counts its double cost: the base raised and the fit removed, a sweet tree lost and a bitter one planted in its place.
list_adds: its orchard proverb pairs the promotion with a removal, so the folly is an exchange of good for bad rather than a single mistaken trust.
audit_text_issue: pazhamozhi_nanooru:104 line 1 ஊழாயினார் is uncertain.

note: Naladiyar 345 says a dog fed from a golden bowl still eyes leftovers, so honouring the base does not change their deeds; Pazhamozhi 105 says giving the small the honour due to the great is like laying a seat for a dog.
teaches: Both use the honoured dog, but the Naladiyar faults the dog, which stays a dog, and Pazhamozhi faults the one who honours it, who has also taken the honour from the great.
list_adds: it moves the blame from the honoured base to the giver and adds the loss to the great whose due was given away.

note: Naladiyar 347 says the base, though they have come into wealth, are known by their deeds, as a golden sandal is still for the foot; Pazhamozhi 106 says the worthless whom a patron lifts out of distress into faultless prosperity do not become men of good family.
teaches: The Naladiyar says wealth does not change deeds; Pazhamozhi adds that it does not change rank either, even when the wealth is a patron's gift and is used without fault.
list_adds: it names the patron's favour as the source of the wealth and denies the base the standing of குடி, a claim of rank the quatrain does not make.
audit_text_issue: Pazhamozhi 106 line 2 ஆசறு செய்யாராய் is ambiguous.

note: Naladiyar 70 tells the high not to answer the low, as no one bites back a biting dog; Pazhamozhi 107 sets the base man's slighting talk as a dog barking at the moon.
teaches: Read together the dog moves from biting to barking out of reach: the Naladiyar asks the great to refrain from answering, and Pazhamozhi shows the insult never reaches them anyway.
list_adds: its proverb puts the insulted great man out of the dog's range, so restraint is backed by the insult's harmlessness, which the quatrain does not claim.

note: 107 has the base set the great level with themselves in speech; 122 has the unrestrained rise while the worthy withdraw.
teaches: The two verses give the same inversion at two scales, one man's insolent equal talk and a whole order where stone floats, and show the first as the seed of the second.

note: Naladiyar 329 says the small-minded think of the next world only in want and illness; Pazhamozhi 108 gives the base man who denies it outright and urges the fill of desire.
teaches: The pair sets two degrees of the same neglect, forgetting the next world when able and denying it as a creed, and Pazhamozhi's proverb names the cost the Naladiyar leaves implied, brick eaten in tears.
list_adds: it quotes the denier's own words and answers them with an image of the trade he offers, where the quatrain only describes the forgetter's timing.

note: Kural 850 says one who says 'it is not' to what the world says is will be reckoned a demon; Pazhamozhi 108 names one such denial, of the next world, and its practical upshot.
teaches: The couplet leaves blank what is denied; the pairing fills it with the next world and shows the denier's error as a bad exchange, not only a social stigma.
list_adds: it fills the couplet's blank with a named denial and a proverb that judges it by what is lost, not by the world's verdict.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 16 says that before the worthless anger is good and nobility bad, as good meat is wasted in a biting dog's mouth; Pazhamozhi 109 says good done to the graceless base puts the doer in danger.
teaches: Holding them together shows the two halves of one counsel: Sirupanchamoolam says kindness to the base is wasted, Pazhamozhi that it is also dangerous, the tiger's face being closer than the dog's mouth.
audit_text_issue: sirupanchamoolam:16 line 3 கோய்வாயிற் கீழுயிர்க்(கு)ஈ துற்று is hard to construe. | sirupanchamoolam:16 line 3 கோய்வாயிற் கீழுயிர்க்கு is hard to construe. | 16 line 3 hard to construe | sirupanchamoolam:16 line 3 is hard to construe.

note: Kural 1078 says the base yield their use only when crushed like sugar-cane; Pazhamozhi 110 asks whether the wicked ever come under control because they have suffered and answers no. The conflict holds on the reading that the Kural's crushing and Pazhamozhi's suffering are both pressure applied to the base.
teaches: The pair splits on whether pressure works on the base: the Kural finds something sweet to be pressed out, Pazhamozhi finds clay that no binder will make into a wall.
list_adds: its proverb puts the fault in the material itself, so that no admixture of hardship helps, against the couplet's cane that yields under force.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 98 says the base, though bound and scoured, show their dirt; Pazhamozhi 110 says suffering does not tame the wicked, as unfit clay makes no wall.
teaches: Both deny that working on the base changes them, and together they cover the two methods of correction, scouring from outside and mixing in from within, each failing on the material.

note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from deeds; Pazhamozhi 111 lays the quarrelsome temper on those small by lineage. The conflict holds on the reading that குலத்துச் சிறியார் ranks by birth rather than naming the mean ones of a family.
teaches: Set beside the Kural, the verse shows the ethics books divided on whether baseness is inherited: the couplet ranks by deeds, Pazhamozhi traces a vice to the family one comes from.
list_adds: it attaches a specific behaviour, turning on peacemakers, to a birth group, the very link between birth and worth the couplet denies.

note: Naladiyar 68 says the anger of the low keeps spreading and never dies; Pazhamozhi 111 shows it spreading onto those who come to part the fighters.
teaches: Pazhamozhi gives the Naladiyar's spreading anger its concrete path, from the quarrel to the peacemakers themselves, so that intervention becomes one of the ways it spreads.
list_adds: its proverb shows the attempt to settle the quarrel as what overturns it, a turn the quatrain's general claim lacks.
audit_text_issue: Lines 3-4 வெண்மாத் தலைக்கீழாக் காதி are obscure. | Lines 3-4 வெண்மாத் தலைக்கீழாக் காதி விடல் are obscure. | 111 proverb obscure (வெண்மாத் தலைக்கீழாக் காதி விடல்)

note: Kural 888 says a family with inner enmity wears itself down like gold rubbing a file; Pazhamozhi 112 says provoking the defiant within one's own house is pulling the axle-pin from inside the cart.
teaches: Together they show inner enmity as both a slow wearing and a sudden collapse, and Pazhamozhi places its cause with the householder who provokes it, not with the enmity alone.
list_adds: its proverb makes the head of the house the agent of the ruin, sitting inside what he dismantles, where the couplet speaks of the family as a whole.

note: Kural 451 says greatness fears small company while smallness takes it at once as kin; Pazhamozhi 113 says fostering and living with the shameless is binding worms into a wound.
teaches: The couplet explains why the great fear such company, and the pairing supplies what they fear: harm that grows under one's own care, sealed in by the very bandage of fellowship.
list_adds: its proverb makes one's care for the base the means of one's injury, a mechanism the couplet's fear leaves unstated.

note: 109 warns against doing good to the graceless base; 113 against fostering and living with the shameless.
teaches: Read in order the two verses rise from a single favour to a shared life, and the danger rises with them from a tiger's sudden bite to a wound eaten from within.

note: Kural 127 says those who do not guard the tongue suffer from the fault of their words; Pazhamozhi 114 shows the hiding fool betrayed by his own evil speech, like the frog in the sand.
teaches: Pazhamozhi adds what the Kural does not consider, that the unguarded tongue undoes even a man who has hidden himself, so concealment is no substitute for restraint of speech.
list_adds: its proverb sets hiding against speaking and lets speech win, a contrast the couplet's single command lacks.

note: Kural 182 ranks backbiting with a false smile as worse than open wrongdoing; Pazhamozhi 115 asks why blame the backbiter at all, since he is past disgrace.
teaches: The Kural's ranking condemns the backbiter most severely, and Pazhamozhi warns that this condemnation does him no harm, since a man without shame is beyond the reach of blame.
list_adds: its proverb turns from judging the backbiter to judging the use of blaming him, adding a limit of blame the couplet does not raise.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 10 says the base are bound with iron after goading while the worthy are bound by courtesy; Pazhamozhi 116 says the qualityless cannot be restrained by words.
teaches: Together they mark a limit of persuasion: courtesy binds the worthy, but words are wind to the base, so only force is left, as the Nanmanikkadigai says outright.

note: Naladiyar 70 says the high do not answer the low with their own mouths; Pazhamozhi 116 says it is hard to restrain loose talkers by speech at all.
teaches: The Naladiyar's refusal to answer the base is a matter of dignity, and Pazhamozhi adds a practical ground: answering is useless, since words cannot catch wind.
list_adds: its proverb gives a reason of futility beside the quatrain's reason of rank.

note: Kural 448 says a ruler without rebukers perishes even with no one to ruin him; Pazhamozhi 117 says one who will not take the words of the great and does not guard himself makes others into thieves.
teaches: The Kural's ruin needs no enemy; Pazhamozhi adds that the unguarded man's ruin creates its own agents, so the thief is partly his making.
list_adds: it carries the couplet's claim from the king to anyone and its proverb shifts guilt from the thief to the man who would not heed counsel.

note: Kural 821 calls the friendship of those close without inner consent an anvil for striking when the chance comes; Pazhamozhi 120 calls the arrogant, concealing men one has honoured gravel in a sandal.
teaches: The two images of hidden ill will differ in timing: the Kural's waits for its moment to strike, Pazhamozhi's galls at every step, so the false intimate is shown as both a threat and a constant wearing.
list_adds: its proverb turns hidden hostility into a present, continuous injury, where the couplet looks to a single future blow.

note: Kural 510 says that doubting one already trusted brings endless trouble; Pazhamozhi 121 says raising a man to intimacy and casting him off without cause is a deed of smallness.
teaches: The Kural counts the cost of withdrawing trust to the one who withdraws; Pazhamozhi judges the character of the act, a child's play with a grove, so the error is both costly and mean.
list_adds: its proverb names the fault as whim and smallness, a moral judgement beside the couplet's prudential one.

note: Naladiyar 368 says the old wealthy and the worthy decline while concubines' sons and the base flourish, the world upside down; Pazhamozhi 122 says the worthy withdraw while the unrestrained rise, the gourd sinking and the stone floating.
teaches: Both read social inversion through an image, but the Naladiyar mixes birth and wealth into its ranks while Pazhamozhi measures only by speech and restraint, showing the complaint can be made on conduct alone.
list_adds: it drops the quatrain's birth and wealth markers and ranks by conduct, and its proverb calls the inversion impossible in nature, not merely a turned umbrella.

note: Naladiyar 348 lists the base as harsh, without kindly regard and scornful of all; Pazhamozhi 123 names the same traits and adds the absence of fear of evil deeds and a verdict of hell.
teaches: The quatrain describes and stops; Pazhamozhi takes nearly the same portrait and passes sentence, so the pairing shows the description turning into a judgement.
list_adds: its proverb closes the portrait with a verdict, making such men hell's own, where the quatrain gives only the list.

note: Kural 1122 calls the bond between the lover and the girl the bond of body and life, using the word நட்பு; Pazhamozhi 124 says friends take each other as a whole body, more than the god who took Uma as half.
teaches: Both measure the closest bond by the body, but the Kural's lovers are body and life, two in one frame, while Pazhamozhi uses the divine half-woman to claim that friendship joins two wholes completely, setting friendship above even the god's marriage.
list_adds: its proverb from the god's half-body adds a ranking the couplet lacks: friendship is placed above the divine marriage, not only likened to lovers.

note: 124 says friends take each other as a whole body; 132 says the faultless take a friend's fault as their own.
teaches: The union pictured in 124 as one body is given its moral cost in 132: if the friend is one's own whole body, his faults are one's own too.

note: Kural 819 calls bitter the bond with those whose words and deeds differ; Pazhamozhi 125 says between true friends the words and their meaning are one, and twisting them is betrayal.
teaches: The Kural tests the speaker for a gap between word and deed; Pazhamozhi tests the hearer for a gap between word and meaning, so the demand for oneness falls on both sides of a friend's speech.
list_adds: its proverb of acceptance turned to weapon carries the fault to the listener who re-tells, a party the couplet does not consider.

note: 125 condemns re-telling a friend's words in a twisted sense; 130 says a chosen friend is not blamed among many.
teaches: Read together the two verses govern what one says of a friend to others: neither distort his words nor publish his faults, so a friend's speech and his failings are both kept from the crowd.

note: Naladiyar 76 says one should not abandon those one has mingled with, since parting is hard even for beasts; Pazhamozhi 126 uses nearly the same words and closes with the proverb that parting hurts even from a demon.
teaches: The quatrain grounds staying in patience with a friend's hurts, while Pazhamozhi drops the hurts and adds that parting is painful even from a demon, so the reason to stay becomes the bond itself, whatever the companion is worth.
list_adds: its proverb adds a claim the quatrain lacks: the pain of parting does not depend on the friend being good.

note: Naladiyar 220 says parting after closeness hurts even from a deadly snake, so test friends first; Pazhamozhi 126 says parting hurts even from a demon, so do not abandon those one has joined.
teaches: The same image of a painful parting from a dangerous companion yields opposite advice: the quatrain draws caution before the bond, Pazhamozhi draws loyalty after it, and together they show the image argues for testing first and keeping afterwards.
list_adds: its proverb is used after the bond is formed, where the quatrain uses the same thought before it, so the pair divides friendship into two stages.

note: Kural 788 says friendship removes distress at once, like the hand that catches a slipping garment; Pazhamozhi 127 says a friend's distress is not removed by words, as dew does not fill a tank.
teaches: The Kural gives the speed and instinct of true help; Pazhamozhi names what does not count as help, kindly words, and its dew-and-tank proverb shows that even sincere sympathy falls short of the deed.
list_adds: its proverb adds the negative case the couplet leaves out: words, however ungrudging, are dew and not water for the tank.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 துனியால் is an odd opening for the address and may be corrupt.

note: Naladiyar 369 says those whose hearts do not ease the pain a dear one tells them had better leap from a cliff; Pazhamozhi 127 says the remedy for a dear one's distress is not accomplished by words.
teaches: The quatrain makes a heart moved by a friend's pain the minimum of friendship; Pazhamozhi sets the bar higher, since feeling expressed in speech still leaves the tank empty, so the pair moves from compassion to remedy.
list_adds: its proverb ranks deed above sympathy where the quatrain asks only that the heart be moved.
audit_text_issue: pazhamozhi_nanooru:127 lines 2-3 (முனியார் செயினும், துனியால்) are hard to construe. | pazhamozhi_nanooru:127 lines 2-3 (முனியார் செயினும், துனியால்) are uncertain.

note: Kural 791 says nothing ruins like befriending without inquiry; Pazhamozhi 128 says there is no need to insist on worthy friends and one should take anyone's friendship, since a befriended dog brings in a hare.
teaches: On a plain reading the two disagree on whether a friend must be tested first: the Kural fears the bond one cannot leave, while Pazhamozhi counts the profit even a low friend brings, so the pair shows two grounds of valuing friendship, by its risk and by its yield.
list_adds: its proverb measures a friend by what he brings in, a ground of judgement the couplet does not use, and so drops the inquiry the couplet requires.

note: Naladiyar 213 says hold close those like a dog, which wags its tail with its master's spear in its body, and leave those like an elephant; Pazhamozhi 128 says a befriended dog brings in a good hare.
teaches: Both take the dog as the model friend but for different virtues: in the quatrain it is loyal even when wounded, in Pazhamozhi it is useful as a hunter, so the same animal serves a test of character and a reckoning of gain.
list_adds: its proverb keeps the quatrain's dog but changes its merit from loyalty to yield.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu 34 names as sweet leaving the friendship of worthless people even when they embrace one; Pazhamozhi 128 says one should take friendship whoever's it is.
teaches: Within the same group of works the counted verse and the proverb verse take opposite sides on befriending the unworthy, which shows the group does not speak with one voice on choosing friends.

note: Naladiyar 310 says that where old acquaintance stands as a post (பழமைகந் தாக) one may ask what intimacy allows; Pazhamozhi 129 speaks of friends who lean on old acquaintance as a post (பழமை கந்தாக) and closes that a span of respect beats a cubit of friendship.
teaches: The two use the same phrase of old acquaintance as a tethering post: the quatrain lets one lean on it to ask for help, while Pazhamozhi warns that leaning on it while dropping care wears the friendship out, so the post is a support with a limit.
list_adds: its proverb ranks a little respect above much intimacy, a measure the quatrain does not apply to the same post of old acquaintance.

note: Kural 801 defines old friendship as friendship that does not cut down the liberties intimacy gives; Pazhamozhi 129 says a span of respect is better than a cubit of friendship when intimacy is presumed upon without care.
teaches: The Kural asks the friend to bear the liberties of intimacy; Pazhamozhi sets a limit from the other side, that intimacy which forgets care and respect is worth less than a little regard, so the liberties of old friendship do not cancel the duty of regard.
list_adds: its proverb ranks two measures, respect and friendship, where the couplet only defines one.

note: Naladiyar 227 says the worthy see no fault in those they have joined, and those who bring out a friend's wrongs are lower than he; Pazhamozhi 130 says those who chose friends after sifting do not blame them among many, as no one tells a shameful dream.
teaches: The quatrain ranks exposing a friend as worse than his wrong; Pazhamozhi gives the reason through the dream: a friend chosen by oneself is part of oneself, so publishing his fault is publishing one's own shame.
list_adds: its proverb of the shameful dream adds why the exposer is shamed, which the quatrain asserts without a reason.

note: Kural 820 warns against those friendly at home who defame one in the assembly; Pazhamozhi 130 says those who chose friends after sifting do not blame them among many.
teaches: The Kural describes the false friend from the victim's side; Pazhamozhi describes the true friend from the speaker's side, and the pair makes the public gathering the place where a friendship is proved or broken.
list_adds: its proverb gives the true friend's reason for silence, the shameful dream one does not tell, where the couplet only names the false friend's fault.

note: Kural 808 praises those whose intimacy is strong enough not to listen to reports of a friend's lapse; Pazhamozhi 131 says one does not burn against a friend one has made even for faults seen with one's own eyes.
teaches: The Kural guards the friend against hearsay; Pazhamozhi goes further, to faults one has witnessed, and grounds the restraint in having made the friend oneself, as one does not watch one's own calf die.
list_adds: its proverb of the dying calf extends the couplet's case from reported faults to seen ones and gives the reason, that the friend is one's own.

note: Elathi 15 counts not burning against those dear as one's eyes (கண்போல்வார்க் காயாமை) among five good things; Pazhamozhi 131 says one does not burn against (காய்ந்தீயார்) a friend one has made even for faults seen with one's own eyes.
teaches: The counted verse lists the restraint as one good among five; Pazhamozhi sets the hardest condition on it, faults seen with one's own eyes, and argues it by the calf one would not see die.

note: Naladiyar 223 says it is right to bear with friends even when they do great wrong and closes with ஒருவர் பொறையிருவர் நட்பு; Pazhamozhi 132 closes with the same proverb after saying the faultless take a friend's fault as their own.
teaches: The two works close on the same proverb but frame it differently: the quatrain asks the injured friend to bear the wrong, while Pazhamozhi has the faultless friend own it as 'our fault', so the one who bears becomes the one who shares the blame.
list_adds: it applies the shared proverb to a different act, owning the fault rather than enduring the injury.

note: Kural 803 asks what use long friendship is if one does not accept a friend's liberty as if one had done it oneself; Pazhamozhi 132 says the faultless take a friend's faults as their own.
teaches: The Kural asks one to treat a friend's liberties as one's own acts; Pazhamozhi carries the same identification to his faults, so what began as tolerance of intimacy becomes sharing of blame.
list_adds: its proverb of one's patience as two's friendship extends the couplet from liberties to wrongs.

note: Innaa Narpathu 26 counts telling one's own trouble to those who do not care (பரியார்க்குத் தாமுற்ற கூற்று) as painful; Pazhamozhi 133 says one should tell one's want to one moved with care (பரிந்து) who will remove it.
teaches: The two say the same thing from two sides, the painful telling to the uncaring and the fitting telling to the caring healer, so together they make the listener's care the condition of disclosure.

note: Naladiyar 369 condemns those whose hearts do not ease the pain dear ones tell them; Pazhamozhi 133 says the sufferer should tell his want to one who will remove it, as the sick do not hide disease from the physician.
teaches: The quatrain speaks to the friend who hears; Pazhamozhi speaks to the friend who suffers and tells him to choose a hearer able to cure, so the pair completes the exchange of telling and easing from both ends.
list_adds: its proverb of patient and physician adds the sufferer's duty to disclose, which the quatrain assumes.

note: Naladiyar 284 says a thousand gather like crows while there is wealth and none asks after one in want; Pazhamozhi 134 says a thousand eat at a man's house while he lacks nothing, and in the Kali age the ruined have no friends.
teaches: The two share the thousand who feed on the prosperous, but Pazhamozhi places the desertion in the Kali age, turning the quatrain's account of poverty into a mark of a fallen time.
list_adds: its proverb with the Kali age frame adds a cause in the age itself, where the quatrain gives only the man's change of fortune.

note: Kural 796 says ruin has one benefit, that it measures one's people to full length; Pazhamozhi 134 says in the Kali age the ruined have no friends.
teaches: The Kural treats ruin as a rod that sorts true friends from false; Pazhamozhi reports what the rod finds in this age, nothing at all, so the couplet's consolation becomes a bleak verdict.
list_adds: its proverb gives the result of the measuring the couplet describes, the thousand eaters reduced to none.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 62 counts that want of close friends is learned in ruin (கெழியின்மை கேட்டா லறிக); Pazhamozhi 134 says the ruined have no friends.
teaches: The counted verse makes ruin a means of knowing; Pazhamozhi adds the crowd of eaters who vanish and puts the fact in the Kali age, so a test of friends becomes a judgement on the time.

note: Naladiyar 110 says what was fixed at birth does not shrink or grow and so asks why grieve at ruin; Pazhamozhi 135 turns the same fixed term against a friend turned murderer, who cannot shorten it.
teaches: Together they show the fixed-term doctrine working in two directions: the Naladiyar uses it to quiet grief over loss, while Pazhamozhi uses it to quiet fear of betrayal, making fate a shelter against human malice.
list_adds: its proverb pictures Death as the guard of a life until its portion is eaten, so the fixed span becomes protection from a plotting friend rather than a reason for calm at ruin.

note: Both picture Death as an eater: Nanmanikkadigai 40 says it does not take its food at anyone's bidding, Pazhamozhi 135 that it guards a man until his eating is done.
teaches: Put together, Death's refusal to eat at command explains the Pazhamozhi consolation: no plotter can order Death to take a man early, so the same appetite that cannot be bribed cannot be hurried either.

note: Naladiyar 218 asks what use is a close friend who gives not even a fly's foot of help; Pazhamozhi 136 names the friend kept as a reserve who gives none at need and adds that he first set one in danger.
teaches: The pair separates two failures the word 'useless friend' joins: the Naladiyar's friend merely gives nothing, while Pazhamozhi's raises one into peril and then withdraws, so the worst friend is the one whose help began.
list_adds: the ladder proverb adds the stage the quatrain lacks, being helped up and then stranded, which makes a half-given help worse than none.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 அச்சிடை இட்டு is compressed and its sense uncertain. | Line 3 அச்சிடை இட்டு is compressed; its sense is uncertain.

note: Kural 788 says friendship clears distress there and then, like the hand catching a slipping garment; Pazhamozhi 137 shows a friend who chose penance over battle, help offered when the festival is over.
teaches: Read with the Kural's 'there and then', the Balarama story shows that timing is the whole of friendship's help, so even a holy act done for the friend fails if it replaces help at the moment of need.
list_adds: it sets an epic case and a proverb of lateness against the couplet's simile of speed, and ranks the friend's present help above pious works done on his behalf.
audit_text_issue: site's text lacks line 1; graded on the packet text

note: Naladiyar 238 is a vow to put one's life in a distressed friend's hands; Pazhamozhi 137 condemns the friend who went off to penance instead of fighting beside his friend.
teaches: The vow and the story are the two halves of one rule: the Naladiyar says what the friend owes in the hour of danger, Pazhamozhi shows a famous figure who withheld it and calls his religion a late shoulder.
list_adds: it supplies a named failure for the quatrain's oath, so the duty to risk one's life is shown being broken by a pious withdrawal rather than by cowardice.
audit_text_issue: Site text lacks line 1 (flagged).

note: Kural 839 calls the friendship of fools very sweet because parting from them brings no pain; Pazhamozhi 138 closes with the proverb that the friendship of fools is painful afterwards. The tension holds if the Kural's line is read plainly rather than as irony.
teaches: The two place the pain of a fool's friendship differently: the Kural finds none at the parting because there was no real bond, while Pazhamozhi finds pain later because the fool believes slander and breaks the bond.
list_adds: it ranks friends by how they take slander, highest against lowest, and so names the cause of the later pain, which the couplet does not.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 தெரிதலால் is ambiguous between heeding and speaking the tale-bearing.

note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken by cruel slander like a shielded flame; Pazhamozhi 138 makes the same steadiness the mark of the highest friend, who finds no rift even when looking, against the lowest, who believe.
