teaches: The pair moves resistance to slander from a private virtue to a test of friendship: the Naladiyar's steady heart protects itself, Pazhamozhi's protects the bond between two other people.
list_adds: it sets the steady man against his opposite and names what the credulous one's belief costs, the friendship's later pain.

note: Naladiyar 229 says that when those taken as one's own prove otherwise, one should honour them all the more and keep it within; Pazhamozhi 139 calls heart's friendship given to the shameless moonlight shed in the forest.
teaches: Read together, the Naladiyar's counsel to keep honouring the false friend meets its limit in shamelessness: where the other has no shame within, the honour reaches no one, and Pazhamozhi counts it wasted.
list_adds: its proverb names the outcome the quatrain leaves out, that continued regard for the shameless lights an empty forest.

note: Kural 805 says that when friends do what hurts one should read it as folly or great intimacy; Pazhamozhi 140 says one should not act as one who knew them of old but break with them as they broke.
teaches: The two give opposite rules for the old friend who turns unfriendly: the Kural asks for a generous reading of the hurt, Pazhamozhi denies old acquaintance any claim and prescribes the break as a cure.
list_adds: its proverb treats breaking off as a medicine, so ending the friendship becomes a remedy rather than a failure of the patience the couplet asks.

note: Naladiyar 226 asks whether anyone cuts off his own hand because it poked his eye, so a friend who hurts should not be cast off; Pazhamozhi 140 says breaking with one who breaks is the remedy.
teaches: The images decide the rule: the Naladiyar makes the friend one's own limb, so cutting him off is self-harm, while Pazhamozhi makes the broken friendship an ailment, so the cut is the cure.
list_adds: the medicine proverb answers the quatrain's body image with one of cure, turning the same separation from mutilation into healing.

note: Naladiyar 375 uses the eel that shows one end to the snake and the other to the fish for women of double conduct; Pazhamozhi 141 calls the man who courts both friends and enemies a brand burning at both ends.
teaches: Both books picture double dealing as one body with two ends, but the eel profits by fitting each side, while the brand burns whoever holds it, so Pazhamozhi makes the two-sided man a danger to both sides rather than a clever survivor.
list_adds: it moves the two-ended image from the courtesan to the go-between among friends and foes, and its proverb names the harm to the holder that the eel image does not.

note: Pazhamozhi 139 counts love given to the shameless as wasted; 140 goes on to say what to do when a friend turns unfriendly: break with him.
teaches: Read in order, the two verses move from loss to action: once the love is seen to be moonlight in a forest, the next counsel is to stop shedding it and answer the break with a break.

note: Kural 505 makes one's own deeds the only touchstone of greatness and smallness; Pazhamozhi 142 says one part seen of a person, like one ladle from the pot, suffices to judge the whole.
teaches: Together they turn the Kural's touchstone into a method of sampling: one need not watch all a person's deeds, since a single act examined stands for the whole as one ladle stands for the pot.
list_adds: its cooking image and proverb add the claim that a small sample is enough, which the couplet's touchstone does not say.

note: Kural 271 says the five elements within laugh at the deceiver's hidden conduct; Pazhamozhi 143 says the wrongdoer who thinks his deed screened by a mountain is pierced by others' eyes, sharper than arrows.
teaches: The pair names two witnesses the hider cannot escape, his own body within and other people's eyes without, so concealed wrong is seen from both sides at once.
list_adds: it moves the witness from the body's elements to the onlookers and gives the wrongdoer's false belief, the mountain, that the proverb answers.

note: Kural 824 warns of deceivers whose faces smile while their hearts are bitter, so the face hides malice; Pazhamozhi 144 says the deceitful are known on sight because the face tells what the heart intends even when they conceal it.
teaches: Read together they disagree on whether a deceiver's face can be trusted to betray him: the Kural fears the face that masks, the Pazhamozhi trusts the face to leak, so the reader must ask whether the skill lies in the face or in the one who reads it.
list_adds: its flood image claims the sign comes before the deed and cannot be held back, a confidence the couplet denies.

note: Kural 706 says the face, like crystal, shows what is strongest in the heart; Pazhamozhi 144 applies this to deceit held under concealment (ஒளிப்பினும்).
teaches: The pair extends the Kural's claim from feeling that shows freely to intent that is actively hidden, and holds that concealment does not stop the face's showing.
list_adds: it narrows the couplet to கள்ளம் and adds the condition of hiding, with the flood's dampness as the sign that runs ahead.

note: Kural 708 says it is enough to stand and look at the face of those who read the inward; Pazhamozhi 145 says for those who know faces the face suffices to know intention, as a mirror shows one's unseen limbs.
teaches: The Kural speaks of the petitioner who needs only show his face to a perceptive master, and the Pazhamozhi gives the reason it suffices: the face works as a mirror that makes the unseen inward visible.
list_adds: its mirror image supplies the mechanism the couplet assumes, and its proverb frames face and mind as offspring and source.

note: Naladiyar 127 asks who can examine another's mind, since minds and deeds differ; Pazhamozhi 146 opens with nearly the same words (ஒருவர் ஒருவர்தம் உள்ளத்தைத் தேரும்) and grants the difficulty, but answers that people take the colour of their kin.
teaches: The two share the question almost word for word and part on the answer: the Naladiyar leaves the mind unknowable because conduct misleads, while the Pazhamozhi finds an outside mark, lineage, that it trusts more than conduct.
list_adds: its proverb turns the Naladiyar's closing despair into a method, making kin the visible plumage of a hidden nature.

note: Kural 959 says a sprout shows the soil and speech shows the lineage one was born in; Pazhamozhi 146 runs the inference the other way, using lineage to read the hidden mind, as land shows in a bird's colour.
teaches: In the Kural lineage is what is inferred from speech, and in the Pazhamozhi lineage is the evidence from which the mind is inferred, so the pair shows kin serving as both sign and signified in this ethics.
list_adds: its bird image matches the Kural's soil image but makes kin the key to another's mind rather than the thing to be found.

note: Kural 972 holds birth alike for all living beings and distinction to come from the work done; Pazhamozhi 147 says one's own birth-group (தஞ்சாதி) shows through any concealment, as in the keeper's daughter.
teaches: The pair sets two views of what makes a person's standing side by side: for the Kural deeds make the difference, for this verse birth leaves a mark no change of house can hide.
list_adds: its exemplum and proverb make birth an ineradicable trait shown in a habit of eating, where the couplet makes birth equal and conduct the divider.
audit_text_issue: pazhamozhi_nanooru:147 lines 1-2 are obscure: காப்பான் twice and the rare மேய்ப்பாட்டது.

note: Naladiyar 195 calls good and bad caste mere words and makes lineage from austerity, learning and effort; Pazhamozhi 147 says one's own சாதி breaks through concealment.
teaches: Within the same group of ethics works the Naladiyar denies that caste has substance while the Pazhamozhi treats it as a nature that betrays itself, so the group holds no single view of birth.
list_adds: its story gives birth an observable trait, which is just what the quatrain denies birth has.
audit_text_issue: line 2 episode obscure

note: Kural 454 says understanding seems to be in the mind but lies in one's company; Pazhamozhi 148 makes company the test by which others, sages included, are known.
teaches: The Kural's claim about where understanding lives becomes, in the Pazhamozhi, a rule of evidence: if a person's nature is in their company, then the company is what an observer should read, even of a sage.
list_adds: it extends the couplet to the judging of முனிவர் and sets company above witnesses and inquiry as proof.

note: Pazhamozhi 146 reads a hidden mind by kin; Pazhamozhi 148 reads it by the company kept, without inquiry or witnesses.
teaches: Within one heading the book offers two outward marks of an inner nature, the group one is born into and the group one chooses, and 148 adds that the second applies even to renouncers who have left their kin.

note: Kural 442 bids one cherish as support those who remove an affliction that has come and guard against one to come; Pazhamozhi 149 says one need not seek helpers at all, since each is his own physician.
teaches: The Kural's helper is a physician to the king, and Pazhamozhi takes the same healing image back for the self, so the two disagree on whether one's trouble can be cured from outside.
list_adds: its proverb turns the couplet's healer into the striver himself, denying that another can do one's own work.

note: Kural 410 sets the unlearned to the learned as beasts to men; Pazhamozhi 150 calls wise the man who finishes his task even if he has learned nothing.
teaches: Read together, the two give rival measures of a person: the Kural ranks by what one has studied, Pazhamozhi by what one has completed, and on its reading the unlearned doer outranks the idle learned.
list_adds: its proverb moves rank from learning and age to finished work, a criterion the couplet does not admit.

note: Kural 81 says household life exists for tending guests and doing them good (விருந்தோம்பி வேளாண்மை); Pazhamozhi 151 uses the same pair of words and sets battle valour and freedom from sloth beside them.
teaches: The pairing shows the Kural's purpose of the household needs a means it does not name: hospitality is sustained only by toil, so giving to guests stands with valour as a fruit of effort.
list_adds: it puts hospitality, beneficence and sword-valour in one series closed by toil, making giving an outcome of effort rather than the end of the household alone.

note: Kural 611 forbids slackening because a task seems hard; Pazhamozhi 152 forbids it because a single effort seems too small to help.
teaches: Together they close both exits from effort: the Kural answers the excuse that the task is too great, Pazhamozhi the excuse that one's part is too small.
list_adds: it names the opposite excuse to the couplet's and gives the cost, not surviving even the day.
audit_text_issue: The quotation marks cover only சென்றது பேராதவர், not a whole saying.

note: Pazhamozhi 153 promises that the unwearied never fail to reach their aim; Naladiyar 194 makes manliness standing firm even when the thing does not succeed.
teaches: The pair splits the reward of effort: Pazhamozhi gives the friendless striver success as his warrant, while the Naladiyar holds that persistence is the measure even when success does not come.
list_adds: it ties effort to the excuse of having no kin and guarantees success, where the quatrain detaches manliness from success.

note: Kural 471 bids one weigh the strength of the deed, one's own, the opponent's and the allies' before acting; Pazhamozhi 154 weighs oneself, one's helpers and the gain, using the same verb தூக்கி.
teaches: Pazhamozhi adds the gain to the Kural's weighing of strengths and says what follows without it, so the reckoning is shown to be of purpose as well as of power.
list_adds: it replaces the enemy's strength with the gain in the reckoning and adds, through its proverb, the formless result of unweighed action.

note: Purananuru 39 tells a Chola that, with ancestors who destroyed the hanging fort, killing is not his own fame; Pazhamozhi 155 recalls the same Chola feat of the fort in the sky.
teaches: The puram poem treats the hanging fort as inherited glory a descendant cannot claim, while the ethics verse turns it into a lesson anyone can use: the fort fell to force applied by the right means.

note: Both verses forbid pleading 'I have no kin' as a reason to fail; 153 answers it with unwearied effort, 156 with the image of the long-armed man's great shoulders.
teaches: The pair shows the heading's single counsel argued two ways, by the promise of success and by the sign of strength in one's own body, so the lack of kin is answered both by outcome and by capacity.

note: Kural 691 tells those who attach themselves to kings to stay like fire-warmers, neither far nor near; Pazhamozhi 157 calls those who seek wealth through kings a crow on a pestle.
teaches: The Kural offers a way to keep a safe place by the king, and Pazhamozhi doubts that such a place can be kept: the courtier's perch moves with every stroke.
list_adds: its proverb makes court dependence itself unstable and sets it against wealth won by effort, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: Kural 517 says to examine who will finish a task by what means and then leave it to him; Pazhamozhi 158 shows the task handed out of sloth to those without firm grip, while the master too lets go.
teaches: The Kural's letting go is safe only after examination; Pazhamozhi shows the same handing-over done from sloth, so delegation is a virtue or a ruin depending on why it is done.
list_adds: it names the motive, sloth, and the double loss of grip, which the couplet's rule of choosing assumes away.

note: 149 says no one does for another what that other must do; 159 applies it to the man who waits to have his task done later by someone else.
teaches: 159 supplies the evidence for 149's flat denial: the helper one waits for will not even heat water, so he will not leap into fire for one.

note: Naladiyar 110 says what was set in the early mark neither shrinks nor grows and comes as due; Pazhamozhi 160, on the reading that the smearer rewrites the leaf, says a faulty written fate can be remade.
teaches: The two give opposite answers to what one should do before a fixed fate: the Naladiyar counsels calm acceptance, Pazhamozhi effort that rewrites the leaf, and both reject grieving or idle worship.
list_adds: its proverb casts fate as a palm-leaf document that a later hand can correct, against the quatrain's mark that cannot change.
audit_text_issue: proverb இழுகினான் ஆகாப்பது இல்லையே is obscure

note: Kural 620 says those who toil without flagging see even fate's back; Pazhamozhi 160 says folded hands before the one who fixed fate end no trouble.
teaches: Pazhamozhi names the rival of effort that the Kural leaves unstated, pious resignation, and replaces the Kural's battle image with a scribe correcting a leaf.
list_adds: it sets worship of the fixer of fate against effort, making resignation itself the error.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 இழுகினான் ஆகாப்பது இல்லையே is obscure.

note: Kural 612 warns against letting a task die midway, since the world's regard follows how one deals with unfinished work; Pazhamozhi 161 says what broke off unfinished has no increase and what does not exist has no name.
teaches: Pazhamozhi states as a law of naming what the Kural states as social regard: the half-done work does not earn a poor name but no name at all.
list_adds: its four parallel clauses rank the finished, the broken-off and the capable, ending in the proverb that the undone has no name.

note: Kural 814 prefers solitude to allies like an untrained horse that throws its rider in battle; Pazhamozhi 163 describes those who stir their own side into a quarrel and flee first.
teaches: The couplet's ally fails at the decisive moment; Pazhamozhi adds that the same man often made the battle, so the desertion is the second half of a single betrayal that begins with words.
list_adds: its proverb of the broken food-bowl names the fault as ingratitude to one's own support, where the couplet only weighs such company against being alone.

note: Kural 672 sorts tasks into those to be done slowly and those to be done at once; Pazhamozhi 164 says work with intimates must be carried patiently, since haste ruins it.
teaches: The couplet leaves open how to tell the slow task from the urgent one; Pazhamozhi supplies one test, the closeness of the people involved, and the cost of getting it wrong, that the work turns into trouble.
list_adds: it places the slow kind of task in the circle of one's intimates and adds the condition of keeping to the spoken word, which the couplet does not name.

note: Kural 504 tells the employer to examine both good qualities and faults and take what predominates; Pazhamozhi 165 says not to voice an unsteady helper's faults but to take the benefit.
teaches: The couplet's weighing of faults happens in the employer's mind; Pazhamozhi adds that once the helper is in use, saying the faults aloud is itself a fault, so the examination must stay silent.
list_adds: its proverb of the holed appam turns the weighing into a rule of speech: the faults are counted in choosing and not counted again in the using.

note: Kural 1078 says the worthy are of use at a word and the base only when crushed like cane; Pazhamozhi 166 says to win help by affection, as forcing it is milking a cow with an arrow.
teaches: Read together, the two divide the means by the person: affection draws service from the ordinary helper while force kills what it wants, and the couplet marks the base as the exception who yield only under pressure.
list_adds: its paired images of the calf let in and the arrow loosed rank gentle means over force for ordinary dealings, which the couplet, speaking only of two extremes, does not do.

note: Both use the chisel that will not cut even into a tender shoot unless struck; the Naladiyar applies it to the base, Pazhamozhi 169 to any agent left to do a task.
teaches: The Naladiyar makes the unstruck chisel a mark of base character, but Pazhamozhi uses the same saying of the employer's duty to everyone he employs, so the image shifts blame from the worker's nature to the master's need to keep directing.
list_adds: the quatrain uses the chisel to sort people into kind and harsh-ruled; the Pazhamozhi makes it a rule for the master after the handing over, a stage the quatrain never reaches.

note: 166 says service should be won by affection, not forced; 169 says even entrusted work needs striking like a chisel.
teaches: The two adjacent counsels separate winning a helper from running him: affection is the way to gain his will, but once the task is his, the master's prompting is still needed, so gentleness at the start does not excuse absence later.

note: Naladiyar 345 says a dog fed from a golden bowl still watches for others' leftovers, so honouring the base does not change their deeds; Pazhamozhi 170 says setting the base on a task and sitting back is setting a cat to guard fish heads.
teaches: The quatrain states the base man's fixed appetite; Pazhamozhi turns it into a charge against the employer, whose fault is not only the choice but sitting idle afterwards, so the base nature becomes the master's loss.
list_adds: it moves the quatrain's observation into the employer's domain and adds the second fault of leaving the agent unwatched.

note: Kural 503 says even those who have studied hard books and are flawless are rarely without some blankness; Pazhamozhi 171 says even one who has learnt and is rid of faults should not get a task without clear practical knowledge.
teaches: The verbal echo (learned and faultless) makes the pair a step: the couplet admits learning leaves gaps, and Pazhamozhi draws the employer's conclusion that learning and faultlessness alone do not qualify a man for a task.
list_adds: it adds the decision the couplet leaves open, that the work should wait rather than go to the learned but incapable.
audit_text_issue: pazhamozhi_nanooru:171 lines 2 and 4 are hard to divide (முற்றலை; மற்றதென் பாற்றேம்பல்). | pazhamozhi_nanooru:171 line 4 மற்றதென் பாற்றேம்பல் is hard to divide.

note: Kural 515 says work is not to be given to anyone but one who knows and can do it, merely because he is favoured; Pazhamozhi 172 says not to ask whether a man is kin but to look only at learning.
teaches: The couplet bars favour as a ground; Pazhamozhi names the commonest favour, kinship, and adds a concession the couplet lacks, that even a disobedient learned agent costs no more than the salt fed to a working ox.
list_adds: its proverb weighs the risk of the learned stranger against kin and finds the risk cheap, a cost-reckoning the couplet does not make.

note: 168 says even one's own cart needs grease, so an agent takes his small share; 173 says wealth always clings to those who handle it, so careless handlers must not be chosen.
teaches: Together the two verses accept the handler's share as unavoidable and then limit it: the master budgets for the grease but chooses men who care for the work, so the cut stays a காணி and does not become flight with the goods.
audit_text_issue: Both verses are flagged uncertain; 168 பாணித்தே is ambiguous.

note: Kural 510 says doubting one who has been trusted brings endless trouble; Pazhamozhi 174 says that if an appointee proves bad he should be let go without public exposure.
teaches: The couplet warns against doubt of a trusted man; Pazhamozhi takes the harder case where the doubt is proven, and still counsels quiet removal, so the concern in both is the damage done by open distrust.
list_adds: it adds the case the couplet does not face, the appointee who has truly failed, and the manner of removing him.
audit_text_issue: 174 line 4 proverb uncertain

note: Kural 520 tells the ruler to look daily into those who do his work; Pazhamozhi 175 says raising untrustworthy men and leaving them far off is setting a tortoise loose in a pond and asking it to return.
teaches: The couplet prescribes daily oversight; Pazhamozhi shows what its absence looks like, an agent out of sight and in his own element, and adds that the fault is compounded when the agent lacked honesty of mind from the start.
list_adds: its proverb joins two errors the couplet keeps apart from choosing, raising the wrong man and sending him beyond sight.

note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy for anyone and doing as spoken is hard; Pazhamozhi 176 says the bystander's subtle advice is easy while the doer who enters without inner knowledge perishes.
teaches: The couplet sets saying against doing in one person; Pazhamozhi splits them between two, the adviser at the edge of the board and the player in it, so the cost of easy speech falls on someone else.
list_adds: its dice-board proverb puts the speaker and the doer in different seats, which the couplet's single subject does not.

note: Kural 677 says the doer should learn the mind of one who knows the task from inside; Pazhamozhi 176 warns against the bystander who speaks fine words but does not know the task's hidden state.
teaches: The couplet tells the doer to take counsel; Pazhamozhi adds which counsel to refuse, that of the onlooker who talks subtly from outside, so the test of an adviser is inner knowledge, not subtlety.
list_adds: it sets the false adviser beside the true one the couplet names, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: Naladiyar 350 says small bullocks never learn to draw the cart however well fed; Pazhamozhi 167 says forcing work from a slack man is ploughing with an idle old bullock.
teaches: The quatrain says care cannot supply a missing capacity; Pazhamozhi adds that pressure cannot either, so between them neither feeding nor driving makes the unfit beast or man do the work.
list_adds: it turns the quatrain's verdict on the base into a rule for the employer about sloth and the use of force.
audit_text_issue: பாரித்தவன் (line 3) is uncertain.

note: Kural 506 warns against trusting those cut off from kin, since ties make a person accountable; Pazhamozhi 177 says kinship or friendship is no ground for trusting anyone with one's weak point.
teaches: Together they show ties as a necessary but not sufficient condition of trust: the kinless are not to be trusted, yet kin are not to be trusted with one's exposed point either, since even a god acted for his own ends.
list_adds: its proverb grounds the limit in a universal claim proved from a god's conduct, so the couplet's reliance on attachment meets a rule that self-interest outruns every bond.

note: Kural 1076 likens the base to a beaten drum that proclaims every secret heard; Pazhamozhi 178 likens the choosing of a mean confidant to putting the stick to the drum.
teaches: The drum image moves from the base man to his chooser: the Kural blames the drum for sounding, Pazhamozhi blames the one who sets the stick to it, so the leak begins in a bad choice of confidant over worthy kin.
list_adds: it sets the mean confidant against kin rich in excellence, turning the couplet's description of the base into a fault of selection by the one who confides.

note: Kural 1076 makes carrying on (உய்த்து) secrets the mark of the base; Pazhamozhi 180 says that even pleasant friends cannot refrain from passing on (உயவாது) what they heard, then restricts the rule to the base.
teaches: Read with the Kural, the verse shows the trait the couplet confines to the base is near-universal, so keeping secrets from the base is a minimum measure, not a sufficient safeguard.
list_adds: it widens the couplet's claim from the base to everyone, even agreeable friends, before narrowing it again in the proverb, a turn the couplet lacks.

note: Thirikadugam 55 counts a friendship that does not keep a weighty secret as a spy; Pazhamozhi 180 says that even among pleasant friends no one keeps back what he heard.
teaches: Together they show that the leaking friend is not a rare traitor but the common case, which is why a counted work can number him among the spies inside one's circle.

note: Kural 847 says the man without understanding who lets slip the precious secret (அருமறை) harms himself; Pazhamozhi 181 says telling the precious secret (அருமறை) to the small-hearted is cotton carded on a palm-top.
teaches: The pair names one concrete way the secret slips: handing it to a small heart, and the image shows why the harm the Kural calls self-inflicted cannot be recalled once done.
list_adds: it opposes the noble keepers to the small-hearted hearers, adding to the couplet's lone fool a ranking of who can hold a secret at all.

note: Kural 509 bids one trust no one without examination; Pazhamozhi 182 applies this even to the affectionate and says the unexamined truster perishes.
teaches: The pairing extends the Kural's rule to the case where it is hardest to keep, affection, and fixes the stake at death rather than mere trouble.
list_adds: it ranks the hostile, who need no testing because they are plainly not to be told, below the affectionate, who must be tested, a contrast the couplet does not draw.
audit_text_issue: Pazhamozhi 182's முளிந்தாரை is rare and the sense is flagged uncertain.

note: Pazhamozhi 179 permits telling a secret once the hearer's love is known; Naladiyar 127 asks who has the power to know another's mind, since mind and deed differ.
teaches: Held together they show the condition Pazhamozhi sets may never be met: if love cannot be read from conduct, the counsel to wait for known love becomes a counsel of near-total silence.
list_adds: the Naladiyar quatrain denies the knowledge of minds that Pazhamozhi's proverb of the hunting trail presupposes can be had.
audit_text_issue: 179 lines 2-4 compressed

note: Kural 510 says trusting without examining brings endless trouble; Pazhamozhi 183 gives the case of a ruler who gave without weighing the one who came and lost the world.
teaches: Together they show that the couplet's untested trust covers generosity too: the open-handed king who does not weigh the asker suffers the very trouble the Kural assigns to careless trust.
list_adds: its story turns the couplet's abstract fault into a royal gift, so the failure to examine is shown in the act the ethics books most praise, giving.
audit_text_issue: Verse sense flagged uncertain.

note: Kural 423 asks for the truth of whatever is heard from any mouth; the proverb of Pazhamozhi 185 asks that even what one saw be weighed before it is spoken.
teaches: The pair extends testing from what one hears to what one has seen and from judging to speaking: the Kural doubts others' report, the proverb doubts one's own eyes as a ground for testimony.
list_adds: it moves the test from the hearer's understanding to the witness's speech before a king, adding the shame that makes a worthy man hold back.

note: Both set the millet grain against the palmyra: in Kural 104 a millet-sized kindness is reckoned palm-sized, in Pazhamozhi 187 a millet-grain's gain near at hand is preferred and the palm is the tree too slow to feed its planter.
teaches: The same millet-and-palm scale serves two judgements of value: the Kural enlarges the small out of gratitude, Pazhamozhi prefers the small because it is near and certain, so the image teaches valuing the small for moral and for prudential reasons.
list_adds: it makes the palm stand for delay rather than size, adding time to a scale the couplet uses only for magnitude.

note: Kural 99 asks why one who sees the sweetness sweet speech yields would use harsh words; Pazhamozhi 191 asks the same of those who can tell good speech from mean, and answers that only mean speech brings trouble.
teaches: The two rest one choice on two motives: the Kural on the good that sweet speech brings, Pazhamozhi on the danger harsh speech brings back to the speaker, so the case for sweet speech is both gain and safety.
list_adds: its proverb turns the couplet's rhetorical question into a rule about risk, that sweet speech never endangers, which the couplet does not state.

note: Pazhamozhi 191 says sweet speech never brings anyone into trouble; Thirikadugam 24 names a courtesan's sweet words as a mire that sinks those who step in.
teaches: Read together they show the proverb holds for the speaker, not the hearer: one's own sweet speech is safe, but another's sweet speech may be bait, so sweet speech protects the one who uses it and can trap the one who trusts it.

note: Both close on உடைத்து, 'the world holds such': Kural 277 those bright outside like the kunri seed and black within, Pazhamozhi 194 thieves like peacocks who seem attached by day and rob by night.
teaches: Pazhamozhi moves the Kural's hidden-black ascetic into the household: the false outside belongs to dependants who live with one, and the betrayal is a theft of food and clothing in the hours of sleep.
list_adds: it gives the couplet's single colour image a sequence of acts, night theft and daylight show of attachment, which makes the deceit something one can watch for.

note: Thirikadugam 51 says deceivers stay deceivers even when they keep close and that examination shows them; Pazhamozhi 194 shows deceivers who keep close, appearing attached by day while stealing by night.
teaches: The pair says both that closeness proves nothing and what the examination must look for: the gap between the day's show of attachment and the night's acts.
audit_text_issue: thirikadugam:51 line 1 தூர்ந்துஒழுகி is obscure; the link rests on line 2, which is clear. | thirikadugam:51 line 1 தூர்ந்துஒழுகி is obscure.

note: Kural 426 says understanding lives as the world lives; Pazhamozhi 195 closes on running with the town's way, but first asks for repeated private scrutiny of what one has seen without heeding others.
teaches: The pair shows that going with the world is the end of a private test, not a substitute for it: Pazhamozhi puts one's own repeated examination before conformity, as the Kural's chapter sets 423 beside 426.
list_adds: it ranks the counsels in order, not abandoning dependants, not leaving the renouncers' path, examining for oneself, and only then conforming, so conformity comes last.
audit_text_issue: line 2 uncertain

note: Kural 759 calls wealth the sharpest steel for cutting down enemies' pride (செருக்கறுக்கும்); Pazhamozhi 196 says wealth given cuts off (அறுத்தல்) the senseless better than a spear.
teaches: The pair shows how the Kural's metaphor works in practice: wealth wounds not by being held but by being handed over, so the sharpest blade is a payment that leaves the opponent nothing to resist.
list_adds: its proverb sets the gift and the spear side by side and ranks the gift above force, a contrast the couplet only implies.

note: Kural 753 calls wealth an unfailing lamp that cuts darkness wherever one goes; Pazhamozhi 197 says the rich see well even in the sea, while the same affairs bring the poor to grief.
teaches: Together the two make wealth a means of sight as well as of power: the Kural's lamp travels to any land, and Pazhamozhi carries it into the sea, the place where sight should fail, and adds the poor man for whom the same road is dark.
list_adds: it sets the rich man's ease against the poor man's trouble in the same affairs, a contrast the couplet does not draw.
audit_text_issue: The proverb கடலுள்ளும் காண்பவே நன்கு has no fixed sense.

note: Naladiyar 283 says bees do not go to the hill where the kanthal has not flowered, so the poor have no kin; Pazhamozhi 198 says no one who dug a tank sought out the frogs, so the rich need not seek those who need them.
teaches: Read together, the two nature images state one law from both sides: people are drawn by what can be had, so the rich are sought without seeking and the poor are left without kin, and Pazhamozhi presents as a comfort what the Naladiyar presents as a grief.
list_adds: it states the attraction from the side of the owner, who may wait, where the quatrain states it from the side of the poor man who is abandoned.

note: Kural 752 says all honour the rich and all scorn the poor; Pazhamozhi 199 says even the compassionate praise the rich and gives the reason in its proverb, that two take from the fortunate.
teaches: The Kural states the fact; Pazhamozhi names whom 'all' includes, even those whose compassion should look to need, and explains the praise by interest, since everyone shares in what the rich hold.
list_adds: it divides the Kural's 'all' into the compassionate and the rest and supplies a motive, a reason the couplet does not give.
audit_text_issue: Proverb sense uncertain.

note: Naladiyar 280 counts guarding wealth among its bitter sufferings (காத்தலும் ஆங்கே கடுந்துன்பம்); Pazhamozhi 200 says the wealth one guards guards its owner in return, like the thicket and the tiger. The tension holds on the plain reading of both: the Jain quatrain treats guarding as a cost, the proverb as a mutual defence.
teaches: The two books judge the same act of keeping wealth oppositely: for the Naladiyar the guard is one more place of suffering, for Pazhamozhi it is what makes wealth a shelter, so the dispute is whether wealth is a burden on its owner or a defence of him.
list_adds: its proverb makes guarding reciprocal, which turns the quatrain's one-way burden into an exchange of protection.

note: Kural 478 says a small income brings no ruin if outgo is not wider; Pazhamozhi 201 says a small income gathered daily grows great, like drops into a flood.
teaches: The pair gives two answers to the small income: the Kural makes it safe by limiting what goes out, Pazhamozhi makes it great by what accumulates over time, so a narrow channel is both a limit to respect and a source that time can enlarge.
list_adds: it adds the daily repetition and a second image of gathered light, turning the couplet's balance of channels into growth by accumulation.

note: Kural 667 says not to despise anyone for their form, since the great chariot has its linchpin; Pazhamozhi 202 uses the same words (எள்ளாமை வேண்டும்) of one whose small beginnings are known in town, since the market calf may become a bull.
teaches: The two give different grounds for the same rule: the Kural's small linchpin matters now by where it stands, while Pazhamozhi's calf matters later by what it grows into, so contempt can err about function or about time.
list_adds: it moves the rule from bodily size to known origin or capital, and grounds it in growth over time rather than in present function.

note: Pazhamozhi 201 says small drops gathered make a flood; Pazhamozhi 203 says the licks of a jackal do not dry the sea, so petty thefts do not hurt great wealth.
teaches: Side by side, the two verses show that the book's arithmetic of small amounts runs only toward growth: daily drops add up to a flood, but daily thefts are not allowed to add up to loss, because the scale of the whole decides which small things count.

note: Kural 1043 says poverty destroys at once one's ancient descent and dignity; Pazhamozhi 204 says the great known to the land, though fallen poor, keep their standing, since no dog sniffs at a tiger's head. The tension depends on reading the couplet's தொல்வரவு as inherited standing, as its marks do.
teaches: The two disagree on whether poverty can strip inherited greatness: the Kural says it takes descent and dignity together, while Pazhamozhi holds that renown already known to the land outlasts the wealth that won it.
list_adds: its proverb of the dog and the tiger's head adds the onlookers, the mean who do not dare, where the couplet speaks only of what the poor man loses.

note: Pazhamozhi 89 says the poverty of the great is better than the wealth of the small, as old ghee never sinks below buttermilk; Pazhamozhi 204 says the fallen great are not insulted by the mean.
teaches: Together the two verses build the book's case that greatness is not measured by wealth: 89 ranks the poor great above the rich small in worth, and 204 adds that others still treat them so, since the tiger's head is safe from dogs.

note: Kural 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming are not shaken by affliction; Pazhamozhi 205 applies that foresight to one's own wealth and to the prosperity of one's kin.
teaches: The Kural's foresight is a general shield against calamity; the snail that stores water shows it as stockpiling for a known dry season, so foresight becomes provision for kin as well as self.
list_adds: it joins one's own wealth and the kin's prosperity as one object of forethought, which the couplet leaves unnamed, and gives the snail as the instance.
audit_text_issue: The proverb image (நந்து, சேணோக்கி) is uncertain.

note: Kural 508 warns that trusting an outsider (பிறன்) without examining him brings lasting trouble; Pazhamozhi 206 refuses even eminent men and kin the trust of one's goods until they are tested.
teaches: The Kural's danger is the untested stranger; Pazhamozhi removes the exemption kinship might seem to give, so testing applies inside the family too, and adds that the loss of entrusted wealth cannot be reversed.
list_adds: it names the two pretexts for trust, standing and kinship, and sets both aside, which the couplet does not, since it speaks only of the outsider.

note: Both speak of guarding ஈட்டிய ஒண்பொருள், earned bright wealth: the Naladiyar calls that guarding bitter suffering and wealth the dwelling of suffering, while Pazhamozhi 208 counts guarding it oneself a duty and handing it carelessly to others a folly.
teaches: On the same phrase the Jain quatrain makes custody of earned wealth a burden to be shed, by giving it away, while Pazhamozhi makes it a charge never to be delegated, so the two disagree on whether keeping earned wealth is worth its care.
list_adds: its crow proverb makes the careless handing over the fault, where the quatrain's list of sufferings makes the guarding itself the fault.

note: Both use grass fed to a bullock that will not work: the Naladiyar's small bullocks never take the yoke however much cut grass they eat, and Pazhamozhi 209's grass is fed to a sluggish ox.
teaches: The Naladiyar uses the ox to show that the base cannot be improved by feeding, while Pazhamozhi uses it to show the feeder's loss, so the one image condemns the base man's nature in one book and the owner's choice of keeper in the other.
list_adds: it moves the image from the base man who has come into wealth to the wealth a householder hands to a man of no family, making the image a counsel on custody.

note: Kural 1000 says great wealth got by a man without courtesy spoils like good milk in a faulty vessel; Pazhamozhi 209 says wealth placed in the hands of a man not of good family is grass fed to a sluggish ox.
teaches: The Kural blames the holder's character for spoiling his own wealth, while Pazhamozhi turns this into a rule for the owner who chooses a keeper, and makes birth rather than courtesy the test.
list_adds: it carries the couplet's claim from the man who owns wealth to the man to whom wealth is entrusted, and its proverb makes the loss a waste with no return rather than a spoiling.

note: Kural 535 says the man who slipped by not guarding beforehand grieves afterwards over his own error; Pazhamozhi 210 says neglecting what one had and searching to get it back later is catching a peacock with butter.
teaches: The Kural leaves the negligent man with regret, while Pazhamozhi follows him into his attempt to undo the loss and shows the attempt itself as absurd, so the cost of neglect is wasted effort as well as grief.
list_adds: its proverb mocks the method of recovery, a stage the couplet does not reach, and fixes the neglect on wealth one already had.

note: 206 bars entrusting wealth to untested kin and eminent men; 208 bars handing it carelessly to worthless men; both turn on wealth put into another's hands.
teaches: Read together, the two verses show the danger of entrusting wealth from both sides: the keeper may be untested though respectable, or plainly base, and in each case the owner's own lapse is the fault.

note: 211 says wealth let out of hand does not come back; 212 says a lender who let a loan lie and then asks for it is met with the borrower's anger.
teaches: 212 supplies the mechanism behind 211's maxim: lent wealth fails to return not only by loss but because asking for it turns the borrower hostile, so the loan costs the friendship as well as the goods.
audit_text_issue: 211's proverb கடம்பெற்றான் பெற்றான் குடம் is obscure.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 9 says a debtor's tongue dies when he once sees his creditor; Pazhamozhi 212 says the borrower asked to repay grows angry as if at an enemy.
teaches: The Sirupanchamoolam gives the debtor's shame and Pazhamozhi his anger, and Pazhamozhi ties the anger to the lender's long delay, so shame is seen to turn into resentment once a loan has lain unclaimed.
audit_text_issue: Sirupanchamoolam 9's கடவான் and the last item's sense are uncertain.

note: Kural 113 bids one let go at once any gain that comes from leaving fairness, even if it brings good; Pazhamozhi 213 says the good do not even desire such gain, and gives the reason in the proverb.
teaches: The Kural's command assumes the unfair gain may truly bring good; the proverb denies even that, so renouncing it becomes good sense rather than sacrifice.
list_adds: its proverb and the image of the onrushing wave add a mechanism, that the gain's apparent growth is the first stage of its loss, which the couplet leaves out.

note: Kural 659 says what is taken with tears goes with tears; Pazhamozhi 213 says evil gains perish as they seem to thrive.
teaches: Together the two make ill-gotten wealth self-cancelling twice over: it leaves the way it came, and its swelling is the very shape of the leaving.
list_adds: it sets the claim as a choice the good make in advance, refusing to want such wealth, where the couplet only forecasts its end.

note: Kural 1008 likens the wealth of the unloved to a poison tree fruiting in the middle of town; Pazhamozhi 214 likens the wealth of the irresolute to a mango that fruits and draws the stick.
teaches: The same fruiting tree cuts two ways: in the Kural the fruit is useless to the town, in Pazhamozhi it is coveted and brings blows on the tree, so wealth harms either its neighbours or its holder.
list_adds: it moves the fault from the owner's being unloved to his lacking tested resolve, and turns the tree from an emblem of uselessness into a target.

note: Kural 1009 says others take the wealth gathered by giving up love and virtue; Pazhamozhi 214 says wealth draws attackers when its holder lacks firmness, though the wealth itself is good.
teaches: Losing wealth to others has two causes in the pair: a vice in how it was gathered and a weakness in who holds it, so even rightly gained wealth is not safe in weak hands.
list_adds: it adds a condition the couplet lacks, that the wealth may be நன்மையின் மாண்ட and still be lost, because the danger lies in the owner's want of resolve.

note: Naladiyar 278 says the miser's heirs do not give once the wealth is theirs; Pazhamozhi 215 says that the miser's kin too cling and grow tight while he lives.
teaches: Read together, miserliness is shown as a household trait passed sideways to kin in life and down to heirs after death, not a private vice.
list_adds: it pairs not giving with not enjoying and sets the kin's clinging in the same breath, so the hoard is shown corrupting the whole circle around it.
audit_text_issue: Proverb மரங்குறைப்ப மண்ணா மயிர் obscure.

note: Kural 1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with crores; Pazhamozhi 216 says the drum-proclaimed wealth of such a man is a dog's coconut.
teaches: The Kural says he has nothing; the proverb sharpens this to having something he cannot open, so the miser is not poor but locked out of his own possession.
list_adds: its proverb replaces the couplet's abstract 'nothing' with an image of possession without access, and the drum carries the claim to royal wealth.

note: Naladiyar 9 says the man who only guards his wealth without using or giving it will be thought of as one who has lost it; Pazhamozhi 217 says the non-giver's wealth is a loss like losing an eye with its beauty.
teaches: Both verses answer the miser's fear of loss by calling his keeping the real loss, and the proverb adds that it is a double loss of use and of looks.
list_adds: it grounds the claim in the fall of rulers of the whole earth, an argument from impermanence the quatrain does not make, and turns the miser's own word இழவு against him.

note: Kural 1007 likens the non-giver's wealth to a beautiful woman growing old alone; Pazhamozhi 217 likens it to losing the eye together with its beauty.
teaches: Both images make unused wealth a beauty wasted, but the Kural's beauty fades unseen while Pazhamozhi's is destroyed with the organ, so one is waste by neglect and the other by injury.
list_adds: its proverb replaces slow fading with sudden destruction, matching its frame of kings who vanished like a festival dance.

note: Kural 228 asks whether the hard-eyed hoarders do not know the joy of giving; Pazhamozhi 218 says whether such hoarders fear sin or not makes no difference.
teaches: The pair close the hoarder's two exits: he lacks the joy of giving, and his fear of sin, which might have stood in for it, counts for nothing without the act.
list_adds: its proverb of the blind eye, the same shut or open, rules out piety without giving, a point the couplet's appeal to pleasure does not reach.
audit_text_issue: pazhamozhi_nanooru:218 line 2 மாவினை மாணப் பொதிகிற்பார் is uncertain.

note: Pazhamozhi 218 says the miser's fear of sin is idle; 219 says that those who give nothing toward the next birth keep their wealth and die.
teaches: The second verse supplies the consequence the first only implies: a fear of sin that does not give leaves the next birth unprovided.
audit_text_issue: 218 மாவினை and 219's proverb குடரொழிய மீவேலி are obscure. | 219's proverb குடரொழிய மீவேலி போக்குபவர் is obscure.

note: Kural 1002 says the delusion of clinging without giving brings a மாணாப் பிறப்பு; Pazhamozhi 219 says those who give nothing for the coming birth hoard by attachment and die.
teaches: The Kural names the bad birth as the fruit of hoarding; Pazhamozhi makes giving the provision for that birth, so not giving is a failure to pack for a journey.
list_adds: it frames giving as something owed to the birth that follows (படரும் பிறப்பு) and names the attachment (பற்று) that holds the wealth, and its proverb sets outer guarding against inner loss.
audit_text_issue: proverb குடரொழிய மீவேலி போக்குபவர் is obscure

note: Naladiyar 273 says the fool who hoards and dies is mocked by his own stored wealth; Pazhamozhi 219 says those who keep their wealth and die guard the outer fence while the inner is lost.
teaches: The two verses use the same phrase of keeping and dying and give the hoarder two judges, his wealth's mockery and his own lost next birth.
list_adds: it adds the next birth as the thing lost, where the quatrain stops at the mockery of the wealth that outlived him.

note: Naladiyar 269 likens the giving of fools to rain poured into the sea while the paddy withers; Pazhamozhi 220 says leaving the hunger of kin and lovers unrelieved while helping strangers is like the black palmyra.
teaches: Both make misdirected giving a vice, not a virtue: the Naladiyar faults giving where there is no need, Pazhamozhi names the need passed over, the hunger of one's own kin.
list_adds: it names who is passed over, those who came with love and one's kin, where the quatrain gives only the image of the parched field.

note: Naladiyar 261 says no one counts on the wealth of the worthless, as bats shun the cracked wood-apple; Pazhamozhi 221 lists the faults of the ungiving and calls leaving them leaving an old field's stack.
teaches: The quatrain says people do not approach such wealth; Pazhamozhi adds a counsel, that walking away costs nothing, so shunning the miser becomes a choice, not an instinct.
list_adds: it lists the miser's faults side by side (no giving, no strength, harsh speech, no help in trouble), making stinginess one of a cluster of failures.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu 26 names as sweet the worth of not killing the hope of those who come in desire; Pazhamozhi 222 shows the hope-killer at work, feigning kindness and then withholding.
teaches: The counted verse names the virtue bare; Pazhamozhi shows its opposite as a staged deceit, the gift dangled like grass tied at a beast's neck.

note: Pazhamozhi 222 shows a man who seems about to help and then dashes the asker's hope; 225 says an honest refusal is no fault but that killing hope forfeits the next world.
teaches: Read together, the pair say the wrong is not in refusing but in raising hope and then crushing it, and 225 names the price of what 222 depicts.

note: Kural 223 says not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing', and giving, belong to the well-born; Pazhamozhi 223 condemns pleading 'nothing' to those long close when one could help.
teaches: The Kural measures the plea of poverty against birth; Pazhamozhi measures it against an old bond, so the same words are a fault of lineage in one and a wound to friendship in the other.
list_adds: it adds who is asking, old intimates, and its proverb of the hacked tree says what the false plea does to the bond, which the couplet does not consider.

note: Kural 1067 begs all beggars not to beg of those who conceal; Pazhamozhi 224 says those who beg of hard-minded men get nothing, like seeking alms in a monastery.
teaches: The Kural gives the warning; Pazhamozhi gives the reason in an image, that the hard rich man yields no more than renouncers who own nothing.
list_adds: its proverb equates the hard-hearted rich with those who themselves live on alms, a comparison the couplet does not draw.

note: Naladiyar 279 says the base yield only when strong men press them, like a cow milked by force; Pazhamozhi 224 says those who stand and beg before the hard-minded get nothing.
teaches: Read together, the hard-hearted are moved by force but never by entreaty, so the beggar's mode of asking is the one sure to fail.
list_adds: it fixes the asker's posture, standing before them (முன்னின்று இரந்தார்), as the thing that yields nothing, where the quatrain sets yielding gladly against yielding under force.

note: Naladiyar 111 opens with nearly the same two lines as Pazhamozhi 225: refusing what one cannot give is no disgrace and the way of the world; it then says keeping the asker waiting till hope dies is worse than killing gratitude, where Pazhamozhi says the hope-killer has no world to go to.
teaches: The shared lines show one maxim closed two ways, measured against ingratitude in the Naladiyar and against the next world in Pazhamozhi, so the same fault is given a moral rank and a cosmic penalty.
list_adds: the two verses share their first lines; what Pazhamozhi adds is its proverb, which turns the Naladiyar's comparison of faults into a sentence on the hope-killer's afterlife.

note: Purananuru 196, a bard to the Pandya Nanmaran, says that saying yes to what one can and no to what one cannot are both proper ways of a giver's friendship, while false promises and false refusals wound the asker and lessen the giver's fame.
teaches: The bard's complaint to a king and the ethics verse state the same rule about refusal, which shows the norm of the honest 'no' is older than the ethics works and was first argued from a suppliant's side.

note: Kural 1070 says the asker's life goes out at the word of refusal; Pazhamozhi 225 says refusing what one cannot give is no disgrace, and that the fault lies in keeping the asker in hope and then not sharing.
teaches: The Kural weighs every refusal by the asker's death of spirit; Pazhamozhi exempts the honest refusal and reserves the blame for the one who holds out hope and withholds.
list_adds: it divides refusal into the honest 'I have none' and the hope kept alive and killed, a distinction the couplet, which condemns concealment as such, does not make.

note: Kural 224 says being begged from is painful until one sees the asker's glad face; Pazhamozhi 226 says all that is given to those who do not rejoice in what was done is lost.
teaches: The pair make the receiver's gladness the completion of the gift: the Kural says it ends the giver's pain, Pazhamozhi that without it the gift itself is wasted.
list_adds: it turns the couplet's psychology of the giver into a judgement on the recipient, setting the ungrateful who will not stand by one in need as the wasted object of giving.
audit_text_issue: 226 lines 1-2 elliptic

note: Naladiyar 98 says to give to those who cannot repay is duty and giving to those who repay is only a loan; Pazhamozhi 226 says giving to those who do not rejoice in kindness is all loss.
teaches: Together they say what a gift may and may not ask in return: no repayment, but gladness, so a recipient who cannot repay is fit and one who will not rejoice is not.
list_adds: it adds a condition the quatrain lacks, the recipient's joy in the kindness, without retracting its rule against seeking return.
audit_text_issue: lines 1-2 elliptic

note: Kural 619 grants that the deity may deny the end but says effort still pays the wage of bodily strain; Pazhamozhi 227 asks what effort can do at all once the deity has settled the end.
teaches: Both start from the same concession, that தெய்வம் can deny the goal, and part over what is left: the Kural keeps a wage for effort, while Pazhamozhi leaves it nothing, so the pair locates the precise point where the two works divide on effort and fate.
list_adds: its proverb of a pit dug in vain makes effort's labour itself the loss, where the couplet saves that labour as a wage.
audit_text_issue: Proverb குறும்பியங்கும் கோப்புக் குழி is obscure. | Line 3-4 proverb குறும்பியங்கும் கோப்புக் குழி is obscure.

note: Naladiyar 108 says that when the knowing do blameworthy things it comes from their past deeds; Pazhamozhi 228 says the works of renowned wise men go by their fortune, so fate defeats understanding.
teaches: Together the two verses show fate overriding knowledge in two places, in the wise man's conduct (the Naladiyar) and in the outcome of his works (Pazhamozhi), so knowing what is right secures neither right action nor success.
list_adds: it moves the quatrain's moral puzzle to the success of undertakings and seals it with a proverb that sets fate against understanding outright.

note: Both proverbs turn on உறற்பால, what is bound to befall: 229 proves it by the moon's harm, 230 by an elephant that went to a man of Karuvur.
teaches: Read together the same word covers both directions of fate, harm that strikes the highest and good that finds a man who did not seek it, so உறற்பால in this chapter is neutral lot, not misfortune only.

note: Pazhamozhi 230's proverb repeats almost word for word Naladiyar 109's last line, that wanted or not what is bound to come can hardly be kept from touching one; the Naladiyar applies it to unwanted evil, Pazhamozhi to an elephant that went to a man of Karuvur.
teaches: The pair shows a saying shared between the two works, and that Pazhamozhi re-aims it: the quatrain's line is a warning that unwanted evil cannot be fended off, and the elephant story makes it a promise that unsought good cannot be missed.
list_adds: it takes the quatrain's closing line as a proverb and backs it with a named episode, turning a general warning into a story of fortune arriving.

note: Kural 376 says what is not one's own will not stay though guarded, nor what is one's own leave though thrown away; Pazhamozhi 231 shows a palmyra guarded all night whose fruit still falls to the one it is due to.
teaches: The pairing turns the couplet's abstract 'guard' into a watchman shouting through the night under a tree, and adds a second person the couplet lacks, the passer-by who gets the fruit, so the loss of the guarder is someone else's unearned gain.
list_adds: it gives the couplet a scene with two people, guard and receiver, so fate's allotment is seen as a transfer, not only a keeping or a losing.

note: Kural 463 says the wise do not undertake a deed that loses the capital for the sake of gain; Pazhamozhi 232 says those who did no great good deeds before cannot have great wealth later, for without capital there is no profit.
teaches: The same trader's logic of capital and profit is prudence in the Kural and fate in Pazhamozhi, where the capital is earlier good deeds, so the pair shows the merchant's rule being moved from a counsel about risk to an account of merit.
list_adds: its proverb replaces the couplet's money capital with good deeds done before, so the capital cannot be raised now by any present skill.
audit_text_issue: Pazhamozhi 232 line 2-3 வைப்போடு இகலி is unclear.

note: Naladiyar 93 says wealth gathers when its time to gather comes, whether one gives or withholds; Pazhamozhi 233 says the same of those who serve kings, by the vengai that flowers only on its day.
teaches: The quatrain uses the timing of wealth to remove the miser's excuse, and Pazhamozhi uses it to remove the courtier's hope, so the same rule frees the giver to give and tells the servant of kings his service cannot hasten his reward.
list_adds: it carries the quatrain's rule from the giver's house to the king's court and gives it the image of a tree that flowers only on the right day.

note: 234 says the five got out of the lac house because there is no place without escape for one due to escape; 239 says the Chola's son survived burning and came to rule, for nothing is beyond those who keep their life.
teaches: Both proverbs follow an escape from fire, one from the epic and one from Tamil royal memory, and the second carries the story past survival to kingship, so the chapter makes surviving the fire the first step of a fortune still unfolding.

note: Kural 375 says that in making wealth the favourable can turn bad and the unfavourable good; Pazhamozhi 235 says that for those who are to prosper even what was judged bad turns out good, for the fortunate have no evil day.
teaches: The couplet leaves it open which way a thing will turn, and Pazhamozhi decides it by the person: the same reversal runs only toward good for one with fortune, so the pair shows the couplet's instability resolved by whose lot it is.
list_adds: it makes the reversal depend on the person's fortune and ties it to the reckoning of good and bad days, which the couplet does not mention.

note: Kural 618 says lacking fortune is no one's disgrace; Pazhamozhi 236 says that men who reach a generous king and still get nothing are not to be called dull or small, since gain comes by one's lot.
teaches: The couplet's general absolution becomes a defence of a particular figure, the empty-handed petitioner at court, and the pair shows the Kural's line on blame used to protect a man from the court's contempt rather than to urge him to work.
list_adds: it places the couplet's point at a king's court and adds a proverb of earned luck, so the failure is ascribed to unearned penance, not only excused.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 வீற்று வழி is unclear. | 236 sense flagged uncertain (வீற்று வழி) | 236 line 2 வீற்று வழி is unclear

note: Naladiyar 31 shows those who did no penance before clinging to the outer door of a house, unable to enter; Pazhamozhi 236 says for those who did penance curry falls even into their rice.
teaches: The two verses give both ends of one belief about past penance and present food: one man shut out at the door looking in, the other finding food falling into his plate, so the pair draws the full scale between beggary and luck as the fruit of earlier penance.
list_adds: its proverb shows the reward side that the quatrain leaves implied, and sets it at a king's court rather than at a rich man's house.
audit_text_issue: வீற்று வழி in line 2 is unclear

note: Kural 620 says those who toil without flagging see even fate's back; Pazhamozhi 237 says effort is needless for the fortunate and fruitless for the unfortunate.
teaches: Both name ஆள்வினை and fate together and give opposite verdicts on the same contest, the Kural letting tireless labour outrun fate and Pazhamozhi denying labour any effect in either lot, on the plain reading of both.
list_adds: it splits people into two lots and denies effort a role in each, where the couplet speaks of the single toiler who prevails.

note: Kural 371 says the fate of gain produces tireless effort and the fate of loss produces sloth; Pazhamozhi 237 says the fortunate need no effort and the striving of the unfortunate is fruitless.
teaches: The Kural keeps effort as fate's instrument, while Pazhamozhi makes it idle on both sides, so the pair shows two ways of subordinating effort to fate: as its product, or as beside the point.
list_adds: it pairs the two lots as the couplet does but cuts effort loose from them, so the fortunate prosper without it and the unfortunate strive in vain.

note: Naladiyar 33 says the fool breaks down when the fruit of past deeds arrives, while those who see it as old desert are freed of confusion; Pazhamozhi 238 says those who do not see their suffering as their old deed rage at the foes who cause it.
teaches: The quatrain turns the knowledge of old deeds against grief, and Pazhamozhi turns it against anger at enemies, recasting the foe as a servant carrying out an order, so the same doctrine is shown ending both despair and revenge.
list_adds: its proverb of the servant who burns the town on orders gives the enemy a role, the agent of one's own deed, that the quatrain does not consider.

note: Porunaratruppadai says Karikalan received his inheritance while still in the womb; Pazhamozhi 239 tells of a Chola's son who survived burning, mounted the great elephant and in the end ruled justly, a prince tradition identifies as Karikalan.
teaches: If the traditional identification holds, the same accession is told once as a birthright fixed before birth and once as a survival against fire, and the pair shows the ethics work turning a praised royal memory into proof that a living man can still come to anything.
list_adds: it uses the heroic memory not to praise the king but as a proverb's evidence, so the Chola's rise becomes a general lesson about survival.

note: Naladiyar 110 says that since what was set at the start cannot change, there is no reason to grieve when ruin comes; Pazhamozhi 240 says those who know what is to be done do not fear their distress when fearful things come.
teaches: Both ask for calm before what fate brings, but the quatrain grounds it in the fixity of the lot while Pazhamozhi grounds it in knowing what to do, so the pair shows two routes to the same composure, resignation and readiness.
list_adds: it rests calm on knowing one's course of action, with an image of an elephant sheltering its mate, rather than on the quatrain's sum that cannot be altered.
audit_text_issue: Proverb elliptical; sense uncertain.

note: Kural 541 defines justice as acting without favour to anyone; Pazhamozhi 241 names the hardest case of that 'anyone', one's own people.
teaches: The couplet's யார்மாட்டும் is abstract; the pairing shows where impartiality is actually tested, at the king's own kin, and names the failure there as softness of eye.
list_adds: its proverb turns கண்ணோடாது into a portrait of the king who fails it, the soft-eyed man who cannot punish, so the rule gains a named vice the couplet does not give.

note: 241 demands that the king turn hard-eyed and punish; 256 praises rulers who are not quickly angered even by great harm.
teaches: Together the two separate severity from haste: the king must punish wrong without favour, but the rulers people shelter under are those slow to anger at harm done to them.

note: Kannaki cites the Chola who crushed his own son under the chariot for a cow's grief; Pazhamozhi 242 tells the same episode and adds that the worthy had hidden the deed.
teaches: Kannaki uses the episode to shame a king who killed without inquiry; Pazhamozhi makes it a rule about age, so one exemplum serves both as indictment and as maxim.

note: Pazhamozhi 6 has a young Chola who judges well despite his youth; 242 has a son not spared despite his youth.
teaches: Read together the two Chola stories make youth irrelevant from both sides of the court: it neither disqualifies the judge nor excuses the accused.

note: Kural 118 praises leaning to no side like a level balance; Pazhamozhi 243 applies that to the king's dealing with rich and poor and pictures the lean as milk and water.
teaches: The couplet's balance shows only that something tilts; the pairing names who gains and loses, the rich getting milk and the poor water from one royal source.
list_adds: it moves the worthy man's balance into the king's court and names the two parties, rich and poor, that the couplet leaves unnamed.
audit_text_issue: The packet notes the site lacks pazhamozhi_nanooru:243.

note: Pisirandhaiyar tells the Pandya to take his due like an elephant fed paddy in balls, not one loosed in the field; Pazhamozhi 244 gives the same rule of revenue through the bee that takes and leaves.
teaches: The Sangam poem warns one king of the ruin a greedy collection brings on him and his land; the ethics verse lifts the warning into a general rule of royal taking that should leave no mark at all.

note: 245 says even prosperous subjects should not bear excess levy; 246 says a king's favours funded by excess levy are like feeding a creature its own crest.
teaches: The two close both escapes for over-taxing: the subjects' prosperity does not justify it, and the king's later generosity does not redeem it.
audit_text_issue: 245 lines 3-4 (கோல்தலையே யாயினும் கொண்டீக; பாலதலை) obscure

note: Kural 552 likens a sceptred king's demand to a robber's 'hand it over'; Pazhamozhi 246 follows the extorted wealth into the king's gifts.
teaches: The couplet stops at the taking; the pairing shows the robbery disguised as largesse, so a king can be both robber and giver at once.
list_adds: it sets refuge-seekers harmed, crooked rule, excess levy and later favour in one sequence, so the extortion of 552 is followed to its use.

note: Muthumozhikkanchi 26 says those under an unjust king do not openly censure him; Pazhamozhi 247 says they have no recourse at all.
teaches: The pair gives the reason for the silence: the people do not speak against the unjust king because, with the protector himself the taker, there is no one higher to cover them.

note: 248 says a king who lets things slip is scorned, since all scorn the weak; 250 says an unjust king is scorned by his own allies and yet needs some severity.
teaches: Together they place the king between two contempts, for weakness and for injustice, and make a small severity within just rule the way between them.
audit_text_issue: 248 ஒளியாரை and கைகடத்தல் are ambiguous. | 248 lines 1-2 are ambiguous.

note: Kural 763 says a host of rats roaring like the sea perish at the cobra's breath; Pazhamozhi 249 says a gathered enemy army is nothing to a firm-minded king, one stone for a thousand crows.
teaches: The couplet locates the strength in the cobra alone; the pairing traces it to the king's undivided mind, so numbers fail against resolve, not only against force.
list_adds: its condition, a king not divided in mind, gives the source of the one's power over the many that the couplet's image takes for granted.

note: Kural 562 tells the king to raise the rod sharply and bring it down lightly; Pazhamozhi 250 says kings need a little harshness, since even a cool stick raises the body.
teaches: Both refuse a choice between mildness and terror, and the pairing shows two ways to split it: the couplet splits the act into threat and blow, the quatrain sets a small severity inside just rule.
list_adds: it adds the cost of failing at the other end, that even allies scorn a king who is not just, so severity is fenced by contempt on both sides.
audit_text_issue: Proverb தண்கோல் எடுக்குமாம் மெய் is uncertain.

note: 251 says no rival word can rise under a king's command, as no tree grows under a tree; 253 says keeping would-be leaders on equal footing is living with a snake.
teaches: 251 states the fact of single authority and 253 the danger of breaking it, so together they explain why a king keeps the ambitious beneath him.
audit_text_issue: 253 line 2 ambiguous

note: 252, on a doubtful reading, says a ruler can unmake the men he raised; 253 warns that men raised to equal standing are a snake in the room.
teaches: Read together, 253 limits the confidence of 252: the raised follower stays in the ruler's hand only while he is not raised to the ruler's level.
audit_text_issue: 252 line 3 பாத்தறிவென் மெல்ல is unclear.

note: Kural 890 says living with those not in accord is like dwelling with a snake in a hut; Pazhamozhi 253 uses the same image for a king who keeps aspirants to leadership on his own level.
teaches: The couplet leaves open who the discordant companions are; the pairing names them in a court, ambitious men the king himself has raised, so the snake is one he brought in.
list_adds: it carries the household image into the king's domain and makes the king's own act of raising men the cause of the danger.

note: Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every folly; Pazhamozhi 255 says giving high dignity to the unrestrained is putting a firebrand in a monkey's hand.
teaches: The couplet counts the folly as the king's; the proverb shows it burning outward, since the monkey with fire harms everything near it, not only the one who handed it over.
list_adds: it moves the fault from ignorance to want of restraint and adds wealth to the trust given, so the harm is power and means in an unruly hand.
audit_text_issue: ஒளளியன் (line 3) is likely a slip for ஒள்ளியன்.

note: Kural 155 says the world keeps the forbearing like wrapped gold; Pazhamozhi 256 says the slow to anger rule the world and people shelter under them like a food tree.
teaches: The couplet gives the forbearing esteem; the pairing turns esteem into rule, so forbearance is shown as a ground of authority and not only of reputation.
list_adds: its image reverses the couplet's direction: the forbearing are not kept by others like gold but keep others under their shade.

note: Kural 443 says making the great one's own is the rarest of things; Pazhamozhi 257 shows Lanka's younger prince joining Rama and gaining Lanka.
teaches: The couplet ranks the act as rare; the pairing gives its reward in one epic case, and shows the bond with the great outweighing even the bond with a brother.
list_adds: it proves the couplet's claim by a story, and the story's cost, leaving a brother, is something the couplet's general claim does not face.

note: Kural 717 says the learning of the learned shines among those who can examine words faultlessly; Pazhamozhi 258 says the fierce king's council shows a counsellor's breadth of learning as the flood shows the mountain's rain.
teaches: Together they make the assembly a gauge as well as a stage: the Kural needs fit judges for learning to shine, and the Pazhamozhi adds that what pours out there is the measure of what was stored unseen.
list_adds: its flood-and-rain proverb turns the couplet's claim about where learning shines into an inference from visible effect to hidden quantity, and sets it in a king's dangerous court.

note: Kural 638 makes it the duty of the one at the king's side to tell him his good even when he destroys counsel; Pazhamozhi 259 says the king's faults are laid on those beside him, since no doll is unlike its maker.
teaches: The pair gives the duty of plain counsel its sanction: because the world reads the king as his counsellors' making, the one who stays silent shares the guilt of what the king does.
list_adds: its doll-and-maker proverb adds the consequence the couplet leaves unsaid, that blame for the king's wrongs passes to his attendants.
audit_text_issue: pazhamozhi_nanooru:259 line 2 பயிரறு is obscure.

note: Kural 445 says counsellors are the ruler's eyes and must be chosen with care; Pazhamozhi 260 says one who has not made many around him his eyes is helpless in distress like a lute with cut strings.
teaches: Read together, the eyes the Kural asks a ruler to choose are shown at the moment they are missing: in a crisis the king without them still has his state but can make no response, as a stringless lute keeps its body and loses its sound.
list_adds: it adds the number, many rather than one, and the crisis in which the lack is felt, with an image of form left without function.

note: Kural 441 bids one weigh their worth and take the friendship of the wise who know virtue; Pazhamozhi 261 says to test by discussion those who weigh good and ill and hold them firm, as bull rubs against bull.
teaches: The pair names the means of the Kural's weighing, testing in set speech, and its fruit, a support that runs both ways as two bulls prop each other.
list_adds: its bull proverb makes the tie between chooser and chosen mutual, where the couplet speaks only of what the chooser gains.

note: Kural 442 bids one cherish those who can remove present affliction and guard against what has not come; Pazhamozhi 262 describes guardians restrained in mind, speech and body and says without them life perishes.
teaches: Together they show that the Kural's guarding helpers are, for the Pazhamozhi, first of all men disciplined in all three channels, so the ascetic's threefold restraint becomes the qualification of the king's protectors.
list_adds: it sets the guardians' power beside their threefold self-restraint as its ground and closes with the stark cost of lacking them.

note: Naladiyar 73 asks whether the harsh words of those who love are worse than strangers' smiling sweet words; Pazhamozhi 263 says good ministers press unwanted good on the king and check his evil, so elders' words are painful at first.
teaches: The pair carries the friend's welcome harshness up to the throne and adds time: the bitter word is painful only at first, and the minister must also push the king toward good he resists, not only rebuke.
list_adds: it moves the claim from friends to minister and king, adds the forward push to unwanted good beside the check on evil, and gives the time-order of pain then profit.

note: Kural 448 says a ruler without the guard of those who rebuke perishes even with no enemy; Pazhamozhi 263 says the elders' counsel that saves him is painful at first.
teaches: The pair names the cost of the Kural's safeguard: the rebuke that keeps the king from ruin must be borne as pain before it is known as protection, which is why kings are tempted to do without it.
list_adds: it adds the cost to the hearer, painful first, which the couplet's plain statement of necessity leaves out.

note: Kural 696 bids one know the king's mood and the time and say what is needed and not disliked; Pazhamozhi 264 says the wise, finding the king's favourable moment, will even use guile, as mothers soothe children with the moon.
teaches: Together they show how far reading the king's mood can go: the Kural stops at saying the welcome needful thing, while the Pazhamozhi lets the counsellor treat the king as a child to be steered by a pleasing deception.
list_adds: its mother-and-moon image adds deceit to the couplet's tact and casts the king as a child, a ranking of counsellor over king the couplet avoids.
audit_text_issue: 264 line 4 proverb hard to construe

note: Kural 691 says those who serve quarrelsome kings should be like men warming at a fire, neither too far nor too near; Pazhamozhi 265 says the experienced never even think of what would anger the mighty king, for nothing escapes his force.
teaches: The pair shows the fire's danger from inside the servant's mind: the Kural regulates distance, and the Pazhamozhi says the only safety is never to give the king's anger cause, even when he is in the right.
list_adds: its doubled proverb of deer before tiger and straw before wind adds that once the king's anger rises there is no escape at any distance, so the caution moves from posture to thought.

note: Pazhamozhi 263 praises ministers who afflict the king to tell him his good and stop his evil; Pazhamozhi 265, in the same heading, says the experienced never think of anything that would anger him.
teaches: Side by side the two verses of one heading leave the counsellor between duty and survival: the good minister must hurt the king to save him, yet the king's anger is a tiger no one escapes, so the heading gives no single rule.
audit_text_issue: 265 line 1 தீயன வல்ல is ambiguous.

note: Purananuru 290 has a warrior's king give him toddy before drinking himself, and the warrior will take the spear meant for the king; Pazhamozhi 266 turns the toddy already drunk into the reason a king's man cannot shrink from his task.
teaches: Held together they show the heroic custom of the king's toddy hardening into a courtier's proverb of obligation: what the war poem offers as honour freely returned, the ethics verse states as a debt that forbids hesitation.

note: Pazhamozhi 266 says those who have eaten the king's food cannot shirk his work; 267 says those who have not yet been rewarded cannot refuse it either, since the one who commands will feed.
teaches: Read together the two verses close both exits from service: the servant who has been paid owes the work, and the servant who has not been paid owes it too, so reward never becomes a condition the servant may set.

note: Naladiyar 167 says those who keep close to kings enjoy their wealth without needing to be worthy; Pazhamozhi 272 says whomever the king esteems the people esteem as well.
