teaches: The pair shows royal nearness conferring not only goods but public standing: the Naladiyar's unworthy favourite gets the king's wealth, and Pazhamozhi adds that he gets the town's regard too, poured on from the king like ghee from a filled pot.
list_adds: its proverb of the ghee-filled vessel makes honour a thing that passes from container to container, adding the public as a second recipient that the quatrain's image of shade-giving trees does not have.

note: Kural 363 says there is no fine wealth like not wanting, here or hereafter; Pazhamozhi 273 uses the same word வேண்டாமை to say that a king's servant who asks nothing even in hardship is given all he wants.
teaches: Together they show the renouncer's highest wealth being turned into a courtier's method: the Kural's not-wanting is its own reward, while Pazhamozhi makes it the means by which a king's servant is given everything, so the same virtue serves release and preferment.
list_adds: it carries the couplet's claim from the chapter on cutting off desire into service at court and adds the case of hardship (அல்லுறினும்), where not asking is hardest.

note: Pazhamozhi 273 says the king's servant should ask the king for nothing; 274 says he should not seek help elsewhere either, for that is like sucking the cow's throat while the udder is there.
teaches: Taken together the verses leave the servant no one to ask: not the king, whom he must not petition, and not others, who are a dry source, so all his provision must come unasked from the master he serves.

note: Kural 696 asks the king's counsellor to know the mood and the time before saying what is needed; Pazhamozhi 275 says those who speak to kings at the right moment achieve everything, and that a hunchback inside is better than a minister outside.
teaches: The pair shows that the couplet's timing depends on access: one who knows the right moment is useless unless he is in the room when it comes, so the menial with the inner rooms can outdo the minister the Kural addresses.
list_adds: its proverb ranks a hunchbacked attendant above a minister, adding a ranking by nearness that cuts across office, which the couplet's advice on timing does not consider.
audit_text_issue: உரைப்பாரைக்கொன் (று), line 2, is read as உரைப்பார்க்கு ஒன்று.

note: Kural 691 asks those who serve kings to be like people warming at a fire, neither too far nor too near; Pazhamozhi 276 warns the favourite who answers the king's fierce love with his own and acts without perceiving what lies hidden.
teaches: Together they show that the danger of being too near comes most from the king's own affection: the Kural's fire burns those who press close, and Pazhamozhi shows the courtier being drawn close by love and forgetting to keep distance.
list_adds: it gives the too-near case a cause the couplet leaves out, the king's love itself, and closes it with a proverb of self-betrayal.

note: Kural 698 forbids belittling a king as young or as close kin; Pazhamozhi 277 forbids mocking a king who has lost his greatness and his kin and stands alone, for no one slights a snake as small.
teaches: The pair extends the Kural's bar on belittling from youth and kinship to ruin and isolation, and the proverb's இளைது echoes the couplet's இளையர: in both, smallness of age or fortune is no licence, but Pazhamozhi grounds this in the power still in him, the Kural in the light of his station.
list_adds: it moves the couplet's case from a young king in his strength to a fallen king without kin, and gives a reason by fear of the snake where the couplet gives one by the dignity of the office.

note: Naladiyar 241 says the worthy feel shame and do not advance on humbled enemies, as the eclipse snake does not seize the crescent moon; Pazhamozhi 277 says those who serve a fallen king do not mock him, as no one slights a young snake.
teaches: Set side by side, the two snakes give two different grounds for sparing the fallen: in the Naladiyar the strong one is the snake and holds back from shame, in Pazhamozhi the fallen king is the snake and is spared from fear, so restraint before the weak may be nobility or prudence.
list_adds: it turns the quatrain's image around, making the humbled one the snake, so the same restraint is grounded in the danger of the weak rather than the shame of the strong.

note: Kural 700 says the intimacy that does improper things on the ground of old acquaintance brings ruin; Pazhamozhi 280 says those trusted for their truth who turn to falsehood against the king fell the palm onto themselves.
teaches: The pair names two kinds of capital a servant can spend against himself: the Kural's long familiarity and Pazhamozhi's reputation for truth, and in both the very ground of trust becomes the instrument of the fall.
list_adds: its palm that falls on the one who fells it makes the ruin self-inflicted by the servant's own act, where the couplet says only that the intimacy brings ruin.

note: Pazhamozhi 270 has the ripe palm fruit fall at the foot of its parent tree, and 280 has the felled palm fall on the feller; both use a falling palm for a deed returning to its doer.
teaches: Together the two palm images show one law of return working both ways in the king's service: work done in measure comes back like ripe fruit to its tree, and treachery comes back like a felled trunk on the axeman.

note: Purananuru 73 has Nalankilli say the fool who scorned him will hardly escape, like a blind man stumbling on a sleeping tiger; Pazhamozhi 281 tells the king's wronged servant not to wake the sleeping tiger by acting on his grievance.
teaches: The pairing shows the same sleeping tiger from both sides: the Chola king boasts of being the tiger that the careless rouse to their death, and the ethics verse teaches the king's own servant to treat that tiger as a standing danger to be left asleep.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 என்செய்து அகப்பட்டக் கண்ணும் is obscure; the link does not depend on it.

note: Naladiyar 164 says those who have angered the great do not escape even in a strong fortress, as the snake in its crevice dreads the thunder; Pazhamozhi 282 asks why those who cannot protect themselves are angry with kings at all.
teaches: The pair runs the danger the other way: the Naladiyar speaks of those who have provoked the great and find no shelter, Pazhamozhi of those who themselves feel anger at the king, and both conclude that against royal power the weak have no refuge.
list_adds: it shifts the quatrain's case from another's wrath to one's own anger, and its kongu tree makes the refuge something the angry man climbs himself.
audit_text_issue: வாமான்றோ in line 2 is a doubtful form

note: Kural 699 says the clear-sighted do not do the unacceptable on the thought that they are in favour; Pazhamozhi 283 says that when a king bears an offence with visible displeasure, going on to offend again is a boil on a hump.
teaches: Together they mark two false grounds for presuming: favour in the Kural and forgiveness in Pazhamozhi; the ethics verse adds that the king's patience, shown with displeasure, is a warning the offender misreads as licence.
list_adds: it adds a sequence the couplet lacks, a first offence borne and then repeated, and a proverb of harm piled on harm.

note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken by cruel slander like a flame in a lamp; Pazhamozhi 284 says the wise do not join those agitated by slander spoken to the king, but work out how he may see through it.
teaches: The pair moves steadiness under slander from one's own mind to the court: the Naladiyar's pure heart is not moved when slandered, and Pazhamozhi's wise courtier is not moved when another is slandered before the king, and also helps the king see clearly.
list_adds: it gives the steady one a task beyond composure, clearing the king's judgement, and sets him against a crowd of stilt-dancers moved by alarm.

note: Kural 750 says a fort with every excellence is nothing for those without excellence in action; Pazhamozhi 285 names the missing excellence as courage and adds allies to the fort as a support that fails without it.
teaches: Read together, the outer defences of a ruler, walls and allies alike, are shown to depend on one inner thing, and the Pazhamozhi names that thing as freedom from fear.
list_adds: it sets strong allies beside the fort as a second outer prop and lets the proverb make fear the single cause that empties both.

note: Kural 879 says to cut the thorn tree while young; Pazhamozhi 286 keeps the timing and adds a second step, stripping the young enemy of his friends.
teaches: The pair gives two parts of one tactic: the Kural's when (before the thorn hardens) and the Pazhamozhi's how (leave the tree alone so it cannot become a forest).
list_adds: it joins early action to isolation from allies, a pairing the couplet's single tree image does not make.
audit_text_issue: Lines 2-3 syntax loose (தீர்த்து / தீர).

note: Kural 489 says to do the hard deed at the very moment the rare chance comes; Pazhamozhi 287 applies this to answering an enemy who has struck, and calls delay folly.
teaches: The Kural's general rule of the moment is given a hostile case, where the passing chance is the attacker himself, gone like a snake once it has bitten.
list_adds: it turns the couplet's abstract rare moment into a concrete one with a cost, the snake's fang that cannot be taken once it has fled.

note: Both verses urge acting at once against an enemy; 286 speaks of an enmity still young, 287 of one that has already struck.
teaches: Together they cover enmity before and after its first blow, and say that in neither case does waiting help, once because the enemy grows, once because he escapes.

note: Thirikadugam 24 makes the bowing of hardened enemies a mire; Pazhamozhi 289 says favours shown to enemies set against reconciliation do not take.
teaches: The two verses look at a false peace from both sides: the enemy's submission cannot be trusted, and one's own kindness cannot change him, so neither party's gesture ends a settled enmity.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 60 counts going before those who are not one's own as laughable; Pazhamozhi 290 says why, with the child crying to be carried by those who would not let it follow.
teaches: The counted line names the act as laughable; the proverb shows what makes it so, the asking for closeness from people who deny even distance.

note: Kural 269 says that even leaping past Death becomes possible for those who have gained the power of penance; Pazhamozhi 291 says that even those with the greatness of penance have never clapped Death on the back.
teaches: The two take opposite views of what penance can do against death: the Kural lets austerity overcome it, while the Pazhamozhi, using the demon great in penance who fell, denies that it protects the one who provokes the great.
list_adds: it sets the claim inside a story of a penitent who was destroyed in war, so the power of tapas is tested by a case rather than asserted.

note: Kural 892 says disregard of the great brings ills that do not leave; Pazhamozhi 291 gives an exemplary case, the demon who took enmity with the great without heed and was caught in battle.
teaches: The Kural's general warning gains a named example and a sharper premise, that the offender's own might, even might won by penance, does not change the outcome.
list_adds: it adds the exemplum and the point that the offender was himself great, which the couplet's plain contrast of the great and the heedless leaves out.

note: Naladiyar 178 says enemies' anger cannot reach the weak who have joined good protection, like grass by a stump the plough avoids; Pazhamozhi 292 says the small who attack such dependents only rouse the protector.
teaches: The same situation is seen from both sides: the quatrain promises the protected weak their safety, and the Pazhamozhi warns their attacker that striking them wakes the great one behind them.
list_adds: its bear and wild dog image shows the attacker's fate, which the quatrain's stump and plough, concerned only with the sheltered grass, does not.

note: 291 warns against enmity with the great themselves; 292 extends the warning to enmity with those who depend on the great.
teaches: Read in sequence, the reach of a great man's protection is shown to cover his dependents, so the danger of provoking him begins one step before he is touched.

note: Kural 861 says to avoid opposing the strong; Pazhamozhi 293 says what the weak should do when the strong are already against them: flee far and live by any means.
teaches: The couplet only advises against the contest; the Pazhamozhi carries the advice into defeat and allows any means of escape, since survival keeps future good open.
list_adds: it adds the step of flight and the proverb's promise of later fortune, which the couplet's balanced rule for strong and weak lacks.

note: Kural 969 praises those who, like the yak, give up life when honour is at stake; Pazhamozhi 293 tells the weak to survive by doing anything at all.
teaches: The two give opposite answers on whether life may be bought with loss of standing: the Kural's man of honour dies rather than live shamed, while the Pazhamozhi counts staying alive as the greater good.
list_adds: its என்செய்தே யாயினும் and the promise of the bangle make survival a positive aim, where the couplet makes life itself forfeit to honour.

note: Kural 894 says that when the weak do harm to the strong it is like beckoning Death; Pazhamozhi 294 says the small inflaming the victorious ends in no good.
teaches: The Kural's image makes the attack fatal; the Pazhamozhi's bees warring with the mountain make it pointless as well, an assault that cannot even reach its target.
list_adds: it adds futility to danger: the bees' quarrel with the hill shows the attack does nothing to the strong, not only that it destroys the weak.
audit_text_issue: pazhamozhi_nanooru:294 line 1 நிற்பாறை is likely corrupt for நிற்பாரை. | pazhamozhi_nanooru:294 line 1 நிற்பாறை is likely நிற்பாரை.

note: Thirikadugam 4 names living openly before enemies and taking by the hand one once enraged as the doings of a man about to die; Pazhamozhi 295 says those who swagger and enrage the steadfast become crows' food.
teaches: Both verses treat a way of behaving toward enemies as a sign of death already on its way, the counted work by naming it, the Pazhamozhi by showing the boaster's end as carrion.
audit_text_issue: Pazhamozhi 295 line 1 and இழைத்த திகவாதவர் in line 3 are hard; the sense is uncertain.

note: Kural 874 says the world rests on the greatness of one who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship; Pazhamozhi 296 says old enmity never becomes friendship. On the reading that 874 means turning enemies into friends, the two conflict.
teaches: The two disagree over whether enmity can be converted: the Kural praises the man who makes a friend of a foe, while the Pazhamozhi holds that the old foe, like a tuber, only waits for rain.
list_adds: its tuber image gives a reason for the denial, that enmity lies dormant and revives with its season, which the couplet's praise does not face.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu 17 names winning over those who are not one's allies as sweeter than doing good to the land; Pazhamozhi 296 says an old enemy never becomes a friend and should not be kept close.
teaches: Within the ethics group itself the two verses disagree on the reconciled enemy, one ranking his winning over among the sweetest things and the other counting him a sprout that will rise against one.

note: Kural 882 says not to fear sword-like enemies but the bond with kin-like ones; Pazhamozhi 297 gives the reason as distance, the flood afar against the debt in one's own house.
teaches: The Kural gives the ranking of the two dangers; the Pazhamozhi explains it, since the open enemy works from outside and far off while the false friend consumes the house from within.
list_adds: it sets a flood, a natural force, against a household debt, so the ranking turns on nearness rather than on the enemy's strength.
audit_text_issue: அள்ளில்லத்து is obscure

note: Kural 882 says fear the bond with kin-like enemies more than sword-like ones; Pazhamozhi 298 counts the false intimate's harm in two worlds and ranks the open enemy above him by the proverb of blindness and dim sight.
teaches: The pair shows why the kin-like enemy is worse: the open foe is a known lack one guards against, while the false friend's harm reaches even one's standing in the next world.
list_adds: its rhetorical question and proverb turn the couplet's warning into a ranking of two harms, with the open enemy placed above the false friend as blindness above clouded sight.

note: Naladiyar 219 ranks enmity above the friendship of the undiscerning; Pazhamozhi 298 ranks open enmity above the attachment of those who do not care for one.
teaches: The quatrain blames the friend's lack of understanding, the proverb verse his lack of care, so two different faults in a friend both make plain enmity the better lot.
list_adds: it sets the ranking within strategy of enmity rather than among a list of lesser evils, and grounds it in harm done here and hereafter.

note: Kural 880 says those who do not break the pride of hostile men are as good as dead; Pazhamozhi 299 sets the limit, that once the enemy is killed further rage is waste.
teaches: Together they bound hostility at both ends: one must break the enemy, but anger that outlives the enemy is water poured on a reaped field.
list_adds: its harvest proverb adds an end point the couplet lacks, measuring anger by whether anything is left for it to do.

note: Naladiyar 241 says the worthy are ashamed to advance on a humbled enemy; Pazhamozhi 299 says rage after the enemy's death is fruitless.
teaches: The quatrain stops the worthy from pressing a fallen enemy out of shame, the proverb verse out of futility, so honour and plain economy reach the same restraint.
list_adds: it gives a practical reason, waste, beside the quatrain's reason of honour, and moves the case from a humbled enemy to a dead one.

note: Kural 861 says avoid opposing the strong but favour enmity against the weak; Pazhamozhi 300 says even if the great fight the strong, enmity with the low brings them nothing. The tension holds if புன்பாட்டவர், men of low standing, are the Kural's மெலியார்.
teaches: Where the Kural measures an enemy by strength and picks the weak, Pazhamozhi measures by worth and warns that the petty, though small, can flood one like a light shower.
list_adds: its proverb gives the low enemy a capacity for harm the couplet denies the weak, so the choice of enemy turns on standing and risk, not strength alone.

note: Naladiyar 187 says even enmity with the wise brings dignity while intimacy with the mean brings grief; Pazhamozhi 300 says enmity with the low brings the great nothing.
teaches: The two say from opposite sides that the worth of an enemy is the measure of the quarrel: a wise foe honours one, a petty foe only costs.
list_adds: it adds the hazard the quatrain leaves out, that the petty enemy can still do great harm, as a light shower brings a flood.

note: Pazhamozhi 302 counsels silence before the strong and pressing the weak; 300 says the great gain nothing from enmity with the low.
teaches: Read together the book separates the weak, who may be overrun, from the low, who are not worth fighting, so strength and standing are two different measures of an enemy.

note: Innaa Narpathu 4 counts doing harm to the very strong as painful; Pazhamozhi 302 counsels keeping silent before the strong.
teaches: The counted verse names the pain of provoking the strong, the proverb verse the policy that avoids it and turns force on the weak instead, so the two give cause and remedy.
audit_text_issue: Line 4 வலியலாந் தாக்கு is hard to construe.

note: Kural 873 calls one who alone takes on the enmity of many worse than mad; Pazhamozhi 303 tells the man facing enemies not to trust himself and to rely on numbers, even of poor allies.
teaches: The couplet forbids the lone stand, the proverb verse supplies its positive rule, that number outweighs merit in war, so worthless allies are still worth having.
list_adds: it adds what the couplet lacks, a ranking of number above quality in allies, and a warning against self-admiration.

note: Kural 875 says one alone against two enemies should take one as an ally; Pazhamozhi 304 says against a stronger enemy one should find someone to harass him from behind.
teaches: The couplet makes an ally out of an enemy one already has, the proverb verse recruits a new enemy for one's enemy, so both turn the enemy's own surroundings into one's defence.
list_adds: its ram-and-dog proverb adds the tactic of a rear threat, which halts an advance without meeting it head on, something the couplet's alliance does not name.

note: Kural 887 says a family with inner enmity is not joined though it fits like box and lid; Pazhamozhi 305 shows how an enemy creates that enmity, by flattering one brother that the two together need no one.
teaches: The Kural describes inner enmity from inside the house that suffers it, the proverb verse from the hand that plants it, so the pair shows both the seam and the wedge.
list_adds: it supplies the act of sowing discord, with its quoted boast and bone-among-dogs image, which the couplet's picture of a split family leaves unsaid.

note: Kural 633 names the minister's skill of dividing others; Pazhamozhi 305 shows one way of dividing, by giving allied brothers something to quarrel over.
teaches: The couplet lists division as a skill of office, the proverb verse shows it worked through flattering speech, so the minister's art is seen in practice.
list_adds: it turns the couplet's bare word பிரித்தல் into a scene with a speaker, a boast and its effect.

note: Pazhamozhi 304 sets someone on a stronger enemy's rear; 306 incites an outside power against one's natural enemy and keeps it friendly by favour.
teaches: The two verses together show a graded method: first find a rear threat, then keep the third power warm and let it take the burn, as the monkey's hand stirs the fire.
audit_text_issue: 306 line 3 கறுவழங்கி is uncertain.

note: Pazhamozhi 303 says nothing is mightier than numbers; 307 says one capable man kills the hundred because division is in everyone.
teaches: The book's two proverbs meet: numbers win in the field, but a host can be undone by one man who works its divisions, so number is strength only while it is united.

note: Kural 889 says inner enmity as small as a split sesame seed holds ruin; Pazhamozhi 307 says division is in everyone and an able man can use it to kill a hundred.
teaches: The couplet warns the house of its own small crack, the proverb verse tells the enemy to widen it, so the same fact of universal division is a danger at home and a weapon abroad.
list_adds: it moves the couplet's warning into offence and gives a scale to the ruin, one able man against a hundred.

note: Kural 883 says to fear the enemy within and guard against it; Pazhamozhi 308 says the discerning gain by winning over the enemy within their enemy.
teaches: What the Kural tells one to fear at home the proverb verse tells one to seek in the enemy's camp, so inner enmity is a single force judged by whose house it is in.
list_adds: its doubled proverb, liquor by liquor and thorn by thorn, gives the principle that like cures like, which the couplet's potter's-cutter image lacks.

note: Kural 879 says cut a thorn tree while young before it wounds the hand; Pazhamozhi 308 removes a thorn with a thorn.
teaches: Both read the enemy as a thorn, but the Kural deals with it by timing, cutting early, and the proverb by means, setting one thorn against another.
list_adds: it adds a second way of handling the thorn, by its own kind, beside the couplet's way of cutting it young.

note: Kural 874 praises one who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship; Pazhamozhi 309 says an oppressor whose victim does not fall should come over to him in friendship.
teaches: The couplet makes turning enmity into friendship a mark of character, the proverb verse makes it a move forced by a failed attack, so the same turn can be virtue or prudence.
list_adds: it adds the occasion and the motive, a missed arrow and the need for guard, which the couplet's praise of character does not give.
audit_text_issue: 309 lines 3-4 uncertain

note: Kural 633 names three skills of the minister, dividing others, holding one's own and reconciling; Pazhamozhi 310 names four means of ending enmity, sweet words, gifts, division and measured force.
teaches: The two lists overlap only in division: the Kural's are skills of joining and parting, the proverb verse's a sequence ending in force, so they show two ways of ordering statecraft.
list_adds: it puts the means in an order, words and gifts first and force last and in due measure, which the couplet's three skills do not rank.

note: Pazhamozhi 196 says the senseless are best cut off with wealth, a gift's thrust being stronger than a spear's; 310 puts giving second among the means of ending enmity.
teaches: The earlier verse gives the gift as a weapon by itself; 310 sets it in a sequence with words, division and force, so the book's praise of the gift becomes one stage of a method.

note: Pazhamozhi 311 praises the worthy who, having weighed it, meet the foe whether they or the enemy win; 317 calls attacking without being the enemy's match a harm, like striking a stone.
teaches: Read together, the weighing in 311 does not license fighting any foe: courage indifferent to outcome is admired, but 317 bars the charge against a clearly superior enemy, so the chapter separates accepting risk from courting certain defeat.

note: Both set the silent fighter against the talker: in 311 those who rage within the fort with many words, in 313 the idle who talk and blame the king while the doers stand silent.
teaches: The pair shows the chapter's double charge against talk in war: it is wasted when made from safety, and it becomes slander when the talker turns it on the king.

note: Kural 764 makes an army one that cannot be turned by subversion (அறைபோகாது); Pazhamozhi 312 asks whether one who would give his body for the king could join his enemies.
teaches: The couplet names the quality, incorruptibility, as a property of the army; Pazhamozhi grounds it in the single soldier's willingness to die, so loyalty becomes the consequence of a readiness to give the body rather than a separate virtue.
list_adds: its two-bulls proverb gives a reason the couplet lacks: enmity so settled that the two cannot even share a ford, so desertion is shown as unnatural rather than only forbidden.

note: Naladiyar 346 says the excellent never speak a boastful word even with an emperor's wealth; Pazhamozhi 315 asks the warrior who has killed the strutting foe not to tell his own valour.
teaches: The quatrain's restraint concerns wealth and the base man's swagger; Pazhamozhi carries it to the battlefield, where the deed is real and the praise of others is due, so silence is asked even of one who has earned praise.
list_adds: it moves the rule from wealth to valour and gives the reason in a proverb, that the deed shows itself as a theft cannot be bundled, where the quatrain gives only the contrast of excellent and base.
audit_text_issue: proverb சோரம் பொதியாத வாறு is uncertain

note: Kural 473 says many who did not know their strength rose on zeal and were broken midway; Pazhamozhi 317 says that even capable men who rush on an unequal foe come to harm, like a hand struck on stone.
teaches: The couplet blames ignorance of one's own strength; Pazhamozhi adds that being able (ஆற்றுவாரேனும்) is not enough, since what counts is the match (நிகர்) with the enemy, so the weighing is relative, not absolute.
list_adds: it shifts the measure from the self's strength to the comparison with the enemy and gives the image of injury to the striker, which the couplet's broken-midway leaves general.

note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy and doing as one spoke is hard; Pazhamozhi 318 asks the man in the council of kings not to talk in turn and leave but to resolve to act, undeterred by the enemy's elephants.
teaches: The couplet locates the difficulty in doing; Pazhamozhi names what makes doing hard in war, fear of a strong enemy, and refuses the wait for a safer moment, so resolve is tied to accepting risk.
list_adds: it sets the contrast in the royal council before war and adds the waves proverb, which answers the excuse of waiting that the couplet does not consider.

note: Kural 772 says carrying a spear that missed an elephant is sweeter than an arrow that hit a hare; Pazhamozhi 319 scorns petty men who keep quiet before the strong and overrun the weak.
teaches: Both measure valour by its target rather than its success, and Pazhamozhi names the opposite type the couplet only implies: the man who chooses hares, silent before the guard and pitiless to the helpless.
list_adds: it adds the social side the couplet lacks, the bully's two faces toward strong and weak, and the razor image of sharpness wasted on what offers no resistance.

note: Kural 534 says the fearful have no fortress; Pazhamozhi 320 says the incapable are caught through fear though shut behind walls, like a timid bird that betrays itself in the dark.
teaches: The couplet states that walls do not help the fearful; Pazhamozhi shows how, since fear itself gives them away, as the bird's start reveals it, so the failure is exposure from within, not weak defences.
list_adds: it supplies the mechanism through the bird image, the fear that makes its holder visible, which the couplet's flat 'no fortress' does not give.

note: Kural 428 calls not fearing what should be feared folly and fearing it the work of the knowing; Pazhamozhi 323 denies that the fool's daring, resting on ignorance of dangers, is daring, and grants that knowing brings great fear.
teaches: The couplet makes fear a mark of wisdom in general; Pazhamozhi carries it to the soldier and draws the hard consequence, that the brave man is one who knows the danger and so feels the fear, making courage a matter of holding against it rather than lacking it.
list_adds: it moves the claim into the soldier's domain and turns it against a kind of courage, ruling out the fearless fool as brave, which the couplet does not say.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 பொறிப்பட்டவாறு is obscure; sense uncertain.

note: Kural 768 says that even without striking power or endurance an army gains stature by its படைத்தகை; Pazhamozhi 325 uses the same word for men of good name who lack the drive to march on the enemy.
teaches: The couplet treats bearing as a real asset of a weak army; Pazhamozhi turns it on men, so that bearing without ஊற்றம் becomes their measure, and the concession reads, on this reading, as a limited or ironic praise.
list_adds: its list of generosity, conduct and intelligence as the virtues of reputation sets the warrior's drive apart from them, showing that the civil virtues do not make a fighting man.

note: Purananuru 341 tells of a father who will not give his young daughter even when the king pleads and takes up arms with his tiger-like kin, torn between her wedding tomorrow and death; Pazhamozhi 326 says even the girl's brothers will refuse the king and the only outcome is battle.
teaches: The Sangam poem holds the refusal as a tragic choice and grieves for the town's beauty; the ethics verse keeps the heroic memory but removes the dilemma, so the refusal becomes a fixed rule of a proud house and war the only remedy, said with a kitchen proverb.
audit_text_issue: pazhamozhi_nanooru:326's proverb வாழைக்காய் உப்புறைத்தல் இல் is uncertain in sense.

note: Kural 247 grants as plain fact that this world is not for those without wealth; Pazhamozhi 327 brings that fact into the house and sets money beside a woman's modesty and the body's food as a precondition of the household's work.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's premise about wealth and this world becomes a rule of the house: money is one of three things a household life cannot do without.
list_adds: its run of three 'not without' clauses ranks money with modesty and food, so wealth stands as one of the household's basic needs rather than a worldly power.

note: Kural 85 asks whether the field of one who feeds guests even needs sowing; Pazhamozhi 330 gives the same unfailing yield to the house, but credits the hospitality to the wife who reads the husband's unspoken sign.
teaches: The pair shows the promise of endless plenty for the hospitable house resting in practice on the wife, whose silent understanding of her husband is what keeps the guests fed.
list_adds: its proverb of a water-lift in the sea replaces the unsown field with an inexhaustible source, and it adds the wife's reading of signs, which the couplet does not mention.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 விரும்தோம்பி for விருந்தோம்பி.

note: Kural 67 names the father's good to his son as setting him first in the assembly; Pazhamozhi 331 makes the father's task the child's conduct and warns that a child badly formed afflicts the one who formed him.
teaches: Together they give the father's duty a reward and a penalty: the well-formed son is set before the assembly, the ill-formed one turns on the father like a made thing become a demon.
list_adds: its proverb of the doll that becomes an afflicting spirit to its maker adds the cost of failure, which the couplet's statement of the duty leaves unsaid.

note: Kural 57 says confinement is no use and a woman's own நிறை is the best guard; Pazhamozhi 336 restates this and adds the obverse, that a woman without that restraint is not amended by force however hard.
teaches: The couplet shows only that the inner guard is better; the verse makes the outer guard useless in both cases, needless for the restrained and powerless over the unrestrained.
list_adds: its dog's-tail proverb supplies the second case the couplet does not state, so the claim covers both the woman with restraint and the woman without it.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 90 says a woman without a bond goes as she pleases though guarded; Pazhamozhi 336 says the same of confinement and closes it with the dog's tail.
teaches: The counted verse sets the woman beside desire and hidden murder as natures that outrun control; the proverb makes the same point by a household image of a crookedness force cannot straighten.

note: In Akananuru 146 the wife refuses the bard sent to plead for the husband who goes to the courtesans' street; Pazhamozhi 333 sets the same refusal of the bard in four lines and closes it with the proverb that a feigned sleeper cannot be woken.
teaches: The ethics work takes the akam wife's refusal of the bard and turns it into a general judgement, that a husband who strays knowingly is beyond persuasion, where the Sangam poem left the charge in images and pity.

note: Kural 693 tells the king's servant that once suspicion has arisen nobody can clear it; Pazhamozhi 335 carries the same irreversibility into a friend's house, where the town's rumour leaves no witness.
teaches: The pairing shows one rule about suspicion working at court and in the town alike: since it cannot be undone, the only defence is avoiding the occasion, even for the innocent.
list_adds: its flood-and-dam proverb gives the couplet's 'hard for anyone' a cause, the swell of public talk, and moves it from the king's suspicion to the neighbours'.

note: Naladiyar 141 says the well-born keep their principles though their clothes are rags; Pazhamozhi 329 says the household should keep a bright outward show even in ruin, since the world reads want from dress.
teaches: The two divide dignity in poverty between inner principle, which must never fall, and outward appearance, which the Naladiyar lets go and the Pazhamozhi insists on keeping for the world's eyes.
list_adds: its proverb about the clothed never being asked if they have eaten adds the social reason for outward show, which the quatrain's lion image of inner nature ignores.

note: Kural 90 warns the host that a guest wilts at a changed face; Pazhamozhi 337 turns the duty on the guest: the great should not stay with the poor, whom hospitality strains beyond their means.
teaches: Read together, hospitality has two delicate parties: the guest who wilts at a cold look and the poor host who would wound himself to feed a great guest.
list_adds: its sparrow proverb names the host's cost, which the Kural's chapter on hospitality never counts, and makes restraint a guest's virtue.

note: Kural 92 ranks sweet speech above glad giving; Pazhamozhi 338 says a gift of food, clothes, medicine and shelter is spoiled if the sweet word is withheld at parting.
teaches: Read together, sweet speech is not only the higher of two separable goods but the finishing part of a gift, so its absence cheapens what was given.
list_adds: it names the costly gifts one by one and then the missing word, so the proverb measures the meanness by the gap between a slaughtered buffalo and the spice.

note: Elathi 7 counts sweet speech with mingling, a seat and good food in the host's gift; Pazhamozhi 338 isolates the word given at the guest's leaving.
teaches: Elathi joins the sweet word to food in one welcome, and Pazhamozhi shows the welcome can fail at its last moment, when the departing guest is dismissed without it.

note: Kural 280 says shaving or long hair are not needed if one gives up what the world blames; Pazhamozhi 339 also sets aside the sect's marks and says what penance is: an even mind under the blade and the sandal.
teaches: The Kural removes the outward marks by a negative test, and Pazhamozhi supplies a positive one, equanimity toward harm and honour, as the substance the marks pretend to.
list_adds: its yoke-pin proverb gives the inward test an image of balance the couplet lacks, centring penance on a mind pulled equally both ways.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 செத்துக / சகத்தனாய் odd forms.

note: The Siddhar song says forest, rags and begging bowl gain nothing without inner love; Pazhamozhi 339 says the sect's mark is not penance without an even mind.
teaches: Both deny that garb makes the ascetic, but they put different things in its place, love for the Lord in the Siddhar and Jain-style equanimity in Pazhamozhi.
audit_text_issue: Pazhamozhi 339 line 2 (செத்துக சாந்து படுக்கமனன்) and சகத்தனாய் are corrupt or odd forms.

note: Thirikadugam 62 names the man who wrongly keeps a deposit among three whose line is lost; Pazhamozhi 340 traces how keeping begins, by delaying the return in the hope that the owner will not claim it.
teaches: The pair shows the sin and its root: the Thirikadugam punishes the kept deposit, and Pazhamozhi locates the fault already in stalling when the owner asks.

note: Kural 283 says wealth got by stealth perishes even as it seems to grow; Pazhamozhi 340 applies the same doom to a deposit held back, saying base wealth does not stay.
teaches: Pazhamozhi counts the withheld deposit as stealth without any taking, so the Kural's rule on stolen gain reaches a thing that came into one's hand lawfully.
list_adds: it moves the couplet's claim from theft to trust, the thing placed in one's hand, and adds the time of return as the test.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 63 says small gifts given without calling them of small use bear great fruit; Pazhamozhi 341 says nothing is of no use to something, since even a crab saved a man.
teaches: The two refuse the judgment 'too small to matter' from both sides, of the gift one gives and of the companion one keeps.

note: Pazhamozhi 136 says those cherished as a store against bad days fail one in trouble; Pazhamozhi 341 says even the smallest companion may save one.
teaches: Within one book help is shown to come from where it is not counted on, the crab, and to fail where it was banked on, the cherished friend.

note: Naladiyar 121 sets flesh-eaters among those who do not turn to renunciation; Pazhamozhi 342 says one who has renounced and then eats flesh undoes the whole crossing.
teaches: The Naladiyar makes flesh-eating a mark of the unrenounced, and Pazhamozhi adds that renunciation once achieved can still be sunk by it.
list_adds: its proverb of the sea and the hoofprint ranks the craving overcome against the small appetite kept, a contrast of scale the quatrain does not draw.

note: Pazhamozhi 342 addresses renouncers who eat flesh; 343 addresses those who kill in rage and lack grace.
teaches: The adjacent verses carry the bar on flesh from the renouncer's path to anyone without grace, and give it two roots: leftover appetite and anger.

note: Kural 251 asks how one who eats flesh can hold to grace; Pazhamozhi 343 traces the flesh-eater back through killing to rage, and says he did not walk in grace.
teaches: The Kural states the incompatibility of flesh and grace, and Pazhamozhi gives its order in a life: anger first, then killing, then eating.
list_adds: its chain of rage, killing and eating sets the diet among its causes, and the curd proverb casts grace as the good thing spoiled.

note: Thirikadugam 36 names the flesh-eater who claims compassion; Pazhamozhi 343 says those who eat flesh do not walk in grace.
teaches: Both deny the meat-eater's claim to grace, one by exposing his self-serving reasoning and the other by tracing the habit back to anger.
audit_text_issue: Thirikadugam 36 line 1 has a variant vowel in அருளுடையேம்.

note: Kural 104 says those who know the fruit take a millet's good as a palm; Pazhamozhi 344 asks the knowing to plan always for the good of one who gives them a measure of grain.
teaches: The Kural enlarges a small kindness in the mind, and Pazhamozhi turns that into lasting service toward a provider, framed as a return no trade can match.
list_adds: it moves the couplet from a single favour to a standing tie of maintenance, and its trade proverb puts gratitude in the language of profit.

note: Naladiyar 357 says the worthy bear many faults from one who did them a kindness; Pazhamozhi 345 has the giver bear the anger of the kinsman he fed.
teaches: The pair runs patience both ways along a gift: the receiver bears the benefactor's faults in the Naladiyar, and the giver bears the receiver's rage in Pazhamozhi.
list_adds: it reverses the quatrain's direction and grounds the forbearance in kinship made by giving, with the ghee proverb as its sign.
audit_text_issue: line 2 தான்காயான மன்னே is corrupt

note: Kural 204 says that if one plots another's ruin, aram plots the plotter's; Pazhamozhi 346 says plotting against one's benefactor is cutting the branch one sits on.
teaches: The Kural leaves the return to aram, while Pazhamozhi needs no agent: the benefactor is the plotter's own support, so the ruin is self-inflicted at once.
list_adds: it narrows the couplet to the one who cared for the plotter and joins others to the plot, and its proverb makes the retribution mechanical.

note: Kural 110 says there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him; Pazhamozhi 347 names one form of it, joining the benefactor's enemies and backbiting him.
teaches: The Kural ranks ingratitude as beyond remedy, and Pazhamozhi gives it a concrete shape in speech and alliance, likened to burning the house that fed one.
list_adds: it specifies the ingrate's act as backbiting in company with the estranged and weighs it by the past meals, which the couplet does not name.

note: Both close the heading with ingratitude; 346 is plotting ruin, 347 is backbiting in league with enemies.
teaches: The two proverbs split ingratitude's harm: cutting one's own branch ruins the traitor, burning the house one ate in ruins the benefactor.

note: Kural 521 says honouring old ties when all is lost is found only in kin; Pazhamozhi 352 extends it to kin who were hostile before, and sets them against outsiders who were favoured.
teaches: Together they show that kin loyalty in ruin does not rest on remembered kindness: even a hostile kinsman stands behind, so the bond is of family, not of debt.
list_adds: its contrast of ஒருகுடியார் with பிறர் treated as gold gives the couplet a counter-case, the favoured outsider who still will not come in.

note: Naladiyar 113 says that in trouble few kin claim the relation; Pazhamozhi 352 says those of one family do not part from a man in trouble.
teaches: On the same test, trouble, the two works give opposite verdicts on kin, one of shared family loyalty and one of kin as fair-weather clingers, so the ethics group has no settled view.
list_adds: it narrows kin to ஒருகுடியார் and puts the desertion on outsiders, where the quatrain puts it on kin themselves.

note: Naladiyar 203 says the great never refuse to bear those who depend on them; Pazhamozhi 348 says bearing them is useless unless their trouble is felt as one's own.
teaches: The pair adds an inner condition to the duty of support: carrying dependants as a branch carries fruit is not enough if their trouble is not felt as one's own.
list_adds: its proverb of pounding husk turns support without fellow feeling from a virtue into wasted labour.

note: Naladiyar 201 says a man's distress vanishes on seeing kin who ask after him; Pazhamozhi 350 says good kin are those who remove distress by deeds.
teaches: Read together, the comfort of kin has two measures, being asked after and being helped, and the Pazhamozhi verse ranks the deed as what makes kin good.
list_adds: it defines good kin by their act (வினைமரபின் நீக்கும்) and makes them a remedy at hand, where the quatrain heals by presence alone.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 3 says the use of kin is known when one is ruined; Pazhamozhi 350 says what that use is, removing the distress, and calls it a medicine at home.
teaches: The counted verse gives the test of kin and the proverb verse its content, so ruin both reveals kin and is the thing good kin cure.

note: Kural 529 says kin who left return when the cause of discord is gone; Pazhamozhi 351 says kin who seem never to help will help at last, as rain falls after holding off.
teaches: The couplet makes the return of kin wait on removing a cause, while the rain proverb makes it as sure as weather, so delay in kin's help is no proof of its absence.
list_adds: its rain proverb gives kin help the certainty of a natural cycle and sets it against strangers who never help.

note: Kural 448 says a ruler without those who rebuke him perishes; Pazhamozhi 353 says hurtful counsel should be heard from kin, whose treading, like a mother's, does not lame.
teaches: The pair moves the needed rebuker from the king's council into the family and gives a reason the couplet lacks for bearing him: the bond guarantees the hurt does no harm.
list_adds: its mother-bird proverb explains why rebuke is bearable, which the couplet only declares necessary.

note: Naladiyar 208 says true intimates enter the fire with you like the smith's poker; Pazhamozhi 354 says one taken as kin follows wherever his kinsman goes, as thread follows the needle.
teaches: Both use a craftsman's tool for loyalty, but the poker proves itself in danger and the thread by following, so kin loyalty is shown as obedience to another's course whatever it costs.
list_adds: its needle and thread make loyalty a matter of following the kinsman's lead, where the quatrain's smithy tools sort friends by their behaviour in the heat.

note: Kural 524 makes living surrounded by kin the fruit of wealth; Pazhamozhi 355 says even brothers living long in one dwelling is painful.
teaches: The pair separates being surrounded by kin from sharing a roof with them: the Kural's ideal holds only at a distance, for even brothers wear on one another at close quarters.
list_adds: its proverb that even the goddess of fortune is a bad housemate puts a limit of nearness and time on the couplet's praise.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 49 says living apart from one's companions is hard for the well-born; Pazhamozhi 355 says living long together in one place, even for brothers, is painful.
teaches: Held together, the two verses name a real dilemma of kinship: separation is hard and long cohabitation painful, so kin are best close but not under one roof.
audit_text_issue: Pazhamozhi 355's துச்சு is obscure; the marker flagged the sense.

note: Kural 938 lists what gambling destroys: wealth, truth, compassion; Pazhamozhi 356 shows by the Bharata that dice between kin destroy kinship itself.
teaches: The couplet's loss of compassion becomes, in the epic case, brothers' sons turned into strangers and enemies, so the worst stake at dice is the bond with the other player.
list_adds: its Bharata story names a loss the couplet's list leaves out, the player's kin turned ஏதிலர்.

note: Naladiyar 191 says kin live at ease on what their relative gives, like crops below a tank; Pazhamozhi 349 says the patron's trust in them means nothing unless he sees they do not go in want.
teaches: The pair makes provision the substance of the kin bond: the quatrain shows kin living on the giver, and the proverb verse denies that trust without the meal is any bond at all.
list_adds: its proverb that all is false but cooked food puts feeding above every other proof of kinship, which the quatrain assumes without arguing.
audit_text_issue: 349 lines 1-3 compressed

note: Kural 226 makes relieving the hunger of the destitute the place to store wealth; Pazhamozhi 358 denies the hoard is a reserve and calls aram done at the fit place the reserve for the time of need.
teaches: Both turn the language of saving onto giving, but Pazhamozhi widens the deposit from the hungry poor to any aram placed with discernment, and its proverb names when the store is drawn on, at the time of exhaustion.
list_adds: it joins enjoying wealth, giving it on both sides and choosing the fit occasion as one use set against the hoard, where the couplet names a single act.

note: Kural 335 urges good deeds before the hiccup stops the tongue; Pazhamozhi 361 shows those who wait until illness to begin aram and find it of no use.
teaches: The Kural sets the deadline at the death rattle; Pazhamozhi sets it earlier, at the first sight of illness, and says aram begun then fails because the means is not to hand, as the stone is not when the dog comes.
list_adds: its dog-and-stone proverb adds that the late giver lacks the means as well as the time, a cause the couplet's deadline does not give.

note: Kural 96 says sweet speech of good things makes அல்லவை wane and aram grow; Pazhamozhi 364's proverb says that when aram is done, அல்லவை leave, provided it is given with discernment of the fit place.
teaches: The two share the pair aram and அல்லவை but run the cause differently: in the Kural speech grows aram and wears down evil, in Pazhamozhi aram itself, placed with discernment, drives evil out, so aram is the fruit in one and the agent in the other.
list_adds: it sets good hereafter, growth of wealth and the going of evil together as fruits of one well-placed aram, with discernment as their condition, where the couplet names one fruit of speech.

note: Both use death, old age and disease as the spur: Naladiyar 92 to share wealth while it is in hand, Pazhamozhi 365 to do aram while one can.
teaches: The same triad backs sharing wealth in the Naladiyar and the use of a rare human birth in Pazhamozhi, which ends the triad with death as a stupor that puts one to sleep, so the urgency rests on the rare chance as well as on the threat.
list_adds: it puts the rarity of human birth before the triad of disease, old age and Death, joining a reason of opportunity to the quatrain's reason of threat.

note: Naladiyar 37 says the gains of human birth should not be spent serving the body; Pazhamozhi 365 says the hard-won human birth should be used for aram as far as one can before disease, age and Death arrive together.
teaches: The Naladiyar argues from what human birth is for; Pazhamozhi adds the deadline, so the rare birth has both a purpose and a closing time, and aram is measured by capacity, ஆற்றும் துணையும்.
list_adds: it couples the rarity of the birth with the three that end it, which the quatrain, speaking of gains and the body, does not name.

note: Kural 612 warns against letting a task die midway; Pazhamozhi 366 applies this to aram and says an aram broken off midway is worse than one never begun.
teaches: The Kural guards any task against abandonment; Pazhamozhi makes the rule sharper for aram, ranking the half-done gift below not giving at all, and puts the remedy in the planning that keeps many from being burdened.
list_adds: it ranks the abandoned aram below never beginning, a ranking the couplet does not make, and ties firmness of plan to sparing others the burden.
audit_text_issue: நட்டறான் admits two construals.

note: Kural 33 asks for aram without ceasing, as far as one is able; Pazhamozhi 367 allows that one may not manage it on many days and asks for it on some days with the best things.
teaches: Where the Kural measures aram by constancy within capacity, Pazhamozhi concedes the lapse and moves the measure to the quality of the gift, so a few days of the best is accepted where the couplet asks for every day.
list_adds: it trades frequency for quality, some days with the best things, which the couplet's 'without ceasing' leaves no room for.

note: Naladiyar 280 counts guarding wealth among its bitter sufferings; Pazhamozhi 368 says why guarding is vain: those who eye wealth outnumber those who keep it, as birds take grain under the watcher's eye.
teaches: The Naladiyar finds custody painful; Pazhamozhi finds it futile, since the covetous are always more than the keepers, and under its heading on aram this futility is the argument for giving wealth rather than keeping it.
list_adds: its pairing of grain and wealth makes the watcher's failure an image of all custody, where the quatrain lists custody as one of four pains.

note: Pazhamozhi 208 counts guarding earned wealth oneself a duty and handing it to the worthless a folly; Pazhamozhi 368 says that even wealth guarded with care is outnumbered by those who eye it.
teaches: Read together the book's two verses on custody limit each other: 208 says keep it yourself, 368 says keeping it never wins, so custody is a duty under the wealth heading that the aram heading turns into a reason to give.

note: Kural 249 likens aram done without அருள் to a muddled man's sight of truth; Pazhamozhi 370 calls அருள் the root of aram and its abandonment a loss of the greater for the lesser.
teaches: The Kural shows graceless aram as an empty act; Pazhamozhi names grace as aram's root and adds the cost of leaving it, the hare given up for a crow, so the fault is a bad exchange as well as a blindness.
list_adds: its hare-and-crow proverb ranks grace above whatever aram is done without it, a ranking of goods the couplet's simile of sight does not give.

note: Kural 276 calls those who deceive as if renounced while unrenounced in heart the hardest of all; Pazhamozhi 371 extends false practice to aram as well as penance and says it binds the deceiver in both worlds.
teaches: The Kural judges the false renouncer by his cruelty to others; Pazhamozhi turns the harm back on him, a rope he ties on himself, and carries the blame into the next life, so the fraud is self-ruin as much as an injury.
list_adds: it pairs penance with aram as the two things that can be falsely kept and this life's blame with the next, which the couplet, speaking only of renunciation, does not.

note: Thirikadugam 23 calls giving, faultless conduct and a mind free of possessions a rope that binds good deeds; Pazhamozhi 371 calls penance and aram practised falsely a rope that binds oneself.
teaches: The same rope image holds merit fast in Thirikadugam and holds the person fast in Pazhamozhi, so whether giving and penance are a rope that secures good or one that ties up the doer turns on sincerity.

note: Naladiyar 342 shows the base man refusing with excuses when urged toward the faultless; Pazhamozhi 363 says those who will not take up aram should be made to take it, as a mother feeds a refusing infant.
teaches: The Naladiyar treats refusal of the good as a mark of baseness and leaves it there; Pazhamozhi treats the refuser as a child to be fed by force, so refusal becomes a ground for compulsion rather than contempt.
list_adds: its mother-and-infant image adds a remedy and a motive, the other's lasting good, to the quatrain's bare portrait of refusal.

note: Both name the road after death with செல்வுழி: Naladiyar 328 mocks the fool who does not tie on its provisions; Pazhamozhi 359 shows the worthy making great wealth a protection for it.
teaches: The Naladiyar sets clutching wealth against provision for the road; Pazhamozhi's cane both chewed and boiled into jaggery lets the same wealth serve now and keep for later, so present use and provision are not opposed.
list_adds: its cane-and-jaggery proverb holds enjoyment and provision in one use of wealth, where the quatrain sets the grip on wealth against the provision.
audit_text_issue: Proverb sense uncertain: chewing the cane and then making jaggery may be an impossibility or waste.

note: Naladiyar 98 calls giving to those who will give back a profitable loan; Pazhamozhi 372 shows the same giving as bait cast to land a larger fish.
teaches: The Naladiyar names the return-seeking gift a loan between equals; Pazhamozhi adds the disproportion, a small gift aimed at a large catch, so the fault is not only expecting return but calculating a profit on it.
list_adds: its angler's image adds the ratio of small outlay to large gain that the quatrain's loan does not state.

note: Kural 1009 says others take wealth amassed without love or virtue; Pazhamozhi 373 names the taker, the seizing king, and sets the small gift to the destitute against the hoard.
teaches: The Kural leaves the taker as 'others'; Pazhamozhi makes him the king who drives the hoarder out, and pairs the lost hoard with rain in the wilderness, so the choice is between feeding royal power and feeding the destitute.
list_adds: it sets two ends of wealth side by side, the hoard going to the king and a single gift going to the starving, which the couplet's one fate does not contrast.

note: Kural 215 likens the wise man's wealth to water filling the village tank; Pazhamozhi 374 uses the tank to say discerning giving from long-gathered wealth does not quickly drain it.
teaches: The Kural's tank is wealth open to all; Pazhamozhi's tank is wealth that lasts though drawn on, so the same image answers the giver's fear of exhaustion, on condition that a capable man gives with discernment.
list_adds: it adds to the tank image the time it took to fill and the skill of the one who gives from it, so lasting depends on how the wealth was gathered and how it is given.

note: Kural 1052 says asking is a pleasure if what is asked comes without suffering; Pazhamozhi 375 calls excellent the giver who reads the asker's mind and gives what he wants.
teaches: The Kural conditions the asker's pleasure on getting without pain; Pazhamozhi locates the means in the giver, who spares that pain by reading the need from the asker's manner and giving the fit thing, not stones for the bowl.
list_adds: its begging-bowl proverb adds that the gift must match the need, a requirement on what is given that the couplet does not make.

note: Kural 218 says those who know what is due do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even without means; Pazhamozhi 376 says those long used to giving still relieve dependents when they have nothing to give.
teaches: Read together, the Kural gives the reason, knowledge of what is due, and Pazhamozhi gives the source, long habit of giving, so the giving that survives poverty is both understood and practised into the body like a horse's training.
list_adds: its thin-but-harnessed horse adds that the capacity shows only when put to work, a point the couplet's bare statement lacks.
audit_text_issue: வாய்ப்புத்தான் before the proverb is hard to construe.

note: Naladiyar 141 says the well-born in rags keep their principles, as a starving lion will not eat grass; Pazhamozhi 376 says the habitual giver, wasted, still relieves his dependents, as a thin great horse shows in harness.
teaches: Both use a noble animal reduced by want; the Naladiyar's lion shows what the noble will not do, Pazhamozhi's horse what he still does, so poverty is shown to test both refusal and service.
list_adds: it turns the quatrain's refusal into a positive act, relieving others' distress, so the proof of nobility in want becomes giving rather than abstaining.
audit_text_issue: pazhamozhi_nanooru:376 line 3 வாய்ப்புத்தான் is hard to construe.

note: Kural 220 grants for argument that ruin may come by ஒப்புரவு and calls it worth buying with oneself; Pazhamozhi 377 denies that anyone has ever become poor by giving.
teaches: The Kural meets the objection by accepting the cost; Pazhamozhi meets it by denying the cost exists, so the two show two answers to the fear that giving ruins, one heroic and one reassuring.
list_adds: its proverb flatly denies the premise the couplet entertains, and places the claim of ruin in the mouths of the takers rather than the giver.
audit_text_issue: Address அடுத்தேறல் (line 3) is obscure.

note: Kural 228 asks whether the hard-eyed who hoard and lose do not know the joy of giving; Pazhamozhi 378 asks whether those who hide wealth fearing it will dwindle have not seen the well refill.
teaches: Both ask the hoarder 'do they not know', but the Kural points to the joy he misses and Pazhamozhi to the fact he misjudges, that drawing renews the source, so the hoarder is wrong about both pleasure and arithmetic.
list_adds: its well proverb supplies the hoarder's own reason, fear of dwindling, and answers it with a fact of nature the couplet does not use.

note: Pazhamozhi 374's tank does not quickly run dry; 378's well springs fresh each time it is drawn.
teaches: The tank says giving does not soon exhaust stored wealth; the well says drawing on it renews it, so within one chapter the claim rises from endurance to replenishment.

note: Kural 595 says a water-flower rises to the water's depth and a man's height to his mind; Pazhamozhi 379 uses the same image to say a patron's gifts are great by the measure of his worth.
teaches: The Kural measures a man's rise by his inner drive; Pazhamozhi applies the image to giving, so the size of a gift becomes a reading of the giver's worth and not of the suppliant's rank.
list_adds: it carries the image from striving to giving and sets it against the foolish view that gifts follow the receiver's rank, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: 379 says a patron's gifts are great by his own worth; 380 says givers themselves know the measure of their worth and need no prompting.
teaches: 379 states that the giver's worth sets the gift; 380 adds that the giver knows that measure himself, so the true patron gives unprompted and the poet need not name or press him.
audit_text_issue: pazhamozhi_nanooru:380 lines 1-3 (அடுத்தர, தொடுத்தின்னார்) are hard to construe.

note: Purananuru 116 shows Pari's daughters after his fall, in a thorn-fenced hut counting salt carts; Pazhamozhi 381 shows Pari's daughter giving a bard gold in a drought.
teaches: The Purananuru remembers the daughters as the dispossessed; Pazhamozhi keeps one of them as a giver who feeds a bard even when rain fails, so the ethics work turns the elegy of Pari's house into proof that his giving outlived his fortune.
audit_text_issue: Pazhamozhi 381 line 2-3 (நீருலையுள் பொன்தந்து) uncertain.

note: 376 says habitual givers relieve dependents even with nothing left; 381 names Pari's daughter giving gold in a drought.
teaches: 376 states the rule in general with a horse; 381 gives it a named case from the most famous house of givers, so the chapter pairs the principle with its exemplar.
audit_text_issue: pazhamozhi_nanooru:376 line 3 வாய்ப்புத்தான் is hard to construe.

note: Kural 221 calls every gift but one to the destitute a measured loan; Pazhamozhi 383 says even lavish giving with no eye to return is wage labour if it looks to fame.
teaches: The Kural strips the name of giving from gifts that expect a material return; Pazhamozhi strips it also from gifts that expect only fame, so the wage can be praise as well as goods.
list_adds: it adds fame as a hidden return and names lack of discernment as the giver's fault, which the couplet's loan does not cover.

note: Kural 1051 says that if the worthy giver withholds, the blame is his and not the asker's; Pazhamozhi 384 shows a never-refusing giver hiding what he has because many ask one thing, and puts the fault on the crowd of askers.
teaches: The Kural places the blame for withholding on the giver; Pazhamozhi names a case where withholding comes from pity for those who would be turned away, so the blame moves to the number of askers.
list_adds: its proverb adds the askers' number as a cause of withholding, a condition the couplet's single asker and single giver leave out.

note: Naladiyar 126 likens attaching to one thought worthy who is not to opening a casket for sandal and finding a snake; Pazhamozhi 385 likens seekers who attach to patrons unable to satisfy them to axle grease that soaks away.
teaches: The Naladiyar's failed attachment brings danger, Pazhamozhi's brings slow waste, so the pair shows two costs of attaching without examining: harm from the unworthy and loss to the incapable.
list_adds: it moves the quatrain's failed choice of a friend into the suppliant's choice of a patron, and names the seeker's own great desire as the cause.

note: 373 says the concealed hoard ends as provision for seizing kings; 386 says wealth that escapes its guard and is seized by a great king leaves those who did not give with no remedy.
teaches: 373 sets the hoard's end against the gift's use; 386 adds the hoarder's helplessness after the seizure, so the king's taking appears in the chapter twice, as the hoard's fate and as the moment past remedy.

note: Kural 122 says to guard restraint as wealth, since life has no greater gain; Pazhamozhi 387 sets self-possession above uncounted wealth, good birth, royal property and a king's praise, for both worlds.
teaches: The couplet's metaphor of restraint as wealth becomes a contest here: self-mastery is weighed against real wealth, lineage and court honour and wins in this life and the next, so the figure is cashed out as a ranking.
list_adds: it names the rivals that restraint outranks, wealth, birth, royal goods and royal recognition, and extends the claim over both lives.

note: Kural 126 says drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is a safeguard (ஏமம்) for seven; Pazhamozhi 388 mocks those who do not guard the five early and so make no safeguard (ஏமம்) for the road after the body.
teaches: Both use the same pair, guarding the five and the safeguard it earns, but the Pazhamozhi adds a deadline: the couplet promises a return across births, the proverb shows the loss of one who begins only when the body is falling.
list_adds: it joins the guarding of the five to the 'three' taken up, puts the act in youth (சிறுகாலை), and turns the couplet's promise into a jibe at the late starter.

note: Kural 46 asks what one gains by going the outer way if household life is lived in virtue; Pazhamozhi 389 asks what use is a body that does not renounce once friends, peace, marriage and the house are achieved.
teaches: The two rhetorical questions face each other: on the reading that the Kural's 'outer way' is renunciation, it makes a virtuous household sufficient, while the Pazhamozhi makes the finished household only the stage before the renunciation that alone gives the body its use.
list_adds: it lists the household's tasks (friends made, enemies quieted, a wife joined, a house set up) as completed, so household life becomes a sequence that ends, not a sufficient path.
audit_text_issue: Site lacks this verse (flagged).

note: Pazhamozhi 389 says the body that does not renounce after the household is useless; 390 says those who choose neither household nor renunciation lose both.
teaches: Read together, the two verses give an order and a warning: household life first, renunciation after, and the one fault both condemn is the man who stops in between, holding neither.

note: Naladiyar 365 ranks striving in austerity first and dwelling with loved ones as the middle way; Pazhamozhi 390 condemns those who stand in the middle, choosing neither household nor its absence.
teaches: The word 'middle' moves: for the Naladiyar the middle is the household, a lesser but honest life, while for the Pazhamozhi the middle is indecision between the two lives, and only that is worthless, so neither life is shamed, only failing to commit.
list_adds: it drops the ranking of the two lives and puts the fault in the gap between them, with the image of a pole-carrier who drops both loads.

note: Naladiyar 6 says no one here has leapt clear of Death and escaped (கூற்றம் குதித்துய்ந்தார் ஈங்கில்லை) and urges the wealthy to give; Pazhamozhi 391 closes on the same words as a proverb after a list of wealth, lustre, strength, beauty, youth and birth.
teaches: The same saying about leaping Death serves two ends: the Naladiyar draws from it a duty to give wealth now, the Pazhamozhi uses it to cancel every advantage of fortune and birth at once, showing the saying was a common proof for different counsels.
list_adds: it sets six goods (wealth, lustre, strength, beauty, youth, birth) before the saying, so the proverb strikes a whole inventory, where the Naladiyar names wealth alone.

note: Naladiyar 53 lists home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength as impermanent and says the best renounce them; Pazhamozhi 391 lists wealth, lustre, strength, beauty, youth and birth and says they give no escape from Death.
teaches: Two nearly identical lists of six goods lead to different conclusions: the Naladiyar argues from their passing to renunciation, the Pazhamozhi only to their powerlessness before Death, leaving the remedy to the verses around it.
list_adds: it adds birth (இற்பிறப்பு) and lustre to the goods that fail and drops home and repute, so lineage too is placed among the things Death ignores.

note: Naladiyar 130 asks the heart how long it thinks it will live while it clings to home and pines for children; Pazhamozhi 394 bids the heart not to die speaking fondly of the house, since wives and children are many bonds.
teaches: Both speakers argue with their own heart about house and children, and together they show the form: the Naladiyar shows the heart its brief span and the good deeds that alone remain, the Pazhamozhi pictures the deathbed scene of one still talking of home.
list_adds: it names wives and children together as many bonds in a proverb, and sets the scene at death, where the quatrain asks a question about years.
audit_text_issue: Lines 1-2 are hard (வன்னெஞ்சினார்); the site lacks the verse.

note: Kural 345 asks what further tie (தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்) is left to those cutting off birth, when even the body is excess; Pazhamozhi 395 asks the same question (தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்) of those who left children and wealth, and answers with the elephant whose tail sticks.
teaches: The Pazhamozhi repeats the Kural's very question, and its proverb supplies what the couplet's 'even the body is excess' leaves unpictured: the danger after renunciation is not the great ties but a small remnant that holds the whole back.
list_adds: it names what was given up, dear children and earned wealth, and adds the image of the stuck tail, which ranks the last small tie as the real obstacle.

note: Kural 359 says one who knows the support and lives so that supports perish is freed from clinging pains; Pazhamozhi 397 shows a flame living on wick, bowl and ghee and says that, its supports gone, the self cuts off birth.
teaches: The Kural's abstract play on சார்பு gets a working model in the lamp: the flame is not destroyed by being blown out but goes out when what feeds it is gone, so release is shown as starvation of support, not an act of force.
list_adds: it lists the flame's three supports, wick, bowl and ghee, and adds the water proverb, so the couplet's one word becomes a concrete chain of dependence.

note: Verse 1 offers the book as rain that ends a great famine; the payiram calls the author's hand rain that ends the famine of not learning.
teaches: Together they show the famine pun is the book's own gloss on its title: the five roots cure, and the rain they bring is learning.

note: Verse 1 names killing, lying, meat and theft as the four the book sets aside; verse 20 lists theft, gambling, bad company, harmful speech and meat as what frees one from a flesh body.
teaches: The preface's four abstentions are, by verse 20, the price of release from rebirth, so the book's opening ethic is already a soteriology.

note: Kural 247 says that world is not for those without grace as this world is not for those without wealth; verse 2 gives enjoyment to wealth and dharma to grace, then spells out grace as three refusals.
teaches: Where the couplet only assigns grace its world, the verse says what grace does here: it refuses blame, sin and tale-bearing, so grace is chiefly a restraint of deed and tongue.
list_adds: It pairs wealth and grace as the first two items and then gives grace three more, so the list tips the balance the couplet keeps even.

note: Both counted works place the chaste wife first among things that heal: Thirikadugam calls her shoulders part of a medicine, Sirupanchamoolam calls her amrita.
teaches: In both works the wife's chastity heads a list whose other items are public goods (worthy company, learned friends; land, king, soldier), so the household virtue is ranked as a good of the realm.

note: Kural 402 likens the unlearned man's wish to speak to a woman without breasts desiring womanhood; verse 4 sets the unlearned man's subtlety beside the pride of a woman lacking both ears.
teaches: The two share an old figure of the unlearned as a body lacking its marks, but the verse splits the simile into two separate objects of laughter and adds a third, the poor man's boast.
list_adds: It turns the couplet's single simile into a list of three pretensions, so the woman's pride is no longer a figure for the unlearned but a ridiculous thing of its own.

note: Pazhamozhi 13 says the fine point an unlearned man has found is hard for him to show, so he should not rate himself among the good; verse 4 says that same subtlety makes the good laugh.
teaches: Read together, the pair gives both the cause and the effect: the unlearned man's insight cannot be shown, and so to the learned it is merely comic.

note: Kural 150 says that even one who does wrong does well not to desire another's wife; verse 5 promises fortune to one who does not desire her.
teaches: The couplet values the restraint even without other virtue; the verse makes it the gate to fortune, so the same act is moved from a minimum of decency to a source of gain.
list_adds: It sets not desiring another's wife beside penance, giving and learning as four means to four ends, so this restraint is ranked as one of the means of a whole life.

note: Kural 546 says victory comes from the unbending sceptre, not the spear; verse 6 makes the unbending its beauty and gives the army elephants and the soldier courage.
teaches: The couplet sets the sceptre against force; the verse keeps both, giving force its own beauties and joining the sceptre's straightness to truthful speech by one word, கோடா.
list_adds: It gives the sceptre the same quality as unbending speech and sets it among the army's and soldiers' beauties, so justice is ranked with force instead of against it.

note: Kural 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous who wear kindness to every creature; verse 7 says the பார்ப்பான் is the one who shares his food.
teaches: Both define a priestly title by conduct rather than birth, and the verse makes the conduct a concrete daily act, sharing food, where the couplet names a disposition.
list_adds: It defines the brahmin in a row with the ascetic, the leader and the worthy man, so the birth title is treated as one more role earned by an act.

note: Kural 134 says a பார்ப்பான் can relearn the Veda but his birth is ruined when conduct fails; verse 7 defines the பார்ப்பான் by sharing food alone.
teaches: The couplet keeps birth and makes conduct its condition; the verse drops birth from the definition, so the verse goes further than the Kural in detaching the title from birth.
list_adds: By listing the brahmin with titles anyone can earn, the list removes the birth the couplet still assumes.

note: Kural 575 calls kindly regard the eye's only jewel; verse 8 calls it the eye's beauty and gives four other members their beauties.
teaches: The couplet stops at the eye; the verse runs the same 'X's beauty is Y' through feet, reckoning, song and king, so the last two beauties are other people's praise.
list_adds: It sets the eye's beauty in a series that ends with a king judged by his people, so kindly regard becomes the first of a scale from the body to rule.

note: Kural 403 says the unlearned are good if they can keep silent before the learned; verse 9 says the unlearned man's tongue dies before those who know the good.
teaches: The couplet makes silence a choice that redeems; the verse makes it a shame that strikes, so the same silence is a virtue in one and a punishment in the other.
list_adds: It sets the unlearned man's mute tongue beside the killer's, the false witness's and the debtor's, so ignorance is ranked with guilt as a cause of shame.

note: Kural 1066 says nothing degrades the tongue like begging, even water for a cow; verse 9 says the well-born man's tongue dies when he has eaten and knows it.
teaches: Both place the shame of dependence in the tongue; on our reading of the verse, eating from the wrong hand silences the well-born as begging degrades the asker.
list_adds: It sets the well-born man's shame beside the debtor's, so the list treats owing and being fed as one kind of silencing.

note: Kural 127 says to guard the tongue above all, or suffer through faulty words; verse 10 says abuse is death to the tongue as its own eggs are to the spider.
teaches: The couplet warns of the speaker's suffering; the verse's animals show why: the harm grows from the speaker's own body, as a creature is killed by its own young or horns.
list_adds: It sets abusive speech last after four creatures killed by their own parts or offspring, so the tongue's ruin is shown as self-made.

note: Innaa Narpathu 39 calls liberality in a man who has nothing to give painful; verse 11 calls the generosity of a man without food laughable.
teaches: The two name the same thing from two sides: painful to the would-be giver and laughable to the onlooker, so empty generosity fails both inwardly and in public.

teaches: Both counted works single out meat-eating with a stronger word than their other items (முன்னின்னா, கொடுநஞ்சு), so the ranking is shared across the group.

teaches: Both works put a friend's distress first among painful things, but Sirupanchamoolam pairs it with not giving, so the pain is also a call to help.
