note: Kural 55 praises the wife who worships her husband, not a god, and commands the rain; verse 14 makes walking her husband's way a woman's virtue.
teaches: The couplet gives the wife's devotion cosmic power; the verse sets the same following among son, kin, soldier and subjects, as one case of keeping one's place.
list_adds: It lists the wife's following with the son's, the soldier's and the people's, so the rule for women is presented as one form of a general duty of following.

note: Kural 542 says the people live looking to the ruler's sceptre as the world looks to the sky; verse 14 calls living by the sceptre the virtue of the king's land.
teaches: The couplet speaks of the king's duty to the people's need; the verse turns it into the people's virtue, obedience to the sceptre.
list_adds: It counts living by the sceptre among household and military duties, moving it from the king's chapter into the subject's code.

note: Kural 152 says bear with excess and better still forget it; verse 15 calls bearing a wrong greatness and brooding on harm smallness.
teaches: The couplet ranks forgetting above bearing; the verse names brooding as the opposite of forgetting and calls it smallness, so it supplies the failure the couplet leaves implied.
list_adds: It sets greatness and smallness as a contrasting pair and adds ending enmity as a third good, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: Kural 303 says forget anger at anyone at all, since evils are born of it; verse 16 says anger is good and nobility bad before people without worth.
teaches: On the plain reading of verse 16 the two disagree about the same act: the Kural allows no exception to forgoing anger, while the verse makes the base an exception.
list_adds: It inverts three house virtues at once (anger, nobility, pride) for one audience, so the exception is a rule, not a lapse.

note: Naladiyar 70 says no one bitten by a dog bites it back, so the high do not answer the low in kind; verse 16 uses a barking dog to say goodness to the base is wasted and anger is good.
teaches: Both use the dog for the base man and draw opposite counsels: the Naladiyar asks for restraint, the verse for anger and pride.
list_adds: It sets anger and pride as good beside nobility as bad, so the list reverses the Naladiyar's ranking of forbearance above response.

note: Innaa Narpathu 40 calls fierceness in a man of self-restraint painful; verse 16 says anger is good before people without worth.
teaches: The pair marks a limit: fierceness is unfitting in the restrained man in general, but Sirupanchamoolam carves out the base as the one place it serves.

note: Verse 17 names lying with women and keeping house as the fruits of the unrenounced body; verse 18 says not turning to women who want him is a way out of rebirth.
teaches: The book grants the householder's body its fruits but sets the higher reward, not being born again, on giving up exactly those fruits.

note: Kural 260 says all creatures worship the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; verse 18 says one who does not eat flesh out of craving will hardly take a body again.
teaches: The couplet's reward is honour in this world; the verse's is release from the body, so the same abstention is given a Jain soteriological fruit.
list_adds: It joins refusing meat to truth, honesty and chastity, each tested by its strongest temptation, as joint conditions of release.

note: Verses 18 and 20 both close a list of abstentions, meat last, with the promise that one will not take a body again.
teaches: The book states the same Jain promise twice in three verses, with meat as the final condition each time, which shows how central diet is to its idea of release.

note: Kural 410 says others are to the learned as beasts are to people; verse 19 calls the learned gods and the unlearned ghouls.
teaches: The couplet uses one step, beast to human; the verse widens the scale to god and ghoul and saves the beast for the boaster, so learning is placed on a three-step ladder of beings.
list_adds: It sets learning beside early earning and against nostalgic boasting, ranking each as god, ghoul, wretch or ox.

note: Naladiyar 53 says the best renounce home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength on seeing they do not last; Sirupanchamoolam 23 says those who rely on form, youth, beauty, family and lineage and do not renounce young never see the unshaken state.
teaches: The quatrain gives impermanence as the reason to renounce; the verse adds a deadline, youth itself, and a second obstacle, pride of birth, so delay and lineage join transience as what keeps a man from release.
list_adds: It sets family and lineage (குடி, குலம்) in the same list as the body's goods and makes youth both an item and the time limit.

note: Naladiyar 363 names three bad wives (the defiant, the one who skips the kitchen, the one who withholds food) as weapons that kill the husband; Sirupanchamoolam 24 names five doings of a bad wife.
teaches: The quatrain's faults all lie inside the house and against the husband, the verse's all lie outside it (drink, absence, other houses, prying, bad company), so together they show the period's norm for a wife policing both her service and her movements.
list_adds: Its five faults face outward from the house, where the quatrain's three are failures of service within it.

note: Purananuru 195 tells aged worthies that the axe-bearing one will bind them, so if they cannot do good they should at least avoid harm; Sirupanchamoolam 25 sets four commands under the certainty of Death's coming.
teaches: Both rest counsel on the certainty of death, but the Sangam poem bargains down to a minimum (at least do no harm) while the ethics verse turns the same ground into four positive and negative rules and adds a reckoning after death.

note: Verse 20 lists not stealing, not gambling and not befriending the black-hearted among five abstentions; verse 27 says the friend of outsiders picks up toddy, theft and gambling.
teaches: Verse 20 puts bad company beside theft and gambling as one more abstention; verse 27 shows it as their cause, so the book's ban on bad friends is a ban on the way the other vices are learned.

note: Purananuru 183 says learning is good even at the cost of serving the teacher, giving him wealth and accepting the lower place; Sirupanchamoolam 28 says the true teacher seeks no gain and the fit pupil serves with love.
teaches: The Sangam king accepts payment and service as the price of learning; the Jain verse keeps the pupil's loving service but denies the teacher any gain, and adds that learning without casting off the three faults is a sickness.

note: Naladiyar 135 says learning has no shore and life is short, so the wise choose what to learn; Sirupanchamoolam 30 says no one has learned the whole of the treatises, and no one knows all or nothing.
teaches: The quatrain draws from the boundlessness of learning a method of choosing; the verse draws from the same limit a judgment of persons: no one is complete in knowledge or virtue, and no one wholly lacks knowledge either.
list_adds: It sets the limit of learning beside matching limits on knowing, not knowing and faultlessness, so the shoreless field becomes one case of a rule that no person is complete either way.

note: Kural 261 defines tapas as bearing the pain that comes and harming no life; Sirupanchamoolam 31 keeps both, adds three more, and says penance so made is sweet, not lowly.
teaches: The couplet defines penance by two ethical acts; the verse keeps them, turns bearing pain into forgetting it, and meets an objection the couplet does not raise, that penance degrades the one who does it.
list_adds: It extends the couplet's two marks to five, adding no wrong to another and the giving up of desire and anger, and closes with a verdict on how the penance feels.

note: Kural 134 says a brahmin who forgets the Veda can relearn it but one whose conduct fails loses his birth; Sirupanchamoolam 32 says the brahmin is the one who sacrifices.
teaches: Both tie the birth term பார்ப்பான் to something done rather than to birth alone, but the Kural ties it to conduct and the verse to the rite of sacrifice, two different tests for the same status.
list_adds: It puts the brahmin's defining act in a row with a woman's chastity, a scholar's listening, a poet's mind and the father's gift, so each kind of person is named by one mark.

note: Kural 418 says ears not pierced by listening are deaf though they hear; Sirupanchamoolam 32 says the one who listens is the flawless great scholar.
teaches: The couplet condemns the unlistening ear; the verse makes listening the very definition of the great scholar, ranking it above reading or composing.
list_adds: It sets the listener beside the poet, whose excellence is in his mind, so hearing and composing are named as two separate excellences.

note: Kural 255 says the standing of life lies in not eating flesh and hell will not release the one who eats; Sirupanchamoolam 33 says the one led upward who never begins on flesh is sure to go there.
teaches: The couplet threatens the meat-eater with a hell that does not open; the verse promises the abstainer a sure passage, and ties the abstention to the teacher who leads him, so diet becomes the proof of being led.
list_adds: It ends a list of true titles (liberal man, merchant, teacher) with abstaining from flesh as the condition of the pupil's passage.

note: Kural 247 says that world is not for those without grace as this world is not for those without wealth; Sirupanchamoolam 34 says enjoyment comes of wealth and dharma of melted grace.
teaches: The couplet weighs grace against wealth by the worlds they open; the verse gives each its fruit (enjoyment, dharma) and calls the grace melted, so grace is a softening of the heart, not a possession.

note: Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world; Sirupanchamoolam 35 assigns enjoyment to giving, heaven to penance and release to knowledge.
teaches: The couplet frees giving from any reward; the verse keeps a reward but ranks it lowest, so both deny that giving is the way to heaven, one by indifference to reward and one by a ladder of rewards.
list_adds: It ranks giving, penance and knowledge on one ladder of fruits, enjoyment, heaven, release, which the couplet never builds.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 போதும் does not construe; read as போகம்.

note: Verse 5 says one who wants to be rid of the body does penance and one who wants standing gives; verse 35 says penance brings heaven and only knowledge brings release.
teaches: Read together, the two verses disagree on what ends embodiment: verse 5 credits penance, verse 35 reserves release for knowledge and gives penance only heaven.
audit_text_issue: 35 line 3 போதும் does not construe (perhaps போகம்); 5 lines 2-3 (இடம்பொழிய, மடம்பொழிய, அறிமடம்) divide uncertainly. | 35 line 3 போதும் does not construe as printed (read as போகம்); 5 lines 2-3 (இடம்பொழிய, மடம்பொழிய, அறிமடம்) are hard to divide.

note: Naladiyar 131 says beauty of hair, garment and saffron is not beauty and the beauty of learning is; Sirupanchamoolam 36 says beauty of hair, chest, nails, ears and teeth is not beauty and speech fitted to learning is.
teaches: Both deny outward beauty to praise learning, but the quatrain rests learning's beauty on fairness of heart, while the verse rests it on speech that fits the books, so one makes it inward and the other audible.
list_adds: Its list is all of the body (hair, chest, nails, ears, teeth), not adornments, and it turns on speech rather than learning itself.

note: Kural 1033 says all who do not live by their own ploughing bow to eat and walk behind; Sirupanchamoolam 37 says the worthy do not eat food got by bowing.
teaches: The couplet names the farmer as the one man free of bowing for food; the verse makes refusing such food a rule of the worthy whatever their trade, so the Kural's economic point becomes a point of self-respect.
list_adds: It sets the refusal beside not sleeping in a friend's house and not taking lost goods, so eating by bowing is ranked with small breaches of dignity and honesty.

note: Kural 323 ranks not killing first and not lying after it; Sirupanchamoolam 38 calls not lying, wealth and not killing each good without ranking them.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the verse declines the Kural's ranking of the two vows and admits wealth among the goods between them, a Jain list that values non-killing without making it the single highest good here.
list_adds: It lists not lying, wealth and not killing side by side with wealth in the middle, where the couplet orders the two vows and leaves wealth out.

note: Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every folly; Sirupanchamoolam 39 says giving treasury, accounts and stores to men without understanding is setting a crow to guard rice.
teaches: The couplet locates the fault in the master's fondness; the verse measures the appointee (understanding that does not match his size) and shows the result as the guard eating what he guards.
list_adds: It names the particular offices of trust and closes with the crow image, where the couplet speaks only of trust in general.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 (பாத்தில்லார் உண்டார் அடிசிலே தோழரில்) is hard to construe. | Line 2 பாத்தில்லார் உண்டார் and தோழரில் are hard to construe; the last items are uncertain. | lines 1-2 hard to parse (பாத்தில்லார், தோழரில்)

note: Kural 773 says fierceness is great valour but help to a foe in trouble is its cutting edge; Sirupanchamoolam 40 names five helpless enemies whom true soldiers never approach.
teaches: The couplet makes mercy to the fallen the edge of valour as a principle; the verse turns it into signs a soldier can read on the field, and makes the restraint the definition of a true soldier.
list_adds: It turns the couplet's one principle into five recognisable signs of surrender or helplessness.

note: Purananuru 9 praises a Pandya who warns cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter before he shoots; Sirupanchamoolam 40 names five who give up in battle and must not be approached.
teaches: The Sangam king protects those who never fight by warning them before battle; the verse protects those who stop fighting during it, so together they give both ends of the period's code of sparing in war.

note: Kural 148 calls it manhood not to look at another's wife; verse 41 puts another's wife last in a list of five women men avoid.
teaches: The couplet's one rule becomes a whole map of forbidden women, so the Kural's virtue of restraint is turned into a period code drawn by age, menses and vow.
list_adds: It sets another's wife among a girl, a woman past her menses, a female ascetic and an unguarded woman, so adultery becomes one case of a wider bar by bodily state and vow.

note: Kural 55 praises the wife who does not worship a god but rises worshipping her husband; verse 42 counts worship of the deity, beside the one who brings her fortune, as part of a wife's excellence.
teaches: Read flatly, the Kural sets the husband in place of the god while this verse asks the wife to worship both, so the two works divide on whether her devotion may go beyond the house.
list_adds: It sets the deity's worship as a fifth duty beside income, kin and guests, making religion one household task among others rather than the one the husband displaces.

note: Kural 51 defines the wife by the home's excellence and living within her husband's means; verse 42 opens with knowing the house's ways in proportion to income.
teaches: Both works put income first in defining a wife, and the verse spells out what the couplet's 'excellence of the home' includes: kin kept content, guests and worship.
list_adds: It ranks budgeting first and then lists the duties it must pay for, so the couplet's measure of means becomes the base of a household order.
audit_text_issue: sirupanchamoolam:42 line 2 திருவாக்கும் may qualify தெய்வதை or name the husband.

note: Verse 43 tells one to seek the man who knows five parts of astrology and have him fix the wedding day; Naladiyar 52 calls those who prattle of astrology the greatest of fools.
teaches: Two Jain-era ethics works disagree on the worth of the same learned craft: one treats astrology as the expert's knowledge a marriage needs, the other as a madman's distraction from death.
list_adds: It breaks astrology into five technical parts, treating it as a craft to be mastered, which is exactly what the quatrain mocks as endless prattle.
audit_text_issue: Sirupanchamoolam 43 line 3 (உற்றானும் அல்லானும்) is uncertain.

note: Naladiyar 386 says beauty in a modest woman is like learning in the wise or a sword in a hero's hand; verse 44 says that without modesty and four other qualities even Lakshmi's beauty cannot be held.
teaches: The pair state one claim from both sides: modesty makes beauty serviceable, and beauty without it is ungovernable, so beauty in both works has worth only as the instrument of a virtue.
list_adds: It names four qualities beside modesty and sets them against beauty at its divine limit, a ranking the quatrain's three similes leave implicit.

note: Kural 542 says the people live looking to the king's sceptre as the world looks to the sky; verse 45 says the king rises only as the field bank, water, paddy and people rise beneath him.
teaches: The couplet makes the people depend on the king, while the verse runs the dependence upward from a mud ridge, so read together they show the dependence runs both ways.
list_adds: Its chain of five causes puts the king at the end of a ladder of rises beginning with a field bank, a causal order the couplet does not trace.

note: Kural 1034 says farmers see many kings' umbrellas under their own; verse 45 traces a king's rise to the rising of the field's water and paddy.
teaches: The couplet's claim that farming underwrites kingship is given its mechanism: the height of the crown is measured from the height of the field bank.
list_adds: It sets out each link from field to throne in order, where the couplet states only the end result.

note: Kural 44 says a household that fears blame and shares its food never loses its line; verse 46 counts not blaming and sharing with all among the marks of a good house.
teaches: The couplet's two conditions of a lasting house reappear inside a longer list that adds care for dependants and for the calf, so the house's sharing is carried to its animals.
list_adds: It places sharing beside not milking a calf to death, so household generosity is extended to the livestock, which the couplet does not reach.

note: Kural 328 says gain that comes by killing is the lowest for the worthy however great; verse 47 ends that those who know will not kill whatever they gain.
teaches: The verse takes the couplet's refusal of gain by killing and widens killing to the hope of the needy, the kin's meal, one's generosity and fame, so neglect becomes a kind of slaying.
list_adds: Its pun on கொல் puts killing a life beside killing a hope or a reputation, making non-killing a rule for social conduct as well as for life.

note: Kural 742 names water, open ground, hill and shady forest as a fort; verse 48 names deep water, forest, saline waste, a lofty hill and the people, and makes having them the rule for crowning a king.
teaches: The fort of the couplet gains a fifth wall made of people, and its possession becomes the test for who may be made king rather than a feature of a stronghold.
list_adds: It adds the people as a fifth defence and turns the list into a qualification for kingship, which the couplet's list of terrain does not do.

note: Thirikadugam 100 names a loyal army, a fearless fortress and great treasure as the limbs of kings; verse 48 breaks the fortress into five and makes it the ground of being crowned.
teaches: One counted work treats the fort as one limb among three, the other spells it out as five, with the people among them, so the two together show the fort as both a royal possession and a living defence.

note: Kural 1039 says land left by an owner who does not go to it sulks like a wife; verse 49 counts negligence first among five ruins of the ploughman.
teaches: The couplet's single fault of absence is set at the head of a list that adds pride, unfinished work, quarrels and a broken tie with the craftsman, so a farm fails socially as well as by neglect.
list_adds: It sets negligence among social and moral causes of ruin, where the couplet names absence alone.

note: Verse 12 calls killing and eating flesh poison among five poisons; verse 50 calls not killing good and killing bad, then weighs illiteracy and anger on the same scale.
teaches: Within the book, killing is the fixed first term of two lists, and in each the author sets lesser faults (overpowering the weak, slander, illiteracy, anger) beside it, so its scale of harms keeps killing as the measure.
audit_text_issue: Sirupanchamoolam 12 lines 2-3 and 50 lines 3-4 are hard to divide.

note: Kural 211 says duty seeks no return, as the world gives nothing back to the rain; verse 51 calls it good to host guests without reckoning a return.
teaches: The couplet's principle of giving without return is carried to the guest at the door, and the verse sets it next to fasting and not eating from others' hands, so giving freely and taking nothing are one ideal.
list_adds: It pairs the host who expects no return with the man who will not eat from another's hand, so the list joins the giver's and the receiver's sides of the same refusal.
audit_text_issue: sirupanchamoolam:51 line 1 (று) is an editorial supply

note: Kural 60 calls good children the ornament of a home's excellence; verse 52 counts bearing children first among a wife's medicines that make the husband yield.
teaches: Children, an ornament of the house in the couplet, become in the verse the wife's first hold over her husband, so the same good is read for its effect within the marriage.
list_adds: It sets childbearing beside beauty, accord and restraint in food as means of holding the husband, a use of children the couplet does not name.

note: Verse 44 names five qualities without which a woman cannot be held by her husband; verse 52 names six by which a wife holds him.
teaches: The two verses look at the same marriage from opposite ends: what lets a husband keep a wife within bounds and what lets a wife bring a husband to yield, so the book treats control as running both ways.

note: Kural 57 asks what use guarding by confinement is and puts a woman's own steadfastness first; verse 53 names five men of her family as the ones who guard her.
teaches: Read as a claim about what keeps a woman, the couplet moves the guard inside her while the verse places it in her husband, brother, uncle, son and father, so the two disagree on where chastity is kept.
list_adds: It names the guard as five kinsmen, a list of external keepers that the couplet's single inner guard sets aside.

note: Verse 53 names five kinsmen who guard a woman; verse 54 says she falls if she herself does not guard her restraint.
teaches: Placed side by side in the book, the two verses split the guard between the men of her family and her own நிறை, so the book holds both views the Kural sets against each other.
audit_text_issue: sirupanchamoolam:54: count word ஐந்து with four parts named; lines 3-4 are obscure

note: Naladiyar 139 says the unlearned who keep company with the learned gain sense daily; verse 55 says the unlearned who stay outside the learned's company gain only laughter.
teaches: The quatrain gives the remedy and the verse gives the cost of refusing it, so together they make company, not learning alone, the line between gaining sense and being mocked.
list_adds: It grades rewards (gold, wealth, fame, laughter) by kind of learning and company, setting the unlearned at the bottom of a ladder the quatrain does not draw.

note: Kural 969 says men of honour give up life when honour is at stake, like the yak; verse 56 makes perishing, for the man of honour, the last of five acts of wisdom.
teaches: Death for honour, a matter of nature and pride in the couplet, is counted here as wisdom beside forgiveness and care for living beings, so it is framed as discernment rather than temper.
list_adds: It sets dying for honour beside revealing good, forgetting wrongs and helping living beings, so the list makes it one act of wisdom among gentler ones.

note: Kural 471 says to weigh the strength of the deed, oneself, the opponent and allies before acting; verse 57 says the minister acts after measuring his own state, the work, the opponents' state and the order of things.
teaches: The couplet's four-fold weighing is given to the minister and its fourth term changes from allies to the matchless order of things, so prudence moves from counting forces to reading circumstance.
list_adds: It moves the reckoning to the minister and replaces allies with the order of things, a different fourth term than the couplet's.

note: Kural 501 says a man is trusted after being tested by virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life; verse 58 says the trusted man has wealth, enjoyment, fearlessness, grace at death and rare dharma.
teaches: Where the couplet uses wealth, pleasure and fear as temptations to test a man, the verse treats wealth, enjoyment and fearlessness as qualities he must have, and adds grace, so the same terms change from tests to credentials.
list_adds: It turns the couplet's four tests into five possessions and adds grace that survives death, which the couplet does not name.

note: Kural 1038 ranks manuring above ploughing and guarding above watering; verse 59 lists storing straw, cattle, tools and manure as care that comes before the plough is set.
teaches: Both put the plough after other care, and the verse widens the couplet's ladder to the farmer's stores and animals, then turns the whole into an image for the scholar's finer plough.
list_adds: It sets manure among the farmer's other provisions and closes with the reciter of texts, so the farming list becomes a figure for study.

note: Verse 49 names five ruins of the ploughman; verse 59 names the care he gives before he ploughs.
teaches: The book gives the farmer's life as a pair of lists, what ruins him and what he must tend, so negligence in 49 is answered item by item by the provisions of 59.
audit_text_issue: Sirupanchamoolam 59 lines 1 and 3 (மா டோ, என்றிலை) are doubtful.

note: Kural 890 likens living with those not in accord to living in a hut with a snake; the verse names five such housemates and calls them a disease.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's unnamed discordant housemates become a roster of the house (kin, wife, servant, son, neighbour), so the inner enemy is located in the very people one cannot leave.
list_adds: It names five separate relations of the house and makes them one kind, a disease within, where the couplet leaves 'those not in accord' unnamed.
audit_text_issue: Sirupanchamoolam 61 line 1 is hard, and கரம் may mean poison.

note: Kural 215 likens the wise man's wealth to a village tank full of water; the verse makes the gift of water itself the first of five charities.
teaches: The Kural's tank is a figure for wealth all may draw on; the verse makes it literal and the lowest step of a scale that ends in founding temples and halls.
list_adds: It ranks the charities from a drink of water to founded buildings and puts a condition on charity at home, which the couplet's single image lacks.

note: Both verses list works for others' use of water, land and shelter; 62 promises great enjoyment, 65 heaven.
teaches: Together they mark a scale of public works and fruits: water, shade and halls bring enjoyment, while tanks, roads and wells bring heaven itself.

note: Naladiyar 99 says never call a gift too little, for like the ascetic's bowl it fills slowly; the verse lists the pittances (a handful, begged salt, a rag) given without calling them small.
teaches: The quatrain argues from the receiver's slowly filled bowl and the verse from the poor giver's actual pittances, so the same rule on small gifts is seen from both ends of the gift.
list_adds: It names five concrete pittances, salt the giver himself begged and a torn rag among them, so the rule is tested on gifts a beggar could make.

note: 63 says small gifts not called small bear great fruit; 64 names the melting of the giver's heart as what makes a small gift grow like a hill.
teaches: Read in sequence, the first verse sets the gift's size aside and the second names what replaces it as the measure, the melting of the giver's heart.

note: Naladiyar 38 says a small gift grows vast when it reaches worthy hands; the verse says it grows like a hill when the giver's heart melts.
teaches: Both say a small gift grows huge but place the cause differently: the Naladiyar in the worth of the receiver, Sirupanchamoolam in the melted heart of the giver.
list_adds: It gives five images of melting as the measure of the giver's heart, a condition on the giver that the quatrain does not state.

note: Purananuru 18 urges the Pandya Nedunchezhiyan to build up tanks where the land dips, for those who bind water win wealth hereafter, sole rule and fame; the verse makes tank-digging one of five works that take any doer to heaven.
teaches: The duty the Sangam poet urged on one king becomes in the ethics work a merit open to any man of means, and the promised reward narrows from rule and fame to heaven.

note: Thirikadugam 16 counts one who digs a well of drinking water without stint among three who gain a body that does not die; the verse counts a shared well among five works leading to heaven.
teaches: The two counted works reward the same well differently, one with a deathless name in this world and the other with heaven, so the group divides on where the fruit of public works falls.

note: Kural 280 says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; the verse lists five ascetic forms and says that in the Kali age renunciation is false and the household alone true.
teaches: The couplet discounts the ascetic's marks but keeps renunciation, while the verse, for its own age, discounts renunciation itself, so one critique of outward form reaches opposite ends.
list_adds: It names five ascetic forms where the couplet names two, and ties its judgement to an age (கலி), which the couplet does not.

note: Kural 49 says that what is called virtue is household life; the verse ends that in the Kali age household life alone is true.
teaches: Both favour the household, but the Kural grounds it in what virtue is and the Jain verse in the corruption of the age, so one preference has a timeless and an historical ground.
list_adds: It reaches the household's primacy by eliminating a list of ascetic forms, a route the couplet does not take.

note: 66 rejects the outward marks of ascetics; 68 rejects four austerities and keeps only restraint of the five senses.
teaches: Together the two verses strip ascetic display in two moves, first the marks on the body and then its austerities, leaving only restraint of the senses.

note: Kural 240 says those who live without blame are the ones who live; the verse names the means of a life the worthy bless, beginning with remembering one's birth-house.
teaches: The couplet gives the verdict of blame and fame on a life and the verse the means of earning the good verdict, so memory of lineage becomes a guard on reputation.
list_adds: It sets lineage, self-hold and awareness of others' regard as causes of the good name the couplet only judges, ending on two opposed speeches of others.

note: Kural 343 says the field of the five must be crushed and all desire let go; the verse sets restraint of the five and wanting nothing against four rejected practices.
teaches: The verse supplies what the couplet leaves out, the practices that do not count, so restraint of the senses is defined against bathing and bodily austerity rather than only stated.
list_adds: It sets the couplet's restraint of the five against four rejected practices, a contrast the couplet lacks.

note: Kural 256 says that if none killed to eat, none would sell flesh; the verse divides the sin among killer, consenter, taker, cook and eater.
teaches: The couplet ties the eater to the seller by demand; the verse spreads the sin along the whole chain, so even one who only consented or only cooked is guilty.
list_adds: It names five links of the chain and makes them one guilt, where the couplet names only the eater and the seller.

note: Kural 225 ranks the strength of enduring hunger behind the strength of removing it; the verse names kinds of fasters and promises kingship to those who feed them.
teaches: The couplet ranks feeder over faster, while the verse honours both, making the faster the fit receiver and the feeder the one rewarded, so the ranking becomes a partnership.
list_adds: It names kinds of fasting (alternate days, crescent to full moon) and sets the prisoner among them, and attaches kingship as the reward, which the couplet does not.

note: 71 counts delivering a child, caring for the pregnant and taking up an infant as great virtue; 73 sets out the care of pregnancy, birth and infancy step by step.
teaches: Together the two verses make care of mother and newborn a sequence of virtues, from sheltering the pregnant to medicine for the child, which the Kural does not treat.

note: Purananuru 219 addresses a warrior wasting his body as he sits to die, with many sitting with him; the verse counts those who sit facing north among the needy to be fed.
teaches: The act the Puram honours as heroic resolve the Jain ethics verse counts as a state of need beside age and disease, so the dying hero becomes a receiver of care.

note: 69 argues against flesh from the shared sin of the chain of killing; 74 argues for not eating and not killing from the pains of bearing and rearing a life.
teaches: The book gives two grounds for one abstention: the guilt that runs from killer to eater, and the cost of bringing any life into being.

note: Naladiyar 123 says the old deed of breaking crabs' legs returns as a disease that rots the fingers; the verse says those who once cured disease now live free of it.
teaches: Read together, disease and health are both the return of old deeds, cruelty coming back as rotting fingers and healing as a body without illness, so the law runs both ways.

note: 70 promises kingship to those who feed fasting ascetics; 76 makes feeding the hungry a duty even to the low who are not ascetics.

note: Kural 227 says hunger does not touch one used to sharing his food; the verse says one who shares his food in a famine lives beyond eighty.

note: Kural 691 tells those who join warring kings to be like men warming at a fire, neither far nor near; the verse sets the warring king among things the wise do not befriend, beside the elephant and the tiger.
teaches: The couplet teaches the courtier how to stand near the dangerous king; the verse, for one not bound to serve, says not to go near, so one danger yields a rule of distance and a rule of avoidance.

note: Thirikadugam 19 counts one who grips the tusk of a killing elephant among three who hang by a thread; the verse shuns the place where a fierce elephant is let loose.
teaches: Both counted works use the killing elephant as the type of avoidable danger and set human follies beside it, so folly with people is measured against folly with beasts.

note: Kural 454 says understanding seems to be in the mind but lies in one's company; the verse says blame and fame come from company but understanding from the mind.
teaches: On the plain reading the two divide the same pair the opposite way: the Kural puts understanding in company, while Sirupanchamoolam keeps it in the mind and gives company only reputation.
list_adds: It splits the effect of company by kind, reputation (பழியும் புகழும்) against understanding (மதி), a division the couplet does not make.

note: Naladiyar 245 says people are not as their kind but as their minds; the verse keeps understanding in the mind while granting company power over blame and fame.
teaches: With the Naladiyar the verse forms a Jain answer to the Kural's chapter on company: mind, not kind, decides what a person is, though the verse concedes that company decides their name.
list_adds: It concedes to company what the quatrain does not, blame and fame, while agreeing that the mind decides understanding.

note: Naladiyar 180 says people spotless in mind are scorned for their company, as sandal burns with the scrub; the verse says blame and fame come from company.
teaches: The quatrain shows the cost the verse only states: a spotless mind does not save one from the blame of one's company.
list_adds: It states the rule in two halves, company for name and mind for understanding, where the quatrain gives only the half on reputation.

note: Kural 92 ranks a glad face and sweet speech above giving with a glad heart; the verse joins soft words and a melting gift in one man.
teaches: The Kural separates sweet speech from giving and ranks speech higher; the verse refuses the choice and makes the soft word the manner in which the gift is given.
list_adds: It places soft speech and the melting gift side by side as the last two of five marks, after inner restraints, so speech and gift become one closing act rather than rivals.

note: Kural 134 says forgotten Veda can be relearnt but a brahmin's birth is ruined if conduct fails; the verse asks what a man of five vows lacks without the scriptures.
teaches: Both rank conduct above scriptural recitation, but the Kural keeps the brahmin and his birth in view while the verse makes the point for any man who keeps five lay vows.
list_adds: It names what the conduct is (five vows against attachment, theft, adultery, slander and killing) where the couplet speaks only of conduct in general.
audit_text_issue: ஒத்தினால் (line 4) read as ஓத்து, scripture; the spelling leaves this open. | ஒத்தினால் is read as ஓத்து (scripture); the spelling leaves this open

note: Verse 18 promises no further birth to one who does not lie, steal, desire women or eat flesh; verse 82 lists nearly the same vows and sets them above scripture.
teaches: Read together, the same vows earn two fruits in this book: release from rebirth in one verse, and freedom from needing the scriptures in the other.
audit_text_issue: ஒத்தினால் in sirupanchamoolam:82 line 4 may stand for ஓத்தினால்.

note: Naladiyar 279 makes a cow milked by force the image of the base giver; the verse names milking by a stuffed calf-skin as a cruelty the good refuse.
teaches: The quatrain uses forced milking only as a figure for grudging gifts; the verse shows the literal act was itself judged wrong, so the image carried moral weight before it became a figure.
list_adds: It sets the milking trick in a list that ends with killing creatures, so a small deceit on an animal is ranked with taking life, which the quatrain's figure never claims.
audit_text_issue: line 1 missing on the site; construal of கறந்தபால் uncertain

note: Kural 694 says to suppress whispers and shared smiles before the great; the verse lists five things not wanted where elders sit.
teaches: The couplet's two signs are about what a ruler might read into them; the verse widens the rule to elders generally and adds faults of judgment such as favouring friends.
list_adds: It adds counsel, partiality to friends, enmity and song to the couplet's laughter, and cites the old treatises as its authority, turning a courtier's caution into a code of the assembly.

note: Verse 85 names five subjects that make a first-rank learned man; verse 86 names five arts that make a middle-rank one.
teaches: Together they grade learning in tiers: doctrine, logic and release make the first rank, while arithmetic, music and crafts make only the middle.
audit_text_issue: 86 கண்ணும் unclear

note: Verse 87 calls five men dogs for lacking shame, friendship and reverence or for serving another; verse 88 names shame, friendship, the soldier and reverence as what comes easily.
teaches: The second verse answers the first word for word, so the pair shows the same qualities as failures in one man and as natural ease in their proper holders.
audit_text_issue: 87 line 4 பருத்தி பகர்வழி and 88's ஏண், அளியன் are uncertain.

note: Kural 98 says sweet speech free of pettiness brings joy here and hereafter; the verse runs sweet speech through kinship and grace to release.
teaches: The Kural promises joy in two worlds; the verse names the mechanism, speech producing grace and grace producing release, and sets harsh speech's enmity beside it.
list_adds: Its items are links in a chain rather than peers, so the list becomes a ladder from manners to release, a sequence the couplet does not draw.
audit_text_issue: line 4 விடாய் likely for வீடாய் (cf. Nanmanikkadigai 104); the site lacks line 1

note: Kural 160 grants greatness to those who fast but ranks them after those who bear harsh words; the verse says refusing food befits a rich man.
teaches: The Kural ranks fasting as a whole; the verse makes its worth depend on who fasts, fitting most where food is plentiful and the refusal costs something.
list_adds: It pairs each virtue with the person in whom it costs most (penance with youth, fasting with wealth, beauty with chastity), a matching of virtue to station the couplet lacks.

note: Kural 46 asks what one gains by leaving a virtuous household for the outside way; the verse says household life is better than a mean dharma.
teaches: The Kural's question reaches toward renunciation itself; the verse limits the claim to a poor or false dharma, a narrower comparison from a Jain text that honours the ascetic.
list_adds: It adds the fruit of the household, that feeding the virtuous returns as the means to feed again, which the couplet's rhetorical question does not name.

note: Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world; the verse sets giving with good company and steady hearing and promises the high state.
teaches: The Kural cuts giving loose from reward by a hypothetical; the verse binds it back to a destination, showing the two works disagree on whether the fruit is part of the reason.
list_adds: It pairs giving and company each with its opposite and caps them with hearing as a penance, so giving becomes one step on a road to the high state.

note: The Siddhar verse asks what use ash and bathing are without learning to be born otherwise; the verse ranks worship on the Ganga's bank lowest, below restraint.
teaches: The Siddhar dismisses ritual bathing outright, while the ethics verse keeps Ganga worship as a merit but ranks it beneath restraint of presence and speech.
list_adds: Its ranking into foremost, high and lowest places the rite in an order of merits rather than rejecting it.
audit_text_issue: உரைப்பூசல் கோறல் may mean quarrels and killing.

note: Kural 114 says the worthy and unworthy are seen by what each leaves behind; the verse says the rightness of five kinds of person is known when they die.
teaches: Both defer judgment of worth past the life; the verse applies the rule to five stations and names death as the moment of proof.
list_adds: It runs the test through wife, soldier, ascetic, trader and arbiter, so one rule of posthumous judgment is made to cover every station of life.

note: Both use the god who measured the world with his foot: the invocation worships the stride; the Kural makes all it spanned the reward of a king without sloth.
teaches: The same Trivikrama stride serves the ethics group both as an object of worship and as a measure of worldly gain, so the mythic foot carries devotion in one book and royal ambition in the other.
list_adds: It sets the stride beside two other kicks of the same feet, so the measuring becomes one of three acts that together are the feet worshipped.

note: Kural 794 says a friend of good family who shrinks from blame is worth buying; Thirikadugam makes lasting company with the worthy of an old family a medicine.
teaches: Read together, the couplet gives the price of such company and the verse its use: one pays for it because it cures.
list_adds: It makes the old family's worthy one of three remedies with a chaste wife and a learned friend, so lineage-company is ranked with marriage as a cure.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 repaired (தெடார்ச்சியும் read தொடர்ச்சியும்). | line 2 repaired: தெடார்ச்சியும் read தொடர்ச்சியும்

note: Kural 417 says men of deep heard learning do not speak folly even when mistaken; Thirikadugam says friendship with such men clears the tangle of words.
teaches: The couplet says kelvi keeps its owner's own speech clear; the verse adds that it clears others' confusion, so the virtue passes to the friend.
list_adds: It turns a trait of the learned into a benefit for those who befriend them, and sets it among remedies.
audit_text_issue: line 2 repaired; site differs

note: Kural 134 says a brahmin can relearn the Veda but is ruined if his conduct declines; Thirikadugam asks every gentle person not to let his character decline, and lists following the Veda-knowers as a separate item.
teaches: The pair shows the same verb குன்று applied to conduct in both, but the Kural ranks conduct above Vedic learning inside one birth, while the Thirikadugam keeps them as two equal items for everyone.
list_adds: It moves the rule of undeclining conduct from the brahmin to all gentle people and places Vedic guidance beside it, not above it.

note: Kural 451 says the small take small company as kin; Thirikadugam names living as kin of the unlearned as a ruin that comes from ignorance.
teaches: The couplet explains who seeks low company (the small); the verse names why (ignorance) and what follows (ruin), giving the act a cause and a result.
list_adds: It sets low company beside wife-beating and entering a house with petty men, so all three are failures of a householder's judgment.
audit_text_issue: Thirikadugam 3 flagged uncertain.

note: Kural 882 says to fear the enemy who seems like kin; Thirikadugam counts taking by the hand a man formerly enraged against one as the conduct of one about to die.
teaches: The couplet warns against the hidden foe in general; the verse names the concrete act, taking back a former enemy, and states its outcome as death.
list_adds: It puts this misplaced trust beside living in sight of foes and walking unarmed among cattle, all three plain exposures to known danger.
audit_text_issue: முற்றன்னைக் (line 2) admits two divisions with different senses. | line 3 முற்றன்னை: word division uncertain | முற்றன்னை (line 2) has two possible divisions.

note: Kural 90 says the guest withers at the host's changed face; Thirikadugam counts arriving worn as a guest in a strange town as a road to suffering.
teaches: The Kural measures hospitality by the host's face; the verse looks from the guest's side and counts dependence on strangers as itself a hardship, which is why the host's face matters so much.
list_adds: It sets guesthood beside an unused ford and an unwilling woman, three ventures whose danger lies in the unknown other side.

note: Kural 1191 calls the love of those loved back the seedless fruit; Thirikadugam counts embracing women who do not desire one among roads to suffering.
teaches: The akam couplet praises mutual desire from inside love; the ethics verse states the reverse as a rule of conduct, so the need for mutual desire is affirmed in both kinds of poetry.
list_adds: It moves the claim from a lover's lament into counsel, and likens union without desire to entering water at an unused ford.

note: Kural 773 makes ஊராண்மை the cutting edge of valour, help to a foe in distress; Thirikadugam defines ஊராண்மை by modesty under honour, patience under scorn and unreturned dharma.
teaches: The pair shows one word moving from the battlefield, where it is mercy to the fallen enemy, into everyday conduct, where it is a pride made of self-effacement.
list_adds: It breaks the Kural's single heroic act into three civil ones and calls their sum a pride.
audit_text_issue: line 3 காராண்மை: cloud's giving or farmer's labour

note: Both say learning held by one who fears the assembly is useless: the Kural likens it to a sword in a coward's hand, Thirikadugam to a mute man's dream.
teaches: The two images name different failures: the sword is a power left unused, the mute's dream an experience that cannot be told, so together they say fear of the assembly blocks both action and communication.
list_adds: It sets the timid scholar beside an incapable heir to wealth and a trapped fish, three goods held that cannot be brought out.
audit_text_issue: உள்ளல் (trap or pool) is uncertain | உள்ளல் uncertain (trap or pool)

note: Kural 439 says never admire oneself; Thirikadugam names lineage, learning and victory as things that need not speak of themselves.
teaches: The couplet gives the rule; the verse gives a reason for it in the three strongest cases of worth, each of which has its own witness (an assembly, a king), so self-praise is not only wrong but redundant.
list_adds: It picks the three things most tempting to boast of and attaches to each the audience that proclaims it.
audit_text_issue: வட்டார்த்த (line 3) is obscure. | line 3 வட்டார்த்த obscure

note: Kural 450 ranks leaving the company of the good as ten times worse than many enemies; Thirikadugam counts leaving the company of the great as what fools love.
teaches: The couplet measures the harm of leaving good company; the verse says why people still do it: fools want it, so the harm is chosen.
list_adds: It sets leaving good company beside adulterous desire and base resolve, making all three expressions of a fool's preferences.

note: Kural 322 makes sharing food the chief of all precepts; Thirikadugam counts living beside those who do not share their food as something that yields no good.
teaches: The couplet praises the sharer; the verse shows the cost of the non-sharer falling on his neighbours, so sharing is a public good of a settlement, not only a private virtue.
list_adds: It sets the stingy neighbour beside a town without teachers and an assembly without elders, three lacks that make a place barren.
audit_text_issue: l.3 இம்முன்றும் is a misprint for இம்மூன்றும்

note: Kural 127 says whatever else one fails to guard, guard the tongue; Thirikadugam singles out the unguarded talk of a man who is not drunk.
teaches: Adding 'not drunk' removes the one excuse for loose speech, so the verse sharpens the couplet: unguarded speech when sober is chosen, not lapsed into.
list_adds: It makes careless speech one of three social intrusions (uninvited watching, untrusted visiting) that offend the whole town.
audit_text_issue: sense of விளியாதான், களியாதான், தெளியாதான் is uncertain | விளியாதான், களியாதான், தெளியாதான் are uncertain | thirikadugam:11 negative participles (விளியாதான், களியாதான், தெளியாதான்) are inferred readings.

note: Kural 81 says all household life exists for caring for guests and doing வேளாண்மை; Thirikadugam defines the வேளாளன் as one who does not eat while a guest waits.
teaches: Both books use the vel- word for help to guests; the verse makes it a definition of a person, showing that in this group the name is earned by hospitality, not given by birth or land.
list_adds: It sets the vellalan beside the debt-free man and the grateful man as three kinds of kin worth having.

note: Kural 110 says there is no escape for one who kills a benefit received; Thirikadugam defines the man of principle as one who does not forget.
teaches: The couplet condemns ingratitude as unforgivable; the verse turns gratitude into a mark by which one chooses kin, making it a reason to bind oneself to a person.
list_adds: It makes gratitude a qualification for kinship, alongside freedom from debt and hospitality.

note: Kural 544 says the world embraces the feet of the king who embraces his people; Thirikadugam names such a king as hard to find anywhere.
teaches: The couplet states the reward of the caring king as if it were the order of things; the verse adds that such kings are rare, so the world's embrace is seldom earned.
list_adds: It sets the good king beside a well-conducted youth and a flawless ascetic, three rarities each at odds with his station.

note: Kural 813 says friends who weigh their gains are no better than thieves; Thirikadugam counts the one who clings by fortune and watches for profit as not to be befriended.
teaches: The Kural shames the calculating friend by comparison; the verse adds when he shows himself, at the turn of fortune, which is also when the liar and the hollow man show themselves.
list_adds: It groups the calculating friend with the liar and the one who claims equality in one's fall, three who fail at reversal.
audit_text_issue: sense of பொறியறை, தட்டை and ஊழினால் ஒட்டி is uncertain | பொறியறை, தட்டை and ஊழினால் ஒட்டி are uncertain in sense

note: Purananuru 18 tells a Pandya that those who join water to land give bodies and life; Thirikadugam says one who digs a drinking well without stint gains an undying body.
teaches: The puram poem credits the builder of water works with the lives of his people; the ethics verse credits the well-digger with his own undying body, so the same act of providing water is rewarded outward in one and inward in the other.

note: Kural 233 says only lofty fame stands undying; Thirikadugam names fame as one of three ways to an undying body, with a chaste wife and a public well.
teaches: The couplet makes fame the only deathless thing; the verse widens the routes to it, counting a marriage and a work of public water as equally lasting.
list_adds: It turns the Kural's single route to deathlessness into three, two of them not fame-seeking acts at all.

note: Verse 1 makes a wife chaste as Arundhati a medicine; verse 16 makes the man who won a chaste wife deathless.
teaches: Within the book the chaste wife is given two predicates, cure and deathlessness, so she is valued both for what she does for the husband now and for the name she leaves him.

note: Kural 1134 has love's flood sweep away the raft of shame and manliness; Thirikadugam has three men let go of the raft of learning.
teaches: Both use the raft against a flood, but the Kural's raft is carried off by force while the Thirikadugam's is let go by choice, which makes the ethics verse a charge of fault, not a lament.
list_adds: It shows one raft dropped at three stages of life (old age, marriage, renunciation), not one lover's moment.

note: Naladiyar 92 sets death, old age and disease before the reader and tells him to share before eating; Thirikadugam names old age, separation and disease as things to fear more than thieves.
teaches: The quatrain moves from the threats to a remedy (give now), while the verse stops at the threat and calls it theft, so the pair shows a list that diagnoses beside a quatrain that prescribes.
list_adds: It adds the separation of the joined to old age and disease, putting an akam grief among the bodily dreads.

note: Kural 146 says enmity, sin, fear and blame never leave one who enters another's home; Thirikadugam puts the man at another's door by night between one who runs at a killing elephant and one who plays with a cobra.
teaches: The couplet lists the moral consequences; the verse's company of items makes the danger bodily and immediate, like courting an elephant or a snake.
list_adds: It frames adultery as reckless risk to life by placing it among two plain acts of physical folly.
audit_text_issue: line 4 தூங்குபவர் may be 'hang' or 'sleep heedless'

note: Verse 9 calls lust for women not one's own what fools love; verse 19 says the man at another's door by night hangs by a thread.
teaches: Within the book the same act is first a fool's desire and then a mortal danger, so the book judges it both by the wanting and by the result.
audit_text_issue: தூங்குபவர் may also mean the heedless sleeper | தூங்குபவர் may mean 'hang' or 'sleep'

note: Kural 603 says the family of the slothful fool perishes before him; Thirikadugam counts falling into sloth while one's dependants go hungry as painful to all.
teaches: The couplet gives the end of sloth, the family's death; the verse gives its moment, idling while those bound to one hunger, so the harm is seen as it begins.
list_adds: It sets this sloth beside dependence on others and being scorned as unlearned, three humiliations of a man who fails his station.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu calls giving with knowledge of one's income sweet; Thirikadugam fixes the share at a quarter of what comes in.
teaches: Read together, the two show that 'knowing one's income' had a number attached: the income is known so that a fixed fourth can go out.

note: Sirupanchamoolam calls brooding on harm done to one smallness; Thirikadugam calls not searching out what was done in a quarrel a distinction.
teaches: The pair gives one act two names from both sides, and it supports reading Thirikadugam's doubtful line as forgiving injuries done to one rather than forgetting one's own deeds.

note: Both verses name learning the good after surveying many things and set it beside giving from the household's income.
teaches: The book twice pairs selective learning with measured household giving, so the pairing is a doctrine of the work and not a chance of one list.

note: Kural 361 calls craving the seed of unceasing birth; Thirikadugam makes craving one of three whose seed, once destroyed, ends birth.
teaches: The seed image is shared, but Thirikadugam widens what the seed is made of from an inner craving to include an outward act, false speech.
list_adds: It sets craving beside attachment and false speech, so a lie becomes one of the seeds of rebirth, which the couplet does not say.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 பகையிருள் vs tamilvu புகை இருள்.

note: Kural 360's triad whose end ends pain is desire, anger and confusion; Thirikadugam's triad whose end ends birth is attachment, craving and false speech.
teaches: Comparing the two triads shows the Kural placing the root of suffering wholly in the mind, while Thirikadugam counts a fault of speech among the roots of rebirth.
list_adds: It replaces anger and confusion with false speech, so the counted causes of bondage include an act of the tongue and not only states of mind.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 பகையிருளும் has a witness reading புகையிருளும்.

note: Kural 341 says each thing one leaves removes the pain it would bring; Thirikadugam says a mind that has left many things is a rope to merit.
teaches: The couplet gives detachment a negative yield (pain removed); the verse gives it a positive one (merit bound), so letting go both frees and gains.
list_adds: It sets the detached mind beside the gift and honourable conduct, so the renouncer's letting go and the householder's giving are one kind of rope.

note: Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who want wealth, not love, bring harm; Thirikadugam names a courtesan's sweet speech a sinking mire.
teaches: Kural names the harm; the verse names the mechanism, a pleasing surface over a hook, and its effect, a slow sinking rather than a blow.
list_adds: It groups the courtesan's speech with bait on a hook and an enemy's bowing, so it becomes one of three lures whose sweetness hides the danger.

note: Both use the fishhook: Kural 931 likens gambling winnings to the hook a fish swallows; Thirikadugam names the frog wrapped round a hook as bait.
teaches: The ethics group uses the hook for any pleasure that is the means of capture: the Kural shows it from inside the fish after the gain, Thirikadugam at the bait before it.
list_adds: It turns the hook from an image of gambling gains into one of three snares beside flattery by a courtesan and by a foe.

note: Kural 828 says a weapon hides in an enemy's folded hands; Thirikadugam calls the bowing of hardened enemies a mire.
teaches: The couplet names what the homage hides, a weapon, and the verse what it does to the one who trusts it: he sinks.
list_adds: It puts an enemy's homage beside a courtesan's sweet words, so political and sexual flattery are reckoned one kind of trap.

note: Kural 915 says those of refined understanding do not plunge into the charms of common women; Thirikadugam says the learned do not eat from such a woman's hand.
teaches: The Kural's avoidance is of her body; the verse's is of her food, so the learned man's refusal reaches even to accepting maintenance from her.
list_adds: It groups her with the arrogant petty man and the robber of a charity, so the bar falls on all who live by a wrong means, not on sex alone.

note: Both close by naming three who are called the world: verse 26 a considerate guest, a non-killer and a gentle teacher; verse 34 the brahmin, the just king and orderly people.
teaches: The book defines 'the world' twice, once by three private virtues and once by three estates, so the word means both good persons and an ordered society.

note: Kural 325 makes the one who refrains from killing the chief of all renouncers; Thirikadugam counts him among those who are the world.
teaches: The Kural honours non-killing at the head of renunciation; the verse honours it in ordinary social life, so it is a summit in both ways of living.
list_adds: It sets the non-killer beside a considerate guest and a teacher of good conduct, taking non-killing out of the renouncers' ranking into everyday company.

note: Kural 113 says to let go at once of gain that leaves fairness, even if it brings good; Thirikadugam counts not speaking partially, whatever one gains, as the work of the pure.
teaches: The Kural sets fairness against gain; the verse calls the same refusal a purity, so impartial speech is a cleanliness and not only a justice.
list_adds: It makes impartiality one of three purities with bathing before meals and nobility unto death, joining a bodily rite to two inner virtues.

note: Kural 298 divides outer purity, made by water, from inner purity, seen in truth; Thirikadugam lists bathing before meals with impartial speech and unfailing nobility as the work of the pure.
teaches: The couplet separates the two purities; the verse joins them in one list and implies that a claim to purity needs both at once.
list_adds: It counts the water-purity and two inner purities as one work without ranking them, where the couplet ranks them by kind.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu calls sweet the austerity of one who wants to win and does not rage, and not craving what one lacks; Thirikadugam says the one without austerity who rages to win and the one who craves what he lacks pound husk.
teaches: The two works state the same pair from opposite sides in nearly the same words, so restraint in contest and in craving is both a sweetness and the only labour that bears grain.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu calls sweet not snatching what one sees and desires; Thirikadugam asks for no desire for a thing even once it is in one's hand.
teaches: The pair grades the restraint: not seizing what is seen is the lower step, not wanting what is already held is the higher.

note: Kural 532 says heedlessness kills fame as chronic want kills understanding; Thirikadugam says one who has put away heedlessness in settled wealth keeps lasting fame.
teaches: The couplet states the threat to fame in general; the verse says when it strikes, when wealth seems secure.
list_adds: It places the vigilant rich man beside the courteous giver and the man free of envy, so fame rests on three habits of the wealthy.

note: Kural 1057 tells of the seeker's joy at givers who do not scorn; Thirikadugam gives lasting fame to the man who does not scorn those who seek him.
teaches: The same courtesy pays both parties: the seeker gets inner joy and the giver lasting renown.
list_adds: It turns the seeker's joy into the giver's renown and ranks the courtesy with vigilance and freedom from envy.

note: Kural 322 crowns sharing food and sustaining life as the head of all the authors gathered; Thirikadugam crowns three things as the head of all that is heard: selective learning, unbroken sharing household life, and making wealth by effort.
teaches: Sharing food is the head in both, but Thirikadugam shares the crown with the learning that guides the giving and the earning that supplies it.
list_adds: It divides the couplet's single crown among three, adding learning and self-made wealth to the act of sharing.

note: Kural 424 defines understanding partly as seeing the subtle meaning in others' words; Thirikadugam makes taking the meaning from subtle words a debt the learned owe.
teaches: The couplet describes a capacity; the verse turns it into an obligation that comes with learning.
list_adds: It joins the duty of subtle hearing to two duties of speech, silence when idle words are asked for and speech only to the not-base.

note: Naladiyar 197 says a son props a failing father as aerial roots hold up a termite-eaten banyan; Thirikadugam says a good minister holds the people like the banyan's aerial roots.
teaches: The same image of support from below serves the family and the state: the minister is to the kingdom what a son is to an ageing father.
list_adds: It sets the root-like minister between the sceptre-fearing people and the firm guard as one of a king's three supports.

note: Kural 542 says the people live looking to the king's sceptre as the world looks to rain; Thirikadugam names people who live in awe of the sceptre as a support of the king.
teaches: The sceptre has two faces to the people, hope in the Kural and fear in Thirikadugam, and the verse counts that fear as an asset of rule.
list_adds: It makes the subjects' awe of the rod one of three things a king keeps, with a minister and a guard.
audit_text_issue: line 4 படைவேந்தன் மற்று விடல் obscure

note: Kural 560 says the six-duty brahmins forget their texts when the king fails to guard; Thirikadugam sets the brahmin who has paid his debts beside the just king and orderly people as the world.
teaches: The Kural makes the brahmin's ritual learning depend on good rule; the verse makes it a coordinate pillar beside the king.
list_adds: It lists priest, king and people as three parts of one order rather than as cause and effect.

note: Kural 541 defines justice as investigating (ஓர்ந்து), showing no favour and acting after consideration; Thirikadugam names the king who weighs matters (ஓர்ந்து) and does not bend justice.
teaches: Both put weighing first in justice, but the verse makes the just king only one third of what makes a world.
list_adds: It places the just king between the dutiful brahmin and the orderly people, so justice is one estate's part of a shared order.

note: Naladiyar 135 says learning has no shore and life is short; Thirikadugam praises one who has seen the shore of the texts.
teaches: Read together, mastering a body of texts (நூல்) is possible while learning (கல்வி) itself has no end, so the two claims are about different things.
list_adds: It ranks the one who reached the texts' shore with a steady mind and freedom from delusion as three who stand on truth.

note: Kural 256 says no one would sell flesh if the world did not kill to eat; Thirikadugam names the man who says the killing happens without his consent as self-deceived.
teaches: The verse names the buyer's excuse in his own words, and the couplet supplies the answer: the purchase is the cause.
list_adds: It puts the eater who disclaims the killing beside the flesh-eater who claims compassion and the sacrificer, so three justifications are one kind.
audit_text_issue: line 1 உடையேம்/உடையெம் vowel variant

note: Sirupanchamoolam 69 says the one who consented, the buyer, the cook and the eater share the killer's sin; Thirikadugam mocks one who says the deed is done without his consent.
teaches: Both answer the disclaimer by spreading guilt along the chain: Sirupanchamoolam lists the chain, Thirikadugam ridicules the man who denies his link in it.
audit_text_issue: Thirikadugam 36 line 1 அருளுடையேம் / அருளுடையெம் vowel variant.

note: Kural 259 ranks not killing to eat above a thousand sacrifices; Thirikadugam names one who kills in a desired sacrifice as one who knows only his own view.
teaches: The Kural weighs sacrifice against abstention; the verse drops the weighing and calls ritual killing a self-deception.
list_adds: It groups the sacrificer with two flesh-eaters, so ritual killing is reckoned with ordinary meat-eating rather than above it.

note: Kural 188 asks what those who spread the faults of their intimates will do to strangers; Thirikadugam says the measure of friendship shows in backbiting.
teaches: The couplet reasons from near to far; the verse makes backbiting the gauge by which one learns how far a friendship really reaches.
list_adds: It sets backbiting as a test of friendship beside tests of lineage and of authority, three signs by which hidden worth is known.
audit_text_issue: வாய்மை யடையார் could be negative, which would reverse the predicate.

note: Kural 431 says the prosperity of those without arrogance, anger and smallness is dignified; Thirikadugam names arrogance, anger and the smallness of coveting as an army that breaks wealth.
teaches: The same triad is the condition of wealth's dignity when absent and the force that destroys wealth when present.
list_adds: It turns the couplet's three absent faults into one hostile army and defines the third, smallness, as coveting many things.

note: Verse 38 makes swelling anger part of an army that breaks wealth; verse 40 makes the strength that wears anger thin the work of the wise.
teaches: The book measures anger by quantity, swelling or thinning, and ties the first to lost wealth and the second to old wisdom.

note: Kural 920 names double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those Fortune has left; Thirikadugam names the same three as the work of men without goodness.
teaches: Both name the same three vices, and the verse adds what they share: each is a stupor (மயக்கம்).
list_adds: It calls each item a மயக்கம், so paid sex and dice are made forms of intoxication alongside drink.

note: Kural 913 likens the false embrace of women bought with wealth to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room; Thirikadugam calls it seeking a base stupor (புலைமயக்கம்).
teaches: The couplet's corpse and the verse's புலை both make the bought embrace a contact with something vile, one by image, one by name.
list_adds: It sets the bought embrace in a series of three stupors with drink and dice.

note: Kural 310 says those who renounce anger equal those who renounce all; Thirikadugam names the strength that wears anger thin as the work of the anciently wise beside household duties.
teaches: The Kural lifts quelling anger to the level of renunciation; the verse keeps it as a householder's strength (விறல்).
list_adds: It places anger's control with conduct toward women and sharing food, so it is counted among household virtues rather than set equal to renunciation.
audit_text_issue: Line 2's மகளிர்கட்கு ஒத்த லொழுக்கம் is ambiguous.

note: Kural 955 says an old family does not part from its nature even when its means of giving shrink; Thirikadugam makes the worth that keeps family standing from falling, even when shaken, one of three things chief among all that is heard.
teaches: The couplet observes that old families hold firm; the verse turns that observation into a thing to be taught and ranked first, so constancy of lineage becomes the content of instruction, not only its result.
list_adds: It ranks family constancy with renown from giving to the distressed and with daily widening of friendship, so lineage is made one of three practices that head all teaching.

note: Kural 691 tells those who serve kings to be like men warming at a fire, neither near nor far; Thirikadugam tells the vellala family to behave toward brahmins as toward fire even when familiar.
teaches: The ethics group uses one fire image for two powers: the Kural for the king, the Thirikadugam for the brahmin, so the cultivator's caution toward a birth-group is modelled on the courtier's caution toward the throne.
list_adds: It sets the fire-caution among a farming family's marks of beauty, between refusing gambling wealth and loving the plough, so a rule of birth-rank becomes part of a household's grace.

note: Kural 1033 says only those who live by ploughing truly live; Thirikadugam makes love of farming the beauty of one family, the vellala.
teaches: The couplet gives ploughing to anyone who will live independently; the verse ties its honour to one birth-group, so the same praise of farming reads in one book as a way of life open to all and in the other as a family's mark.
list_adds: It joins love of farming to two other rules for the same family, so the plough becomes one of three marks of a caste-occupation rather than a universal claim.

note: Verse 12 defines the vellalan as one who does not eat while a guest waits; verse 42 names three other marks of the vellala family's beauty.
teaches: Read together, the book defines the vellala by four conducts, hospitality, refusing gambling gain, caution toward brahmins and love of the plough, so the title is built from conduct and occupation together.

note: Kural 127 says guard the tongue whatever else goes unguarded; Thirikadugam makes restraint of the mouth only the first of three restraints, yielding purity, below restraint of deed and of heart.
teaches: The Kural puts the tongue first as the one thing to guard; the verse ranks it lowest of three, so what the Kural sets as the minimum the verse treats as the first rung toward release.
list_adds: It turns restraint into an ascending ladder, mouth, deed, heart, with a rising fruit at each rung, a ranking the couplet does not make.

note: Kural 121 says restraint leads among the immortals; Thirikadugam gives the heavenly state only to restraint of deed and reserves release for restraint of heart.
teaches: The couplet's single reward of restraint, a place among the gods, becomes in the verse the middle of three rewards, so heaven is placed below release.
list_adds: It splits the Kural's one restraint into three with three fruits, purity, the divine state and release, ranking them.

note: Kural 82 says eating alone while a guest waits outside is not to be wished even if the food is ambrosia; Thirikadugam calls a day on which one ate without a guest a sickness to the strong.
teaches: The couplet rejects the guestless meal before eating; the verse counts its cost afterwards as an illness, so the same refusal is given both a motive and a symptom.
list_adds: It sets the guestless day beside the unembraced night and the morning without giving, so hospitality becomes one of three duties that together fill the householder's whole day.

note: Verse 12 says the vellalan does not eat while a guest waits; verse 44 says a day eaten without a guest is a sickness.
teaches: The book treats the guestless meal twice, once as a loss of the title vellalan and once as a sickness of the strong, so the same fault is a loss of rank and of health.

note: Kural 1067 begs beggars not to beg of those who conceal; Thirikadugam sends the one who without love hides from askers what he could give into hell.
teaches: The couplet speaks to the beggar and protects him from the concealer; the verse speaks of the concealer and names his punishment, so the two together cover both sides of the refused request.
list_adds: It sets concealment from askers between tormenting the unable and forgetting death, so withholding is ranked with cruelty and heedlessness as a road to hell.

note: Naladiyar 20 urges keeping Death's stealth in mind and taking provisions in time; Thirikadugam names not reflecting on Death's certain coming as one of three things that lead to hell.
teaches: The quatrain makes remembering death prudent; the verse makes forgetting it a sin with a penalty, so heedlessness is turned from folly into guilt.
list_adds: It places forgetting death beside two acts against others, so an inward lapse is judged on the same scale as cruelty and concealment.

note: Verse 14 names youth, folly and meanness as three the wise do not approach; verse 46, with the same closing line, names an unsound horse, a fierce elephant and the place of an angry man.
teaches: Read together, the book's 'the wise do not go near' covers both inner dispositions and outer dangers, and the angry man of verse 46 stands at the join, a human fault treated like a dangerous beast.
audit_text_issue: கால்தூய்மை / மேல்தூய்மை (lines 1-2) are obscure.

note: Kural 57 says the guarding of women by confinement achieves nothing and their own steadfastness is the best guard; Thirikadugam counts women among three things whose guarding must not be slighted. The tension holds on reading காப்பு in 47 as the householder's watch over women.
teaches: The two books disagree on who keeps a woman's virtue: the Kural moves the guard inside her and calls custody useless, the Thirikadugam keeps it with the man as with his wealth and food.
list_adds: It ranks women with earned treasure and good food as goods to be watched, which is the custodial view the couplet sets aside.

note: Kural 159 says those who bear the harsh words of transgressors are as pure as renouncers; Thirikadugam says the one who takes abuse as sweet speech lives having seen the true thing.
teaches: The couplet praises bearing abuse as endurance; the verse goes further and has abuse heard as sweetness, so the pair shows two grades, enduring the bitter and no longer tasting it as bitter.
list_adds: It sets taking abuse as sweet beside taking gruel as ghee-rice and bitterness as sugar, so patience in speech becomes one case of a general reversal of taste.

note: Kural 1065 says even thin gruel is sweetest when earned by one's own effort; Thirikadugam says the one who values gruel as ghee-rice has seen the truth.
teaches: The Kural makes gruel sweet because it is one's own; the verse makes it sweet because the seer no longer ranks foods, so one ground is self-respect and the other indifference.
list_adds: It puts the gruel among three reversals of speech and taste, so its sweetness comes from a way of seeing, not from how it was earned.

note: Kural 52 says if the wife lacks household excellence the life is nothing whatever else it has; Thirikadugam names a wife who wears the house down by falsehood as one of three who are no security for this life.
teaches: The couplet lays the failure of the household on the wife alone; the verse sets beside her the disobedient junior and the abusive head, so the pair shows the house can be ruined from three places.
list_adds: It distributes the household's ruin across junior kin, the head and the wife, rather than resting it on the wife as the couplet does.
audit_text_issue: பொய்தெள்ளி (line 2) is unclear.

note: Kural 559 says the sky withholds rain when the king bends justice; Thirikadugam names the plundering king as one of three malign planets that stop the rain.
teaches: The couplet ties rain to the king alone; the verse adds deceitful men and a transgressing wife, so the power to cause drought, a royal burden in the Kural, is spread over common people and the household.
list_adds: It sets the king beside commoners and a wife as equal causes of drought, widening the couplet's royal sanction to the whole society.

note: Kural 55 says the wife who worships her husband makes it rain at her word; Thirikadugam says the wife who crosses the bounds of the house cuts the rain off.
teaches: Together the two books give the period's belief in both directions, a chaste wife commands rain and a transgressing one stops it, so the wife's conduct is treated as a lever on the weather.
