list_adds: It sets the wife's transgression beside the king's plunder and men's deceit, so her fault is ranked with misrule as a cause of drought.

note: Kural 822 says the friendship of those who seem kin but are not shifts like a changing mind; Thirikadugam says deceivers stay deceivers even when they keep close.
teaches: The couplet stresses that false friendship changes; the verse that the false friend's nature does not, so the pair separates the shifting surface of conduct from the fixed nature beneath it.
list_adds: It sets the deceiver against the true ally who stays an ally even when estranged, so the list gives a test of constancy in both directions.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 தூர்ந்துஒழுகி and line 3 ஈர்ந்தகல் are obscure.

note: Kural 575 says kindly regard is the ornament of the eye and without it the eye is a sore; Thirikadugam opens with the same ornament and says it is found only with modesty and learning in those of worth.
teaches: The couplet judges the eye by kindly regard; the verse says that regard is not found alone but in the same people as modesty and learning, so it becomes a sign of a whole character.
list_adds: It assigns three ornaments to three wearers, the eye, a woman and the next life, and says all three gather in one kind of person.

note: Kural 1014 calls modesty the ornament of the worthy; Thirikadugam calls it the ornament of a woman in love.
teaches: The Kural gives naanam to the saandror without regard to sex; the verse gives it to the woman, so the same virtue is, in the two books, a mark of nobility and a gendered duty.
list_adds: It sets the woman's modesty between the eye's kindness and learning for the next life, giving each ornament its own wearer.

note: Kural 402 likens the unlearned man's wish to speak to a breastless woman's desire; Thirikadugam sets the unlearned man's eager talk beside a blind man's wife's beauty and lute-music heard by one who cannot tell its modes.
teaches: The couplet's image locates the lack in the speaker; the verse's neighbours locate it in a missing receiver, so the pair shows unlearned speech failing both for want of substance and for want of anyone able to take it.
list_adds: It groups unlearned speech with beauty unseen and music unheard, making it one kind of waste with them rather than a lone figure of incapacity.

note: Kural 584 says a spy examines everyone, the king's servants and kin first; Thirikadugam names a secret-leaking friend, a woman without regard for honour and a rancorous servant as those called spies.
teaches: The couplet turns the king's surveillance inward on his own circle; the verse shows why from the other side, since those closest, friend, woman and servant, are the ones who leak.
list_adds: It names the household's own informers by kind, giving concrete cases of the inward danger the couplet only implies.

note: Kural 131 says conduct gives excellence and must be guarded above life; Thirikadugam makes joining the road of inherited conduct the third of three things that keep the path of excellence open, after letters and the service of parents.
teaches: Both books tie ஒழுக்கம் to விழுப்பம், but the Kural makes conduct its single source, while the verse makes it the last step of a sequence that begins with learning letters and serving parents.
list_adds: It orders conduct in time, after literacy and filial service, so excellence is reached by a sequence rather than by one virtue.

note: Kural 392 calls numbers and letters the two eyes of living beings; Thirikadugam makes learning the letters first the opening step on the path of excellence.
teaches: The couplet values letters as sight; the verse gives them a place in time, first, before the parents and inherited conduct, so literacy becomes the start of a moral sequence.
list_adds: It makes letters the first of three ordered steps (முந்தை ... பிற்பாடு), a sequence the couplet does not have.

note: Innaa Narpathu 31 says singing to an untuned lute is very painful; Thirikadugam says song not measured to the beat is painful to hear.
teaches: One verse faults the pitch and the other the beat, so together they show the period held music to two measures, tuning and time, either of which failing makes song painful.
audit_text_issue: thirikadugam:57 lines 2-3 (தட்டித்து, துச்சிருந்தான் ஆளும் கலம்) are uncertain but do not bear on item 1. | The sense of Thirikadugam 57 lines 2-3 is uncertain. | Thirikadugam 57 is flagged uncertain.

note: Kural 525 says one who gives and speaks sweetly is surrounded by kin layer on layer; Thirikadugam makes giving by old ties, embracing kin and gathering one's people with close words the work of the king's younger.
teaches: The couplet gives anyone the means to gather kin; the verse assigns that work in a royal house to the junior prince, so kin-keeping becomes a delegated office of state.
list_adds: It moves the kin-gathering acts into the royal household and gives them to one office, the king's younger.

note: Kural 523 likens the life of one who does not mingle with kin to a tank filling with water but with no bank; Thirikadugam says the wealth of one who does not help his kin perishes while seeming to exist.
teaches: The Kural's tank shows the water running off; the verse adds that the loss is hidden, the wealth still seems to be there, so the tank looks full while it drains.
list_adds: It groups kinless wealth with untended farming and a drinker's family name as three goods lost while still in sight.

note: Kural 1039 says land the owner does not visit sulks like a wife; Thirikadugam says the farming of one who does not tend the green crop at ripening perishes.
teaches: The couplet asks for the owner's steady presence; the verse names the moment when absence is fatal, the time of ripening, so neglect is located in time.
list_adds: It sets the untended harvest beside kinless wealth and a drinker's lineage, making all three cases of loss that looks like having.

note: Kural 1041 says nothing is more painful than poverty except poverty; Thirikadugam names want as the sorrow proper to human birth, beside the ghost's hunger and the beast's fear.
teaches: The Kural makes poverty incomparable among human pains; the verse explains its place: each kind of birth has its own sorrow and want is the human one.
list_adds: It sets human want beside the hunger of ghosts and the fear of beasts, so poverty becomes the human share of a sorrow common to all births.

note: Naladiyar 174 grants that birth is bitter but says no one would resent it given lasting friendship with the good; Thirikadugam lists the sorrow of each kind of birth with no remedy.
teaches: The verse itemises the bitterness of birth by kind of being; the quatrain names the one thing that makes it bearable, so the pair holds the diagnosis and the consolation apart.
list_adds: It divides the bitterness of birth into hunger, fear and want, by kind of birth, where the quatrain speaks of birth whole.

note: The Kural gives guarding against what is coming as a mark of understanding; the verse makes it one of a great minister's three daily practices.
teaches: Foresight that the Kural praises as a private wisdom becomes, in a minister, an office: one prevents the blow by knowing the enemy king's state every day.
list_adds: It binds foresight to self-discipline and daily watch on hostile kings, so prevention is shown as the minister's working method rather than a trait.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu 30 names as sweet the three virtues whose breach Thirikadugam 62 counts: weighing a kindness, no crooked word in the assembly, not seizing a deposit.
teaches: The two books count the same three acts of trust from both sides, sweetness for keeping them and loss of heirs for breaking them, so the triad was a fixed set in the period's teaching.

note: The Kural says the upright man's wealth is a strength to his descendants; Thirikadugam says the man who speaks crookedly in the assembly loses his descendants.
teaches: Read together, fairness and its breach are both paid in the next generation: the Kural's promise to the heirs of the just has its dark twin in the heirless partial judge.
list_adds: It sets partial speech beside ingratitude and a seized deposit, so unfairness is classed as a breach of trust with a shared penalty.

note: Verse 64 makes tending guests the duty by which a chaste wife is a friend; verse 63 counts a bangled wife who dreads guests among things that yield no good.
teaches: The two adjacent verses give the same rule from both sides: hospitality is the wife's first duty, and failing it alone makes her a loss to the house.

note: The Kural calls good children the ornament of a house's excellence; the verse makes bearing children of an old family the act by which the wife is mistress of the house.
teaches: Children move from ornament to office: what the Kural treats as the crown of a good home, Thirikadugam treats as a debt the wife owes in order to hold her title.
list_adds: It turns three household goods into three roles of one woman, friend, mother and mistress, and frames them all as debts of chastity.

note: The Kural names desire, anger and confusion as the triad whose very names must perish; the verse counts fear, craving and anger as self-consuming.
teaches: Fear takes the place of confusion: Thirikadugam treats terror as a passion of the same kind as craving and anger, burning the one who holds it, which the Kural's triad leaves out.
list_adds: It replaces confusion with fear and gives the triad an image of self-frying in one's own ghee, so the harm is shown as self-inflicted.

note: The Kural says the king who bends the sceptre loses wealth and people together; the verse counts the bent-sceptred king among things not joined with fitness.
teaches: Besides the ruin the Kural predicts, the unjust king is also absurd, like a ring on a man with no servant: injustice is shown as a failure of seemliness as well as of rule.
list_adds: It sets the unjust king beside a husbandless woman's ornament and a servantless man's ring, so royal injustice is judged as an empty sign of rank.
audit_text_issue: கறை in line 1 is uncertain (adornment or stain).

note: Naladiyar 363 calls three kinds of wife weapons that kill the husband; Thirikadugam 67 counts the wife who stands against her husband with bad servants and faulty kin as old karma that devours him.
teaches: The Naladiyar blames the wife as an agent, while Thirikadugam spreads the harm across the whole household and calls it past karma with no remedy, shifting from blame to endurance.
list_adds: It widens the Naladiyar's three bad wives to wife, servants and kin, and explains them as karma ripening in old age.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 61 counts kin, wife, servant, son and neighbour as five household diseases; Thirikadugam 67 counts wife, servants and kin as devouring old karma.
teaches: Two counted works single out the same household cast as a chronic affliction; Sirupanchamoolam calls it disease and adds son and neighbour, Thirikadugam calls it karma and adds old age.
audit_text_issue: Sirupanchamoolam 61 line 1 (அடங்காய், பெண்வியக்க) is hard, so the identity of its first three figures is uncertain.

note: The Kural calls not hurting others the settled stand of the stainless; the verse names doing no hurt to any creature as purity itself.
teaches: The Kural's stainless people are defined by harmlessness, and Thirikadugam draws the conclusion that harmlessness simply is purity, setting it against ritual senses of the word.
list_adds: It sets purity as harmlessness beside giving to the poor and a life shaped by impermanence, as the three marks of those who know the good.

note: The Kural says wealth does not stay, so do at once what stays; the verse lists giving to the needy and the path of one who considers impermanence side by side.
teaches: The Kural derives giving from impermanence as a single argument; Thirikadugam presents them as two coordinate marks of the wise, so awareness of transience is a conduct in its own right.
list_adds: It lists giving and awareness of impermanence as separate items with harmlessness, rather than deriving one from the other.

note: The Kural measures the fruit of hospitality by the guest's worth; the verse prizes the guest who comes in distress after losing his way.
teaches: Against the Kural's ranking of guests by merit, Thirikadugam values the guest by his need: the lost and suffering stranger is the rare prize.
list_adds: It counts the lost guest among hard-to-get goods with a working ox and a maiden, so the guest is valued as a gain to the house, not a cost.

note: Verse 69 counts the lost, suffering guest as hard to come by; verse 76 counts the guest who arrives on a rainy day as hard to tend.
teaches: The same book holds both sides of hospitality: the needy guest is a rare prize and also the hardest burden, so the value and the strain of the guest come together.
audit_text_issue: Thirikadugam 76 line 1 reads வருந்தும்; the count and tamilvu want விருந்தும், and the link rests on that emendation.

note: The Kural likens the wise man's wealth to a village tank filling; the verse calls the man who dug a charitable tank and grove one of the truly rich.
teaches: The Kural's simile is made literal: the public tank is not only like a good man's wealth, its digging is counted as his wealth.
list_adds: It redefines the rich as three givers, of a tank, of Vedic learning and of shared food, so wealth is measured by what one has made common.

note: The Kural likens the brief want of the renowned rich to rain-clouds running dry; the verse counts the poverty of men with the manliness to give as a sight the eye cannot bear.
teaches: Both treat a giver's poverty as a public loss rather than a private one; Thirikadugam adds the witness's pain, so the giver's want hurts those who watch.
list_adds: It sets the giver's poverty beside two shameful sights, so the generous man's want is ranked as a kind of indignity.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 division of பெண்டிர் is uncertain.

note: The Kural tells one to let go that day of gain that comes from leaving fairness; the verse says ill-gotten wealth itself fears the man who keeps dharma in mind.
teaches: The Kural asks for an act of renunciation, while Thirikadugam makes it a property of the person: for the dharma-minded, wrong gain never comes near enough to refuse.
list_adds: It sets dharma beside steadiness and valour as three strengths that make things fear their holder, a ranking of inner strengths the couplet lacks.

note: The Kural calls nothing harder than the hardness that would end poverty by begging; the verse counts the man who would build wealth by begging among three who dare the hard.
teaches: Thirikadugam pushes the Kural's case further: begging not to escape poverty but to grow rich, and it ranks this with crossing the sea as a reckless venture.
list_adds: It sets begging-for-wealth beside trusting a roving woman and a sea voyage, so the folly is judged as a physical gamble.

note: The Kural says the asker's heart rejoices at givers who give without scorn; the verse counts the man who laughs at one asking for a gift among those who hold to nothing.
teaches: The Kural shows the asker's side and Thirikadugam the scorner's: mocking an asker is not just meanness but a sign of a man without any principle.
list_adds: It sets mocking a beggar beside killing to eat and presuming on the great, so contempt for the asker is ranked with flesh-eating as a lack of rule.

note: The Kural says killing is the absence of grace and eating the flesh is not right; the verse counts the man who lives by killing and eating among three who keep no rule.
teaches: The Kural argues from grace, Thirikadugam from discipline: flesh-eating is condemned on both grounds, in one as cruelty and in the other as want of a firm rule.
list_adds: It sets killing to eat among faults of social conduct, so non-killing is read as part of self-rule rather than of compassion alone.
audit_text_issue: kural:254 as printed begins ருளல்லது, dropping the initial அ of அருளல்லது.

note: Naladiyar 386 uses the learning of a man with understanding and bright wealth in a generous man's hands as similes for a modest woman's beauty; Thirikadugam 75 counts the same two as solid heartwood.
teaches: The same paired figures served two works with different ends: the Naladiyar borrows them to praise a woman's beauty, Thirikadugam keeps them as goods in their own right with a heartwood image.
list_adds: It treats the two figures as things in themselves, joined by a leader who knows fit unions, under one tree image.

note: The Kural likens wealth in a just man's hands to a fruit tree ripening in town; the verse likens wealth in a generous man's hands to a tree hardened without hollow.
teaches: Both use a tree for the good man's wealth, but the Kural praises its fruit given to all and Thirikadugam the soundness of its wood, so the same image teaches use and durability.
list_adds: It sets wealth beside learning and a fit leader as three sound trees, ranking generosity with understanding.

note: The Kural says men of unsteady heart touch women who join with them while their hearts are elsewhere; the verse counts the courtesan whose heart is elsewhere yet never fails in business as hard to keep.
teaches: Both note the courtesan's divided heart; Thirikadugam adds that her business never fails, so the danger is a reliable trade without love.
list_adds: It sets the courtesan beside a rain-day guest and a defiant servant, so she is counted among household burdens rather than vices.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 வருந்தும் should be விருந்தும் (tamilvu).

note: The Kural says those who resolve to live by a spotless lineage do nothing unworthy through deceit; the verse says three positive habits are found only in those of spotless family.
teaches: The Kural shows lineage as a restraint on wrongdoing; Thirikadugam shows it as a source of positive conduct, so a pure line both forbids and produces.
list_adds: It names three habits of a good family, avoiding the base, constancy in friendship and guarding against blame, where the couplet gives one restraint.

note: The Kural says inner purity is seen through truth; the verse counts purity, truth and evil unspoken in mind and word as the ascetic's practice.
teaches: The Kural ties purity to truth; Thirikadugam gives each its own fruit, boldness and beauty, and adds silence of the mind as a third discipline.
list_adds: It separates purity and truth into two items with different rewards and places them in the ascetic's domain.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 துணிவாம் தொழிலகற்றும் can be parsed differently.

note: Verse 78 names the practices of those strong in penance; verse 80 counts penance taken up by one without restraint of heart as wasted seed.
teaches: The two verses together give the condition and its failure: penance bears fruit with purity and restraint of mind, and is seed lost in a thicket without them.

note: The Kural says penance comes to those who have it and is futile for others; the verse counts penance taken up by one without restraint as seed cast in a thicket.
teaches: Thirikadugam names what the Kural leaves circular: the missing quality is restraint of the heart, so the futility is located in the will.
list_adds: It ranks futile penance with unjust headship and unruly beauty, so the failure is shown as a general rule of gifts without their inner condition.

note: The Kural says beauty without subtle understanding is a clay doll; the verse says beauty in one who does not perfect his conduct is wasted seed.
teaches: The two place the condition of beauty in different places, learning for the Kural and conduct for Thirikadugam, so beauty needs both mind and conduct to count.
list_adds: It moves the test of beauty from understanding to conduct and sets it with rank and penance.

note: The Kural says the man who fears his wife fears to do good to the good; the verse calls the man who lives in fear of his wife an ox whose eating grieves the heart.
teaches: The Kural names the harm, Thirikadugam the scorn: a wife-fearing husband is useless to others and also a beast, set beside the shameless and the lapsed ascetic.
list_adds: It ranks the wife-fearing husband with the blame-fearless man and the lapsed ascetic, as three who should not even be fed.

note: Kural 920 names double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those Fortune has left; Thirikadugam names the courtesan, the gambler and the money-dealer themselves as sinking in craving.
teaches: The couplet ruins the customer of these trades; the verse drowns the traders too, so vice is shown to consume both sides of the bargain.
list_adds: It replaces liquor with the money-dealer, so all three are people who live by others' wants and are judged by their own greed rather than by the harm they do.

note: Naladiyar 371 says a harlot's love ends when the hand is empty, like a lamp without oil; Thirikadugam says the courtesan herself sinks in the sea of craving.
teaches: The quatrain explains why her love fails (it follows money); the verse names the cost to her, so the same greed that makes her love brief also drowns her.
list_adds: It sets the courtesan beside the gambler and the usurer, making her one of three money-trades rather than a figure of false love.

note: Kural 720 says holding forth before those not of one's group is nectar spilled in a drain; Thirikadugam counts not saying what the unreceptive will not accept, even when provoked, as part of a good person's path.
teaches: The couplet gives the reason for silence before the wrong audience as waste; the verse makes that silence a mark of standing, kept even under provocation.
list_adds: It sets restraint before the unreceptive beside being acknowledged by the worthy and the intimate, so the silence counts as one of three signs of a good person's standing.

note: Kural 112 says the wealth of the upright does not decay and supports those after them; Thirikadugam says the upright are like rain.
teaches: The couplet keeps the yield of rectitude within the upright man's line; the rain image sends it outward to all, so rectitude is shown both lasting and shared.
list_adds: It sets the upright against two images of dissolution (salt in water, friendship under a lie), so rectitude stands as the one thing in the list that gives instead of melting.
audit_text_issue: the closing predicate of thirikadugam:83 is uncertain

note: Verse 15 says the man who lives by lies is not to be befriended; verse 83 says a lie dissolves friendship's thriving shoot as water dissolves salt.
teaches: One verse keeps the liar out of friendship at the start and the other shows a lie undoing friendship already grown, so the book makes falsehood fatal to friendship at both ends.

note: Kural 408 says wealth in the hands of the unlearned is more painful than poverty among the good; Thirikadugam counts the unlearned among those already joined to poverty.
teaches: Read together, the unlearned rich man is poor twice: the couplet makes his coin a grief and the verse makes him poor in what he never took in, so poverty is a lack of intake as well as of money.
list_adds: It sets the unlearned with a tank whose inlet fails and an infant not fed full, so lack of learning becomes a vessel that cannot fill, a kind of poverty the couplet does not name.

note: Kural 585 asks a spy to have an appearance that raises no suspicion and to let nothing spill; Thirikadugam asks him to be of a despised kind, to forget nothing he hears and to report the hidden matter fully.
teaches: The verse makes the couplet's unsuspected look specific: contempt is the cover, because people do not guard their words before the despised, and it adds the report that the couplet's silence serves.
list_adds: It pairs the disguise with memory and accurate report, so the spy's work is a sequence (hear unseen, keep, deliver) where the couplet gives only concealment.

note: Verse 9 lists what utter fools love, beginning with moving away from the company of the great; verse 87 lists who are utter fools, including the man who enters a company remote from learning.
teaches: The two verses share the predicate முழுமக்கள் and both define the utter fool by the company he leaves or joins, so the book makes the choice of company the first test of folly.

note: Kural 1001 says one who stores great wealth and does not eat it is dead; Thirikadugam says one who buries wealth without enjoying it is born yet unborn.
teaches: The couplet counts the hoarder dead at the end; the verse counts him never born, so between them the hoarder's life is cancelled at both ends.
list_adds: It sets the hoarder beside the graceless heart and the overreaching harsh tongue, so hoarding becomes one of three refusals (of grace, of use, of measure in speech) that unmake a birth.

note: Naladiyar 273 says the fool who neither enjoys nor gives his wealth is mocked by that wealth and by the world's compassion; Thirikadugam counts the graceless heart and the buried wealth as two separate items.
teaches: The quatrain fuses the failure of compassion and the failure to use wealth into one mockery; the verse separates them, showing the Naladiyar's single fault as two distinct ways of being unborn.
list_adds: It counts the graceless heart and the buried treasure as two items with harsh speech as a third, where the quatrain treats compassion only as the hoarder's judge.

note: Kural 243 says those whose hearts are joined with grace do not enter the painful world of darkness; Thirikadugam names gracious speech, earning for giving and study for dharma as three ways not to reach the dark world.
teaches: The couplet locates the escape from the dark world in the heart; the verse carries grace into speech and adds two practical means, so the escape becomes a matter of how one talks, earns and studies.
list_adds: It turns grace from a state of heart into a manner of speaking and sets it beside wealth and learning used for their ends, so three daily practices replace one inner condition.

note: Verse 89 names the graceless heart, buried wealth and harsh speech as unmaking a birth; verse 90 names earning for giving, studying for dharma and gracious speech as the way past the dark world.
teaches: Verse 90 answers 89 item for item on wealth and speech, so the book shows the same two goods (wealth, words) as either cancelling a life or saving it, depending on use.

note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction differs by what one does; Thirikadugam counts the man not born in an excellent line as born yet unborn, on the reading that விழுத்திணை is a high birth-group, not conduct.
teaches: The ethics group splits on whether lineage can void a life: the couplet places worth in work, the verse places a birth condition beside illiteracy and boasting as equal disqualifiers.
list_adds: It puts low birth in one row with two faults one can mend, so birth is treated as a fault of the same kind as conduct, which the couplet denies.

note: Verses 89 and 92 share the predicate 'born yet unborn'; 89 lists failures of grace, use of wealth and speech, 92 failures of birth, letters and speech.
teaches: Both lists include a fault of speech, but 92 adds birth and literacy where 89 has grace and wealth, so the book's 'unborn' joins conditions one chooses with a condition one cannot.

note: Kural 410 says others stand to those learned in the shining books as beasts stand to people; Thirikadugam says one who knows not a single letter is born yet unborn.
teaches: The couplet lowers the unlearned to beasts; the verse goes further and denies them birth, and sets the bar at one letter rather than at the great books.
list_adds: It sets the illiterate beside the low-born and the boaster, pairing a lack of letters with a lack of lineage as one kind of void life.

note: Kural 360 says pain perishes when the very names of desire, anger and confusion perish; Thirikadugam names a world passing in darkness, anger that speaks without knowledge and desire for worthless things as what belongs to a creature in folly.
teaches: The verse gives each of the Kural's three its mark (confusion as a darkened world, anger as speech without knowledge, desire as love of the worthless), so the couplet's bare names gain definitions.
list_adds: It describes each member of the triad by its effect and assigns all three to the fool, where the couplet only names them as what must be destroyed.
audit_text_issue: Kural 360 is printed இநவ்முன்றன் for இவ்மூன்றன்.

note: Kural 57 asks what use guarding women by confinement is and makes their own steadfastness the chief guard; Thirikadugam counts the man who neglects guarding his woman among those without right conduct.
teaches: The couplet moves a woman's guard inside her; the verse keeps an outer guarding as the husband's duty and faults him for neglecting it, so the group holds both views of where the guard lies.
list_adds: It ranks neglect of guarding a woman with courting the unfriendly and faulty speech, so it becomes a lapse of the man's own conduct, not a question of the woman's virtue.

note: Kural 225 says the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, though it ranks below relieving others' hunger; Thirikadugam counts hunger that eats away wisdom as one of three forces that drive out good deeds.
teaches: The verse shows why enduring hunger is a strength in the couplet: hunger is an army against merit, so bearing it is holding a line, and relieving it removes the enemy itself.
list_adds: It sets hunger in one army with desire and anger, so a bodily need is ranked as a moral enemy beside two passions.
audit_text_issue: line 2 செறிவழங்க is likely செறிவு அழுங்க

note: Verse 93 gives anger and desire to the creature in folly; verse 95 sets anger and desire beside hunger as an army that drives out good deeds.
teaches: Read together, the book treats anger and desire both as the condition of folly and as the force that removes merit, and swaps the third member, delusion, for hunger.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 செறிவழங்க is read as செறிவு அழுங்க per tamilvu.

note: Kural 55 says that if the wife who rises worshipping her husband says 'rain', it rains; Thirikadugam gives the same rain-command to the wife who knows her husband's mind, the ascetic true to his undertaking and the king who shuns cruelty.
teaches: The Kural gives the power over rain to the wife alone; the verse shares it with the ascetic and the king, so it becomes the reward of anyone who keeps the line of his station.
list_adds: It names three holders of the rain-power from household, renunciation and rule, turning the couplet's single wonder into a rule about keeping one's station.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 குறிப்பறிவான் is masculine for the wife; line 3 repaired from சொய்வான்.

note: Acharakkovai 16 names the king, teacher, mother, father and elder brother as the peerless elders to be worshipped as gods; Thirikadugam counts refusing the five elders' command as the act of those without goodness.
teaches: Acharakkovai supplies who the ஐங்குரவர் are and the positive rule; Thirikadugam names the breach and ranks it with lying in friendship and casting off a chaste wife, setting obedience to elders in one ethic with loyalty to friend and wife.

note: Verse 86 calls letting go of the raft of chastity and the loss of friendship's grace an enmity; verse 97 names forsaking a chaste wife and false dealing in friendship as acts of the graceless.
teaches: Verse 97 names plainly the husband's act of forsaking a chaste wife beside a breach of friendship, which supports reading 86's letting go of chastity as his act rather than hers.

note: Verse 96 gives the rain-command to the wife, the ascetic and the king; verse 98 makes the fire-priests, the just king and the obedient wife the seed of the month's three rains.
teaches: The pair shows the book's rain list is fixed on king and wife but varies its third member between ascetic and fire-priest, and moves from command to seed, from a single word to a monthly cause.

note: Kural 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and the men of six duties forget their books; Thirikadugam sets the fire-priests' dharma and the king's just rule side by side as seeds of rain.
teaches: The couplet makes priestly learning depend on the king's protection; the verse makes priest, king and wife coequal causes of the rains, flattening the Kural's order of dependence into a joint one.
list_adds: It adds the wife who follows her husband as a third cause beside priest and king, joining the household to the ritual and royal orders as one seed of rain.

note: Verse 90 names giving, study for dharma and gracious speech as the way past the dark world; verse 99 names forsaking the learned, self-will and unchecked wrongdoing as barring the good world.
teaches: Study is on one list and the abandonment of the learned on the other, so the book makes learning the hinge between the dark world and the good one.

note: Kural 381 names six limbs of a king (army, people, resources, ministers, allies, fort); Thirikadugam names three: a loyal army, a fort fearless of numbers, and uncountable treasure.
teaches: The Thirikadugam's king needs only the three material limbs and drops people, ministers and allies, a narrower and more martial account of what makes a king than the Kural's.
list_adds: It selects three of the six and qualifies each (loyal, fearless, uncountable), so the list sharpens the quality of each limb where the couplet only counts kinds.

note: Kural 1134 has the lover say the flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness; Thirikadugam names letting go the great raft of chastity out of desire as an enmity that brings fault.
teaches: Both make a virtue the raft that desire tears away, but the love couplet voices it as a lover's helpless loss while the ethics verse judges the same release as a culpable fault.
list_adds: It sets the abandoned raft of chastity beside a loosened bond of love and friendship's lost grace, so the release becomes one of three broken bonds that turn into enmity.

note: Naladiyar 52 says the best reflect on impermanence, disease, old age and death and do their own work; Thirikadugam names disease eating one, Death consuming life and wealth passing without worth as what unsettles the raft.
teaches: The quatrain draws the conclusion, do your own work now, while the verse shows what that work is threatened by, so the pair gives both the danger and the answer to it.
list_adds: It adds the passing of wealth to disease and Death as a third force shaking the raft, so loss of goods is ranked with bodily ruin where the quatrain counts only the body's fates.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 பிணைசெல்வ மாண்பின்று இயங்கலிவை is fused and its sense uncertain.

note: Kural 539 says to think of those ruined by negligence when one is swollen with joy; Thirikadugam counts speaking heedlessly at a time of gain as a sign of the body that does not last.
teaches: The couplet treats elated negligence as a danger to be remedied by memory, while the verse reads the same heedless word as a mark of mortality, so forgetting at a gain is shown to be forgetting that one will die.
list_adds: It sets heedless speech at a gain beside the cry at the end and shame at a withering body, so negligence is ranked with dying itself as a sign of a perishable life rather than as a tactical fault.
